text: Bootstrapped the Quillbase repository today, the read-later app that will anchor everything else Larkspur Labs builds. Went with Next.js 15 on the app router from the start rather than pages router, mostly because server components make the reader view and archive list cheap to render without shipping a client bundle for every clip card. Database is Postgres 16 running in a local docker-compose service, and after a short debate we picked Drizzle ORM over Prisma: Drizzle stays close to SQL, its migration files are plain readable SQL we can hand-edit, and it does not require a long-running query engine binary, which matters for the self-hosted story where users run this on tiny VPS boxes. Defined the first schema in lib/db/schema.ts with a clips table: id uuid default gen_random_uuid, userId uuid, url text, canonicalUrl text, title text, siteName text, contentHtml text, contentText text, state text default pending, savedAt timestamptz default now. Ran drizzle-kit generate to produce migration 0001_initial.sql and wired a migrate script into package.json. Chose pnpm as the package manager and set engines to Node 20. Tailwind is in but unconfigured beyond defaults; actual layout work is a separate session. Also stubbed app/api/clips/route.ts with a POST handler that just echoes the payload so I could verify the route wiring and confirm that route handlers in Next 15 need the async request APIs now, which briefly threw me because headers() returning a promise broke a copy-pasted snippet from an older project with the error headers is not a function when awaited incorrectly. Decisions recorded: Postgres 16 as the only required datastore for a minimal install, Drizzle over Prisma for SQL transparency and lighter runtime, uuid primary keys over bigserial because clips will eventually sync across devices and we do not want guessable sequential ids in share URLs. Also set up the local development story properly before it could rot, a docker-compose bringing up Postgres 16 and a Redis alongside the Next dev server, seeded by a small script that creates the dev user and a handful of sample clips so a fresh clone is one command from a working app rather than an afternoon of yak-shaving, and wrote the getting-started steps into the readme while they were fresh. Committed a .env.example enumerating every variable the app reads with a comment on each rather than leaving people to discover them from runtime crashes, since undocumented environment variables are how self-hosted software earns a reputation for being fiddly. Open threads: no auth at all yet, everything is a hardcoded dev user until the clearharbor service exists; no dedup strategy, so saving the same URL twice makes two rows; and I have not decided whether contentHtml belongs in Postgres long term or in object storage once articles pile up. Next session is the ingest parser, which is the actual heart of the product.

Spent the whole session on the clip ingest parser, the piece that turns an arbitrary URL into clean readable article content, living in lib/ingest/parser.ts. First decision was the fetch layer: using undici request directly instead of global fetch so I can set a hard 15 second body timeout, cap redirects at 5, and stream the body with an abort once it passes 5 MB, because early testing showed a couple of sites happily serving 60 MB of inline base64 images. Set a desktop browser user agent string after finding three major news sites return a consent interstitial to unknown agents. Second decision, and the bigger one: DOM parsing with linkedom instead of jsdom. Benchmarked both on a saved 2.1 MB article page and linkedom parsed it in roughly 180 ms with 40 MB heap growth while jsdom took about 1.4 seconds and 210 MB; jsdom is more spec-complete but we never execute scripts, so linkedom wins for a pipeline that will eventually run inside ferrite-driven jobs at volume. The extraction itself is a Readability-style scoring pass I wrote from scratch rather than importing the Mozilla port wholesale: score candidate blocks by paragraph density, comma count, and link density, penalize nav and footer class name patterns, then walk up to the best common ancestor. On my fixture corpus, 40 real pages saved into tests/fixtures/ingest as raw HTML plus an expected-title assertion file, the extractor currently gets clean article content on 34 of 40; failures are two paywalled teasers, one single-page app that renders client-side, one recipe site with content split across widgets, and two where boilerplate sneaks in. Hit a nasty charset bug: a page declared UTF-8 in its Content-Type header but the bytes were windows-1252, so smart quotes decoded as mojibake; fix was sniffing the meta charset tag from the first 1024 bytes and preferring it when the header and meta disagree, using TextDecoder with the sniffed label. Also fixed a crash where an empty body made the extraction throw TypeError: Cannot read properties of null reading textContent because I assumed document.body always exists; linkedom returns a document without body for empty input, so there is now an explicit guard that marks the clip failed_parse with a stored error string. Content sanitization is deliberately not done here, that belongs to the render path; parser output is contentHtml scoped to the extracted article subtree plus contentText from textContent with whitespace collapsed, plus title, siteName from og:site_name falling back to the hostname, byline when a rel=author or meta author is present, and a wordCount. Errors are typed: FetchError, ParseError, ExtractError, each carrying a retryable boolean so the future job runner can decide whether to retry; DNS failures and 5xx are retryable, 404 and robots-style 403 are not. Wired the parser into the POST /api/clips flow synchronously for now, so saving a URL blocks for a couple of seconds, which is obviously wrong long term and is exactly the motivation for the Rust job runner we keep talking about. Spent a chunk of the session on the tokenizer that feeds contentText, because naive textContent collapsed adjacent block elements without spacing so the end of one paragraph fused into the start of the next, producing run-on words that later wrecked both the excerpt and the eventual search vector; the fix walks the extracted subtree and inserts a single space at block-level boundaries before collapsing runs of whitespace, and a fixture asserts that two stacked paragraphs never yield a glued word. Also decided on a boilerplate blocklist keyed by class and id substrings, share, related, newsletter, comments, promo, subscribe, that get pruned before scoring rather than merely penalized, after finding that a high-density related-articles widget occasionally out-scored the real article on listicle-shaped pages; pruning up front was cleaner than trying to out-tune the scoring constants against adversarial layouts. Measured the parser end to end on the fixture corpus and the median extraction runs in about 210 milliseconds including fetch-free parse, with the p95 dominated by two pathological pages carrying tens of thousands of DOM nodes, and I noted that once this moves into ferrite the per-job budget wants a hard node-count ceiling that fails a page as too complex rather than spending seconds on a hostile document. One more decision recorded: the byline and published-date extraction now consults JSON-LD Article blocks when present as a higher-confidence source than meta tags, parsing the first application/ld+json script that declares an Article or NewsArticle type, with a guard against the surprisingly common case of a malformed JSON-LD block that would otherwise throw and take the whole parse down, so a bad LD block degrades to the meta-tag path instead of failing. Open threads: paywalled sites need at least a graceful teaser capture, AMP pages should redirect to canonical before extraction, PDFs are completely unhandled and currently produce garbage contentText, and the scoring constants are hand-tuned magic numbers that deserve a proper eval harness once we have more fixtures. Also noted for later: lazy-loaded images use data-src attributes on several sites and the extractor keeps the empty src placeholder, so images vanish in the reader; that fix goes with the metadata pass planned in a few sessions.

Short layout session on Quillbase. Built the application shell: a left sidebar with Archive, Starred, and Settings entries, a top bar with the save-URL input, and the main clip list column, all in app/(app)/layout.tsx with Tailwind. Decided on the class strategy for dark mode rather than media queries so a manual toggle is possible later, and defined a small set of design tokens as CSS variables consumed through Tailwind config: surface, surface-raised, ink, ink-muted, accent. Clip cards show title, siteName, savedAt as relative time, and a two-line excerpt from contentText using line-clamp-2. Fixed a hydration mismatch warning caused by rendering relative timestamps on the server; the server said 3 hours ago while the client computed 4 hours ago across a timezone difference, so timestamps now render an absolute ISO date on the server and are enhanced to relative time client-side in a tiny use client component. Also pinned the sidebar with position sticky instead of a separate scroll container after the nested scrollbars looked terrible. No open threads worth recording, this was pixel-pushing to make the thing feel like an app instead of a database viewer, though the empty-state illustration is still a gray rectangle with an apology in it.

Focused session on the save endpoint, app/api/clips/route.ts, turning the stub into a real POST handler. Input validation with zod: clipCreateSchema requires url as a string that parses with the URL constructor and is http or https only, plus optional title override and optional source field for telling apart the web form, the future browser extension, and imports. Validation failures return 422 with a flattened zod error object; malformed JSON bodies return 400; the distinction matters because the extension should treat 422 as a user-facing message and 400 as its own bug. The meat of the session was URL normalization, which now lives in lib/ingest/normalize.ts as a pure function with its own test file: lowercase the hostname, strip default ports 80 and 443, remove utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, utm_content, fbclid, gclid, and ref query params from a maintained strip list, sort remaining query params alphabetically for stable ordering, collapse duplicate slashes in the path, drop trailing slash except at the root path, and drop the fragment entirely except when it matches a page anchor pattern like #page=12 used by some doc viewers. Spent a while on whether stripping params could break sites that genuinely need utm-like params; decided the strip list is conservative and explicitly enumerated rather than pattern-based, so no wildcard utm_* matching that might eat a legit param. The normalized form is stored in canonicalUrl while the raw submitted URL is kept in url, so we never lose what the user actually gave us; that felt important for debugging future dedup complaints. The handler currently runs the parser inline and returns 201 with the full clip once parsing completes, but I added a state column flow anyway, pending to parsed to failed_parse or failed_fetch, so the response shape will not change when parsing moves into the background runner; the API contract is designed for a 202-style async world even though today it blocks. Also decided idempotent behavior is out of scope for this session since dedup design deserves its own dedicated pass, so right now double-saving still duplicates. Small fix along the way: the URL constructor accepts whitespace-padded input in some runtimes and not others, so input is trimmed before validation, and a test now covers a URL with a trailing newline pasted from a chat app. Open threads: rate limiting per user is completely absent, the endpoint trusts the hardcoded dev user until clearharbor lands, and normalize.ts needs a decision about whether http URLs should be upgraded to https for canonicalization, which interacts directly with the upcoming dedup work.

Dedup design session for Quillbase, the thing I punted on when building the save endpoint. Core decision: dedup keys off a sha256 of the canonical URL, stored in a new urlHash column, with a unique composite index on userId plus urlHash so deduplication is strictly per-user; two different users saving the same article each get their own clip, which matters because highlights and read state are personal. Wrote migration 0003_dedupe.sql adding the column and index, and a backfill script at scripts/backfill-url-hash.ts that recomputes canonicalUrl with the current normalize.ts and hashes it, because a handful of early rows were saved before the normalizer stripped gclid. The interesting question was what happens on conflict. Decided the save endpoint uses Drizzle onConflictDoUpdate targeting the unique index, bumping savedAt to now and incrementing a new saveCount integer, so re-saving an article resurfaces it at the top of the archive rather than erroring; that felt like the behavior a person actually wants when they hit save on something twice, and saveCount becomes a cheap personal-importance signal for search ranking later. Deliberated a long time on scheme handling: http and https versions of the same page were hashing differently, and probing HSTS or following upgrade redirects at hash time is too slow, so the canonical hash input is now host plus path plus sorted query with the scheme dropped entirely; recorded the known risk that a site serving genuinely different content on http versus https would collide, judged acceptably rare. Also debated content-level dedup for the syndicated-article case where the same text lives at two URLs; sketched a 64-bit simhash over contentText with hamming distance 3 or less as the near-duplicate test, but explicitly deferred it because it needs a banding index to avoid pairwise comparison and this session was already deep enough — wrote the sketch into a comment block at the top of a future lib/ingest/simhash.ts so the thinking is not lost. Ran the backfill against my own instance and found 68 duplicate rows accumulated over three weeks of dogfooding; wrote a one-off merge in the same script keeping the earliest savedAt as the surviving row, summing saveCount, and repointing nothing because no child tables exist yet, which is a luxury that will not last. Verified the unique index by hammering the endpoint with a small concurrent loop, 50 parallel saves of one URL produced exactly one row with saveCount 50, no serialization errors, because the upsert resolves the race at the index level rather than with a select-then-insert. One subtle bug found and fixed on the way: normalize.ts sorted query params with default array sort which is lexicographic on the joined key=value string, and two params whose values contained an ampersand-encoded sequence sorted unstably across encodings; switched to sorting on the decoded key alone with a stable tiebreak on value. Spent real time on the interaction between dedup and the state machine, because a save that upserts onto an existing parsed clip should not blindly reset it to pending and re-run the whole fetch pipeline; decided the onConflictDoUpdate path only bumps savedAt and saveCount and explicitly does not touch state or contentHtml, so re-saving an already-parsed article is a cheap metadata write rather than a redundant fetch job, while re-saving a clip that had previously landed in failed_fetch does flip it back to pending and re-enqueues, on the theory that a manual re-save of a dead link is a human asking us to try again. That split is expressed as a conditional in the save handler and covered by two tests, one asserting a re-save of a healthy clip enqueues nothing and one asserting a re-save of a failed clip enqueues exactly one fetch job. Also confronted the canonicalization-drift problem head on: because canonicalUrl and therefore urlHash are computed by normalize.ts, any future change to the normalizer silently changes the identity of every clip and would break dedup against already-stored rows, so I stamped a normalizerVersion integer into a column alongside urlHash and wrote the backfill script to be re-runnable and version-aware, recomputing hashes only for rows whose stored version is behind current; this makes normalizer evolution a migration rather than a landmine, and the reasoning went into a comment at the top of normalize.ts in bold because it is exactly the kind of thing a future me forgets. Benchmarked the upsert path under a synthetic burst of 500 saves spread across 50 distinct URLs and it held a steady sub-10-millisecond write with the unique index resolving conflicts in-engine, no measurable lock contention, which was reassuring since the whole point of index-level conflict resolution was avoiding a read-modify-write race. Open threads: the simhash follow-up, whether imports should also bump savedAt on conflict or stay silent (leaning silent, an import should not shuffle the archive), and surfacing saveCount in the UI somewhere honest without turning it into a gamification widget.

Parser hardening session on Quillbase after a week of dogfooding produced a folder of misbehaving URLs. Built out a dedicated metadata module, lib/ingest/meta.ts, extracting a title with a fallback chain of og:title then twitter:title then the title element then the first h1, trimming site-name suffixes like pipe or dash followed by the site name when og:site_name is known; that suffix stripping alone fixed a dozen ugly titles in my archive. AMP handling got a real decision: when a fetched page declares itself AMP or the URL matches an amp path pattern, the parser now looks for link rel=canonical and refetches the canonical URL once, with a loop guard so a canonical pointing back at the AMP page cannot cycle; extraction quality on the canonical pages is consistently better since AMP strips the markup my scorer relies on. Paywalled sites now degrade gracefully instead of storing an empty husk: when extracted contentText is under 400 characters but the page has og:description, the clip stores the description as a teaser, gets a new state partial instead of parsed, and the reader view will eventually badge it as a teaser-only capture rather than pretending that is the whole article. Fixed the lazy-image problem noted last week: the extractor now swaps data-src and data-srcset into src and srcset when the original src is a placeholder pattern like a 1x1 gif or an inline svg blur, and picks the largest candidate from srcset when only that is present, capping at 2000 pixels wide. Also normalized relative image URLs against the final post-redirect URL rather than the submitted one, which was quietly breaking images on any site that redirected. Fixture corpus grew from 40 to 55 pages and the clean-extraction count went from 34 of 40 to 49 of 55; the remaining failures are the client-side rendered app, two PDFs, and three sites doing aggressive bot detection that will probably never work without a headless browser, which I am not adding — recorded that as an explicit non-goal for now since a headless Chrome dependency would wreck the small-VPS self-hosting story. Also added a small per-parse metrics line logging extraction outcome, word count, and elapsed time, which immediately made it obvious which sites were slow versus which were simply failing, and confirmed that the metadata pass added negligible time, about 3 milliseconds median, since it reads tags already in memory rather than re-walking the document. Recorded a firm non-goal while the temptation was fresh: no headless browser for the client-side-rendered holdouts, because a bundled Chrome would balloon the install footprint and the memory budget and quietly break the entire small-VPS story the whole architecture is built to protect. Open threads: the partial state needs UI treatment, and byline extraction is still hit or miss on sites using JSON-LD, so parsing application/ld+json Article blocks is queued for a future pass.

Long session building the Quillbase reader view, the page the whole product exists to serve, at app/read/[clipId]/page.tsx as a server component. The load-bearing decision was sanitization. The stored contentHtml comes from arbitrary websites and must never execute in our origin, so it gets sanitized at render time, not at ingest, because sanitizing at ingest freezes the policy — any future tightening would require reprocessing every stored clip, and any bug in an old sanitizer version would be baked into the database forever. Render-time means the policy is always the current one. For the library, compared DOMPurify and sanitize-html: DOMPurify is the household name but wants a real DOM, which server-side means dragging jsdom back in after I deliberately chose linkedom for the parser, and running DOMPurify over linkedom is an unsupported pairing I do not want to debug at the security boundary. sanitize-html works on strings server-side with an explicit allowlist model, which reads better in review: you can see exactly what is permitted. Configured the allowlist in lib/render/sanitize.ts: p, headings h2 through h4 with h1 reserved for our own title, a, img, blockquote, pre, code, em, strong, ul, ol, li, figure, figcaption, table elements, hr, br; attributes limited to href on a, src, srcset, alt, width, height on img; href schemes restricted to http, https, and mailto so javascript: URLs die at the boundary; all class and style attributes stripped since our typography owns the presentation. Typography itself is Tailwind prose classes with a customized measure — max width 68ch after trying 60 and 75, line-height 1.7, and a serif stack for body with the UI staying sans. Font size preference is a client-side island: a small use client toolbar writes a scale value to localStorage and sets a CSS variable on the article container, wrapped in try-catch since localStorage can throw in private windows, defaulting to medium. Heading anchors get generated ids with a visible-on-hover link icon. Images are still hotlinked from origin servers, which leaks reader IP addresses to the sites; set referrerpolicy no-referrer on the article container as a partial mitigation and recorded a proper image proxy as an open thread with real tradeoffs around storage and copyright. External links get target blank with rel noopener noreferrer. Also fixed the first genuinely scary bug of the project while testing: a fixture page had an onerror attribute on an img that survived my first sanitize config because I had passed allowedAttributes with a wildcard entry while experimenting; the final config is strict enumeration only and there is now a regression test asserting that onerror, onclick, script tags, and javascript: hrefs are all stripped from a nasty fixture document. Spent a while on the link-handling policy inside sanitized article bodies, since raw href values from arbitrary sites are a menagerie: protocol-relative slashes, relative paths, mailto, tel, and the occasional data URI hiding a payload. Settled the rules explicitly in sanitize.ts, relative and protocol-relative links are resolved against the clip canonicalUrl at render so they point somewhere real instead of at our own domain, http and https and mailto survive, tel is allowed because it is harmless and occasionally useful, and everything else including data, javascript, and vbscript is dropped by turning the anchor into a plain span so the link text survives even when the destination dies. Added a regression fixture with one anchor per hostile scheme and asserted each one either resolves to an absolute safe URL or degrades to inert text, and that no anchor ever retains a javascript or data href. Also made a real decision about images that I had been avoiding: the sanitizer now strips width and height attributes that disagree wildly with intrinsic proportions to stop layout-shifting placeholder dimensions from sites that lie, and forces loading lazy plus decoding async on every img so a long article with forty images does not block the main thread on load, which measurably dropped time-to-interactive on image-heavy fixtures. The srcset handling got hardened too, since a malformed srcset descriptor could previously survive into the output and confuse the browser layout, so srcset is now parsed, validated candidate by candidate, and re-serialized rather than passed through as an opaque string, with anything unparseable dropped in favor of the plain src. One genuinely subtle bug surfaced while testing the anchor resolution: a clip whose canonicalUrl had a path but the article contained a bare fragment link like a table-of-contents anchor was getting the fragment resolved against the full canonical path correctly, but an empty-href anchor used purely as a scroll target was being rewritten to point at the article URL and hijacking in-page navigation, so empty and pure-fragment hrefs are now left untouched as same-document links. Open threads: estimated reading time in the header, a scroll progress indicator, code block syntax highlighting which is currently unstyled monospace, and the partial-state teaser badge from the paywall work needs its banner here.

Distilled notes on the reader view session for Quillbase. Built app/read/[clipId]/page.tsx as an RSC and spent most of the time on how to make stored third-party HTML safe to render. Settled on sanitizing at render rather than ingest so the sanitization policy stays current for all historical clips instead of being frozen into stored data at whatever version the sanitizer was on save day. Library choice went to sanitize-html over DOMPurify: DOMPurify needs a DOM implementation on the server which would reintroduce jsdom alongside the linkedom decision from the parser work, while sanitize-html operates on strings with a declarative allowlist that is easy to audit. The policy in lib/render/sanitize.ts enumerates permitted tags (paragraphs, h2-h4, links, images, blockquotes, pre and code, lists, figures, tables, hr, br) and per-tag attributes, restricts href to http, https, mailto schemes, and strips every class and style attribute so site CSS cannot fight our typography. Speaking of which: prose styling landed on a 68ch measure, 1.7 line height, serif body against the sans UI chrome. Reader font size is adjustable through a small client island that persists a scale to localStorage behind a try-catch and applies it as a CSS variable, so the server render never mismatches. Remote images keep their origin URLs for now with referrerpolicy no-referrer on the container to limit IP leakage to origin servers; a real proxy is deferred and noted. During testing caught an XSS hole in my own experimental config where a wildcard attribute allowance let an inline onerror handler through sanitization; locked the config to strict enumeration and added a regression fixture asserting script tags, event handler attributes, and javascript: links are all removed. Remaining threads carried forward: reading time estimate, scroll progress, syntax highlighting for code blocks, and a badge for teaser-only paywall captures.

First pass at search for Quillbase. Kept it deliberately boring: Postgres full-text search, no external engine. Migration 0004_search.sql adds a searchVector tsvector column to clips, populated as a generated column from to_tsvector with the english config over title concatenated with contentText, plus a GIN index on it. Went with a generated column over a trigger after confirming Postgres 16 handles stored generated tsvector columns cleanly with Drizzle, though Drizzle itself has no first-class tsvector type so the column is declared via a customType wrapper in lib/db/types.ts and the generated expression lives in hand-edited migration SQL, which is exactly why we picked an ORM that tolerates hand-edited SQL. Query side is a new GET /api/search route taking a q param, running plainto_tsquery against the vector, ordering by ts_rank, limiting to 50. On my archive of about 3000 clips a typical query returns in roughly 45 ms including the round trip, completely fine for now. The ranking is naive: raw ts_rank with no weighting means a word appearing forty times deep in a long article outranks the same word in a title, which already feels wrong when searching for a half-remembered headline. Stemming produced one fun surprise: searching for postgres does not match postgresql under the english config because they stem differently, noted as a genuine relevance issue rather than a curiosity since half my archive mentions one or the other. No phrase search, no operators, no typo tolerance, all deferred deliberately. Wired a search box into the top bar that navigates to /search?q= with results rendered server-side reusing the clip card component. Made a deliberate call to keep the search route stateless and cache-friendly, no session-bound scoring or personalization yet, so a query is a pure function of the archive contents and the parameters, which keeps it easy to reason about and easy to benchmark before any ranking sophistication muddies the picture. Also added an empty-query guard returning the recent archive rather than running an expensive match-nothing tsquery, and a hard cap on q length to stop a pathologically long pasted query from becoming an accidental denial of service against the parser. Open threads: weighted vectors so titles count more, some recency signal so a search does not surface a five year old clip above yesterday's save of the same topic, and the postgres/postgresql stemming gap which might want a small synonym layer. This sets up a proper ranking session next.

Marathon search ranking session on Quillbase, all in and around lib/search/rank.ts, turning the naive v0 into something that actually finds the clip you are thinking of. Started by restructuring the vector: instead of one undifferentiated tsvector over title plus contentText, the generated column is now setweight(to_tsvector(english, title), A) concatenated with setweight over siteName as B and contentText as C, so the ranking function can price a title hit far above a body hit; migration 0005_weighted_search.sql rebuilds the column and the GIN index, which on my now 5000-clip archive took about 40 seconds of table rewrite, acceptable for self-hosters at this scale but worth a note in the eventual upgrade docs about running it during off hours on big archives. Switched scoring from ts_rank to ts_rank_cd with the normalization flag that divides by document length plus one, because without length normalization my handful of pasted 20000-word longreads dominated every query they vaguely matched; flag choice was empirical, tried 0, 1, 2, and 4 across the golden queries and 2 gave the best ordering with 4 close behind. The second big piece was recency. A pure text score treats a clip saved yesterday and one saved two years ago identically, but a read-later archive has a strong prior that recent saves are more likely to be what you want; multiplied the text score by 0.7 plus 0.3 times an exponential decay exp of negative age over halfLife, and tuned halfLife by feel across the golden queries: 14 days was too aggressive, burying a three-week-old clip I was explicitly hunting, 30 days kept old classics reachable while still boosting fresh saves, so 30 it is, with both constants exported from rank.ts as named parameters rather than buried inline, since I already suspect a future session will want them user-configurable. saveCount from the dedup work joins the party as a small multiplicative bonus, 1 plus 0.05 times log of saveCount, so repeatedly-saved references drift upward without dominating. Third piece: typo tolerance. Full-text search returns nothing for a single-character typo, which is brutal for a search box people type into from memory, so I added a pg_trgm fallback: when the tsquery path returns fewer than 3 results, a second query runs word_similarity against titles with a 0.3 threshold and merges results below the exact matches, deduplicated by clip id. That required the pg_trgm extension, which is bundled with stock Postgres, so the self-host constraint survives, and a trigram GIN index on title. To measure any of this honestly I built a tiny benchmark: 25 golden queries in a fixture file, each a query string plus the clip id I consider the right answer, drawn from my own memory of my own archive, run by a script that reports top-1 and top-3 hit rates. Before this session the naive ranking scored 9 of 25 top-1 and 14 of 25 top-3; after weighting, normalization, recency, and the trgm fallback it lands 16 of 25 top-1 and 21 of 25 top-3. The four remaining top-3 misses are instructive: two are stemming vocabulary gaps like the postgres versus postgresql split noted last session, one wants a phrase match the plainto path cannot express, and one is a genuinely ambiguous query where the golden answer is arguably wrong. Latency moved from a p95 of about 38 ms to 88 ms when the trgm fallback fires, since it only fires on sparse result sets I judged that acceptable, and the common path stays around 45 ms. Ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the main query and confirmed the GIN index is used with a bitmap scan; also turned fastupdate off on the search GIN index after reading about pending-list stalls causing unpredictable insert latency spikes, preferring slightly slower steady-state writes over occasional multi-hundred-millisecond cleanup pauses in the middle of a save. Seriously considered, and rejected, pulling in a dedicated search engine: meilisearch or typesense would give better typo tolerance and faceting out of the box, but each is another process to run, another port to expose, another thing to back up, and the entire product thesis is that a self-hosted Quillbase needs exactly Postgres and nothing else; wrote that reasoning into a decision note in the repo because future me will absolutely be tempted again. Before any of the tuning I had to fix the evaluation itself, because tuning ranking without a repeatable measure is just moving numbers around until the last query you tried looks good while silently breaking five others. So the first hour went into the golden query harness: a fixture file of 25 query strings each paired with the clip id I consider the single right answer, drawn from my own memory of my own archive, plus a runner script that executes the full ranking pipeline against a snapshot of the database and reports top-1 and top-3 hit rates, and crucially prints a diff of which specific queries regressed since the last run so a change that helps in aggregate but breaks a query I care about is visible rather than hidden inside a summary number. That harness is the reason every decision below has a number attached, and I already suspect it is the seed of a real eval suite once it grows past single right answers into graded relevance. On the weighting, the setweight decision was not just A for title and C for body, I actually tested three weight profiles against the golden set: title-heavy where a title match nearly always wins, balanced, and body-favoring, and the title-heavy profile won on the half-remembered-headline queries that dominate how I actually search while costing almost nothing on the content-recall queries, so title gets A, siteName B, and body C, and the ts_rank_cd normalization flag was chosen empirically by sweeping 0, 1, 2, and 4 with flag 2 giving the best ordering because it divides rank by document length and stops my handful of pasted twenty-thousand-word longreads from dominating every query they vaguely touch. On recency I was careful not to let freshness bulldoze relevance, so the final score is 0.7 times the normalized text score plus 0.3 times an exponential decay of age, deliberately a minority weight, and the 30 day half-life came from watching the golden runner as I swept it: 14 days buried a three-week-old clip I was explicitly hunting, 45 days barely moved fresh saves up, 30 kept old classics reachable while still surfacing yesterday's save of the same topic, and both constants are exported as named parameters from rank.ts because I am nearly certain a future session makes them user-configurable. The trigram fallback needed its own guardrails: it only fires when the exact tsquery path returns fewer than 3 results, so the common path never pays for it, it uses word_similarity against titles with a 0.3 threshold tuned to catch single-character typos without dragging in loosely-related titles, and merged results always sort below exact matches so a fuzzy guess never outranks a real hit, deduplicated by clip id. I ran an honest latency accounting across all of this rather than just the happy path: the common query stays around 45 milliseconds, the trigram fallback pushes p95 to about 88 when it fires but it fires only on sparse result sets so the amortized cost is small, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirmed the main query rides the GIN index via a bitmap scan rather than degrading to a sequential scan as the vector grew. I also turned fastupdate off on the search GIN index after reading about pending-list stalls, where deferred index maintenance batches up and then blocks a random later insert with a multi-hundred-millisecond cleanup pause right in the middle of someone saving a clip, and I decided predictable slightly-slower steady-state writes beat occasional latency spikes for an interactive save, a classic tail-latency-over-throughput call that I wrote up because it will look arbitrary to a future reader who does not know the failure it prevents. The whole session moved the golden set from 9 of 25 top-1 and 14 of 25 top-3 to 16 of 25 top-1 and 21 of 25 top-3, and I made a point of understanding the four remaining top-3 misses rather than celebrating the wins, because the misses are the roadmap: two are stemming vocabulary gaps like the postgres versus postgresql split, one wants a phrase match the plainto path cannot express, and one is a genuinely ambiguous query where I suspect my golden answer is wrong. And I seriously considered and firmly rejected pulling in a dedicated search engine, since meilisearch or typesense would hand us better typo tolerance and faceting for free, but each is another process to run, another port to expose, another store to back up, and the entire product thesis is that a self-hosted Quillbase needs exactly Postgres and nothing else, so I wrote that reasoning into a decision note in the repo specifically because future me, staring at the postgres-versus-postgresql miss, will absolutely be tempted to reach for one. Open threads carried out of this session: the english config is hardcoded so non-English articles are stemmed wrong, wanting per-clip language detection; result snippets need ts_headline which was too slow in a quick test, deferred to its own session; the golden query set should grow past 25 and gain graded relevance instead of single right answers, which starts to look like a real eval harness; and phrase support via websearch_to_tsquery syntax is an easy future win.

Kicked off clearharbor, the shared auth and billing service that will sit under Quillbase and whatever we build next. Plain Node service, and after weighing Express against Fastify went with Fastify: schema-validated routes out of the box, better raw-body control which I already know Stripe webhook signature verification will demand, and the plugin encapsulation model keeps auth and billing concerns from bleeding into each other. Postgres 16 again, same Drizzle setup as Quillbase for consistency, with its own database rather than sharing Quillbase's, since the whole point is multiple products hanging off one auth service. Started with sessions in src/session.ts and made the foundational call early: server-side sessions in a Postgres sessions table with an opaque random id, not JWTs. Reasoning recorded at length because this always gets relitigated: revocation must be instant when a user resets a password or we detect abuse, JWT revocation requires a denylist which reintroduces the database lookup JWTs supposedly avoid, and at two products and dozens of users the statelessness benefit is imaginary while the footguns are real. Session ids are 32 random bytes base64url encoded, stored hashed with sha256 so a database leak does not hand out live sessions, delivered in a cookie named ch_session. Password hashing is argon2id via the argon2 package with memory cost 19456 and time cost 2, matching current OWASP guidance; wrote a small benchmark confirming a hash takes about 90 ms on the Fly shared CPU we will deploy to, slow enough to resist cracking, fast enough for login. Signup and login routes exist with fastify schemas validating email shape and password minimum of 10 characters, no maximum silliness, no complexity rules. Login failures return an identical 401 body for unknown email and wrong password, message invalid email or password, to avoid account enumeration; timing still differs since unknown emails skip the argon2 verify, mitigated by hashing a dummy value on the unknown-email path. Also decided early on the database boundary between products, clearharbor owns its own Postgres database rather than sharing Quillbase's, because the whole reason clearharbor exists is to sit under multiple products and a shared schema would couple their migrations and blast radius together in exactly the way a shared auth service is supposed to prevent. Wrote a short architecture note stating that products talk to clearharbor only over its HTTP API and never reach into its tables directly, a boundary that is cheap to hold now and expensive to reconstruct later once someone has taken a shortcut across it. Open threads: cookie attributes and expiry policy need their own careful session, there is no session listing or revoke-all endpoint yet, and the verify endpoint that Quillbase will call does not exist, which blocks the integration work.

Integration session: wiring Quillbase authentication to clearharbor, ending the era of the hardcoded dev user. Built the verify endpoint on the clearharbor side first, GET /v1/session/verify reading the ch_session cookie, hashing it, looking up the session row, returning userId and email with cache headers explicitly disabled. On the Quillbase side, middleware.ts now runs on all app routes and API routes except public ones, forwards the incoming cookie header to the verify endpoint, and either annotates the request with the userId via request headers or redirects to the clearharbor login page. The cookie topology decision took real thought: in production both services will live under one parent domain, quillbase.larkspur.dev and auth.larkspur.dev, so ch_session is set with domain .larkspur.dev making it visible to both; in development Quillbase runs on localhost 3000 and clearharbor on localhost 4000, and cookies on localhost ignore ports, so the same cookie flows naturally and no special dev proxying is needed, which pleasantly surprised me. A per-request verify call adds a round trip to literally everything, so Quillbase caches verify responses in an in-process LRU keyed by the session cookie hash with a 60 second TTL, capped at 10000 entries; the tradeoff is that a revoked session can live up to 60 seconds inside Quillbase, judged fine for now and recorded, with the note that a future push-based invalidation or shorter TTL is the fix if it ever matters. The login redirect flow carries a returnTo param so you land back where you were, and that param is validated hard on the clearharbor side against an allowlist of registered product origins, because an open redirect on an auth domain is a phishing gift; wrote the allowlist as a REGISTERED_ORIGINS env var parsed at boot, failing startup loudly if malformed. Migration on the Quillbase side finally makes userId a real foreign concept: the dev-user placeholder rows got assigned to my actual first account via scripts/adopt-orphan-clips.ts. Also handled the annoying middleware edge where API requests should get 401 JSON rather than a 302 redirect to a login page, switched on the accept header and path prefix, so the future extension and CLI get sane errors. Tested the whole loop: login on 4000, redirected back to 3000, clips load under my user, revoking the session server-side kills Quillbase access within the cache TTL. Open threads: no logout button in the Quillbase UI yet, the LRU cache should be shared across the eventual multi-instance deploy story or at least documented as per-instance, and clearharbor still has no signup email verification, meaning any typoed email becomes an orphan account.

One-off personal automation session, nothing to do with the products. Quarterly estimated taxes were due and the spreadsheet ritual annoyed me enough to script it: a Python script, quarterly_tax.py in my personal tools folder, that reads the bank export CSV, filters deposits matching client invoice patterns, sums the quarter's income, applies the safe-harbor calculation against last year's total tax, and prints the federal and state voucher amounts with the due date. Pandas felt like overkill so it is csv module plus a dataclass, under 200 lines. The one real decision was rounding: the worksheet wants whole dollars and banker's rounding versus round-half-up changed the answer by a dollar, went with round-half-up to match what the official worksheet produces. Also discovered my bank quietly changed the CSV date format from MM/DD/YYYY to YYYY-MM-DD in their export sometime this spring, which silently zeroed a quarter until I noticed the filter matched nothing; the script now parses both formats and refuses to run if fewer than 5 transactions match, a cheap sanity tripwire. Printed the vouchers, paid the thing, moved on with my life. Next quarter the only manual step left is downloading the CSV.

Started ferrite today, the Rust job runner that will take background work off Quillbase's request path, beginning with the fetch and index pipeline. Set up a cargo workspace with two crates: ferrite-core holding the queue, lease, and worker machinery as a library, and ferrite-cli as the binary for running workers and poking at jobs, structured this way so Quillbase-specific job definitions can eventually live in their own crate without touching core. Tokio for the async runtime, sqlx for Postgres with compile-time checked queries, tracing for structured logs. The foundational decision, argued out loud in the readme before any code: the queue lives in Postgres, not Redis. Reasons, in order of weight: jobs are enqueued in the same transaction as the application writes that spawn them, so a clip insert and its fetch job commit or roll back together and there is no dual-write window where a clip exists but its job vanished; the self-host story stays one database; and the known scaling ceiling of a Postgres queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is thousands of jobs per second, while Quillbase at wild success needs maybe tens. Redis stays in the stack for caching and rate limiting but owns no durable state. Recorded the revisit trigger explicitly: if sustained throughput needs ever exceed roughly 500 jobs per second or queue depth regularly passes a million, reopen the question. Sketched the jobs table shape and the state machine, queued to leased to done or failed with retries looping back to queued, but left the actual schema and dequeue query for the next session so it gets full attention. Also decided version pinning policy, tokio and sqlx pinned to exact minor versions in workspace Cargo.toml since a job runner is the wrong place to absorb surprise dependency behavior changes. Also set the observability and error-handling posture up front, tracing spans around every future job execution and anyhow for error propagation in application code with thiserror for the typed library errors in ferrite-core, on the principle that a job runner whose failures are opaque is worse than no job runner at all, and I would rather pay the small ceremony of typed errors now than retrofit context onto a pile of stringly-typed failures later. Wrote the crate boundary rule into the readme too, ferrite-core stays free of any Quillbase-specific job logic so the runner remains a general library, with product-specific handlers living outside it, a separation that is trivial to keep on day one and painful to extract on day two hundred. Open threads: everything, but concretely the queue schema session, then lease semantics which I already suspect is where the correctness dragons live, then the worker loop.

Queue schema session for ferrite, all in src/queue.rs plus the first sqlx migration. The jobs table: id bigserial primary key, kind text, payload jsonb, state as a Postgres enum over queued, leased, done, failed, run_at timestamptz for delayed jobs defaulting to now, attempts int default 0, max_attempts int default 5, last_error text, created_at, and updated_at maintained by a trigger. Chose bigserial here over uuid deliberately, opposite of the Quillbase clips call, because job ids never leave the backend, ordering by id is a useful tiebreak, and btree locality on a hot table matters more than unguessability. The dequeue query is the classic shape: select from jobs where state equals queued and run_at is at or before now, ordered by run_at then id, limit N, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then flip the selected rows to leased in the same statement via a CTE returning the claimed rows. Getting sqlx to typecheck the enum through the CTE took longer than writing the SQL; the fix was deriving sqlx Type on the JobState enum with the postgres type name attribute matching the migration exactly, after a confusing mismatched types error citing job_state versus jobstate that came down to a missing underscore in the migration. Enqueue is a plain insert exposed as Queue::enqueue taking kind and a serde_json Value payload, plus enqueue_in for delayed jobs; both are generic over an executor so callers can pass their own transaction, which is the whole transactional-enqueue selling point from the design session. Wrote integration tests against a dockerized Postgres using sqlx test macros: enqueue then dequeue returns the job, two concurrent dequeuers claiming from a pool of 10 jobs never claim the same job across 200 iterations, delayed jobs stay invisible until run_at passes. One correctness detail settled now rather than discovered later: dequeue ordering by run_at then id makes retried jobs with a backoff run_at naturally interleave with fresh jobs instead of jumping the line or starving. Also settled the payload serialization contract early, jobs carry a serde_json Value rather than a strongly-typed enum in ferrite-core, because core must not know the shape of every product's job payload, and each handler deserializes its own payload into a typed struct at the top of the function, failing the job with a clear error if the payload does not match rather than panicking, which keeps a malformed or version-drifted payload from taking a worker down. Wrote a test enqueuing a job whose payload is missing a required field and asserted it lands as a failed job with a deserialization error in last_error rather than a crash, since a bad payload should be a data problem, not an availability problem. Open threads: the leased state currently has no expiry so a crashed worker orphans its jobs forever, which is precisely the lease semantics session queued next; no priority concept; failed jobs just sit there with no dead-letter separation; and payload schema versioning is unaddressed, noted with a suspicion it will bite around the first payload shape change.

The session where Quillbase and ferrite finally meet: moving clip fetching off the request path and into the job runner. The architectural question was where parsing lives, because the parser is TypeScript in lib/ingest/parser.ts and the job runner is Rust, and I refuse to maintain two extraction implementations. Considered three shapes. One, port the parser to Rust: rejected, the parser is the most behavior-dense code in the product and its fixture suite and iteration speed live in the TS world. Two, ferrite calls a Node HTTP endpoint that does everything, fetch included: rejected because the network-heavy retry-prone fetch step is exactly what a job runner with backoff is for, and funneling it through Next.js route handlers means paying their timeout and memory constraints for arbitrary slow origins. Three, the split that won: ferrite owns network IO, Quillbase owns parsing. A fetch_clip job in ferrite fetches the URL with redirects, size caps, and timeout enforcement in Rust, stores the raw bytes and final URL into a clip_snapshots table, then calls a thin internal Next.js route, POST /api/internal/parse, which loads the snapshot, runs the existing parser, and updates the clip row. The internal route is guarded by a shared secret in an x-ferrite-token header, compared with a constant-time equality check, with the token injected into both deploys from the same secret store; recorded that this is service-to-service auth of the crudest workable kind and that mTLS or signed requests are the upgrade path if the surface ever grows. Retry semantics defined per failure class using the retryable flags already present in the parser error types, mirrored on the Rust side for fetch errors: DNS and connect timeouts and 5xx retry up to max_attempts 5 with exponential backoff, base 30 seconds, factor 4, full jitter, capped at one hour; 404 and 410 fail terminally on first attempt; the parse callback returning 422 fails terminally since retrying a deterministic parser on identical bytes is a waste of everyone's time. The save endpoint now inserts the clip in state pending and enqueues fetch_clip in the same transaction, exactly the transactional-enqueue pattern ferrite was designed around, and returns immediately; end-to-end save-to-readable latency on my instance is p50 about 2.1 seconds, p95 around 6 seconds dominated by slow origins, and the UI clip card shows a subtle pending shimmer until a light poll notices the state flip. Failure surfaces properly now too: terminal fetch failures set clip state failed_fetch with a human-readable reason from last_error shown in the card, replacing the old behavior where a failed synchronous save just error-toasted and left nothing. The clip_snapshots handoff between the Rust fetcher and the Node parser needed a contract decision, since the two processes share a table but neither should assume the other's timing: ferrite writes a snapshot row with the raw gzipped bytes, the final post-redirect URL, the fetched-at timestamp, and a contentHash, then calls the parse route with the snapshot id, and the parse route is the only writer of the parsed clip fields, so ownership of each column is unambiguous and there is no field two processes both write. The contentHash on the snapshot turned out to earn its place immediately as an idempotency key, because the fenced-completion overlap window in the lease design means the parse callback can genuinely fire twice for one fetch, so the parse route now no-ops if the clip already carries the same snapshot contentHash it is being asked to parse, making a double-fired callback a cheap read instead of a redundant parse and a racy double write. Timeouts got split thoughtfully: the Rust side owns the network timeout at 15 seconds per attempt with the size-cap abort, while the parse callback has its own separate 30 second budget on the Node side since parsing a genuinely enormous document is CPU work unrelated to network slowness, and conflating the two had previously let a huge-but-fast-to-download page blow the fetch timeout for the wrong reason. Wired structured logging across the boundary with a shared clipId and a jobId so a single save can be traced from enqueue through fetch through parse in the logs, which paid off within the hour when a clip stuck in pending turned out to be a parse route returning 500 on a specific malformed document, invisible from the ferrite side alone but obvious once the two log streams shared a correlation id. Also measured the split architecture honestly: moving fetch to Rust and keeping parse in Node adds one internal HTTP round trip per clip, about 4 milliseconds on the private network, a rounding error against multi-second origin fetches and completely worth the clean language boundary. Open threads: the poll for state changes is crude and wants server-sent events eventually; clip_snapshots will grow unboundedly in Postgres and I already suspect object storage is its real home; and there is no per-user fairness in the queue, so a future bulk import could starve interactive saves, noted before it hurts because I can feel the bookmarks importer coming.

Session cookie hardening for clearharbor, the careful pass promised when sessions were first built. Locked the ch_session cookie attributes in src/session.ts: HttpOnly always, Secure in production, SameSite Lax rather than Strict, and Lax took actual deliberation: Strict breaks the case where someone follows a link to their own Quillbase archive from an email or chat message, arriving with no cookie and bouncing through login despite being logged in, while Lax still blocks the cross-site POST shapes that matter for CSRF. Since Lax leans on top-level-GET semantics, state-changing endpoints must never be GET, audited both services to confirm, found and fixed one offender, a logout implemented as GET in a leftover route, now POST with a CSRF-safe body. Expiry policy: sliding 30 day idle window, absolute 90 day cap, both enforced server-side from lastSeenAt and createdAt on the session row rather than trusting cookie max-age, with lastSeenAt updated at most once per hour to keep verify reads from becoming writes on every request. Session fixation handled by issuing a brand new session id at every login and privilege boundary, deleting the old row; wrote a regression test that logs in twice and asserts the ids differ and the first is dead. Added session rotation on password change plus a revoke-all-other-sessions call, and a GET /v1/sessions listing active sessions with creation time, rough user agent, and a current-session marker, the raw material for a sessions page in account settings someday. One deploy wrinkle: Secure plus the parent-domain cookie meant local testing over plain http on localhost was exempt as browsers treat localhost as trustworthy, but the Fly preview environment on a non-production hostname needed Secure too, so the cookie config now derives from a single COOKIE_SECURE env flag rather than NODE_ENV guessing. Also audited the cookie against the parent-domain topology one more time, since ch_session is scoped to the shared parent domain so both products can read it, and confirmed that the SameSite Lax plus HttpOnly plus Secure combination behaves correctly across the auth subdomain and the product subdomain, with a test hitting the verify endpoint from a simulated cross-subdomain request to prove the cookie flows where it should and nowhere it should not. Wrote the reasoning for choosing a shared cookie over per-product cookies into the session module docs, since a future self will wonder why auth cookies are visible to every product and the answer is that single-sign-on across products is the entire point of a shared auth service. Open threads: no anomaly signals on sessions at all, even country-change logging would help; and the once-per-hour lastSeenAt batching means idle expiry has an hour of slop, documented as intentional.

Built the first browser bookmarks importer for Quillbase, starting with the lowest common denominator: the Netscape bookmark file format, that ancient DL DT DH tag soup every browser still exports. Parsing uses linkedom, consistent with the ingest parser, walking the nested DL structure recursively in lib/import/netscape.ts; the format nests folders as DL inside DT with an H3 folder title, and real-world exports are full of unclosed tags, which linkedom tolerates the same way browsers do, one of the quiet reasons to parse with a browser-grade parser instead of regex heroics. Each bookmark yields url, title, addDate from the ADD_DATE attribute in epoch seconds, and folderPath as the joined chain of enclosing H3 titles; tags do not exist in Quillbase yet, so folderPath is stored as plain text on the clip row, an explicit bridge decision recorded so the future tags feature can promote these into real tags with a migration script instead of losing the structure now. The import flow: upload the file to POST /api/import/bookmarks, parse and validate, then insert clips in state pending and enqueue fetch_clip jobs, in batches of 100 clips per transaction so a 5000-bookmark file does not hold one giant transaction open, with each batch reusing the dedup machinery from the urlHash work. Dedup interplay got its own decision: imports use onConflictDoNothing rather than the manual-save behavior of bumping savedAt, because a re-import should be idempotent and silent, not a stampede reshuffling the entire archive to the top; this split the conflict behavior by source, which the source field on the save endpoint conveniently already supports. savedAt for imported clips comes from the bookmark addDate rather than import time, so a decade of bookmarks lands with its real history and the archive timeline means something; clips missing addDate fall back to import time. Ran it on my own Chrome export, 4832 bookmarks: parse took under a second, insert plus enqueue took about 90 seconds total across the batches, 214 duplicates skipped against clips I had already saved by hand, and the fetch pipeline then chewed through the backlog for half an hour, ending with 371 clips in failed_fetch, almost all dead links from the mid 2010s, which honestly is its own little memento mori. The import currently starves interactive saves exactly as predicted in the ferrite integration notes, a manual save during the backlog took 40 seconds to get fetched; queue priority or fairness is now a real need rather than a theoretical one, flagged loudly for the ferrite backlog. The parsing itself surfaced a pile of format reality that the happy-path fixtures had not: real Netscape exports from a decade of browser versions are wildly inconsistent, with some emitting the ADD_DATE attribute in seconds and others in microseconds, some double-escaping ampersands in titles so a title reads amp amp, and Chrome specifically injecting a synthetic Bookmarks bar folder plus an Other bookmarks folder that should map to folder paths but not pollute every clip with a meaningless top-level segment. Handled the timestamp ambiguity by sniffing magnitude, a value past the year 5000 in seconds is obviously microseconds and gets divided, which is crude but correct across every fixture and documented as such; handled the entity double-escaping by decoding HTML entities exactly once after linkedom hands back the text, since linkedom already decodes the outer layer; and stripped the synthetic root folders from folderPath while keeping genuine user folders, matching on the well-known folder names browsers inject. Decided the importer must be resilient to partial garbage rather than all-or-nothing, because a 5000-line export with three malformed entries should import 4997 clips and report 3 skips, not reject the whole file, so parsing collects per-entry errors into a report array and continues, and the upload response carries counts of imported, deduped, and skipped-with-reason rather than a boolean. Also made an explicit call on ordering and memory: the parser yields bookmarks lazily as it walks the DOM rather than materializing the entire flattened list, so even a pathologically large export streams into the batch inserter at bounded memory, and the batches commit in document order so the archive timeline reconstructs the user's real bookmarking chronology from the addDate values. Tested against exports from three different browsers plus a hand-corrupted file with an unclosed folder tag and a bookmark missing its href entirely, confirming the corrupt entries are skipped with distinct reasons and the surrounding good entries survive, which is exactly the robustness a migration tool lives or dies on since nobody re-exports a clean file just because ours choked. Open threads besides fairness: no progress UI during the backlog chew, the upload just returns counts and the user watches clips trickle in, server-sent events or polling a progress endpoint both plausible; Firefox JSON backups and Safari plists are unhandled, Netscape HTML only; and dead-link clips should perhaps be visually distinct or quarantined rather than littering the archive with failure cards.

Small Quillbase bugfix session on a timestamp bug that made imported clips display several hours off from their real save times. Symptom: a clip saved at 9pm showed as saved the next day. Root cause was a mode mismatch in the Drizzle column config: savedAt was declared as timestamp with mode string, so rows came back as bare strings without timezone offsets, and new Date on the client parsed them as local time while the values were UTC, shifting everything by the viewer's offset. Fix was switching the column to mode date so Drizzle returns real Date objects hydrated as UTC, then rendering through a single formatDate helper in lib/format.ts using Intl.DateTimeFormat with the viewer locale, replacing the four slightly different inline formatting spots that had accumulated. Also audited every other timestamp column for the same mode mismatch and fixed two more, lastSeenAt on the session cache mirror and createdAt on imports. Added a regression test that round-trips a known UTC instant through insert and select and asserts the epoch millis survive untouched. The deeper note recorded for the team: timezone bugs here are almost always at the ORM hydration boundary, not in Postgres itself, since timestamptz storage was correct the whole time. Took under an hour including the audit.

Worker loop session for ferrite, src/worker.rs. The shape: a Worker struct owning a sqlx pool, a registry mapping job kind strings to handler functions, and a run loop that dequeues batches and spawns each job as a tokio task, with a Semaphore capping in-flight jobs at a configurable concurrency, default 8, chosen as a starting point for the network-bound fetch_clip workload where most time is spent awaiting slow origins. Handlers are async functions from a job payload to a Result, registered at startup; unknown kinds fail the job immediately with a clear unregistered kind error rather than silently requeueing forever, a failure mode I have been bitten by in other systems. Graceful shutdown got most of the session. On SIGTERM the loop stops dequeuing, then waits for in-flight jobs with a deadline of 25 seconds, chosen because Fly gives 30 between SIGTERM and SIGKILL and I want margin; jobs still running at the deadline are abandoned, which is safe precisely because lease expiry will make them reclaimable, a nice example of the lease design paying for itself before it is even fully built. Shutdown signaling uses a tokio watch channel checked between dequeue cycles and passed into handlers as a CancellationToken so long-running handlers can bail early at their own safe points. Panics in handlers were the tricky bit: a panicking job task must not take the worker down, so each job runs in its own spawned task and the JoinError is caught and converted into a job failure with the panic message captured into last_error, verified by an integration test with a deliberately panicking handler followed by a healthy job on the same worker. Also added a tiny jittered sleep between empty dequeue polls, 500 milliseconds plus up to 250 of jitter, to stop multiple idle workers from synchronizing their polling. Also decided the worker registry maps job kind strings to handlers at startup and is immutable thereafter, so the set of runnable kinds is fixed for the lifetime of a worker process and a deploy is the only way to change it, which I preferred over any dynamic registration because a job runner whose capabilities shift at runtime is a debugging nightmare, and an unknown kind failing loudly and immediately is far better than one silently requeueing forever waiting for a handler that will never appear. Wrote a startup log line enumerating every registered kind so an operator can see at a glance what a given worker process can actually run, which will matter once different process groups run different subsets of kinds. Open threads: concurrency should eventually be per job kind rather than global, cancellation tokens are plumbed but no handler actually honors them yet, and there is no observability at all beyond tracing logs, no counters, no queue depth gauge, noted for a metrics session.

Deep session on lease semantics in ferrite, src/lease.rs, the correctness heart of the whole runner. The problem: a worker claims a job, then crashes, hangs, or gets partitioned; the job must eventually run elsewhere, but the original worker must not be able to stomp the successor's work if it wakes back up. Design settled after a lot of whiteboarding: no separate leases table, instead two columns on the jobs row, leased_until timestamptz and lease_token uuid, because a separate table adds a join to every dequeue and the lease has exactly the lifetime of the claim anyway. Dequeue now sets state leased, leased_until to now plus 30 seconds, and a fresh random lease_token, returning the token to the worker. Workers heartbeat every 10 seconds via extend_lease, an update guarded by both job id and lease_token that pushes leased_until forward another 30; the 3-to-1 ratio of lease length to heartbeat interval gives two missed heartbeats of grace before reclamation. Reclamation is not a background sweeper but a predicate folded into the dequeue query itself: a job is claimable when state is queued, or state is leased with leased_until in the past; this means orphaned jobs get picked up lazily by the next hungry worker with zero extra moving parts, and a dedicated reaper only becomes necessary if we ever want orphan metrics faster than natural dequeue pressure provides. The fencing piece is the part I care most about: completion and failure updates are guarded by lease_token match, update jobs set state done where id equals X and lease_token equals Y, so a worker that lost its lease gets zero rows affected and knows it; the handler result is then discarded with a warning log. This is not hypothetical: reproduced the exact scenario in an integration test by claiming a job, letting the lease expire without heartbeats, having a second worker reclaim and complete it, then having the first worker attempt completion, asserting the stale write bounces; also hit it accidentally and delightfully while stepping through a worker in a debugger, which froze heartbeats, expired the lease, and had a background worker steal the job out from under my breakpoint, at which point the fencing check did its job in real life on day one. Clock skew got explicit treatment: every time comparison uses the database clock via now() in SQL, workers never compare their local clocks to leased_until, they only ask Postgres to do it, so skew between workers is irrelevant and only DB clock jumps matter, which is a much better failure surface. Considered and rejected Postgres advisory locks as the lease mechanism: they vanish when the connection dies which sounds perfect, but that couples job claims to connection lifetime, breaks over pooled connections through pgbouncer in transaction mode, and makes leases invisible to plain SQL inspection; a timestamp column can be read, debugged, and reasoned about with a select statement. One residual risk documented honestly in the module docs: fencing protects the jobs table state machine, but a handler with external side effects, like the parse callback HTTP call, can still double-fire during the overlap window between lease loss and the fenced completion attempt, so handlers must be idempotent, and the parse callback already is since it writes deterministic output keyed by clip id. Spent extra time reasoning through the exact failure interleavings on paper before trusting the design, because lease bugs are the kind that pass every test and then corrupt one job in ten thousand in production. Walked four scenarios: a worker that dies mid-handler leaves leased_until in the past and the job is reclaimed cleanly, verified; a worker whose heartbeat task survives but whose handler hangs forever keeps extending the lease indefinitely and the job never reclaims, which is correct because the worker genuinely still holds it, and the mitigation for a truly wedged handler is a max-handler-duration ceiling I noted as future work rather than pretending the lease solves it; a network partition where the worker can reach the origin but not Postgres means heartbeats fail, the lease expires, another worker takes over, and the partitioned worker's eventual completion write is fenced out, verified; and the nastiest, two workers both believing they hold the lease during the handoff instant, resolved by the fact that only one lease_token is current so at most one completion write ever lands and the other sees zero rows. Also settled the heartbeat implementation detail that the heartbeat runs as its own tokio task spawned alongside the handler and sharing a CancellationToken, so when the handler finishes the heartbeat is torn down immediately rather than firing one last stray extension against a job that is already done, a small race I caught in testing where a completed job briefly showed a leased_until in the future because the heartbeat task outlived the completion by a few milliseconds. The extend_lease query returns the number of rows affected and the worker treats a zero there as a hard signal that it has lost the lease, logging a warning and cancelling its own handler through the shared token rather than wasting effort on work whose result will be fenced anyway, which turns lease loss from a silent overlap into an early, observable bailout. Wrote all four scenarios up in the module docs with the exact SQL guards that make each one safe, because the next person to touch lease.rs, quite possibly me in a year, needs the reasoning and not just the code, and a lease module without its threat model written down is a loaded gun. Open threads: lease duration and heartbeat interval are constants that should move to worker config; no metric yet counts fenced-off completions, which is exactly the number that would reveal lease-thrash in production; and a long CPU-bound handler that blocks the runtime could starve its own heartbeat task, noted with a pointer at spawn_blocking as the likely answer.

Session notes, ferrite lease work in src/lease.rs. Tackled the crashed-worker problem: claimed jobs must become reclaimable, and a zombie worker returning from the dead must not be able to overwrite the successor. Went with lease state embedded on the jobs row, a leased_until timestamptz plus a lease_token uuid, rather than a standalone leases table, keeping dequeue join-free since lease lifetime equals claim lifetime. Claims stamp a 30 second lease and a random token; a heartbeat call extends the lease by another 30 every 10 seconds, guarded by token match, giving roughly two missed beats of slack before the job is up for grabs. Expired leases are reclaimed opportunistically, the dequeue predicate treats leased-and-expired identically to queued, so no sweeper process exists at all; the next worker looking for work inherits orphans naturally. All completion paths are fenced: the update that marks done or failed requires the current lease_token, so a worker whose lease was reclaimed sees zero rows updated and logs a stale-completion warning instead of corrupting state. Proved the fencing twice in one day, once with a purpose-built integration test that stages the reclaim-then-stale-write sequence, and once by accident when a debugger pause suspended heartbeats long enough for another worker to steal the job mid-breakpoint, exactly the failure the design anticipates. Time handling rule: only the Postgres clock ever judges lease expiry, workers never evaluate leased_until against local time, eliminating worker clock skew as a failure class entirely. Explicitly turned down advisory locks despite the attractive auto-release-on-disconnect property, since they misbehave behind transaction-mode poolers, tie claims to connection health rather than worker health, and cannot be inspected with an ordinary select the way a timestamp column can. Wrote into the docs the one limitation fencing does not cover: side effects outside Postgres can still execute twice in the window between lease expiry and the fenced write bouncing, therefore every handler is required to be idempotent, which the clip parse callback satisfies today. Also worth restating the reason a separate leases table was rejected: it would add a join to every dequeue for state whose lifetime is exactly the claim's lifetime, so folding leased_until and lease_token onto the jobs row keeps the hot path join-free and lets an operator inspect a job's lease state with a plain select rather than correlating two tables. And the reason advisory locks lost despite their tidy auto-release-on-disconnect property is that they tie a claim to connection health rather than worker health, misbehave behind a transaction-mode pooler, and cannot be read with ordinary SQL, whereas a timestamp column can be inspected, debugged, and reasoned about by anyone with a psql prompt. Left open: hardcoded lease and heartbeat constants belong in config, a counter for rejected stale completions would be the canary for lease thrash, and heartbeat starvation under a CPU-hogging handler needs the spawn_blocking treatment eventually.

Reader view polish session on Quillbase, clearing threads left open since the sanitization work. Code blocks finally get syntax highlighting: went with shiki, rendered server-side at view time in the RSC, using a lazily initialized singleton highlighter with a trimmed language set of about fifteen common languages to keep memory sane, since a full shiki grammar load was adding roughly 80 MB of heap. Considered highlighting once at parse time and storing the colored HTML, but that bakes theme and grammar versions into stored data, the same argument that put sanitization at render time, so consistency won and highlighting happens at render with an in-process LRU cache keyed by content hash plus language plus theme, which makes repeat views free. Language detection for fenced blocks is heuristic, class name hints like language-rust when present, otherwise a cheap keyword sniff, otherwise plain monospace, no shame in plain. Theme uses shiki dual light and dark output wired to the existing class-based dark mode. Estimated reading time landed too: wordCount from the parser divided by 230 words per minute, shown in the header, clamped to a minimum display of 1 min; picked 230 as a middle-of-the-road adult silent reading rate and moved on with my life rather than bikeshedding it. Scroll progress bar shipped as a thin client island using a passive scroll listener writing to a CSS variable, throttled with requestAnimationFrame, no layout thrash measurable in the profiler. The image proxy question came up again and got explicitly re-deferred with a note: it is a storage and bandwidth commitment masquerading as a privacy toggle, and it deserves its own session with numbers.
