Also fixed a small layout bug where a very long unbroken URL in article text blew out the 68ch measure, solved with overflow-wrap anywhere on the prose container. The teaser badge for partial paywall captures finally rendered, an amber banner reading partial capture with the og description styled distinctly from real article text so nobody mistakes a teaser for the article. Also spent a few minutes on the shiki singleton lifecycle since a highlighter that reinitializes per request would be a memory and latency disaster, so it lives as a lazily-created module-level singleton guarded so concurrent first-requests do not each trigger a full grammar load, and I confirmed with a quick load test that fifty concurrent cold requests initialize the highlighter exactly once rather than fifty times. Recorded that the trimmed fifteen-language grammar set is a deliberate ceiling, since loading every grammar shiki ships would add roughly 80 MB of heap for languages nobody in a read-later archive is realistically saving code in, and the plain-monospace fallback for unrecognized languages is honest rather than a failure. Open threads: shiki singleton warmup adds about 400 ms to the first highlighted view after a cold start, might want eager init behind a flag; and the reading time should probably subtract code blocks for technical articles where wordCount lies.

Queue redesign marathon on ferrite, the session where the simple queue grows up because the bookmarks importer exposed its naivete. Four workstreams: priorities, batch dequeue, dead-lettering, and wakeup latency, plus an unplanned index surgery. Priorities first, the direct fix for imports starving interactive saves: a priority smallint on jobs, default 100, lower runs first, and the dequeue ordering becomes priority, then run_at, then id. Interactive saves enqueue fetch_clip at 100 while bulk imports enqueue at 200, so a manual save cuts the entire import backlog line; deliberately did not build fair-share scheduling or per-user quotas, recorded as a real gap with a concrete trigger to revisit when multi-user instances exist, because a two-tier static priority solves the actual problem we have today with two integers. Per-kind concurrency limits went into static config, a ferrite.toml read by ferrite-cli mapping kind to max in-flight, considered a kind_limits database table for runtime tweakability and rejected it, config redeploys are cheap at our scale and a DB-driven limiter needs cache invalidation machinery that is pure overhead right now. Batch dequeue: the loop was claiming one job per query, and under load the per-claim round trip dominated; the dequeue CTE now claims up to 16 jobs in one statement, distributing them to the semaphore-gated tasks. Benchmarked with a synthetic no-op handler on my dev box against local Postgres: single-claim managed about 40 jobs per second per worker, batch-16 hit around 310, and at a queue depth of 10000 the p99 claim latency sat near 4 milliseconds. Those numbers comfortably embarrass our actual needs, which is the point, headroom means the queue disappears from conversations. Dead-lettering: jobs exhausting max_attempts now move to a jobs_dead table carrying the full original row plus an errors jsonb array accumulating every attempt's error and timestamp, instead of rotting in the main table as state failed; this keeps the hot table small and makes the failure archive greppable, and ferrite-cli gets a dead ls and dead requeue pair for inspection and resurrection. Backoff logic moved from inline arithmetic in the worker into ferrite-core backoff module with property tests: 30 seconds times 4 to the attempt power, capped at one hour, with full jitter, meaning the delay is uniform between zero and the computed value, which the tests actually caught me implementing wrong the first time, I had jitter only above half the computed value, a classic. Index surgery: the original btree on state and run_at bloated hard under churn because every job transitions through three states and dead rows piled up between autovacuums; replaced it with a partial index on run_at, priority where state equals queued, which is the only slice dequeue ever scans, cutting the index to a tenth of its size and making autovacuum's job tractable, plus lowered autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.01 on the jobs table specifically after watching bloat rebuild between default-cadence vacuums under sustained enqueue pressure. Wakeup latency: the 500 millisecond idle poll meant a freshly enqueued job on an idle system waited up to half a second, and multiple idle workers were collectively hammering pointless polls; added LISTEN NOTIFY, enqueue fires a notify on a ferrite_wake channel and idle workers select over the notification and a 5 second fallback poll, keeping the poll as belt and suspenders since notifications are advisory and lost on reconnect. Idle CPU across four workers dropped from a steady 2 percent to effectively 0.2, and enqueue-to-claim latency on an idle system went from a mean around 250 milliseconds to under 10. Stepping back, the reason this session was a redesign rather than a tweak is that the bookmarks importer exposed every latent assumption in the simple queue at once, and I want the reasoning behind each of the four workstreams recorded because each one had a tempting over-engineered alternative I turned down. On priorities, the real problem was narrow and concrete, a bulk import of thousands of low-urgency fetch jobs starving the handful of interactive saves a person makes while the import runs, measured at a 40 second wait for a manual save during an import backlog, and the minimal fix that actually solves it is a single priority smallint defaulting to 100 with imports enqueuing at 200 and the dequeue ordering becoming priority then run_at then id, so an interactive save cuts the entire import line. I deliberately did not build weighted fair queuing or per-user quotas, and I wrote down the concrete trigger for revisiting, the arrival of real multi-user instances where one tenant's import should not starve another's, because a two-tier static priority solves the problem we actually have today with two integers and no scheduler, and inventing fairness machinery now would be solving an imaginary problem with real complexity. On concurrency limits I made the same kind of call, per-kind limits live in a static ferrite.toml read at startup rather than a database table, and I explicitly rejected the runtime-tunable DB-driven limiter because it needs cache invalidation machinery that is pure overhead at our scale where a config redeploy is cheap and frequent. On batch dequeue the motivation was measured rather than assumed: under load the single-claim query's per-round-trip cost dominated, so the dequeue CTE now claims up to 16 jobs in one statement and hands them to the semaphore-gated task pool, and I benchmarked it honestly with a synthetic no-op handler against local Postgres, single-claim managing about 40 jobs per second per worker versus batch-16 hitting around 310, and at a queue depth of 10000 the p99 claim latency sat near 4 milliseconds, numbers that comfortably embarrass our actual needs, which is exactly the point because headroom is what makes the queue disappear from conversations. On dead-lettering, jobs exhausting max_attempts now move to a jobs_dead table carrying the full original row plus an errors jsonb array accumulating every attempt's error and timestamp, rather than rotting in the hot table as state failed, which keeps the main table small and its indexes tight and makes the failure archive greppable, and ferrite-cli grew a dead ls and dead requeue pair for inspection and resurrection. Along the way the backoff logic moved out of inline arithmetic in the worker into a ferrite-core backoff module with property tests, 30 seconds times 4 to the attempt power capped at one hour with full jitter meaning uniform between zero and the computed value, and the property test earned its keep by catching that my first implementation jittered only above half the computed value, a classic mistake that would have left a thundering-herd correlation between retries that the full-jitter design exists specifically to break. The unplanned fifth workstream was index surgery, because the original btree on state and run_at bloated hard under churn, every job cycling through three states and dead rows piling up between autovacuum runs, so I replaced it with a partial index on run_at and priority where state equals queued, the only slice dequeue ever scans, which cut the index to a tenth of its size and made autovacuum tractable, and I lowered autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.01 on the jobs table specifically after watching bloat rebuild between default-cadence vacuums under sustained enqueue pressure. And the wakeup-latency piece, the 500 millisecond idle poll that made a freshly enqueued job on an idle system wait up to half a second while multiple idle workers collectively hammered pointless polls, got LISTEN NOTIFY, with enqueue firing a notify on a ferrite_wake channel and idle workers selecting over the notification and a 5 second fallback poll kept as belt and suspenders since notifications are advisory and lost on reconnect, dropping idle CPU across four workers from a steady 2 percent to about 0.2 and enqueue-to-claim latency on an idle system from a mean around 250 milliseconds to under 10. Open threads leaving this session: recurring or cron-style jobs do not exist and the nightly reconcile idea from the billing side will need them; per-user fairness remains config-tier only; the errors jsonb in jobs_dead has no retention policy and will grow forever; and the metrics session keeps getting displaced, queue depth and fenced-completion counters are still invisible outside of psql.

Search snippets session for Quillbase, closing the ts_headline thread from the ranking work. The naive approach, ts_headline over contentText for every result row, cost about 120 milliseconds per row on longform articles because headline generation re-tokenizes the entire document, which at 50 results would be a six second search page, obviously dead on arrival. Two-stage fix: the ranking query runs as before and returns ids and scores only, then a second query computes headlines for just the top 10 visible results, dropping worst-case headline work by four fifths before any caching. Tuned the headline options: MaxFragments 2 so a snippet can show two separate matching passages with an ellipsis between, MinWords 6 and MaxWords 18 per fragment, StartSel and StopSel emitting a mark element that the clip card styles with a soft highlight, and ShortWord 3 to stop tiny stopwords from anchoring fragments. Even limited to 10 rows, repeat searches were paying the same headline cost every time, so snippets now cache in Redis keyed by clip id plus a hash of the normalized query, TTL one hour, invalidated implicitly by the TTL rather than on clip update since a stale snippet for an hour is harmless. Measured on my archive: search page p95 went from about 210 milliseconds with 10 uncached headlines to 95 with warm cache, and the cold case sits around 160 after the two-stage split. One correctness wrinkle: ts_headline uses the same text search config as the query, and with the english config hardcoded the snippets inherit the same wrong-stemming behavior on non-English clips that ranking has, the language detection thread grows another dependent and I have noted it again, this is becoming the most-referenced open thread in the project. Also fixed the snippet fallback for clips whose match is only in the title, where contentText headlines came back empty; those cards now show the first 30 words of contentText instead of a blank line. Also made a deliberate decision to cache snippets keyed by clip id plus a hash of the normalized query rather than trying to invalidate them on clip edits, accepting that a snippet can be up to an hour stale after a rare clip re-parse, because a stale highlight fragment for an hour is harmless while a precise invalidation scheme would add write-path complexity for a payoff nobody would notice. Confirmed the two-stage split, ranking the full result set first then generating headlines only for the visible top ten, holds up under a query matching thousands of clips, since headline cost scales with rendered results rather than matched results, which is the whole reason the naive per-row headline approach was dead on arrival. Open threads: the mark highlight color needs a dark mode pass, and query hash normalization currently lowercases but does not sort terms, so semantically identical queries in different word orders miss the cache, minor and noted.

Home infrastructure interlude, no product work. The apartment wifi had been dropping video calls for two weeks and I finally sat down with it. Diagnosis: the router was on a 2.4 GHz channel overlapping three neighboring networks, and band steering was bouncing my laptop between bands mid-call, which presented as one to two second freezes exactly matching the disconnect logs in the router admin. Fixes applied: pinned 2.4 GHz to channel 11 which a scan showed cleanest, disabled band steering entirely and gave the 5 GHz network its own SSID so devices stop negotiating, set static DHCP leases for the desk machines and the printer because the printer kept wandering to a new address and breaking its queue, and updated the firmware which was 14 months stale and whose changelog mentioned a memory leak in the DHCP server, plausibly related to the weekly slowdowns. Also moved the router off the floor and away from the microwave line of sight, which is free signal margin people pay money to avoid learning about. Calls have been stable for three days since. Left a note in my personal wiki with the channel scan results and the admin password hint so future me does not rediscover all of this from scratch next year.

Stripe checkout session for clearharbor, the first billing work in the stack. Scope was getting a user from a pricing page to a paid subscription with the webhook skeleton in place, not full entitlement enforcement. Products and prices are created by an idempotent seed script, scripts/stripe-seed.ts, which looks up products by a metadata key before creating, so re-running against the same Stripe account never duplicates; two products for now, Quillbase Plus monthly and yearly, with lookup keys quillbase_plus_monthly and quillbase_plus_yearly referenced in code by key rather than hardcoded price ids, keeping test and live mode configs symmetrical. Checkout uses Stripe-hosted checkout sessions rather than embedded elements, a deliberate call: hosted checkout outsources card UI, SCA flows, tax display, and most compliance surface to Stripe at the cost of a redirect, and for a two-person company the redirect is a bargain. POST /v1/billing/checkout creates the session with client_reference_id set to our userId, customer_email prefilled, success and cancel URLs pointing back at the Quillbase settings page with a session id param for a friendly confirmation state, and subscription mode with the price resolved from the lookup key. The webhook endpoint skeleton went into src/webhooks.ts: a Fastify route at POST /v1/stripe/webhook with raw body preserved for signature verification, currently just verifying the stripe-signature header with constructEvent, logging the event type, and returning 200 fast; actual event handling is next session, and I resisted the temptation to half-implement it now, an unhandled logged event is honest while a half-handled one is a lie. Local testing loop established with the stripe CLI, stripe listen forwarding to localhost 4000 and stripe trigger for synthetic events; also played with test clocks briefly to preview renewal event sequences and wrote down which events a monthly renewal actually fires since the docs list is longer than what practically arrives. One gotcha burned twenty minutes: Fastify's default JSON body parser consumes the stream so the raw body was gone by verification time; fixed with the rawBody config on that single route rather than globally. Also made a deliberate scope call to build the webhook endpoint as a verify-and-log skeleton this session rather than half-implementing event handling, because an unhandled logged event is honest about doing nothing while a half-handled one silently drops billing state changes, which is the worst possible bug in a payments pipeline. Wrote down the local testing loop in the readme, stripe listen forwarding to the local port and stripe trigger plus test clocks for synthetic renewal sequences, along with the actual list of events a monthly renewal fires in practice, which is shorter than the documentation implies and worth capturing so the next session does not rediscover it. Open threads: no webhook event handling yet, no entitlements model, no customer portal wiring for cancellation, and the userId to Stripe customer mapping table exists but only fills at checkout, meaning a user who pays twice from two tabs could create two customers, needs an idempotency guard.

Content-level dedup finally landed in Quillbase, the simhash design sketched during the URL dedup session months back in comment form. The target problem: the same article syndicated at two URLs, or a canonical and a mirror, both passing URL dedup because the URLs genuinely differ, cluttering the archive with twins. Implementation in lib/ingest/simhash.ts: contentText is tokenized, lowercased, and shingled into overlapping 3-grams of words, each shingle hashed with a 64-bit FNV-1a, and the classic simhash bit-voting produces a single 64-bit signature stored as a bigint column on clips, computed at parse time in the internal parse route so it rides the existing pipeline with zero new jobs. Candidate lookup is the part that needed actual design: comparing a new signature against every clip is quadratic nonsense, so the signature is split into four 16-bit bands stored in a clip_simhash_bands table, four rows per clip with bandNo and band16, indexed on band16 and bandNo; by pigeonhole, any two signatures within hamming distance 3 share at least one identical band, so candidates are fetched by band equality and then verified with an exact popcount of the xor, distance 3 or less flags a near-duplicate. Tested against my archive of about 6200 clips: the backfill script computed signatures and bands for everything in 41 seconds, then a full self-scan flagged 11 pairs, of which 3 were genuinely syndicated articles I recognized, 6 were legitimate re-saves of updated versions of the same living document which is arguably correct behavior, and 1 was a false positive, two release-notes pages for adjacent versions of the same product sharing enormous boilerplate; 1 more was a pair of my own test clips. The false positive earned a guard: near-duplicate flagging now also requires trigram similarity between titles above 0.25, using the pg_trgm machinery already installed for search, which kills the release-notes pair while keeping the true syndication catches, tuned by hand over the flagged set. The product decision on what to do with a detected near-duplicate deliberately follows the philosophy from URL dedup: never block a save, never auto-merge, only inform; the save proceeds and the clip card plus reader view show a possible duplicate banner linking to the suspected twin, letting the human decide, because a false merge destroys user data while a false banner costs one glance. Wired the check into ingest so it runs on every fresh parse, adding about 8 milliseconds per clip with the banded lookup, and the banner state is recomputed rather than stored so improving the algorithm retroactively improves old clips. Spent a good while on why simhash over shingles rather than the obvious alternatives, and wrote the comparison into the module docs so the choice is defensible later. A straight equality check on a content hash catches only byte-identical duplicates and misses everything with a changed ad or a different timestamp in the footer, useless for syndication. A full pairwise cosine over tf-idf vectors would be more accurate but is quadratic and needs the whole corpus resident, a non-starter for an incremental per-save check. MinHash with LSH banding was the real contender and is arguably more principled for Jaccard similarity, but simhash with the pigeonhole banding trick gives us the same sublinear candidate lookup with a single 64-bit integer per clip and four small band rows, far less storage and a simpler query than MinHash's many hash-permutation rows, and at our scale and target distance-3 threshold the accuracy difference is noise, so simhash won on operational simplicity. The 3-gram shingle size was itself tuned, tried unigrams which made every article about the same topic look similar and produced a flood of false candidates, tried 5-grams which were so specific that lightly-edited re-publishes stopped matching, and 3-grams sat in the sweet spot where genuine syndication matched and merely-related articles did not. Also handled a subtle correctness issue in the banding table: because a clip can be re-parsed and its signature can change, the four band rows must be deleted and reinserted transactionally with the clip's signature update, otherwise a stale band row points a future candidate query at a signature that no longer exists, so the parse route wraps the signature write and the band rewrite in one transaction and a test asserts a re-parse leaves exactly four band rows with the new values and none orphaned. Measured the candidate-lookup selectivity on my archive to make sure the pigeonhole was not degenerating into near-full scans, and the average band-equality query touched about 30 candidate rows before the exact popcount verify, which is the sublinear behavior the whole scheme promises, versus the 6200-row full scan the naive approach would cost per save. Open threads: no UI to dismiss the banner permanently on a false positive, the threshold pair of hamming 3 and title similarity 0.25 is tuned on one archive and should be revisited with more data, and simhash over shingles handles prose well but code-heavy articles produce jittery signatures since whitespace tokenization mangles code, noted with low priority.

Tags landed in Quillbase. Schema: a tags table with id, userId, name, color, and a clip_tags join table with clipId and tagId, composite primary key on the pair. Uniqueness took a decision: tag names should be case-insensitively unique per user so Rust and rust do not become two tags, and the options were the citext extension or a unique expression index on userId, lower(name); chose the expression index to avoid adding an extension dependency for one column, consistent with the keep-the-install-boring principle, and normalized display casing at write time to whatever casing the user first typed. API surface: POST and DELETE on /api/clips/[id]/tags for attach and detach, POST /api/tags for create with a merged create-or-attach convenience path since the common gesture is typing a tag onto a clip whether or not it exists yet, and a rename endpoint that just updates name since the join table is id-based and rename is free. UI is a tag chip row on clip cards and a combobox editor in the reader view header with typeahead over existing tags, arrow key navigation, and enter-to-create; the combobox is a client island talking to the API optimistically with rollback on failure, the first genuinely optimistic UI in the app and the rollback path got a test since optimistic bugs are silent data lies. The promised bridge from the bookmarks import finally happened: scripts/promote-folder-tags.ts walks clips with a non-null folderPath, splits on the separator, takes the last two path segments as tag candidates, creates tags idempotently through the same lower(name) uniqueness, and attaches them, leaving folderPath in place as provenance rather than nulling it; ran it over my archive and 4100 imported clips gained tags from their old bookmark folders, which instantly made the tag filter feel inhabited instead of empty. Decision recorded on hierarchy: folders are trees but tags are flat, and I am not building nested tags, the two path segments compromise loses some structure and that is accepted, flat tags with good search beats a taxonomy nobody maintains. Also thought through the delete semantics, since removing a tag from the system versus detaching it from one clip are different gestures with different blast radius, and settled that a rename is free because the join table is id-based, a detach touches one join row, and a full tag delete cascades its join rows but never touches the clips themselves, so deleting a tag can never accidentally delete a clip, a guarantee I wrote a test for because destructive operations deserve proof rather than confidence. Recorded the optimistic-UI rollback path as the one genuinely risky piece, since an optimistic attach that fails to persist must visibly revert rather than leaving the UI claiming a tag the database does not have, and that rollback got its own test because optimistic bugs are silent data lies. Open threads: no tag management page for merge and bulk delete, tag color is stored but no picker exists, and the archive filter bar only supports a single tag at a time while the query layer already handles arrays, small UI gap noted.

Performance session on Quillbase after the archive page started feeling sticky around 7000 clips. Profiling with the React flight trace and query logs found three separate sins. First, a textbook N+1: every clip card fetched its tags with its own query, so a 50-card page ran 51 queries; the temptation was Drizzle's relational with tags syntax generating one joined query, but the join multiplies clip rows by tag count and the payload bloats, so I went with the two-query pattern instead, one page of clips then a single where clipId in query for tags, stitched in memory, dropping the page from 51 queries to 2 with a smaller wire size than the join. Second sin, offset pagination: page 100 of the archive ran limit 50 offset 5000 and Postgres dutifully scanned and discarded 5000 rows, measured at 380 milliseconds; replaced with keyset pagination on savedAt, id descending, where the cursor is the last row's savedAt and id encoded as an opaque base64 param, and the same deep page now reads in 9 milliseconds flat off a new composite index on userId, savedAt desc, id desc; the index also covers the common no-cursor first page. Infinite scroll in the UI consumes cursors instead of page numbers now, with the back-forward cache behaving since the cursor is in the URL. Third sin, everything above the fold waited on everything below it: the tag sidebar counts, which aggregate over the whole archive, were computed in the same server component as the first page of clips, so the slowest query gated first paint; wrapped the sidebar in a Suspense boundary with a skeleton and let RSC streaming deliver the clip list first, then counts, and while in there cached the tag counts in Redis for 5 minutes since they drift harmlessly. Measured results end to end on production-ish data: archive page TTFB from about 640 milliseconds to roughly 180, deep pagination from 380 to 9, query count per page from 51 to 2, and the flight payload shrank 40 percent from dropping the join duplication. One regression caught before shipping: keyset ordering broke for clips sharing an identical savedAt from the bookmark import batches, cards shuffled between pages because the sort was unstable, which is exactly why the cursor includes id as tiebreak, the first implementation compared only savedAt and the test with duplicate timestamps caught it. Also turned on Drizzle query logging in dev permanently with a 50 millisecond slow-query warn threshold, cheap tripwire for the next N+1 before it ships. A fourth issue surfaced once the first three were fixed and the page got fast enough to expose it: the archive was selecting the full contentText column on every clip just to render a two-line excerpt, dragging entire article bodies, some tens of kilobytes each, across the wire and through the ORM for fifty cards, so the query was fast but the payload and the serialization were fat. Added a stored excerpt column populated at parse time with the first roughly 280 characters of contentText at a word boundary, migrated the existing rows with a one-off backfill, and changed the archive query to select excerpt instead of contentText, which cut the per-page flight payload by another third on top of the join-dedup win and dropped ORM hydration time noticeably since it was no longer materializing giant strings it would immediately truncate. While instrumenting I also found that the relative-time rendering was recomputing Intl formatting per card on every render, cheap individually but measurable at fifty cards times frequent re-renders during infinite scroll, so the formatter is now memoized and the absolute timestamp is precomputed server-side, shaving a bit of main-thread work on scroll. Reasoned carefully about the keyset cursor encoding under filters, since a cursor is only valid within the sort and filter context that produced it, and decided the opaque base64 cursor encodes only the sort position, savedAt and id, while filters live in their own URL params and are reapplied fresh on every page fetch, so a cursor cannot smuggle stale filter state and a filtered infinite scroll cannot leak unfiltered rows at a page boundary, a bug the first draft actually had when the cursor query forgot to reapply the tag join and which is now guarded by a test seeded with interleaved tagged and untagged clips. Documented the whole investigation as a short perf note in the repo with the before and after numbers, because the N+1 and the offset-pagination traps are exactly the mistakes that will recur the next time someone adds a feature to the archive query in a hurry. Open threads: tag counts caching means the sidebar can contradict a just-added tag for up to 5 minutes, acceptable but worth an eventual bust-on-write; the clips list still selects contentText for the excerpt when a stored excerpt column would avoid dragging full article text through every page render, migration sketched but not run; and search pagination still uses offset since result sets are capped at 50, fine until it is not.

Quick Quillbase fix session on favicons, which had been quietly broken since the beginning. The clip cards were hotlinking a big search company's favicon service, which worked but ships every reader's browsing pattern to a third party and violates the self-host ethos anyway, so it got removed. The replacement fetches favicons ourselves at parse time in the internal parse route: try link rel icon and apple-touch-icon from the parsed document preferring the largest declared size, fall back to /favicon.ico at the site root, follow at most one redirect, cap the download at 100 KB, and accept only image content types. Storage decision: not Postgres bytea and not the future object store, favicons land on the local volume under data/favicons keyed by hostname hash with a single shared file per host rather than per clip, since a host's icon is a host property; the archive page serves them through a tiny route with long cache headers and an etag from the file hash. Hosts with no discoverable icon get a deterministic generated placeholder, a colored circle with the first letter of the hostname, color derived from the hostname hash so it is stable across renders, which honestly looks better than half the real favicons. Backfilled icons for the roughly 900 distinct hosts in my archive with a small script running 8 fetches concurrently, took about 4 minutes, 71 hosts had nothing fetchable and got placeholders. One amusing failure: a site served its favicon with content type text/html, an error page with status 200, which passed the naive check and stored garbage until the content type gate went in. Open thread: icons never refresh once fetched, a host that rebrands keeps its old icon forever, fine for now, noted a 90 day staleness rule as the eventual fix.

Archive filtering session for Quillbase, making the URL the single source of truth for list state. The archive page now reads filters entirely from search params: q for text search, tag, site, state for filtering to failed or partial captures, and star, all composable, so any filtered view is a shareable, bookmarkable, refresh-stable URL, which for a bookmarking product feels almost legally required. Considered the nuqs library for typed search param state and decided against one more dependency for what is six params, hand-rolled a small parseArchiveParams helper in lib/params.ts with zod validation that clamps junk values to defaults instead of erroring, since a mangled URL should degrade to the unfiltered archive rather than a 400 page. Filter changes navigate with router.replace for refinements like toggling a tag, but router.push when the text query changes, on the theory that search queries are meaningful history entries while filter fiddling is not, and testing the back button through both paths confirmed the browsing feel is right. The filter bar UI shows active filters as removable chips with the tag chips colored from the tags work, and an explicit clear-all; empty filter states render a purpose-built empty view naming the active filters rather than the generic no-clips illustration, small thing, big feel. Query layer composes the filters into one Drizzle query builder chain, and the keyset pagination cursors from the performance session survive filtering because the cursor encodes only sort position while filters re-apply on every page fetch; verified a filtered infinite scroll does not leak unfiltered rows at page boundaries, which the first draft did when the cursor query forgot to reapply the tag join, caught by a test seeded with interleaved tagged and untagged clips. One subtle app router behavior documented for the team: navigating with only search param changes still re-runs the server component by default, there is no shallow routing in the pages router sense, so the two-query archive fetch happens on every chip toggle, acceptable at 2 queries and 180 ms TTFB but worth remembering before anyone adds an expensive aggregate back into the critical path. Also made a deliberate choice to clamp malformed filter values to sensible defaults rather than erroring, so a mangled or hand-edited URL degrades to the unfiltered archive instead of a 400 page, which matters because filtered URLs are meant to be shared and pasted and a shared link that 400s because a param drifted is a broken promise. Wrote parseArchiveParams as the single place all six filter params are validated and normalized, so no route or component reinvents its own interpretation of the query string, and covered it with a test throwing junk values at every param to assert each one falls back gracefully rather than propagating a bad value into the query builder. Open threads: no date range filter yet though the URL schema reserves from and to, multi-tag filtering still pending from the tags session, and the site filter matches exact hostname only, wanting a domain-suffix match so a blog and its www twin group together.

Full-text search upgrade session for Quillbase, finally paying down the two oldest search debts: query syntax and the hardcoded english config. Query parsing moved from plainto_tsquery to websearch_to_tsquery, which understands quoted phrases, a leading minus for exclusion, and OR, matching what fingers type into search boxes from years of habit; this immediately fixed the phrase-shaped golden query miss from the original ranking session. The bigger piece was language. Every clip now gets a lang column detected at parse time using franc over contentText, mapped from ISO codes to the Postgres text search configs we support, english, spanish, german, french, portuguese, italian, with anything else falling back to the simple config which does no stemming but at least does not stem wrongly; detection runs on the first 2000 characters which benchmarked as accurate as full-text for this corpus and much cheaper, and clips under 200 characters skip detection and take simple since franc is unreliable on tiny inputs. The searchVector generated column had to become a regular column maintained by trigger, because a generated column cannot reference another column to choose its config dynamically, a genuine loss of tidiness recorded with mild grief; the trigger builds setweight vectors using the row's lang config, same A B C weighting as before. Query-side language selection was the thorniest decision: searching should not require declaring a language, and querying six configs and unioning is slow and noisy, so the query runs against the user's dominant language config, computed as the modal lang across their archive and cached, plus the simple config, unioned and deduplicated by id keeping max score; recorded honestly that a Spanish-dominant user searching for a German article by a stemmed German word will miss, and the mitigation is that title words are usually unstemmed enough to hit via simple, plus the trigram fallback still exists below 3 results. Re-vectorizing the archive took 2 minutes 10 seconds for about 7100 clips inside a single migration transaction, and the migration got a comment warning self-hosters with large archives to expect proportional time. Reran the golden queries: 23 of 25 top-3, up from 21, the two recovered being the phrase query and a Spanish article previously stemmed as english garbage; the remaining misses are the postgres versus postgresql vocabulary gap, stubborn as ever and now clearly wanting a small synonym dictionary, and the ambiguous query I keep refusing to redefine. Latency held steady, the dual-config union adds about 12 milliseconds at p95, and EXPLAIN confirmed both index scans stay bitmap-and-ed rather than degrading to sequential. The migration from a generated tsvector column to a trigger-maintained one deserved more care than I first gave it, because a trigger that runs on every insert and update of a large table is easy to get subtly wrong. The trigger only recomputes the vector when title, contentText, siteName, or lang actually change, checked with an IS DISTINCT FROM guard so an unrelated update like bumping saveCount does not pointlessly rebuild a vector over a long article, which measurably cut write amplification during the import backfill where many rows get touched repeatedly. Getting the trigger to select the right text search config dynamically from the row's lang column meant building the tsvector with a regconfig cast resolved at runtime rather than a compile-time config literal, and I had to map our supported lang codes to actual config names in the trigger body with an explicit CASE rather than trusting the code to equal the config name, since our lang column stores ISO codes like en and de while the Postgres configs are named english and german. A genuinely nasty bug ate an hour: the initial trigger built the vector correctly but I had forgotten to also fire it on the language-detection backfill update, so freshly re-detected clips kept their old english-config vectors until touched again, and search results looked half-migrated in a way that made me suspect the query side before I found the trigger coverage gap; the fix was an explicit one-time UPDATE that forced a no-op distinct write to rebuild every vector after the lang backfill completed, and I added a assertion query to the migration that counts vectors whose config disagrees with the row lang, which must return zero. Also reconsidered whether to store the detected lang confidence and decided against persisting it, since franc returns a best guess and a stored confidence would invite building logic on a number I do not trust; instead clips under 200 characters or with an ambiguous detection simply take the simple config, a conservative default that never stems wrongly, and that rule lives in one place in the parse route rather than being reconstructed at query time. Open threads: the synonym layer, growing the golden set which now clearly underrepresents non-English queries, and the dominant-language cache has no invalidation beyond a daily TTL so a user whose archive flips language majority sees it a day late, documented as delightfully unlikely.

ferrite-cli session, giving the job runner a face for operators, meaning us at two in the morning. Built out the command surface with clap derive: jobs ls with filters by kind, state, and age plus a limit flag, jobs inspect taking a job id and printing the full row including payload pretty-printed and the error history when dead, jobs retry, jobs cancel, and the dead subcommands from the redesign session wired properly, dead ls and dead requeue. Output formatting went through comfy-table for the list views with a plain flag emitting tab-separated values for piping into awk, and inspect prints a readable key-value block rather than a table since single-record tables are silly. Retry semantics needed a real decision: naively resetting attempts to zero lies about history, so retry sets run_at to now and state to queued while leaving attempts intact and incrementing a separate manual_retries counter, meaning a job manually retried past max_attempts can run again but the record shows the full story; if it fails again it dead-letters again immediately rather than earning a fresh five attempts, which matches the operator intent of one more try, not start over. Cancel is restricted to queued state only, cancelling a leased job would race the worker holding it and the lease machinery already handles abandoned work, so the CLI refuses with a message pointing at the lease timeout instead of pretending to control a running job. All mutating commands print what they did and support a dry-run flag, and connection config comes from the same DATABASE_URL and ferrite.toml the workers read so the CLI never contradicts the running system. One bug found while building: jobs ls ordered by created_at descending was using a sequential scan past a few hundred thousand historical rows since only the partial queued index existed, added a plain btree on created_at after confirming with explain, listing dropped from 800 milliseconds to 12. Also made a firm decision that every mutating CLI command prints exactly what it changed and supports a dry-run flag, because an operator running destructive commands against a production queue at two in the morning deserves to see the blast radius before committing, and a CLI that silently mutates state is how outages get worse rather than better. Pulled the connection config from the same DATABASE_URL and ferrite.toml the workers read rather than a separate CLI config, so the CLI can never accidentally point at the wrong database or contradict the running system, a small consistency that removes an entire category of confusing operator mistake. Open threads: no jobs stats summary command yet showing depth by kind and state which is the thing you actually want at a glance, no requeue-by-filter bulk operation for mass dead-letter recovery after an outage, and the CLI has no JSON output mode which the eventual metrics or web dashboard work might prefer to scrape.

Product-shaped session on Quillbase around RSS, or more precisely around deciding not to build RSS yet. The ingest parser now detects feed declarations while it is already parsing the document, link rel alternate with an rss or atom type, and stores the first discovered feedUrl on a per-host sites record alongside the favicon machinery, essentially free data capture riding an existing parse. Then came the actual question: Quillbase users keep asking versions of can it subscribe to this blog, and the pull toward becoming a feed reader is real. Wrote the argument out in DECISIONS.md and it came down firmly against, for now: a read-later app is an intentional space holding things you chose, a feed reader is an obligation engine generating unread counts, and bolting subscriptions on turns the calm archive into another inbox; competitively the feed reader space is crowded with excellent dedicated tools while calm read-later is exactly our wedge; technically it drags in polling schedules, feed dedup against clip dedup, and per-feed state, a large surface for a two-person team mid-stride on billing work. The compromise position recorded: feedUrl capture stays because it costs nothing and preserves optionality, and the someday-shape sketched is not subscriptions but a weekly digest suggestion, surfacing that a site you save from often has a feed, still leaving the choosing to the human. Also cleaned up the sites table while in there since it now carries hostname, favicon path, and feedUrl: gave it a proper unique index on hostname and migrated the favicon path column over from its temporary spot on clips, one less denormalization. Open threads: none new, the decision is the artifact, though the DECISIONS.md file is getting long enough to want a table of contents, which is a good problem.

Deep Stripe webhooks session on clearharbor, turning the logging skeleton into the real billing state machine. First, the transport layer hardening: signature verification via constructEvent was already in, but a deploy-eve incident made it earn its keep, verification suddenly failing on every event with the error message No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload, which smelled like key rotation but was actually a trailing newline in the webhook secret as stored in the Fly secrets manager, invisible in every echo I ran; the fix trims the secret at load time and the config loader now trims all secrets on principle, plus a startup log of each secret's byte length, enough to spot padding without leaking values. Idempotency next, because Stripe explicitly retries and duplicates: a webhook_events table stores every received event id with a unique constraint, processing runs inside a transaction that inserts the event id first, and a conflict on that insert means already processed, return 200 and do nothing, making redelivery a no-op by construction rather than by handler discipline. Then the events themselves. checkout.session.completed resolves the user from client_reference_id, creates or reuses the customer mapping row, and hands off to entitlement computation; customer.subscription.updated and deleted drive the ongoing lifecycle; invoice.payment_failed only logs for now since the subscription updated event carries the status change that actually matters. Entitlements got their own module, src/entitlements.ts, with the central decision of the session: entitlements are computed and stored, not derived per request. The mapping is a pure function from subscription status and price lookup key to a plan enum, free or plus, with past_due keeping plus for a 7 day grace window from the status transition timestamp, after which it drops; the function is pure so it is exhaustively unit tested across the status and time matrix, thirteen cases, and the stored entitlements row per user carries plan, source subscription id, and computed_at. Freshness rides two rails: webhooks update entitlements the moment Stripe tells us anything, and a nightly reconcile job re-derives every active user's entitlement from the Stripe API to heal any missed or misordered webhook, and that reconcile job is a ferrite job, the first cross-product use of the runner from clearharbor, enqueued on a schedule which currently means a cron hitting an enqueue endpoint since ferrite still lacks native recurring jobs, a dependency called out in the notes. Ordering hazards got explicit handling: Stripe does not guarantee event order, so entitlement writes carry the event created timestamp and a stale event, older than the last applied one for that subscription, is discarded with a log line rather than applied, which the test suite proves by replaying an update pair in reverse. Tested the whole flow with stripe CLI listen and trigger plus a test clock walking a subscription from trial through active into past_due and cancellation, watching the entitlements row move through plus, grace-period plus, and free at exactly the boundaries intended. Spent meaningful time on the customer mapping table and its idempotency, because the double-tab-checkout hazard flagged in the earlier checkout session is a real way to end up with two Stripe customers for one user and a split billing history that is miserable to untangle. Resolved it by making the user-to-customer mapping row the point of serialization: the checkout handler upserts the mapping under a unique constraint on userId before creating the checkout session and passes the resolved customer id into the session, so two concurrent checkouts converge on one customer row rather than minting two, and if Stripe has already created a customer for that email we adopt it by looking up rather than creating a duplicate. Also worked through the ordering guarantees more rigorously than the summary suggests, because Stripe explicitly warns that events can arrive out of order and even be duplicated, and a subscription that goes active then past_due then active again could, if applied in the wrong order, leave a paying customer downgraded. The fix layers two defenses: the webhook_events unique constraint makes redelivery a structural no-op, and the entitlement write carries the Stripe event created timestamp and refuses to apply anything older than the newest already applied for that subscription id, so a late-arriving stale event is discarded with a log line rather than clobbering fresher state, proven by a test that replays an update pair in reverse and asserts the final entitlement matches the newer event. The nightly reconcile job is the belt to that suspenders: it re-derives every active user's entitlement directly from the Stripe API and heals any drift from a missed or misordered webhook, and running it as a ferrite job was the first time clearharbor reached across into the Rust runner, which needed a small internal enqueue endpoint since ferrite has no native cron yet and the schedule is currently an external timer poking that endpoint, a dependency I called out loudly for the ferrite backlog because a billing reconcile that silently stops running is a slow-motion incident. One operational decision recorded: the reconcile intentionally never downgrades a user inside a webhook-driven grace window, it only corrects genuine disagreements, so a user legitimately in their 7 day past_due grace is not yanked to free by a reconcile that reads a raw past_due status without the grace logic, which meant the grace computation had to live in the shared pure entitlement function that both the webhook path and the reconcile path call, not duplicated. Open threads: the customer portal for self-serve cancellation is still unwired, Quillbase does not yet read entitlements so plus is currently a database row with no powers, webhook_events has no retention policy, and the grace window length is a product guess awaiting contact with reality.

Session notes on the clearharbor Stripe webhook build-out, moving from skeleton to functioning billing pipeline. Spent the first stretch on a verification outage that turned out to be environmental: every incoming event failed signature checking with No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload, and after chasing imaginary key rotation the culprit was a newline appended to the webhook secret in the secrets store; secrets are now trimmed on load across the board and the boot log prints byte lengths per secret so whitespace contamination is visible without printing values. Duplicate delivery is handled structurally: each event id lands in a webhook_events table under a unique constraint inside the processing transaction, so a redelivered event conflicts on insert and short-circuits to a 200, removing any reliance on individual handlers being careful. Event handling covers checkout.session.completed for the initial purchase, mapping client_reference_id back to our user and establishing the customer link, plus customer.subscription.updated and deleted for lifecycle changes, with invoice.payment_failed logged but not acted on since subscription status transitions carry the authoritative signal. The design centerpiece is src/entitlements.ts: plan state is materialized into an entitlements row rather than computed from Stripe on request, derived by a pure function mapping subscription status and price lookup key to free or plus, including a 7 day past_due grace period measured from the transition time; purity made the thirteen-case unit test matrix trivial. Staleness protection compares event created timestamps and refuses to apply an event older than the newest already applied for that subscription, verified by a reversed-replay test, since Stripe ordering is best-effort. Two mechanisms keep stored entitlements honest: immediate webhook-driven updates, and a nightly full reconcile against the Stripe API that runs as a ferrite job, notably the first time clearharbor work rides the Rust runner, though scheduling it currently needs an external cron poke because ferrite has no recurring-job support yet, a gap now on ferrite's plate. Exercised everything with the stripe CLI forwarding to local plus a test clock marching one subscription through trial, active, past_due, and cancelled, confirming the entitlements row tracked plus, grace, and free on the intended boundaries. Worth restating the central architectural call, that plan state is materialized into a stored entitlements row rather than computed from the Stripe API on every request, because a per-request Stripe call would couple our request latency and availability to a third party and burn rate limits, while a stored row derived by a pure function is fast, testable, and inspectable, with the two freshness rails of immediate webhook updates and a nightly reconcile keeping it honest. Also restating why the reconcile runs as a ferrite job rather than an in-process timer, since it made clearharbor the first consumer of the shared runner and gives the reconcile the same retry, backoff, and dead-letter guarantees every other job gets, at the current cost of an external cron poke standing in for the native recurring-job support ferrite still lacks. Still open after this session: customer portal integration for cancellation, actual enforcement of plan limits inside Quillbase which currently ignores entitlements entirely, retention for the ever-growing webhook_events table, and validating the 7 day grace number against real customer behavior someday.

Non-product session: outlined my talk for a regional JavaScript meetup, working title Your Reading List Is a Distributed System. The conceit is walking through building a read-later tool as an excuse to teach three unsexy production topics to app developers: queues with leases instead of fire-and-forget async, sanitization boundaries and why render-time beats ingest-time, and Postgres full-text search before reaching for a search service. Outline landed at five sections: opening bit about bookmark graveyards and the 4832-bookmark import as the cold open; the fetch pipeline story with the lease-fencing debugger anecdote as the emotional peak since a debugger breakpoint losing a job to a rival worker demos distributed systems better than any diagram; the XSS near-miss with the wildcard attribute config as the security section, self-deprecation as pedagogy; the search ranking numbers as the data section, 9 of 25 to 16 of 25 top-1 with each change attributed; closing argument that boring infrastructure choices are a form of user respect for self-hosted software. Twenty five minutes plus questions, budget one minute per slide, so roughly 22 slides, demos pre-recorded as gifs because live demos at meetups are a tax on everyone's evening. Deliberately fictionalizing nothing and naming no companies beyond our own products, the real numbers are the material. Next step is drafting slides and doing a timed run against the kitchen wall; submission deadline is in three weeks.

Rate limiting session for Quillbase, closing the oldest open thread on the save endpoint. Implementation is a token bucket in lib/ratelimit.ts backed by Redis: bucket per user for clip saves, capacity 30, refill rate one token every 2 seconds, implemented as a small Lua script doing the read-refill-consume atomically server-side so concurrent requests cannot race the bucket state, script loaded once via SCRIPT LOAD and invoked by sha. Chose token bucket over fixed or sliding windows because bursts are legitimate here, someone clearing browser tabs saves ten things in thirty seconds and should not be punished, while sustained abuse should be, and the bucket expresses exactly that shape. Limited endpoints: POST /api/clips at 30 burst with the 0.5 per second refill, and the search endpoint got a gentler 60-capacity bucket after noticing the typeahead work coming down the road will multiply search calls. Import endpoints are explicitly exempt from the per-clip bucket since imports batch through their own controlled pipeline with queue priorities handling fairness at the ferrite layer, and double-limiting them would just break big imports; the exemption keys off the source field that keeps earning its existence. Responses on limit are 429 with a Retry-After header computed from the token deficit, and the UI save box shows a soft countdown message rather than a raw error toast. The self-host purity debate resurfaced since this adds a Redis dependency to the request path: considered a Postgres-based limiter for dependency minimalism, but Redis is already required for snippet caching and the tag count cache, so the marginal dependency is zero; still, wrapped the limiter behind a RateLimiter interface with an in-memory fallback implementation activated by config for single-instance installs that want to run without Redis, correctness caveat documented that in-memory state resets on restart and does not share across instances, acceptable for the tiny-install audience it serves. Tests cover burst-then-sustain behavior against a real Redis in CI using time injection into the Lua script via a passed-in now parameter rather than mocking Redis, which keeps the atomicity claims honest. Also made the deliberate call to wrap the limiter behind a RateLimiter interface with an in-memory implementation selectable by config, so a single-instance self-host that wants to run without Redis can, at the documented cost that in-memory buckets reset on restart and do not share across instances, which is an honest tradeoff for the tiny-install audience it serves rather than a hidden limitation. Recorded that imports are intentionally exempt from the per-clip bucket because they batch through their own controlled pipeline where the ferrite queue priorities already handle fairness, and double-limiting them would just break large imports for no benefit, an exemption that keys off the same source field that keeps earning its existence. Open threads: no per-IP limiting on unauthenticated surfaces like the login page, which is clearharbor territory and got a note passed over the fence, and limits are constants that plausibly become plan-dependent once entitlements start meaning something.

Bookmarks import marathon, round two, the session that turns the Netscape-only importer into a real multi-browser migration path, and incidentally the session where several past decisions get cashed in at once. Format support first. Chrome and Edge export the Netscape HTML already handled. Firefox backups are a different animal, a JSON tree of places nodes with GUIDs, type discriminators, and microsecond timestamps, parsed in lib/import/firefox.ts with a zod schema loose enough to survive the format drift between Firefox versions, since fixtures from three versions showed field renames like title going absent versus empty. Safari was the boss fight: bookmarks live in a binary plist, so the importer takes Bookmarks.plist directly, decoded with the bplist-parser package after weighing writing a minimal bplist reader and deciding a maintained parser for a stable binary format is the correct dependency to accept, recorded with reasoning since it cuts against the dependency-minimalism reflex; the plist nests WebBookmarkTypeList and WebBookmarkTypeLeaf nodes with the reading list living under a specially named list node, and Safari reading list items carry a preview text field that maps beautifully onto our teaser concept for partial captures. All three formats normalize into a shared intermediate, a BookmarkNode tree defined in lib/import/normalize.ts with url, title, addedAt, and children, so the downstream pipeline is format-blind; folder paths map to real tags now via the promote logic built in the tags session, joined with a slash separator and capped at depth 3 from the leaf upward, deeper ancestry discarded as noise, matching the flat-tags philosophy. The infrastructure story is where the past caught up with us. The v1 importer parsed uploads inside the Next.js route handler, and a 40 MB Safari plist from a decade-old machine spiked route memory past 512 MB and got the dev server killed; parsing now happens off the request path entirely, the upload streams to the local volume, the route enqueues an import_bookmarks ferrite job with the file path and returns immediately, and the job parses, normalizes, and then feeds clips into the pipeline in batches of 100, reusing the batch shape from v1 but now inside the runner where memory is budgeted and failure is retryable. Fetch jobs spawned by imports enqueue at priority 200 against the interactive 100, which is precisely the two-tier priority machinery built in the queue redesign paying off, and a manual save mid-import now gets fetched in seconds instead of the 40-second starvation measured back then. Progress became visible: an import_progress row per import tracks total, parsed, inserted, deduped, and failed counts, updated by the job every batch, and the UI polls a progress endpoint every 2 seconds rendering a progress card with per-category counts; considered server-sent events again and deferred again, polling every 2 seconds for a minutes-long operation is undignified but completely fine, the SSE debt is now consolidated across three features and will be paid once, later. Numbers from the live test: a 12400-bookmark Firefox backup imported end to end in 4 minutes 40 seconds, job memory steady around 140 MB, 1832 duplicates skipped by urlHash conflict, 96 dead links surfaced as failed_fetch, and the archive timeline landed with correct historical savedAt from the backup timestamps. Edge cases collected along the way and handled with counters shown in the final report rather than silent drops: javascript scheme bookmarklets skipped, place scheme Firefox internal rows skipped, data URI pseudo-bookmarks skipped, and duplicate URLs within the same import file collapsed pre-insert to avoid intra-batch conflict churn. The fixture suite for the importers grew to 14 files covering the three formats plus adversarial cases, including a hand-built plist with a cycle in its object table which bplist-parser survives but our tree walk needed a visited-set guard against, found by the fixture before production found it for us. It is worth spelling out how much past design this session cashed in, because that is the real story of the round-two importer, it barely wrote new infrastructure and instead collected debts that earlier sessions had deliberately taken on. The format work alone was substantial. Chrome and Edge were already covered by the Netscape HTML parser, but Firefox exports a JSON tree of places nodes with GUIDs, type discriminators, and microsecond timestamps, which needed a zod schema deliberately loose enough to survive the field drift between Firefox versions since fixtures from three versions showed a title field variously absent, empty, or present, and Safari was the boss fight because its bookmarks live in a binary plist, so the importer takes Bookmarks.plist directly and decodes it with the bplist-parser package after I weighed writing a minimal bplist reader myself and decided that a maintained parser for a stable binary format is precisely the dependency worth accepting, a call I recorded because it cuts against the dependency-minimalism reflex that governs most of these decisions. The three formats normalize into a shared BookmarkNode intermediate tree in lib/import/normalize.ts with url, title, addedAt, and children, so everything downstream is format-blind, and folder paths map to real tags through the promote logic built back in the tags session, joined with a slash and capped at depth 3 from the leaf upward with deeper ancestry discarded as noise, consistent with the flat-tags philosophy that folders are trees but tags are flat. The infrastructure payoff is where the past really caught up with us. The v1 importer parsed uploads inside the Next.js route handler, and a 40 MB decade-old Safari plist spiked route memory past 512 MB and got the dev server killed, which was the concrete event that justified moving parsing off the request path entirely: the upload now streams to the local volume, the route enqueues an import_bookmarks ferrite job with the file path and returns immediately, and the job parses, normalizes, and feeds clips into the pipeline in batches of 100 inside the runner where memory is budgeted and failure is retryable, exactly the shape the ferrite integration was designed to enable. The fetch jobs those imports spawn enqueue at priority 200 against interactive saves at 100, which is the two-tier priority machinery from the queue redesign paying off directly, and a manual save mid-import now gets fetched in seconds instead of the 40-second starvation I measured back when priorities did not exist, a satisfying closed loop from problem to design to payoff across three sessions. Progress finally became visible through an import_progress row per import tracking total, parsed, inserted, deduped, and failed counts, updated by the job every batch, with the UI polling a progress endpoint every 2 seconds, and I considered server-sent events yet again and deferred yet again on the grounds that polling every 2 seconds for a minutes-long operation is undignified but completely fine, consolidating the SSE debt across three features that will pay it once, later, together. The live numbers were reassuring: a 12400-bookmark Firefox backup imported end to end in 4 minutes 40 seconds with job memory steady around 140 MB, 1832 duplicates skipped by urlHash conflict, 96 dead links surfaced as failed_fetch, and the archive timeline landed with correct historical savedAt from the backup timestamps rather than collapsing everything to import time. And the edge cases got handled with visible counters in the final report rather than silent drops, because a migration tool that silently loses data destroys the trust it exists to earn: javascript-scheme bookmarklets skipped, Firefox place-scheme internal rows skipped, data-URI pseudo-bookmarks skipped, and duplicate URLs within a single import file collapsed before insert to avoid intra-batch conflict churn, each with its own count. The fixture suite grew to 14 files across the three formats plus adversarial cases including a hand-built plist with a cycle in its object table, which bplist-parser survives but our tree walk needed a visited-set guard against, a cycle found by the fixture before production found it for us. Open threads: no cancel for a running import, the job would need a cooperative cancellation check between batches which the worker cancellation tokens already support in principle, just unwired; per-user fairness remains priority-tier-only which multi-tenant instances will eventually feel; and reading list preview text is captured for Safari but no equivalent enrichment exists for the other browsers, minor asymmetry, noted.

Data model session for Quillbase highlights and annotations, groundwork before any UI exists. The highlights table: id uuid, clipId, userId, color from a fixed palette of five, note text nullable for attached commentary, createdAt, and the anchoring payload, which is where all the design weight went. Rejected character offsets into contentHtml immediately: offsets shatter whenever the sanitizer policy changes or a re-parse of a snapshot regenerates markup, and both are explicitly allowed to happen in this architecture, render-time sanitization being a standing decision. Went instead with quote-based anchoring in the style of the W3C annotation selector model: each highlight stores exact, the selected text itself, plus prefix and suffix context strings of up to 64 characters on each side, and anchoring at render is a search for exact with prefix and suffix used to disambiguate between multiple occurrences, scored by context match quality. When re-anchoring fails outright, the highlight is not discarded but rendered in an orphaned state listed below the article with its text and note intact, because a note someone wrote must never silently vanish on a re-parse; that principle went into the module docs in bold. Implemented the anchoring engine in lib/annotate/anchor.ts as pure functions over plain strings so the whole thing unit tests without a DOM, with a fuzz pass that mutates documents by inserting and deleting sentences around highlights and measures re-anchor survival, currently 96 percent across the mutation corpus, orphan rate under 4 percent with zero false re-anchors, and false re-anchors are the metric that matters since a highlight jumping to the wrong text is worse than orphaning. API routes for create, update note, recolor, and delete are in, gated by clip ownership through the usual middleware, with highlight creation validating that exact is non-empty and under 4000 characters to keep someone from highlighting an entire article into a single row, and the routes are exercised by integration tests. Storage decision recorded: highlights reference clipId and survive clip re-fetches, but if a clip is deleted its highlights cascade, debated soft-preserving them as orphaned quotes and decided deletion should mean deletion, users own their data including its destruction. Open threads: no selection UI in the reader yet, that is its own session with all the range-and-selection browser pain implied; exports should eventually include highlights inline; and the color palette is hardcoded pending the tag color picker that also does not exist, two features now waiting on one tiny color component, which is how backlogs are made.

Storage architecture session for Quillbase, prompted by an alarming number: the clip_snapshots table, holding raw fetched HTML since the ferrite integration, had grown the database to 9.4 GB while actual queryable data is a fraction of that, and backup times had stretched past twenty minutes. Decision: raw snapshots move out of Postgres into object storage, and the split principle is recorded plainly, Postgres holds what queries touch, parsed contentHtml and contentText and vectors, while immutable blobs live in an object store addressed by key. Went with the S3-compatible object storage on Fly for production since we already deploy there, but the code targets the S3 API generically through a thin client in lib/storage/blobs.ts, and the self-host docs will name MinIO as the reference alternative, keeping the no-vendor-lock principle intact; the client is deliberately minimal, put, get, delete, presign, with retries and a size guard, no SDK-wide dependency dragged in beyond the S3 signing lib. Key layout is userId slash clipId slash fetchedAt timestamp dot html dot gz, snapshots gzipped on write which averaged 78 percent size reduction across a sample of a thousand snapshots, text compresses like it wants to disappear. Retention became a real policy instead of never: keep the two most recent snapshots per clip, delete older ones on write, reasoning that the current parse plus one history step covers re-parse and diff needs while unbounded history is a cost with no user-facing story; the policy runs inline at snapshot write rather than as a sweeper, one less background job. The migration itself moved about 41000 snapshots: a script streaming rows oldest-first, uploading gzipped, verifying by size and a sampled content hash, then deleting the Postgres row in the same loop iteration, run at a deliberate pace over 55 minutes with a resumable cursor checkpoint written every 500 rows since a migration that cannot be interrupted is a hostage situation; database size dropped from 9.4 GB to 1.1 GB and the nightly backup fell from 22 minutes to 3. Access paths updated: the internal parse route now pulls snapshot bytes from the blob store, and a debug route serves a stored snapshot through a presigned URL with a 5 minute expiry rather than proxying bytes through Node. One migration surprise: about 60 snapshots failed gzip round-trip verification with truncated content, traced to the earliest days of the fetch pipeline before the size-cap abort was flushed properly, ancient bug, already fixed upstream, the damaged snapshots were logged and skipped and their clips flagged for re-fetch. Spent real design time on the blob key layout and the immutability guarantees, because an object store is only pleasant if keys are deterministic and content never mutates under a key. Keys are userId slash clipId slash fetchedAt dot html dot gz, which sorts naturally by user then clip then time and makes the two-most-recent retention query a simple key-prefix list plus a sort, and because the fetchedAt timestamp is part of the key each snapshot is write-once, a new fetch writes a new key rather than overwriting an existing one, so a reader that holds a key never sees its bytes change beneath it. The retention policy, keep the two newest snapshots per clip and delete older ones on write, runs inline at snapshot creation rather than as a sweeper, which I chose deliberately to avoid yet another background job and its schedule, accepting that a delete failing mid-write leaves an orphan blob that the eventual consistency-check script will reap. The migration itself was the risky part and got the most caution: 41000 snapshots streamed oldest-first, each gzipped and uploaded, then verified by comparing the uploaded object size and a sampled content hash against the source before the Postgres row was deleted in the same loop iteration, with a resumable cursor checkpoint written to a small progress table every 500 rows so an interrupted migration resumes rather than restarts, because a 55-minute migration that cannot be paused is a hostage situation and I have been burned by exactly that before. Ran it at a deliberate throttle to avoid saturating the database or the object store and watched the database shrink from 9.4 GB to 1.1 GB with the nightly backup falling from 22 minutes to 3, which was the entire point. The verification caught 60 snapshots that failed gzip round-trip with truncated content, traced to the earliest days of the fetch pipeline before the size-cap abort flushed its buffer correctly, an ancient and already-fixed bug whose damaged artifacts were logged, skipped, and their clips flagged for a clean re-fetch rather than migrated as garbage. Also made the access paths lazy and cheap: the debug snapshot viewer serves bytes through a presigned URL with a 5 minute expiry so Node never proxies large blobs, and the internal parse route fetches snapshot bytes directly from the store, both changes keeping big binary payloads out of the application process entirely. Open threads: favicons still live on the local volume and arguably belong in the blob store for multi-instance futures, deferred until multi-instance is real; blob deletion on clip deletion is wired but there is no orphan sweep for blobs whose delete failed, wanting an eventual consistency check script; and self-host docs describing the MinIO setup do not exist yet, the code is ready but the words are not.

Metrics session for ferrite, the observability debt finally paid. Wired the prometheus crate into the worker binary, exposing a /metrics endpoint on a dedicated port 9090 separate from any job traffic, containing: job_duration_seconds as a histogram labeled by kind with buckets tuned for our bimodal reality, tight sub-second buckets for the parse callback and wide ones out to 30 seconds for fetch_clip against slow origins; jobs_completed_total and jobs_failed_total counters by kind; jobs_fenced_total counting completions rejected by lease token mismatch, the lease-thrash canary explicitly promised back in the lease design session, now real; queue_depth as a gauge labeled by state and kind, refreshed by a 10 second poller running one aggregate query, with the poll interval chosen after confirming the group-by on the partial index costs under 2 milliseconds even at depth; and heartbeat_extensions_total because a heartbeat rate that diverges from in-flight job count is an early sign of the runtime starvation issue noted in the lease docs. Grafana dashboard JSON checked into ops/dashboards/ferrite.json covering depth, throughput, duration percentiles by kind, failure rate, and a fencing panel that should read zero forever and now will be noticed if it does not. First day of real data immediately produced insight, which is the whole sales pitch of metrics: fetch_clip p95 sits at 8.4 seconds, dominated by a long tail of slow origins, while p50 is 900 milliseconds, confirming the per-request 15 second timeout is doing its job and the tail is origin slowness rather than our stack, no action needed but now it is known rather than felt. Also spotted queue_depth for the parse callback kind briefly spiking during an import test while fetch depth stayed flat, which is the priority tiers working exactly as designed and was oddly satisfying to watch on a graph. Deployment note: the metrics port is internal-only on Fly private networking, scraped by a tiny prometheus instance on the same network, nothing exposed publicly. Also chose the histogram buckets deliberately rather than accepting defaults, since fetch_clip and the parse callback have wildly different latency profiles and a single default bucket set would blur both into uselessness, so job_duration_seconds carries tight sub-second buckets that resolve the fast parse callback and wide buckets out to 30 seconds that capture the slow-origin tail of fetch_clip, and getting the buckets right is the difference between a histogram that tells you something and one that just says most things were fast. Recorded that the metrics endpoint deliberately lives on its own internal port scraped over the private network, never exposed publicly, because a metrics surface leaks operational detail and occasionally sensitive labels, and the least-privilege default is to keep it off the public internet entirely. Open threads: no alerting rules yet, the dashboard is a window not a pager, and dead-letter table size should join the gauges since jobs_dead growth is currently invisible until someone runs the CLI; also the CLI stats command idea from the tooling session would now trivially read from these same aggregates, noted as a cheap follow-up.

Short Quillbase fix session on right-to-left language support in the reader, prompted by an Arabic article rendering as a left-aligned mess.
