Root cause was simple: the article container hardcoded no direction and inherited ltr, so RTL text ran against the wrong margin with punctuation scattered to the wrong ends of lines. Fix was dir auto on the article container, letting the browser derive direction from the first strong directional character of the content, which handles whole-article RTL correctly and gracefully leaves mixed content to per-paragraph bidi resolution. The subtler breakage was in our own chrome around the text: blockquote styling used border-left and padding-left, which in RTL puts the quote bar on the wrong side, so all physical properties in the prose styles were swept to logical ones, border-inline-start, padding-inline-start, margin-inline-end and friends, about a dozen declarations across the prose css; the heading anchor icons and the scroll progress bar were audited and left as physical since they belong to the app frame, not the text flow. Also set unicode-bidi plaintext on code blocks inside RTL articles so embedded code stays visually LTR, which matters for technical Arabic and Hebrew writing quoting terminal output. Tested against saved Arabic and Hebrew articles plus a mixed Hebrew-with-English-code post, all reading correctly now; the lang detection column from the search work conveniently already identifies these clips, so a future refinement could set the dir attribute from stored lang instead of auto-detection, noted but not needed while dir auto behaves. One remaining wrinkle documented: the reading time badge and byline still render on the same side regardless of direction, mildly awkward next to an RTL title, cosmetic, queued behind actual RTL user feedback rather than guessed at.

CI and deploy pipeline session across all three repos, consolidating the ad hoc scripts into GitHub Actions and Fly deploys with actual gates. Quillbase workflow: pnpm install with a frozen lockfile, typecheck, lint, then vitest with a Postgres service container and a Redis service container so the integration tests that hit real databases run in CI exactly as locally, then a Next.js build, and only on main after all green does a deploy job run flyctl deploy. ferrite workflow: cargo fmt check, clippy with warnings denied which caught a pile of accumulated lint I had been ignoring, cargo test against a Postgres service container using the sqlx offline query metadata so compile-time query checking works without a live database at build time, generated by cargo sqlx prepare and committed as .sqlx, a step that itself needed documenting since a stale .sqlx directory fails the build confusingly with a query mismatch error that looks like a code bug. clearharbor workflow mirrors Quillbase's shape. The cross-cutting decision was database migrations in deploy: migrations run as a release_command in each fly.toml before the new version takes traffic, not baked into app boot, so a migration failure aborts the deploy cleanly rather than crash-looping new instances against a half-migrated schema; recorded the ordering rule that migrations must be backward compatible with the currently-running version since there is a window where old and new code share the database during a rolling deploy, which retroactively justified the expand-then-contract shape I had been informally following. Secrets flow from Fly secrets into the runtime and from GitHub Actions secrets into CI, never crossing, and the ferrite-Quillbase shared token plus the Stripe secrets are documented in a SECRETS.md listing every secret, where it lives, and its rotation procedure, without values. Caching tuned to keep CI under 4 minutes: pnpm store cache, cargo registry and target cache with a clippy-aware key, and the Rust build went from 6 minutes cold to about 90 seconds warm. One flaky test surfaced under CI parallelism that never failed locally: two integration tests sharing a hardcoded user email collided when vitest ran them concurrently against the same database, fixed by generating unique emails per test rather than serializing the suite, the right fix since serial tests are a slippery slope. Deploy safety net: each fly.toml has health checks and a rolling strategy with max-unavailable one, so a broken deploy pauses rather than replacing every instance with a sick one. The migration-as-release-command decision deserved the scrutiny it got, because the failure mode of migrations baked into app boot is a crash-loop of new instances hammering a half-migrated schema, so migrations run once as a release_command in each fly.toml before the new version takes traffic and a failed migration aborts the deploy cleanly with the old version still serving. That safety only holds if every migration is backward compatible with the currently-running code, since a rolling deploy has a window where old and new instances share one database, which retroactively justified the expand-then-contract discipline I had been following informally: add a nullable column and backfill in one release, start writing it in the next, make it non-null and drop the old path in a third, never renaming or dropping in a single step that the still-running old code depends on. Wrote that rule into a DEPLOY.md with a worked example so neither of us shortcuts it at midnight. The sqlx offline metadata story ate real time and earned its own documentation: ferrite's compile-time query checking needs a .sqlx directory of cached query metadata committed to the repo so CI can typecheck queries without a live database, generated by cargo sqlx prepare, and a stale .sqlx fails the build with a query-mismatch error that reads exactly like a code bug and sent me hunting in the wrong place for twenty minutes before I remembered to regenerate it, so DEPLOY.md now names that error and its real cause. Caching got tuned aggressively to keep CI under 4 minutes since a slow pipeline is a pipeline people skip: the pnpm store is cached across runs, the cargo registry and target directories are cached with a key that includes the clippy toolchain so a toolchain bump busts it cleanly, and the Rust build went from about 6 minutes cold to roughly 90 seconds warm. A flaky test surfaced only under CI parallelism and never locally, two integration tests sharing a hardcoded user email that collided when vitest ran them concurrently against the same database, and I fixed it the right way by generating a unique email per test rather than the tempting wrong way of serializing the suite, since serial tests are a slippery slope toward a suite that takes ten minutes and hides real concurrency bugs. Secrets flow was documented in a SECRETS.md listing every secret, where it lives, and how to rotate it, with no values, covering the ferrite-Quillbase shared token and the Stripe keys, because a two-person team with undocumented secrets is one sick day away from being locked out of its own production. Open threads: no staging environment, deploys go straight to production behind health checks which is honest for two people but will not scale to caring users; no smoke test post-deploy beyond the health check; and the ferrite worker is deployed as a separate Fly process group from its metrics scrape which is wired but undocumented for anyone else who might run this.

Dotfiles session, purely personal tooling maintenance, no product code. Finally migrated my shell config from a pile of sourced bash scripts accreted over years into a cleaner structure and switched the login shell to zsh to match the machine default and stop fighting it. The chezmoi setup now manages the dotfiles across my two machines with templated differences for the work laptop versus the desktop, mostly diverging on git email and a couple of machine-specific paths, so a fresh machine is one bootstrap command instead of an afternoon. Consolidated three overlapping git aliases and wrote a couple of new ones, the useful one being a graph log alias I keep retyping. Prompt moved to starship for the async git status which stops the prompt hanging in big repos, and pruned about forty dead aliases pointing at tools I no longer use, the kind of archaeology where you find an alias for a service that shut down years ago. Set up fzf key bindings for history and file search properly instead of the half-configured state they had been in, and the ctrl-r history search alone is worth the whole session. Also fixed a genuinely annoying bug where my PATH had the same three directories five times each because every shell nesting re-appended them, adding a dedup guard in the profile that keeps first occurrence order. Nothing here touches Quillbase or the other products, just sharpening the tools. Committed the whole thing to my private dotfiles repo with a real README this time so the next fresh-machine me is not spelunking.

Stripe customer portal and billing UI session on clearharbor plus Quillbase, wiring the parts that let a paying human manage their own subscription without emailing us. Portal first: POST /v1/billing/portal creates a Stripe billing portal session for the mapped customer and returns the URL, the settings page links to it, and the portal handles plan changes, payment method updates, and cancellation entirely on Stripe's side, which for a two-person team is exactly the right amount of billing UI to build, which is almost none. Cancellations and plan changes flow back through the same customer.subscription.updated webhook and entitlement machinery built earlier, so the portal needed no new state handling, it just generates events the pipeline already digests, a payoff from doing the webhook state machine properly the first time. The portal config, which products can be switched to and whether cancellation is immediate or end-of-period, is set once in the Stripe dashboard and referenced by a portal configuration id in env, end-of-period cancellation chosen so a canceling user keeps plus until their paid time expires, matching the grace philosophy. Then the actual gating, since plus had been a database row with no powers: Quillbase now reads entitlements. A getEntitlement helper in lib/billing.ts fetches the user's plan from clearharbor via an internal endpoint, cached in the same request-scoped way the session verify is, and the first real limit landed, free tier caps stored clips at 1000 with saves past the cap returning a 402 and a friendly upgrade prompt, plus tier unlimited. Chose a hard cap with a clear number over a soft nag both because it is honest and because it is trivial to reason about, and existing over-cap users at rollout are grandfathered by checking account age against the feature launch date rather than yanking access, which would be a hostile way to introduce a limit. The limit check reads a maintained clip count rather than counting rows on every save, a counter column on the user updated in the same transaction as clip insert and delete, since counting to 1000 on every save is silly and the counter is cheap; audited that imports and dedup-driven deletes keep the counter honest, and wrote a reconcile query for the nightly job to heal any drift. UI shows current usage against the cap in settings as a quiet progress bar, not a nag, appearing only past 80 percent. Open threads: annual versus monthly proration is entirely Stripe's problem now which is the point, but the UI does not surface which plan you are on very prominently; the grandfather check is a date comparison that will look arbitrary to future readers so it got a heavy comment; and there is no dunning email flow for failed payments, past_due currently degrades silently after grace, which needs at least one heads-up email before the free-tier drop, flagged as the next billing thread.

Highlights UI session on Quillbase, the browser-selection work deferred when the anchoring model was built. This was as fiddly as feared. Selection capture uses the Selection and Range APIs in a client island wrapping the article, and turning a live DOM Range into our stored anchor model, exact plus prefix and suffix context, meant walking text nodes to extract the selected string and its surrounding 64 characters across element boundaries, since a selection routinely spans a bold span or a link mid-sentence; wrote that extraction carefully against the range's common ancestor with a TreeWalker over text nodes, and it is the kind of code that is either right or haunted. On selection a small floating toolbar appears at the range's bounding rect offering the five highlight colors and a note affordance, positioned with careful attention to not overflow the viewport near the edges, and creating a highlight optimistically paints the range immediately then persists via the API from the annotations model session, rolling back the paint if the write fails, matching the optimistic pattern from tags. Rendering stored highlights on load is the inverse of capture: the pure re-anchor engine from lib/annotate/anchor.ts finds each highlight's position by searching for exact disambiguated by context, and then the client wraps the located range in a mark element with the highlight color, done after sanitization and outside React's control since we are decorating server-rendered prose, which meant reconciling with React by treating the highlight layer as a manually managed overlay and being disciplined about cleanup on navigation. Overlapping highlights forced a real decision: two highlights covering overlapping text cannot both wrap the same nodes cleanly, so overlaps render as layered background tints computed by splitting the union into segments by highlight membership, which looks correct for two overlaps and acceptably muddy for three, and nobody sensibly makes four, documented as a known ceiling. Orphaned highlights, the ones that fail to re-anchor after a re-parse, render in a panel below the article showing their text and note with a subtle explanation that the article changed, honoring the never-lose-a-note principle from the data model session, and each orphan offers a re-attach affordance that re-runs anchoring against the current text in case a later edit restored the context. Notes attached to highlights show as a margin marker that expands on click. Performance check: an article with 40 highlights re-anchors and paints in about 30 milliseconds, imperceptible, and the TreeWalker extraction on selection is instant. Found and fixed a nasty bug where highlighting text that contained a sanitizer-stripped element boundary produced an exact string with collapsed whitespace that then failed to re-anchor against the rendered text whose whitespace differed; normalized whitespace identically in both the capture and the search path, a single shared normalize function, and the re-anchor rate on real highlights jumped back to match the fuzz-test numbers. That whitespace bug deserves more detail because it was instructive about the whole render-time architecture: the sanitizer collapses runs of whitespace and drops certain inline elements, so the text the user visually selects in the reader is not byte-identical to the contentText the parser stored, and my first capture implementation extracted the exact string from the live DOM while the re-anchor search ran against a differently-normalized string, so highlights created and immediately painted would fail to re-anchor on the very next page load. The fix was to route both the capture path and the search path through a single shared normalizeForAnchor function that applies identical whitespace collapsing and the same treatment of zero-width and non-breaking spaces, so the string stored at capture is guaranteed to be findable at render, and I added a property test that takes a random article, selects a random span, normalizes through both paths, and asserts the captured exact is a substring of the normalized rendered text every time. Overlapping highlights forced a genuine rendering decision since two mark elements cannot cleanly wrap the same text nodes: the renderer computes the union of overlapping ranges, splits it into maximal segments by which set of highlights covers each segment, and paints each segment with a background tint blended from its covering highlights, which looks correct for two overlaps, acceptably muddy for three, and I documented four as a ceiling nobody sensibly reaches. The orphan panel got real care because the never-lose-a-note principle from the data-model session is load-bearing for trust: a highlight that fails to re-anchor after a re-parse is not discarded but listed below the article with its text and note intact and a re-attach affordance that re-runs anchoring against the current text, so a later edit that restores the surrounding context can rescue an orphan. Reconciling a manually-managed highlight overlay with React was its own subtlety, since we decorate server-rendered prose outside React's control, so the overlay is applied after hydration and torn down explicitly on navigation with a cleanup effect, and getting that teardown right mattered because a leaked overlay from a previous clip painting onto a new one was a real bug I hit and fixed. Measured the whole pipeline: an article with 40 highlights re-anchors and paints in about 30 milliseconds, imperceptible, and the TreeWalker-based extraction on selection is effectively instant, so the fiddly correctness work did not cost interactivity. Open threads: touch selection on mobile is untested and the toolbar positioning assumes a mouse, a whole mobile pass looms; highlights do not yet export with the article; keyboard-only highlight creation is unsupported, an accessibility gap flagged with intent to fix since selection-only interaction locks out keyboard users; and there is no highlights index across clips, a someday view of everything you ever marked, which several people have now asked for.

Data export session for Quillbase, building the take-your-data-and-leave feature that self-hosted software has a moral obligation to ship, and which conveniently cashes in nearly every prior decision in the corpus. GET /api/export streams a zip: a manifest.json describing format version and counts, a clips.jsonl with one line per clip carrying url, canonicalUrl, title, siteName, savedAt, tags as a name array, saveCount, folderPath provenance, and highlights inline as an array of exact plus prefix plus suffix plus color plus note, and an html directory with one readable standalone file per clip containing the sanitized contentHtml wrapped in a minimal self-contained template with inlined typography so an exported article opens and reads in any browser with no Quillbase around it. The format decisions were deliberate: JSONL for the machine-readable spine because it streams and greps and a truncated export still yields valid lines up to the cut, standalone HTML for the human-readable body because the entire point of a read-later archive is the reading and an export that loses readability is a betrayal. Streaming was the engineering core, since a large archive cannot be assembled in memory: the route is a ReadableStream piping through a zip encoder, pulling clips in keyset-paginated batches using the exact cursor machinery from the performance session, fetching each clip's snapshot-derived contentHtml, sanitizing it through the same render-time lib/render/sanitize.ts so the export inherits the current safe policy rather than any stored state, and writing entries as it goes, so peak memory stays flat regardless of archive size, verified at about 90 MB steady while exporting my 7000-clip archive into a 340 MB zip over roughly 3 minutes. Highlights export inline rather than as a sidecar because a highlight without its article is meaningless, and the exact-plus-context anchor model from the annotations work turns out to be a perfect portable format, self-describing and re-anchorable by any future importer including our own, a nice unplanned dividend of choosing quote anchoring over offsets. Images in exported HTML remain remote URLs with a documented caveat that a fully offline archive would need the deferred image proxy to localize them, an honest limitation rather than a silent one, and the manifest records which optional pieces are present so a re-import can reason about completeness. The export runs as a synchronous stream for now rather than a ferrite job, judged acceptable because it is read-only, self-throttling through backpressure, and rate-limited to one concurrent export per user through a Redis lock so nobody accidentally launches five; recorded that a truly enormous archive might eventually want the job-plus-download-link shape the bookmarks import uses in reverse, but the streaming route serves every real archive size today. Tested a full round trip by exporting, then writing a throwaway import that reads the manifest and clips.jsonl back, confirming tags, highlights, savedAt history, and readable HTML all survive, which doubles as validation that the format is genuinely portable and not just a dump only we can read. Spent real thought on why streaming was non-negotiable rather than the simpler assemble-then-send approach: a user with a large archive could easily produce a multi-hundred-megabyte zip, and buffering that in memory to compute a Content-Length before sending would blow the process memory budget and reintroduce exactly the out-of-memory failure that pushed the bookmarks importer off the request path. So the route returns a ReadableStream piping through a zip encoder that emits entries incrementally, the clips are pulled in keyset-paginated batches using the same cursor machinery from the performance session, and peak memory stays flat regardless of archive size, verified at about 90 MB steady while producing a 340 MB zip from my 7000-clip archive over roughly 3 minutes. Backpressure falls out naturally, since a slow client consuming the download slows the stream and therefore the pace of database reads, so the export is self-throttling and cannot stampede the database no matter how large; the only added guard is a Redis lock giving one concurrent export per user so nobody accidentally launches five parallel full exports and defeats the throttle. The format decisions each had a reason worth recording: JSONL for the machine-readable spine because it streams line by line and a truncated export still yields valid parseable lines up to the cut, which a single giant JSON document does not, and standalone self-contained HTML for the human-readable body because the entire point of a read-later archive is the reading, and an export that loses readability the moment Quillbase is gone would betray the whole self-hosted promise. Sanitizing exported HTML through the same render-time sanitize.ts rather than dumping stored contentHtml means the export inherits the current safe policy rather than any historical stored state, consistent with every other consumer of that module, and it means an exported article is exactly as safe to open in a browser as one viewed in the app. Highlights export inline as exact-plus-prefix-plus-suffix anchors rather than as offsets or a sidecar file, which turned out to be a quiet dividend of choosing quote anchoring months ago, because the anchor model is self-describing and portable and re-anchorable by any future importer including our own throwaway prototype, whereas character offsets into now-absent markup would export as meaningless numbers. Validated the whole thing by writing a small import that reads the manifest and clips.jsonl back and confirmed tags, highlights, savedAt history, and readable HTML all survive the round trip, which doubles as proof the format is genuinely portable and not a dump only we can read. Open threads: no scheduled or incremental export, every export is a full snapshot; the standalone HTML template does not embed a stylesheet toggle for dark mode, exports are light-only, cosmetic; and an official documented import-from-Quillbase-export path does not exist yet though the throwaway prototype proves it is a short session away, which matters because portability you cannot reverse is only half a promise.

Keyboard shortcuts and command palette session for Quillbase, the polish pass that makes a reading app feel like a tool for people who read a lot. Built a command palette on the ubiquitous cmd-k, a client island rendering a filtered command list with fuzzy matching over a registered command set, each command carrying a title, an optional keybinding hint, and a run function; registration is centralized in lib/commands.ts so the palette and the global key handler read one source of truth rather than drifting, which they always do when shortcut definitions get scattered. Global shortcuts landed with care around focus: j and k move selection through the clip list, enter opens the selected clip, s stars it, e archives it, slash focuses search, g then a jumps to archive and g then s to starred in a two-key sequence, and everything is suppressed while focus is in an input or the reader is capturing a text selection for a highlight, because a shortcut that fires while you are typing a note is a bug that makes people distrust the whole feature. In the reader, j and k scroll by paragraph rather than by line, which sounds fussy but reading by paragraph is how the eye actually moves and it felt right immediately. The accessibility thread from the highlights session got partially paid here: highlight creation is now reachable by keyboard, extend a selection with shift-arrow as browsers already allow and then a shortcut opens the same highlight toolbar, closing the keyboard-only gap that had locked out non-mouse users, though full screen-reader annotation of existing highlights remains open and honestly needs someone who lives in a screen reader to test rather than my guessing. A discoverability decision: a small keyboard hint appears in the corner on first visit and a full shortcuts cheat sheet opens on question-mark, generated from the same command registry so documentation cannot fall out of sync with behavior, which is the kind of single-source discipline that pays for itself the third time you add a command. Persisted the one genuine preference, whether cmd-k or a leader key drives the palette, to localStorage behind the usual try-catch. Tested the sequence-key handling carefully since g-then-a style chords are a notorious source of stuck-state bugs where a timeout never clears; the implementation uses a short 800 millisecond window after a prefix key with an explicit reset on any non-matching key, and a test drives prefix-then-wrong-key and prefix-then-timeout to prove the state machine always returns to idle. Open threads: the shortcuts are not yet remappable which power users will eventually want and the registry is already shaped to allow it, mobile obviously has no keyboard story so this is desktop polish, and the fuzzy matcher in the palette is a simple subsequence scorer that could grow smarter but is completely fine for a command set this size. That closes out the interaction-polish arc, and with export shipped last session the product finally feels like something a person could adopt and trust rather than a demo.

Session centered on designing and implementing the retry and backoff ladder for ferrite-core, the piece that decides what happens after a job handler returns an error, and it ended with a working ladder merged behind a feature flag. The starting point was the embarrassing status quo: every failure in src/worker.rs was retried immediately and forever, which last week turned a single misbehaving Quillbase fetch job into roughly 40k retries per hour hammering the same dead origin server. The first decision was to split errors into two classes at the type level rather than by string matching, so the JobError enum in ferrite-core now has Retryable and Terminal variants, and handlers must choose one explicitly when they construct the error; the reasoning was that implicit classification based on error text is exactly how the earlier prototype ended up retrying 404s for six hours. The second decision was the shape of the ladder itself: exponential with base 2 starting at 5 seconds, so 5s, 10s, 20s, 40s, and so on, capped at 15 minutes, with a default max_attempts of 10 after which the job moves to the failed state with the final error message preserved in a last_error text column on the jobs table. The cap value got debated for a while; 15 minutes was chosen over 1 hour because Quillbase fetch jobs are user-visible (someone saved a link and is waiting for the clip to render) and a link that fails for 15 minutes straight is probably down for the day anyway, whereas index jobs that genuinely need long patience can override the ladder per job type via the new RetryPolicy struct, which is stored serialized in a policy jsonb column so a job carries its own policy rather than looking it up at retry time. That storage choice matters for upgrades: if the default policy changes in a deploy, in-flight jobs keep the policy they were enqueued with, which makes behavior predictable during rollouts. Implementation-wise the ladder lives in a new retry_at computation in src/queue.rs, and the dequeue query gained a retry_at <= now() predicate; a partial index on (retry_at) WHERE state = 'retryable' keeps that query from scanning completed rows, and EXPLAIN on a synthetic table with 500k jobs showed the dequeue staying under 1.2ms with the index versus 210ms without it. Jitter was added as a plus or minus 20 percent multiplier on the computed delay because the earlier immediate-retry behavior demonstrated how well correlated failures synchronize themselves; the jitter uses the rand crate seeded per worker. One subtle bug found during testing: attempt count was being incremented in the worker after handler completion but the retry_at computation ran in the queue layer using the stale count read at dequeue, so the first retry used attempt 0 delay twice; fixed by making the queue layer own the increment inside the same UPDATE that transitions the state, so the count and the delay can never disagree. Tests cover the ladder math with a table-driven test asserting the exact delay sequence for attempts 1 through 12, and a Postgres integration test in ferrite-core/tests that enqueues a job whose handler fails three times then succeeds, asserting the observed retry timestamps are monotonically spread. Two things deliberately punted: dead-lettering beyond the simple failed state (there is a sketch of a dead letter queue in the notes but no table yet), and per-error-code retry hints like honoring HTTP Retry-After headers, which would be genuinely useful for the Quillbase fetcher but requires plumbing header data through JobError and can wait. Open threads for next session: wire the Quillbase fetch handler in lib/ingest to actually classify its errors instead of marking everything Retryable, decide whether max_attempts exhaustion should notify anything (right now it is silent, which feels wrong for user-visible fetches), and remove the feature flag once the ladder has a week of prod time. Also noted for later: the backoff cap plus jitter means worst-case a job can wait 18 minutes between attempts, and the ferrite-cli status output still shows raw retry_at timestamps in UTC which is unreadable during debugging; a small quality-of-life fix for the cli crate to render relative times would pay for itself.

Short but consequential debugging session on the ferrite backoff ladder that shipped two sessions ago: staging showed synchronized waves of retries every few minutes despite the jitter that was supposed to prevent exactly this, with the queue depth graph looking like a comb, spikes of 300 to 400 dequeues at a time separated by dead air. The investigation started from the assumption that jitter was broken and that assumption turned out correct in an annoying way: in src/queue.rs the delay computation applied jitter first and the 15 minute cap second, so once a batch of jobs climbed the exponential ladder past the cap, every one of them got its jittered value clamped to exactly 900 seconds, erasing the randomness at precisely the point where correlated failures pile up. The fix was to reorder the operations, clamp the exponential value to the cap first, then apply the plus or minus 20 percent jitter to the clamped value, so capped jobs now land anywhere between 720 and 1080 seconds. A regression test asserts that a thousand simulated jobs at attempt 12 produce at least 900 distinct retry_at values. While in the file, also fixed a secondary issue the graphs surfaced: the dequeue query ordered purely by retry_at, so the retry wave always ran ahead of freshly enqueued jobs with a retry_at of now; changed the ordering to (priority, retry_at) with fresh jobs and retries getting equal treatment, which is a placeholder until real priority lanes exist, a thread that keeps coming up and keeps getting deferred. Deployed the fix to staging and watched for 40 minutes; the comb pattern flattened into noise, p95 dequeue latency held at 1.4ms, and no handler regressions appeared. One open question written down for the queue backend discussion: the wave analysis was only possible because Postgres made it trivial to run ad hoc aggregate queries against the jobs table, worth remembering when the SQLite-for-self-hosters argument comes back around. Next step is letting the ladder run against real Quillbase fetch traffic in prod and checking whether the 20 percent jitter width is enough at fleet scale or whether it needs to widen to 30.

Quillbase session, the first one consuming ferrite for real: moved clip fetching out of the Next.js request path and into background jobs, which has been the plan since ferrite got a stable enqueue API. Previously app/api/clips/route.ts fetched the saved URL inline, ran the parser, and wrote the clip in one request, which meant slow origins held the POST open for up to 30 seconds and Fly would sometimes kill the request mid-parse, leaving half-written clips with a null content_html that the reader page renders as an empty grey card. The new flow has the route validate the URL, insert a clips row in state pending, enqueue a fetch_clip job in ferrite with the clip id as payload, and return 202 with the clip id immediately, measured at 45 to 60ms end to end versus the old 2 to 30 seconds. The ferrite handler lives in a new worker crate that calls back into the same Postgres database, and the first design argument of the session was whether the worker should talk to the database directly or go through an internal Quillbase HTTP API; direct database access won because both processes already share the schema via Drizzle migrations and an internal API would just be a second serialization layer to keep in sync, though the losing side was noted since it becomes right again if the worker ever runs on separate infrastructure without database reach. Error classification got wired properly against the new JobError enum: DNS failures, timeouts, and 5xx map to Retryable so the backoff ladder from the earlier ferrite work applies, while 404, 410, and SSL certificate validation failures map to Terminal and transition the clip to state failed with a user-visible reason string. The pending state needed frontend work too, the clips list now shows a subtle pulse animation on pending cards and polls a lightweight status endpoint every 3 seconds with capped exponential backoff on the polling itself, chosen over websockets because the payoff did not justify the infrastructure for a two-person product. Migration path for existing data: a one-off script re-enqueued the 217 clips that were stuck with null content_html from the old inline path, and 195 of them recovered on the first pass, the rest hit Terminal errors which is honestly the correct outcome for links that are actually dead. Open threads: the status polling endpoint does a full clip select when it only needs the state column, trivial to tighten with a narrower Drizzle select; the fetch handler does not yet honor robots.txt which needs a decision rather than an accident; and there is no per-domain rate limiting, so saving twenty links from the same site enqueues twenty simultaneous fetches against one origin, which is impolite and will eventually get the fetcher IP blocked by someone.

Long ferrite session on crash recovery, the scenario where a worker dies holding leased jobs and those jobs need to come back without human intervention. The starting behavior was genuinely bad: a leased job whose worker vanished stayed in state running forever, and the only remedy was a manual UPDATE in psql, which happened twice last week after Fly rescheduled the worker VM. The design that landed has three cooperating parts. First, leases got real expiry: the leases table in src/lease.rs now stores lease_expires_at, set at claim time to now() plus a per-job-type TTL defaulting to 60 seconds, and workers renew their leases every 20 seconds via a heartbeat that extends the expiry; the 3x ratio between TTL and heartbeat interval was chosen so a worker can miss two consecutive heartbeats to transient network trouble without losing its lease, since the failure mode of losing a lease on a live worker is worse than a dead worker taking an extra 40 seconds to be discovered. Second, a reclaim sweep: every worker, not a dedicated janitor, runs a sweep every 30 seconds that finds jobs whose lease_expires_at is in the past and transitions them back to state ready with attempt count incremented, the reasoning for incrementing being that a crash mid-job might be caused by the job itself (a parser segfault on pathological input, say) and a poison job that crashes workers should climb the backoff ladder toward failed rather than crash-looping the fleet at full speed; this exact scenario happened with the earlier prototype when a 90MB HTML page OOMed the worker repeatedly. Making every worker run the sweep instead of electing a janitor avoids a leader election problem entirely, and the sweep UPDATE is written to be idempotent so concurrent sweeps from multiple workers are harmless, they just race to move the same rows and the losers update zero rows. Third, startup reconciliation: a worker that restarts after a crash may find leases in the table still bearing its own worker_id from the previous life, so workers now generate a fresh UUID identity per process and treat any lease held by a worker_id not currently heartbeating as expired-equivalent during the sweep, rather than trying to resume their old leases, because resuming requires proving the old process is really dead and a fresh identity sidesteps the whole question. Testing was the bulk of the session: an integration test spins up a worker via the test harness, lets it claim a job whose handler sleeps forever, kills the worker process with SIGKILL, starts a second worker, and asserts the job is reclaimed and completed within the TTL plus sweep interval budget, which passes reliably at around 95 seconds worst case. A property worth writing down: this design gives at-least-once execution, not exactly-once, since a worker that stalls longer than its TTL (a long GC pause equivalent, a network partition) will have its job reclaimed and run twice. The handlers are supposed to be idempotent already, the Quillbase fetch handler is, since it writes clip content keyed by clip id, but nothing enforces idempotency and the duplicate-execution window makes me nervous enough that fencing tokens went on the roadmap: a monotonically increasing token per lease that storage-side writes could check, so a zombie worker holding a stale token gets rejected at write time. Also deferred: the sweep currently scans with a full predicate on lease_expires_at < now() and there is no index on that column yet, fine at current volume of a few thousand rows, needs the partial index treatment before the index rebuild workloads arrive. Metrics got a stub, reclaimed_jobs_total counter increments but nothing scrapes it yet. Next session should wire the fencing token schema before the memory of this design fades, and decide whether reclaim on increment should skip the backoff delay for the first reclaim since a Fly reschedule is not the job's fault and delaying a user-visible fetch by 5 seconds for infrastructure reasons is a worse default than retrying immediately once.

Marathon design session on the ferrite queue backend question, the SQLite versus Postgres debate that has been simmering since the crate split, written up at length because the arguments deserve preserving even though no final call was made until the follow-up session. The context: ferrite currently assumes Postgres, the jobs and leases tables live in the same Postgres 16 instance as Quillbase, and everything works, but the stated ambition for ferrite as an open source crate is to be the job runner a solo developer reaches for, and solo developers self-hosting a read-later app on a single VPS may not want to run Postgres at all. The SQLite case, argued as strongly as possible: zero operational surface, the queue is a file, backups are a file copy, the ferrite-cli could ship a demo mode that works with no infrastructure, and for a single-node deployment SQLite write throughput is comfortably beyond what a personal Quillbase generates, benchmarked during the session at roughly 8k single-row inserts per second with WAL mode on the dev laptop against maybe 200 jobs on a busy day for a heavy user. Latency is also better, claim-and-lease as one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction measured around 90 microseconds versus 1.2ms over the wire to local Postgres. The Postgres case: ferrite already depends on it, every operational lesson learned so far, the partial indexes from the backoff work, the reclaim sweep semantics, the ad hoc debugging queries that saved the jitter investigation, all of it is Postgres-shaped; SKIP LOCKED has no true SQLite equivalent so multi-worker claim contention would need a different design, effectively a single-writer model with worker dispatch in process, which is a different architecture, not a port; and the multi-node story dies instantly with SQLite since two Fly machines cannot share the file, meaning SQLite mode caps ferrite at single-node forever, or until someone writes a litestream-flavored escape hatch which is exactly the operational surface the SQLite case claimed to remove. The middle path examined in detail: a QueueBackend trait in ferrite-core abstracting enqueue, claim, heartbeat, complete, reclaim, with postgres and sqlite implementations. Sketched the trait during the session and immediately hit the leaky parts, the claim operation wants to express claim-N-jobs-atomically-with-lease and the natural Postgres implementation is one CTE with SKIP LOCKED while the natural SQLite implementation is a serialized transaction with retry-on-busy, and the trait can hide the syntax but not the semantics: under Postgres claims are concurrent, under SQLite they serialize, which changes worker tuning defaults, changes what the metrics mean, and doubles the integration test matrix for every queue feature from here forward, the fencing tokens, the priority lanes when they land, the sweep behavior, all of it tested twice or silently broken on the backend that CI exercises less. Also examined what other ecosystems did, the general pattern being that job runners that promised backend plurality early spent years dragging the lowest common denominator behind them, and the ones that picked one store and leaned into its semantics got depth instead of breadth. The genuinely new argument this session versus previous rounds of this debate: the reclaim and fencing designs from the crash recovery work depend on multi-worker visibility of lease state through the shared store, and the SQLite single-writer model would get crash recovery essentially for free through process supervision instead, which means the two backends do not even want the same recovery design, strengthening the two-architectures-not-one-abstraction read. Current lean at end of session, stated explicitly for the record: Postgres as the only supported backend for the foreseeable future, SQLite revisited only if ferrite ever grows a genuine embedded use case, and the QueueBackend trait shelved as premature abstraction, though the trait sketch is preserved in a design note in the repo because the exercise of writing it is what surfaced the semantic leaks. Not merged as a decision yet, sleeping on it, follow-up session to make the call and write it down properly. Side observations captured while benchmarking: the Postgres claim CTE spends a third of its time on the jsonb policy column deserialization which nobody has needed to read at claim time since the policy moved into the retry_at computation, worth a look; and BEGIN IMMEDIATE contention behavior under SQLite means the busy_timeout pragma matters enormously, 5 seconds default hid real serialization stalls in the benchmark until it was set to 50ms to make the contention visible, a good reminder that default timeouts are a way of lying to yourself about latency.

Short decision session closing out the queue backend debate from yesterday: Postgres is the sole supported ferrite backend, decided and written into DECISIONS.md in the repo root alongside the reasoning, with the QueueBackend trait sketch explicitly rejected as premature abstraction and archived in docs/design-notes/sqlite-backend.md for whenever the question resurfaces. The tipping argument on reflection was the test matrix, every future queue feature costing double integration coverage or rotting on the less-exercised backend, which is a permanent tax to serve a hypothetical user, while the actual known user base is two people and one Postgres instance. Consequences applied immediately: removed the two dyn-dispatch seams that had crept into src/queue.rs in anticipation of the trait, inlined the claim path back to direct sqlx calls which shaved the claim benchmark from 1.2ms to 1.05ms by dropping a boxed future, and deleted a speculative feature flag in ferrite-core Cargo.toml that gated nothing. Also acted on yesterday's side observation, the claim CTE no longer selects the policy jsonb column since nothing reads it at claim time, which cut claim latency to 0.85ms on the synthetic 500k-row table. Documented the single-node SQLite story honestly in the README instead of promising it: ferrite requires Postgres, and a solo deployment can run Postgres in the same Fly app with a volume, which is what Quillbase production does anyway. Open thread noted for the ferrite-cli crate: the demo-mode idea that motivated half the SQLite argument could be served by a dockerized Postgres one-liner in the quickstart instead, worth trying before anyone reopens the debate.

Quillbase session on index rebuilds, making the search index rebuildable from scratch through ferrite instead of the current situation where lib/search/rank.ts assumes the index rows were populated once by a migration and drift is forever. The trigger was noticing that clips saved during the two-day window when the parser was mangling whitespace have subtly broken tsvector rows, lowercase runs fused together, and the only remedy was hand-running SQL. Built an index_clip job type in the worker crate that recomputes the search document for one clip, title weighted A, excerpt B, body C in the tsvector, matching what rank.ts expects at query time, and an admin endpoint plus ferrite-cli invocation that enqueues index_clip for every clip id in a given range, batched into enqueue calls of 500 ids at a time to avoid one giant insert. The interesting decision was rebuild granularity: one job per clip rather than one job per batch of clips, chosen because per-clip jobs make progress visible in the jobs table, make failures isolated and retryable by the existing backoff ladder without wrecking a whole batch, and let the reclaim sweep from the crash recovery work handle a mid-rebuild worker death for free, all at the cost of enqueue volume, and 30k clips at per-clip granularity is 30k rows in the jobs table which the completed-jobs cleanup will digest. Ran the first full rebuild against the production dataset in the evening: 31,204 jobs enqueued, completed in 19 minutes with 4 workers, 12 failures all with the same error, tsvector document exceeds maximum size, which turned out to be three enormous clips (one was a saved single-page documentation dump) whose body text blows past the 1MB tsvector limit; handled by truncating body text to 400KB before vectorization with a truncated flag stored on the search row so the UI can eventually disclose it, and re-enqueued the 12, all green. Wrote down but did not act on: the rebuild saturated the queue for 19 minutes and any user-facing fetch_clip job enqueued during that window waited behind index jobs, which is the first concrete argument for priority lanes in ferrite rather than the abstract one from the backoff session; also the search row schema has no version column so there is no way to know which analyzer version produced a row, adding index_version now costs one migration and will make every future rebuild a targeted where-clause instead of a full sweep, next session candidate.

Ferrite session dedicated to worker fencing, the follow-through on the nervousness recorded at the end of the crash recovery work about at-least-once execution and zombie workers. The scenario being defended against: worker A claims a job, stalls past its lease TTL (long parser hang, network partition, Fly host trouble), the reclaim sweep hands the job to worker B, then A wakes up and finishes, and now two workers both believe they own the completion, with A potentially writing stale results over B's fresher ones or double-firing side effects. The design that landed is classic fencing tokens adapted to the Postgres queue: the leases table gains a fence bigint column backed by a per-job monotonic counter, incremented every time a lease is granted on that job, and the claim query returns the fence value to the worker, which must present it on every subsequent state-changing call, heartbeat, completion, failure, retry scheduling. All four of those paths in src/lease.rs and src/queue.rs now carry a WHERE fence = $presented predicate, so a zombie worker holding fence 3 after the job was reclaimed at fence 4 simply updates zero rows, and the worker code treats a zero-row update as LeaseLost, a new error variant that aborts the handler task via a cancellation token rather than letting it run to completion for nothing. Getting the abort right was most of the session: the handler future is now raced against a lease_lost watch channel, and handlers doing non-transactional side effects (the Quillbase fetcher writing files, eventually) are documented as needing to check the token at their own commit points, since Rust cannot preempt arbitrary code and cancellation only lands at await points. Deciding what heartbeat does on LeaseLost was the subtle part; the first instinct was to have the worker retry the heartbeat, which is exactly wrong, a lost lease is unrecoverable by design and any retry path would just be a mechanism for zombies to fight the living, so heartbeat failure due to fencing immediately cancels the local job task and increments a lease_lost_total counter. Wrote a targeted integration test that manufactures the zombie scenario deterministically: claim a job, directly UPDATE the lease in the test to simulate a reclaim bumping the fence, then drive the original worker's completion path and assert it gets LeaseLost, the job row is untouched by the zombie, and the counter incremented. Also proved the ordering property matters with a second test where the zombie completion races the legitimate worker's claim inside two concurrent transactions, which shook out a real bug: the completion path read the fence in one statement and updated in a second, a classic check-then-act window, rewritten as a single conditional UPDATE returning the row so the check and the act are atomic. Downstream consequences noted: the Quillbase worker handlers all write to Postgres keyed by clip id so their writes are naturally last-write-wins and the fencing mostly protects against wasted work and metric pollution there, but the planned side-effecting job types, webhook-style notifications and file exports, get real correctness from this, and the fencing token should be passed into handler context so side-effect targets can do their own fence checks eventually, that plumbing exists now as a fence field on JobContext. Not done: fencing for the enqueue-dedupe path, which does not need it, and any storage-side fence enforcement for external systems, which is documented as the handler author's problem with the JobContext fence as the tool. Perf check after all the WHERE clause additions: claim, heartbeat, and complete all within noise of their previous numbers on the 500k-row synthetic table, the fence predicate rides the existing primary key lookups. Next session pull: the reclaim sweep currently increments attempt count on reclaim, and with fencing in place a reclaim caused by pure infrastructure delay arguably should not consume an attempt, revisit the increment-on-reclaim decision from the crash recovery session with the new machinery in mind.

Clearharbor session on webhook resilience, provoked by Monday's incident where Stripe sent invoice.payment_failed during a clearharbor deploy, the handler 500ed on a connection pool that was mid-drain, and the customer's entitlement stayed active for three days until a manual reconciliation caught it. The immediate fix was making src/webhooks.ts do almost nothing in the request handler: verify the Stripe signature, insert the raw event into a new webhook_events table with a unique constraint on the Stripe event id, and return 200, with all actual processing moved to an async drainer that reads unprocessed rows, applies them, and marks them done. Stripe retries delivery on non-200 for up to three days, which is a real safety net, but the incident showed the failure mode where the handler is what breaks, so the new posture is accept-everything-verify-first, and let processing fail internally where it can be retried without Stripe's involvement. The drainer runs on a 10 second interval, processes events in Stripe timestamp order per customer rather than global order (global ordering is a lie anyway given Stripe's delivery semantics), and retries failures with a simple doubling backoff persisted in a next_attempt_at column, capped at 10 minutes, deliberately echoing the ferrite ladder design because the reasoning transfers even though pulling ferrite itself into a Node service was rejected as cross-runtime overkill. The unique constraint on event id gives idempotent ingestion, so Stripe redelivering an event the handler already stored is a clean no-op insert conflict, and processing idempotency is handled by making each event application an upsert against the subscriptions and entitlements tables keyed by customer id rather than an increment or state machine step; the one genuinely order-sensitive pair, subscription.updated versus subscription.deleted arriving swapped, is resolved by trusting the Stripe object's own status field over the event type name. Backfilled the missing three days by replaying events from the Stripe dashboard export through the new path, which itself validated the idempotency since half of them had been partially applied already. Left open: the drainer is in-process with the web server so a crashed deploy still pauses processing until the next instance boots, acceptable at current scale but noted; and there is no alerting when an event exceeds five processing attempts, which needs at least an email before this bites again.

Quick ferrite metrics session, first pass at observability beyond tailing logs: added the metrics crate facade to ferrite-core with counters for jobs_enqueued_total, jobs_completed_total, jobs_failed_total, jobs_retried_total, and reclaimed_jobs_total (finally hooking up the stub left by the crash recovery work), plus lease_lost_total from the fencing session, all labeled by job_type and nothing else, a deliberate cardinality decision after reading one too many postmortems about per-id labels. Gauges for queue_depth and running_jobs are computed by a 15 second poller running one aggregate query against the jobs table rather than trying to maintain counters incrementally, because the table is the truth and incremental gauges drift the moment any process restarts. Exposition is a tiny hyper endpoint on port 9100 in the worker binary serving Prometheus text format via metrics-exporter-prometheus, gated behind a metrics feature flag so library users of ferrite-core do not inherit an HTTP server. Verified scrape output locally with curl and wired a Fly internal service so a future Prometheus can reach it, but actual collection infrastructure is explicitly deferred, the immediate payoff is that ferrite-cli gained a stats subcommand that hits the same aggregate query and prints a one-screen summary, queue depth by state and type, oldest ready job age, retry ladder distribution, which already replaced the three psql aliases used during every debugging session this month. Histograms for job duration and queue wait time are sketched but not merged, pending a decision on bucket boundaries, since fetch jobs and index jobs have wildly different duration profiles and one shared bucket set serves neither, next session problem.

Personal side project session, nothing to do with the products: built a wedding RSVP site for college friends getting married in May. One evening, one page, deliberately boring stack after a week of queue semantics: plain Next.js app with a single form, name lookup against a guest list CSV exported from their spreadsheet, meal choice radio buttons, plus-one logic driven by a column in the CSV, and submissions written to a Google Sheet through a service account so the couple can watch responses arrive in the tool they already use. Resisted the urge to add an admin dashboard, authentication, or a database; the guest list is 140 names and the couple can edit the sheet directly. The only mildly interesting engineering was fuzzy name matching for the lookup, guests type their name to find their invitation and nobody types their name the way it appears on the list, so it does case-insensitive comparison after stripping accents and punctuation, then falls back to a trigram similarity threshold, tested against the real list with deliberately mangled inputs until common misspellings of the trickier names resolved. Also added a hidden honeypot field and a 2-request-per-minute rate limit on the submit endpoint, less against attackers than against a bored cousin submitting forty RSVPs. Deployed to Fly on the smallest machine with the couple's custom domain, total hosting cost effectively zero, handed over the sheet link and called it done. They asked for a photo carousel; said yes because it is their wedding, that goes in next weekend.

Unsettling ferrite session that started as routine metrics review and ended with a confirmed duplicate execution bug in production. While checking the new stats output after Tuesday's deploy, jobs_completed_total for fetch_clip was 14,982 against 14,876 enqueued over the same window, a hundred-odd surplus completions that should be impossible, and cross-checking the Quillbase side found 41 clips whose fetched_at timestamp was overwritten twice within the same minute by different worker ids recorded in the audit column. So two workers ran the same job to completion, despite the lease machinery, despite fencing having shipped, which specifically exists to make this scenario end in LeaseLost for one of the pair. Spent the bulk of the session narrowing when it happens rather than why: correlated the 41 duplicate pairs against deploy timestamps and worker lifecycle logs, and every single pair straddles a window where the reclaim sweep ran on one worker while another worker was mid-claim, all during the Tuesday deploy when the fleet briefly ran 6 workers instead of 4 and lease timing was chaotic. Pulled the exact log lines for one pair: worker w-7f21 claims job 88412 at 14:02:11 with fence 1, heartbeats normally at 14:02:31, and completes successfully at 14:02:44; worker w-a940 claims the same job at 14:02:39 with fence 2 and also completes successfully at 14:02:58, no LeaseLost anywhere, both completion UPDATEs matched rows. That should be flatly impossible under the fencing predicates, w-7f21 held fence 1 and the reclaim that granted w-a940 fence 2 should have made the first completion update zero rows, unless the completion of w-7f21 read or matched against lease state from before the reclaim committed, which smells like a transaction visibility or predicate ordering problem in how complete joins jobs to leases in src/queue.rs. The heartbeat at 14:02:31 is also suspicious, it succeeded 8 seconds before the reclaim, meaning the lease was live and the reclaim should not have fired at all, so the sweep's expiry predicate may be reading a stale expires_at or the heartbeat's extension write landed after the sweep's read in a way the row locking was supposed to prevent. No fix attempted yet, deliberately, because guessing at concurrency fixes is how bugs get buried instead of killed; instead the session ended by adding forensic logging to the sweep (log every reclaimed job id with the observed expires_at and fence at reclaim time) and to the completion path (log matched-row count and fence presented), deployed behind a debug flag, plus a hand-written incident timeline in docs/incidents/duplicate-execution.md. The 41 affected clips were re-verified and all content converged correctly thanks to idempotent writes, so no user damage, which is the fencing session's real payoff even though fencing itself apparently has a hole. Next session: build a deterministic reproduction before touching any production code, likely a stress harness with aggressively short TTLs and a synthetic slow handler, because this class of bug only dies when it can be summoned on demand.

Session spent chasing a production anomaly in ferrite: the completion counters and enqueue counters disagree in the wrong direction, roughly a hundred more fetch_clip completions than enqueues since Tuesday, and the audit trail on the Quillbase side shows 41 clips finalized twice within a minute by two different workers. Duplicate execution straight through the fencing that shipped precisely to prevent it, and with no LeaseLost errors emitted at all, both workers in each pair believed they completed legitimately, both their completion updates matched a row. Worked one pair end to end from logs as the anchor case: job 88412 claimed by worker w-7f21 with fence 1 at 14:02:11, a successful heartbeat at 14:02:31 extending the lease, then the reclaim sweep on another worker seizes the job at around 14:02:39 handing fence 2 to w-a940, and both workers complete cleanly at 14:02:44 and 14:02:58 respectively. Two impossible things in one timeline: the sweep reclaimed a lease that had been extended 8 seconds earlier and should have been nowhere near expiry, and the fence 1 completion succeeded after fence 2 was issued, so either the sweep read a pre-heartbeat expires_at or the completion matched pre-reclaim lease state, both pointing at transaction visibility between the sweep, the heartbeat, and the completion path in src/queue.rs and src/lease.rs rather than at the fence arithmetic itself. Established the shape of the trigger from the other 40 pairs before going deeper: every one lands inside the Tuesday deploy window when 6 workers were briefly live and the sweep cadence overlapped heavily with claims and heartbeats, so it is a genuine race with a small window, widened by deploy-time churn, invisible in normal steady state. Chose not to attempt a speculative fix, the discipline this time being reproduction before remediation since concurrency patches applied on vibes have a way of narrowing races instead of closing them. Concrete outputs of the session: forensic debug logging added to both the sweep (reclaimed job id, the expires_at value the sweep observed, fence before and after) and completion (fence presented, rows matched), shipped dark behind a flag; an incident write-up started at docs/incidents/duplicate-execution.md with the anchor timeline; and confirmation that all 41 duplicated clips converged to identical correct content because the Quillbase handler writes are idempotent by clip id, meaning user impact was zero and the blast radius of this bug is currently wasted work and broken invariants rather than corruption. Plan for the follow-up session is a repro harness, short lease TTLs measured in hundreds of milliseconds, a handler that sleeps configurably, many workers in-process hammering claims and sweeps, run until the duplicate signature appears, then start removing coincidences until the race stands alone.

Ferrite session on the duplicate execution investigation, building the reproduction harness planned after the incident analysis. Wrote a new stress binary in ferrite-core/tests/stress that runs entirely in-process against a real Postgres: 12 workers with lease TTL squeezed to 400ms, heartbeat every 130ms, reclaim sweep every 200ms, and a handler that sleeps a random 100 to 900ms so a meaningful fraction of jobs straddle multiple heartbeats, plus a churn thread that kills and restarts a random worker every 2 seconds to imitate deploy chaos, since every production pair happened inside the deploy window. Each job records its executions into a side table keyed by an execution UUID, so duplicates are detected by counting rows per job id after the run rather than by trusting the counters under test. First three runs of 10k jobs each produced zero duplicates, which was disheartening, then lowering the TTL-to-heartbeat ratio from 3x to 2x and running 50k jobs produced 7 duplicate executions, signature matching production exactly: no LeaseLost anywhere, both completions matched rows, and the forensic logging (ported into the harness from the prod debug flag) showed the same double impossibility, sweep reclaiming leases whose observed expires_at predated a heartbeat that had already committed successfully from the worker's perspective. Reproduction reliability is now roughly 1 in 7k jobs under the tightened timings, enough to iterate with. One genuinely useful negative result: disabling the churn thread entirely still produced duplicates at a lower rate, so deploy churn amplifies the race but does not cause it, the race lives in steady-state sweep-versus-heartbeat interleaving. Also captured the exact isolation level in play, everything runs at read committed, and jotted the hypothesis list for next session in the incident doc, ranked: sweep SELECT reading a snapshot older than the heartbeat commit then acting on it in a separate UPDATE statement, heartbeat extending via a non-locking read-modify-write on expires_at, or the sweep and completion joining jobs to leases in a way that lets the join see mixed-generation rows. Suspicion is heaviest on the first, the sweep is two statements where it should be one. No fixes yet, harness merged behind a dev-dependency so it does not ship, next session is bisection by candidate.

Quillbase session prompted by fallout from the parser: fetch jobs for a handful of academic publisher pages were timing out at the 30 second handler deadline, failing as Retryable, and climbing the entire ferrite backoff ladder before dying at max_attempts, ten expensive doomed attempts per clip. The root cause split into two halves. First, lib/ingest/parser.ts runs readability extraction and sanitization on the same tick as the fetch, and these publisher pages are 5 to 12MB of markup with tens of thousands of DOM nodes, so parse alone was eating 20+ seconds; profiling with a saved fixture showed 80 percent of that inside a quadratic-looking sanitizer pass that walks ancestors for every node it visits. Patched the immediate pain by capping extraction input at 3MB of HTML with a truncation marker, which brought the worst fixture from 24s to 3.1s, and filed the sanitizer rewrite as its own thread rather than heroically fixing it at midnight. Second, the timeout classification was wrong at the ferrite boundary: a handler deadline exceeded was mapped to Retryable on the theory that slowness is transient, but for parse-bound jobs the duration is a property of the document, perfectly deterministic, and retrying is pure waste. Introduced a third disposition in how the Quillbase worker maps errors, still only two variants in ferrite's JobError but the handler now tracks phase, and a timeout during fetch maps Retryable while a timeout during parse maps Terminal with a reason of document too complex, on the argument that network conditions change and documents do not. Also added a per-job-type deadline override so fetch_clip keeps 30s but the future index jobs are not bound by a limit tuned for fetches, using the RetryPolicy jsonb plumbing from the backoff work which happened to generalize nicely. Re-enqueued the 9 stuck publisher clips after the fix: 7 completed under the new parse budget, 2 went Terminal as too complex, which is the correct honest outcome pending the sanitizer rewrite. Open threads: the 3MB cap is a blunt instrument and the truncation marker is not yet surfaced in the reader UI, and the phase-aware timeout mapping deserves a small design note because the pattern (classify by phase, not by error type) will recur for every handler with mixed IO and compute.

The duplicate execution bug in ferrite is dead, and the session that killed it is worth documenting properly because the root cause was both of the ranked hypotheses at once, interacting, which is why each looked insufficient alone. Recap of the setup: the stress harness reproduces duplicate executions at about 1 in 7k jobs with tightened timings, signature being a reclaim of a freshly heartbeated lease followed by two fenced completions both matching rows. Bisection started with hypothesis one, the sweep being two statements, a SELECT collecting expired lease ids followed by an UPDATE transitioning those jobs, and the theory that the heartbeat commits between them. Rewrote the sweep as a single UPDATE with the expiry predicate inline, ran 200k jobs, and duplicates dropped roughly 5x but did not vanish, 4 survivors, which was the moment the investigation got interesting because the single-statement sweep should have been airtight if hypothesis one were the whole story. The surviving mechanism took three hours and a lot of statement-level logging to corner, and it lives in the heartbeat: heartbeat was implemented in src/lease.rs as read-modify-write, SELECT the lease row, check the worker still owns it, then UPDATE expires_at to now() plus TTL in a second statement, and under read committed the check and the write are not atomic, so the interleaving that survived was: heartbeat SELECT sees a valid owned lease; the single-statement sweep runs in another session, its predicate evaluates against the current committed expires_at which is genuinely past expiry because the heartbeat has not written yet (the worker was slow this cycle, timing jitter under load); the sweep reclaims, bumps the fence to N+1, transitions the job to ready; a third worker claims it at fence N+1; then the original heartbeat UPDATE lands, and here is the actual bug, the heartbeat UPDATE's WHERE clause matched on job id and worker id but not on fence, so it happily updated the lease row that now belongs to the new worker, stomping expires_at and, because the ownership check had passed in statement one, the old worker carried on believing the lease was its own. From there both workers heartbeat the same lease row indefinitely, both pass their ownership checks against a row they take turns rewriting, and both completions succeed because the completion path checked fence against the leases table, and the zombie's heartbeats kept resurrecting enough shared state for the check-then-act completion (also two statements, same disease) to race through. So the full causal chain needed three separate check-then-act windows lining up, sweep, heartbeat, completion, which explains the 1 in 7k rarity and why the fencing work, which fixed the fence arithmetic but implemented its predicates as read-then-write in two of three paths, reduced the bug without eliminating it. The fix is uniform and boring, exactly as it should be: every lease mutation is now a single conditional UPDATE carrying the full predicate, job id, worker id, AND fence, with RETURNING to learn the outcome, and a zero-row result maps to LeaseLost everywhere, no SELECT-then-UPDATE anywhere in the lease lifecycle. The heartbeat one-liner is the load-bearing change: WHERE job_id = $1 AND worker_id = $2 AND fence = $3. Ran the harness for 1.2 million jobs across the evening at the nastiest timings, zero duplicates, LeaseLost events firing exactly where reclaims interleave, counters balancing to the job. Also promoted two harness assertions into permanent integration tests, the heartbeat-after-reclaim scenario and the completion-race scenario, both driven deterministically with manual fence manipulation rather than relying on stress timing, so the regression is caught by CI in seconds rather than by production in weeks. Cleanup: removed the forensic debug flag logging from production, closed the incident doc with the full chain written up, and left one paragraph of commentary for future selves about the general lesson, every one of the three windows was individually reviewed and looked fine because each was a small sensible pair of statements, and the review technique that would have caught it is asking of every read, what if the world changes before the write, which is now a line in the ferrite code review checklist. Follow-ups deliberately spawned rather than done tonight: the reclaim-consumes-an-attempt question from the crash recovery session is now safe to revisit since reclaims are trustworthy; queue_depth gauge undercounted during the bug and the poller deserves a sanity assertion; and the stress harness should run nightly in CI at moderate settings, 20 minutes, because this class of bug regresses silently and the harness is the only tripwire that has ever actually fired.

Follow-through session on the ferrite race fix, turning the emergency surgery into something maintainable. The uniform conditional-UPDATE pattern from the root cause session was applied under pressure, so today was consolidation: extracted the lease mutation predicates into a single helper in src/lease.rs, lease_guard(job_id, worker_id, fence), that all four mutation paths (heartbeat, complete, fail, retry-schedule) compose into their UPDATEs, so the full three-part predicate can never again be partially applied by a path that forgets fence, which is precisely how the heartbeat hole happened. The helper is a query-builder fragment rather than a wrapper function around the whole UPDATE, chosen so each path keeps its own RETURNING shape and SET clause while sharing the guard, and a unit test asserts via string inspection that every lease mutation in the crate contains all three guard columns, a slightly gross test that would have caught the original bug and is therefore worth its grossness. Second thread: made LeaseLost handling consistent at the worker layer in src/worker.rs, previously heartbeat LeaseLost cancelled the handler task but completion LeaseLost logged and moved on, now both route through a single on_lease_lost that cancels the task, increments lease_lost_total, and emits one structured log line with job id, held fence, and phase where the loss was detected, because during the incident the asymmetry made the logs genuinely misleading. Third: revisited the increment-attempt-on-reclaim decision as planned, and split the behavior, a reclaim now records a reclaim_count separately from attempt count and only counts against the backoff ladder when the previous holder was heartbeating normally until the end (suggesting the job itself is poison) versus vanishing outright (suggesting infrastructure), the discriminator being whether the lease was reclaimed while expired for more than two heartbeat intervals; infrastructure reclaims re-enqueue at the front with no delay, poison-suspect reclaims climb the ladder as before. This gives Fly reschedules a fast path while keeping the crash-loop protection that motivated the original increment, at the cost of one heuristic that is documented with its failure modes in the code. Ran the nightly-candidate stress configuration for 40 minutes as a smoke test, clean, then wired the harness into GitHub Actions as a scheduled nightly workflow with a 25 minute budget and failure notification, using a Postgres service container, which took embarrassingly long because the harness assumed a superuser role for its truncate-between-rounds step and CI's service container did not grant it, fixed by scoping the harness to its own schema. Loose ends recorded: the string-inspection guard test should extend to any future table with fenced mutations, and the poison-versus-infrastructure heuristic deserves a metric split so the two reclaim flavors are graphable separately once the metrics histogram work lands.

Clearharbor session on entitlement caching, addressing the fact that every authenticated Quillbase request currently makes a synchronous call to clearharbor to check entitlements, adding 15 to 40ms per request and creating a hard availability coupling where clearharbor being down means Quillbase is down even for reads. Introduced a Redis cache in front of the entitlements lookup in src/entitlements.ts, keyed by user id, TTL 60 seconds, storing the full resolved entitlement object (plan tier, clip limit, feature flags) rather than individual booleans, so one cache entry answers every entitlement question for a request. The TTL choice is a deliberate consistency trade: a downgrade or cancellation can be stale for up to a minute, which for a read-later app means someone might save one extra clip after their plan lapsed, an acceptable cost, whereas an upgrade being stale for a minute is a genuinely bad first impression for a paying customer, so writes that improve entitlements (the webhook drainer applying an upgrade event) actively delete the cache key, giving upgrades read-your-writes behavior while downgrades ride out the TTL. Stampede protection matters because Quillbase fans out several entitlement checks during a page load: used a soft-TTL scheme where entries carry a refresh_after timestamp at 45 seconds, the first request past it triggers an async background refresh while still serving the cached value, and only a hard miss blocks, plus a per-key in-flight guard in the Node process so concurrent misses for the same user coalesce into one clearharbor call. Also settled the failure posture: on Redis being down, fall through to direct clearharbor calls (slower, correct); on clearharbor being down with a warm cache entry, serve stale up to 10 minutes past TTL with a served_stale counter incremented; on both down, fail open for read paths and closed for write paths, the reasoning being that letting someone read their own saved clips during an outage is nearly riskless while letting saves through unchecked has actual quota consequences. Measured impact on staging with synthetic load: p50 entitlement check went from 22ms to 0.4ms, cache hit rate 97 percent after warmup, clearharbor request volume down 30x.
