Left open: cache invalidation on the downgrade path could be added cheaply from the same webhook drainer hook that upgrades use, the asymmetry is a policy choice not a technical one and deserves a revisit once someone actually complains; and the 10 minute stale window has no metric distinguishing it from normal hits yet.

Ferrite tuning session using the first two weeks of real production numbers from the backoff ladder, now that the metrics stats output makes the retry distribution visible. Findings from the data: 91 percent of fetch_clip retries succeed on attempt 2 or 3, meaning most transient failures clear within 15 seconds, then there is a long desert where attempts 4 through 7 almost never succeed, 0.7 percent combined, and a tiny bump at attempts 8 to 10 that on inspection is entirely origin servers doing daily maintenance windows, sites that were down for 20 to 90 minutes and came back. The current ladder, 5s base doubling to a 15 minute cap over 10 attempts, spends its middle attempts in exactly the zone where nothing succeeds, so it was reshaped per the evidence: attempts 1 through 3 stay fast at 5s, 10s, 20s to harvest the transient-failure mass, then the ladder now jumps hard, 5 minutes, 15 minutes, then three final attempts spaced at the new 45 minute cap to reach into the maintenance-window bump, with max_attempts dropped from 10 to 8 since two rungs were pure waste. Modeled the change against the two weeks of historical failure timestamps before shipping it, replaying each real failure sequence against both ladders: the new shape recovers 96 percent of eventually-successful jobs within 25 minutes versus 52 minutes for the old ladder, while total wasted attempts per eventually-failed job drop from 9.2 to 6.1, mostly from the removed rungs. The 45 minute cap exceeds the old 15 and that decision is user-facing for fetch jobs, but the data shows nothing succeeds between 15 and 45 anyway, so the old cap was buying responsiveness against attempts that never worked, an illusion of care. Also widened jitter from 20 to 30 percent at the cap after confirming the fleet-scale question from the jitter fix session, at 4 workers the comb pattern never returned but the synthetic 12-worker harness runs showed mild re-synchronization at 20 percent, and 30 flattens it. Shipped with the per-job-type policy override mechanism carrying the new defaults, existing in-flight jobs keeping their enqueued policies as designed during the original ladder work, which made the rollout a non-event. Recorded a small methodology note in the repo: the replay-against-history trick is cheap and should be the standard bar for any future retry tuning, gut feelings about backoff shapes have now been wrong twice.

Home infrastructure evening, no product work: swapped the failing disk in the NAS. Monthly scrub flagged mounting read errors on one of the four drives in the ZFS raidz1 pool, SMART showing 312 reallocated sectors and climbing week over week, so the replacement 8TB drive that has been sitting on the shelf for exactly this day finally went in. Process was uneventful in the way good preparation makes things uneventful: offlined the sick disk from the pool, shut down, swapped the sled, booted, ran a short SMART self-test on the new drive to catch infant mortality before committing, then zpool replace and let the resilver run. Resilver took 9 hours 40 minutes for 5.1TB of actual data, throttled it slightly during the evening so streaming to the living room stayed watchable, let it run full speed overnight. Scrub after resilver came back clean, zero errors, pool back to full redundancy. The old drive gets a secure wipe and a trip to electronics recycling, it lasted six years which is a fair innings. One improvement made while in there: the case fan curve was aggressive enough to keep drives near 28C which is colder than needed and louder than wanted, adjusted to target 34C for a noticeably quieter closet. Also finally labeled the drive sleds with serial numbers on tape, because identifying the physical position of a failing disk by serial number through the case grille with a flashlight was the worst part of the whole exercise. Reminder set to price a cold spare again, shelf stock is now zero and the remaining three original drives are the same age as the one that just died.

Ferrite session on crash recovery hardening, running the torture regimen that has been on the list since the lease machinery stabilized post-race-fix. Built a kill loop script around the stress harness: 6 workers processing a steady 50 jobs per second of synthetic work, and every 5 to 15 seconds (randomized) one worker chosen at random receives SIGKILL, no drain, no warning, then restarts 2 seconds later with a fresh worker identity per the crash recovery design, run maintained for four hours over the afternoon. Invariants checked continuously by a verifier thread against the side-table execution log: no job lost (every enqueued job eventually completes or fails terminally), no job executed twice to completion (the race fix's promise), and no job stuck (nothing sits in running with a dead worker longer than TTL plus sweep interval plus grace). Results: 719 forced kills, 61,344 jobs, zero lost, zero duplicated, 100 percent reclaimed within the expected window, worst reclaim latency 96 seconds against the theoretical 95 second budget which turned out to be a measurement artifact of the verifier polling at one second granularity, satisfying. Two real findings though. First, the startup path had a thundering herd: a restarting worker immediately ran a reclaim sweep before its first claim, by design so recovery is fast, but with the kill loop restarting workers constantly, sweeps overlapped heavily and the sweep UPDATE contention showed up as lock waits in pg_stat_activity; fixed by jittering the initial sweep by 0 to 5 seconds and having the sweep take a small advisory lock so at most one sweep runs fleet-wide per interval, with the others skipping rather than queueing, safe because sweeps are idempotent and any single sweep covers the whole table. Second, the fresh-identity-per-process design leaks worker rows: 719 kills means 719 dead worker identities in the workers registry table, harmless functionally but unbounded growth, so added a janitor step to the sweep that deletes worker rows with no heartbeat for over an hour, measured as removing all corpses within the run. Merged both fixes, re-ran a one-hour confirmation, clean. The kill loop script is checked in under tests/torture with a README, intended cadence is before every release rather than nightly since four hours of CI Postgres hammering daily is more spend than the risk justifies given the deterministic regression tests already guard the known races. Next thread from the backlog: the metrics histograms, which keep getting displaced by more urgent work and are now the oldest open item on the ferrite list.

Quillbase session on fetch pipeline dedupe, closing a hole that has been wasting work since the pipeline moved to ferrite: saving the same URL twice, or two household members saving the same article, enqueued two full fetch and parse cycles producing two identical clips. The fix has two layers with different semantics, deliberately. First layer is URL-level dedupe at enqueue time in app/api/clips/route.ts: URLs are canonicalized (lowercase host, strip default ports, sort query params, drop known tracker params like utm_*, resolve trivial redirects is deferred) and hashed, and a save whose canonical URL hash matches an existing clip for the same user within the household returns the existing clip id with a deduped flag rather than enqueueing, which turns the double-save case into a no-op costing one indexed lookup. The tracker-param strip list is explicit and conservative, twelve params, because overzealous canonicalization that merges genuinely different pages (some sites put content ids in query params) is a worse failure than occasional duplicate fetches. Second layer is content-level: the fetch handler computes a SHA-256 of the parsed content and stores it on the clip, and when a fetch completes with a content hash matching another clip from the same canonical domain fetched within 24 hours, the parse and index phases are skipped and the stored parse result is copied, which catches the syndicated-content and AMP-variant cases the URL layer cannot see. Content-level dedupe is copy-not-reference, each clip keeps its own rows, on the reasoning that reference-sharing content between clips creates deletion and edit anomalies (annotations land on shared content, one user deletes, whose content is it) that are not worth the storage savings at this scale, storage being the cheapest thing in the whole system. Wired both layers with metrics, dedupe_url_hits and dedupe_content_hits, and backfilled canonical hashes for the existing 31k clips with a ferrite batch of index-style jobs reusing the per-clip granularity pattern from the rebuild work, 11 minutes, uneventful, the priority lane absence noted once again as fetches queued behind the backfill. One decision explicitly recorded against future confusion: dedupe never crosses households even for identical content, privacy boundary trumps efficiency, the content hash comparison is scoped within the household key. Open: canonical URL resolution of redirects (the t.co problem) needs the fetcher to report the final URL back into the canonical hash, half-plumbed, finishing next session.

Ferrite metrics session, finally landing the histogram work that has been the oldest open item on the list, plus a first real Grafana dashboard. The bucket boundary question that stalled this for weeks got resolved by refusing to answer it globally: job duration histograms are now registered per job_type with per-type bucket sets declared alongside the handler registration in the worker builder API, so fetch_clip gets buckets tuned for network work (100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2.5s, 5s, 10s, 30s) while index_clip gets compute-shaped buckets (10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 1s, 5s), and a job type registered without explicit buckets gets a broad default with a startup warning nudging the author to choose, the warning being the actual enforcement mechanism since nobody reads docs. Three histograms per type landed: run_duration measuring handler execution, queue_wait measuring enqueue-to-claim which is the number users actually feel, and total_latency measuring enqueue-to-completion including all retry waiting, the third one added after realizing the first two cannot be summed across retries to reconstruct user-perceived latency. Implementation detail that took real thought: queue_wait for retried jobs was ambiguous, does the wait clock reset per attempt or run from original enqueue, and the answer chosen is per-attempt with the original-enqueue view living in total_latency, because per-attempt wait is the signal that detects queue congestion (what the metric is for) while cumulative wait conflates congestion with backoff policy, and a note to this effect went into the metrics docs because the next person to touch this will absolutely re-ask the question. The Grafana dashboard, built against a Prometheus now actually scraping the 9100 endpoints via Fly internal DNS, has four rows: queue health (depth by state and type, oldest ready age, claim rate), outcomes (completion and failure rates, retry ladder distribution as a heatmap which immediately visualized the ladder reshape from the tuning session, the abandoned middle rungs visibly empty), lease integrity (reclaims split by the poison-versus-infrastructure heuristic from the race fix follow-through, lease_lost events, sweep contention skips from the torture-test fix), and per-type latency (p50, p95, p99 from the new histograms). Building the lease row surfaced one small real bug: the infrastructure-flavored reclaim counter was never incremented on the fast-path re-enqueue branch, only the poison branch counted, so the split ratio was fictional, one-line fix with a test. Also rationalized metric naming while everything was on screen, three counters renamed to consistent _total suffixes with the old names kept as deprecated aliases for one release since the ferrite-cli stats command scrapes them, breaking the cli with a metrics rename would be a self-inflicted wound. Deliberately rejected during the session: per-worker-id labels on any metric, still the correct cardinality call even though the lease debugging would occasionally enjoy them, the worker id belongs in logs not labels; and pushing metrics to a hosted service, Prometheus on a small Fly machine is fine at this scale and keeps the self-hosted story honest for eventual ferrite open source users. Dashboard JSON is checked into the repo under docs/observability with a screenshot in the README, and the stats cli subcommand gained a percentiles flag reading from the new histograms. Open threads: alerting rules exist for exactly nothing, queue depth stuck high and reclaim rate spiking are the two obvious candidates and should be wired before they are needed rather than after, and the parse-phase timing from the Quillbase side lives in Quillbase logs where it is invisible to this dashboard, worth deciding whether handler-side phases get a ferrite-blessed sub-span mechanism or stay an application concern.

Ferrite session on graceful shutdown, the drain path, which mattered less when deploys were rare and matters a lot now that the torture testing proved crash recovery works but every deploy still relies on it, treating SIGTERM like SIGKILL and paying the reclaim latency tax (up to 95 seconds of a job sitting orphaned) for jobs that a polite shutdown could have finished or handed back instantly. Implemented the drain in src/worker.rs: on SIGTERM the worker stops claiming immediately, lets in-flight handlers run against a drain deadline (default 20 seconds, configurable per deployment since Fly gives 30 by default before SIGKILL), and for any handler still running at the deadline, cancels it via the same cancellation token machinery the fencing work installed, then explicitly releases its leases back to ready state with the fast-path no-attempt-consumed treatment from the reclaim heuristic, since a deploy is infrastructure not poison. The explicit release is the payoff: a drained job is claimable by another worker within milliseconds instead of waiting out TTL plus sweep, measured on staging as re-claim within 300ms of release versus the old worst case near 95 seconds. Decision on in-flight jobs versus the deadline: first instinct was to extend leases during drain so slow jobs are not reclaimed mid-drain by the sweep on other workers, but that is exactly the zombie-adjacent behavior the race investigation taught suspicion of, a shutting-down worker fighting to keep leases alive; instead leases are left to their normal heartbeat cadence during drain, heartbeats continue until each handler exits, and the deadline is set below Fly's SIGKILL grace so the sequence is always drain-then-die rather than a lease tug-of-war. Also handled the sweep interaction, a draining worker no longer runs reclaim sweeps, no reason for a dying process to take the advisory sweep lock and then get killed holding work. Tested with a deploy simulation script: 4 workers under load, rolling SIGTERM with 2 second stagger, asserting zero reclaims-by-sweep occur (everything hands over via explicit release) and no completion gap in throughput beyond the capacity dip; passed after fixing one ordering bug where the claim-stop happened after the final claim batch was already leased, off by one poll cycle, so a drain could pick up new work milliseconds before refusing more, closed by checking the drain flag inside the claim transaction rather than before it. Fly deploys observed after shipping: the queue_wait p95 spike that used to accompany every deploy, previously up to 90 seconds for unlucky jobs, is gone from the graphs entirely, deploy is now invisible in the latency dashboard. Remaining rough edge for a future session: drain deadline versus genuinely long jobs, an index rebuild batch job that legitimately runs minutes will always be cancelled and re-run under this design, wasteful, and the eventual answer is probably checkpointable handlers, which is a big enough idea to deserve its own design session rather than a bolt-on.

Rough Quillbase session dominated by an index rebuild that went sideways in production. Context: shipped the index_version column and analyzer versioning that was proposed after the first rebuild, then kicked off what was supposed to be a routine full rebuild to migrate all 34k clips to analyzer v2 (the one that fixes the fused-whitespace tokens and adds unaccent normalization). The rebuild itself worked, the queue management around it did not: 34,112 index_clip jobs enqueued at 6:10pm flooded the queue, and with no priority lanes, the fetch_clip jobs from actual live users queued behind the entire rebuild, so from 6:10 to roughly 6:50 every newly saved link sat pending with users watching the pulse animation, queue_wait p95 for fetch_clip peaked at 31 minutes, and two users messaged asking if saving was broken, which for a two-person company is a significant fraction of the vocal user base. Mitigated live in two stages: first paused the rebuild by moving 28k not-yet-claimed index jobs to a new paused state via direct UPDATE (a state that did not exist until the moment it was needed, added as a migration on the spot), letting fetches drain in 4 minutes, then dribbled the rebuild back in by moving 2k jobs at a time back to ready whenever fetch queue depth was zero, finishing the full rebuild by 11pm. The searchable outcome is good, analyzer v2 verified against the previously broken clips, fused tokens gone, accented queries now match, and the index_version column means the next analyzer migration can target WHERE index_version < 3 instead of sweeping everything. But the operational lesson is the real content of this session: batch workloads and latency-sensitive workloads sharing one FIFO queue is now a twice-demonstrated failure mode (the dedupe backfill grazed the same problem), and the priority lanes work in ferrite is promoted from recurring backlog item to the next ferrite session, with the design sketch written tonight while the pain was fresh: two lanes, interactive and batch, claim loop draining interactive fully before touching batch, batch enqueue API requiring an explicit lane choice so nobody lands in interactive by default. The improvised paused state is staying, it earned its keep as an operator control and the cli gained pause and resume subcommands wrapping tonight's manual SQL. Also noted for honesty in the incident log: the rebuild was launched at peak evening usage out of pure impatience when it could have waited for 2am, tooling failures and judgment failures compounding, only one of which is fixable in Rust.

Quillbase incident session, the analyzer v2 index rebuild that turned into an unplanned lesson in queue starvation. The plan executed at 6:10pm was straightforward, enqueue index_clip jobs for all 34k clips to migrate them to the new analyzer (unaccent support plus the whitespace-fusion fix), with the fresh index_version column tracking migration state per clip. What was not planned: ferrite still has a single FIFO queue, so 34,112 batch jobs formed a wall in front of every live fetch_clip job, and real users saving links between 6:10 and 6:50 saw their clips stuck pending for up to half an hour, fetch queue_wait p95 hit 31 minutes, and two of the handful of active users wrote in believing saves were down. Live mitigation invented a queue state on the fly: paused, applied via emergency migration and a direct UPDATE moving the 28k unclaimed index jobs out of contention, which drained the fetch backlog within minutes, after which the rebuild was fed back in 2k-job slices during quiet moments and completed by 11pm. Technical outcome fully successful despite the operational mess, analyzer v2 is live across all clips, spot-checked the previously pathological documents, accent-insensitive search confirmed working, and future analyzer bumps become targeted re-indexes via WHERE index_version < N rather than full sweeps. Two durable artifacts came out of the pain: the paused state is now a permanent queue feature with pause and resume verbs in ferrite-cli (the incident's manual SQL, promoted to tooling), and priority lanes graduated from perpetual backlog to committed next ferrite work with the two-lane design sketched immediately, interactive lane strictly drained before batch, and the batch lane mandatory-explicit at enqueue time so accidental defaulting into the interactive lane is impossible. The incident log also records the human factor plainly, the rebuild was started at evening peak because waiting until 2am felt annoying, and no amount of queue engineering fixes launching batch work at peak on purpose. Follow-ups: alerting on queue_wait p95 for the interactive job types (the Grafana dashboard displayed the entire incident beautifully in retrospect while alerting on none of it in real time), and a runbook entry describing the pause-drain-dribble recovery pattern since it worked well enough to standardize.

Ferrite session on jobs table bloat, triggered by the weekly database size check showing the jobs table at 4.1GB while holding only 60k live rows, with autovacuum visibly losing ground, and dequeue p95 creeping from 1.1ms to 3.8ms over two weeks, the slow-burn kind of degradation that eventually becomes an incident. Diagnosis first: pg_stat_user_tables showed 92 percent dead tuple ratio, and the cause is the write pattern the queue naturally generates, every job row is updated at least four times through its lifecycle (claim, heartbeat-adjacent lease writes live elsewhere but state transitions hit jobs, completion), completed rows were being deleted by a nightly cleanup, and the combination of high-churn updates plus bulk deletes is the canonical bloat recipe, each update leaving a dead tuple and the nightly delete carving a fresh 30k-row hole that autovacuum marked reusable but never returned to the OS, while the rebuild-incident spike (34k jobs in one evening) permanently stretched the high-water mark. Considered three remedies and took two. First, taken: stop deleting completed rows from the hot table at all, instead completed and terminally-failed jobs are moved by the nightly job into a jobs_archive table (insert-select-delete in batches of 5k with a sleep between batches to be gentle), so the hot table stays small and the archive is append-mostly where bloat mechanics are benign, and the archive gets the operational benefit that completed-job forensics like the duplicate-execution investigation no longer compete with live queue traffic. Second, taken: set fillfactor 70 on the jobs table so updates have room for HOT chains, avoiding index amplification on the state-transition updates, this being the single highest-leverage knob for update-heavy tables and embarrassing not to have set from the start; applied via a maintenance-window VACUUM FULL at 2am (lesson from the rebuild incident applied, off-peak this time) to rewrite the table compactly with the new fillfactor, taking the table from 4.1GB to 96MB and dequeue p95 back to 1.05ms. Third, considered and rejected for now: partitioning the jobs table by state or by time, which is the textbook answer at bigger scale but at 60k live rows adds partition management complexity, breaks the SKIP LOCKED claim query in subtle ways that would need re-verification against the whole race test suite, and solves a problem the archive split already solved smaller. Also tuned autovacuum per-table settings on the hot table, scale factor from the default 0.2 down to 0.02 with a floor of 500, so vacuum triggers on thousands of dead tuples rather than tens of thousands, verified over the following day as vacuum running every few minutes and dead ratio holding under 5 percent. The archive table got its own design attention rather than being a dumping ground: no indexes beyond the primary key and a completed_at brin index (perfect for time-correlated append order at near-zero cost), a retention policy decision recorded of 90 days then delete for real, and the ferrite-cli stats and history subcommands taught to union hot and archive transparently when asked for older data. One interaction with the priority lanes design committed after the rebuild incident got checked deliberately: the lane column planned for the claim query is on the hot table, small and hot-cached, unaffected by any of tonight, confirmed no conflict between the two workstreams. Follow-ups: the archive mover should emit metrics (rows moved, batch duration) so its silent failure does not quietly regrow the hot table, wired half of it tonight; and pg_repack should be evaluated versus the VACUUM FULL approach before the next compaction is ever needed, since tonight's window took the queue offline for 40 seconds and repack would not.

Clearharbor session on session token rotation in src/session.ts, closing a security posture gap flagged during the last self-review: session tokens were effectively immortal, issued at login with a 30 day expiry and never rotated, so a leaked token (browser extension gone bad, pasted curl command in a screenshot, laptop theft) stayed valid for its full remaining life with no server-side lever short of nuking all sessions for the user. Implemented sliding rotation: sessions now carry a short-lived access token (15 minutes) and a rotation token (30 days sliding window), the access token is what rides on requests, and refresh exchanges the rotation token for a fresh pair, invalidating the old rotation token in the same transaction with a token family id linking the lineage. The family id is the important part, it enables reuse detection: if an already-rotated token is presented again, that is either a race from two tabs or a stolen token being replayed, and the two cases are distinguished by a 10 second grace window, a reuse within grace is treated as a benign concurrent refresh (the second caller gets the same new pair from a short-lived cache keyed by the old token), while reuse after grace kills the entire family, logging a security event and forcing re-login on every device holding that lineage, the standard theft response of burning the family rather than guessing which holder is legitimate. The grace window design came from genuine multi-tab pain during testing, two Quillbase tabs refreshing simultaneously is completely normal behavior and punishing it with logout would be a self-own; 10 seconds was chosen as generous for tab races and useless for an attacker who by definition presents the stolen token well after the victim's next organic refresh. Storage moved from opaque random tokens checked against a sessions table to the same table but with tokens stored hashed (SHA-256, no salt needed for high-entropy random values), so a database read cannot harvest usable tokens, an overdue change that rode along naturally. Migration path for existing sessions: old-format immortal tokens are accepted for 14 more days through a compatibility branch that upgrades them to the new format on first use, after which the branch and any never-seen old tokens die together, and the cutoff date is hardcoded with a startup log line counting down so it cannot be forgotten. Coordinated with Quillbase, which needed its API client taught to refresh on 401-with-rotation-hint instead of bouncing to login, a small change in the shared fetch wrapper. Left open: device metadata on sessions (name, last seen, IP) exists in the table but there is no UI listing active sessions or a revoke button, which is the natural next slice; and rate limiting on the refresh endpoint is inherited from the global limiter but deserves its own tighter bucket since refresh is a machine-speed endpoint.

Small ferrite-cli quality of life session, paying down the annoyances written in the margins of every debugging note this month. The relative-time rendering finally happened, all timestamps in status, stats, and history output now render as 3m ago or in 12m with absolute UTC behind a verbose flag, the tiny change disproportionately improving every future incident. The stats subcommand gained a watch flag re-rendering every 2 seconds with sparkline-style depth trends drawn in plain unicode, which during testing already made the queue breathing pattern visible in a way single snapshots never did. Job inspection improved: show job-id now assembles the full lifecycle from hot and archive tables plus lease history, attempts with their errors and delays, reclaims with the poison-versus-infrastructure classification, fence progression, rendered as a compact timeline, essentially productizing the manual forensic queries from the duplicate-execution investigation so the next race hunt starts from a tool instead of psql archaeology. The pause and resume verbs from the rebuild incident grew a lane filter ahead of the priority lanes work landing, and a dry-run flag that reports what would be paused, both trivially cheap now and obviously wanted the moment lanes exist. Fixed one actual bug found while dogfooding, the enqueue subcommand serialized its payload flag through a serde path that stripped null values from json payloads, silently altering what handlers received, caught because a test payload with an explicit null behaved differently via cli versus via the library API, root cause being a default serde skip attribute on the payload wrapper struct, removed with a round-trip test added. Declined to add: colored output themes and a TUI dashboard mode, both fun, neither worth maintenance while the queue itself still has committed feature work pending, noted so future enthusiasm meets past restraint.

The ferrite priority lanes session, delivering the design committed after the index rebuild incident, and the starvation problem that caused two users to think saving was broken is now structurally impossible rather than operationally avoided. Implementation follows the sketch with one deviation. The jobs table gains a lane column, two values, interactive and batch, and the claim query in src/queue.rs drains interactive completely before touching batch, implemented not as two queries but as a single claim CTE ordering by lane then priority then retry_at, which keeps the claim atomic under SKIP LOCKED and preserves every property the race test suite guards, all of which was re-run green after the change since the claim path is the most invariant-laden code in the crate. The deviation from the sketch: the sketch had strict priority which risks batch starvation under sustained interactive load, and rather than shrugging that off (batch starving is at least operator-visible and less bad than the reverse) an anti-starvation valve was added, one batch job is claimed per worker per 30 claim cycles regardless of interactive depth, roughly 3 percent of capacity reserved, enough that a rebuild makes progress during peak while remaining invisible in interactive queue_wait, and the valve ratio is a config knob with the default chosen from replaying the rebuild incident traffic against a simulation of both policies, strict priority would have delayed the 34k rebuild to 9 hours under that evening's load while the valve finishes it in 5 with interactive p95 unmoved. Enqueue API changed as designed, lane is a required parameter on the batch-capable enqueue path with no default, a deliberate small API breakage forcing every existing call site to declare itself, and the compile errors that followed were exactly the audit wanted, three call sites in the Quillbase worker chose batch (rebuilds, backfills, the archive export) and fetch_clip plus the status-page jobs chose interactive. Migration backfilled existing rows, index adjusted to (lane, priority, retry_at) partial on claimable states, claim latency measured before and after at no meaningful change, 0.9ms p95. The pause and resume cli verbs gained their lane filter for real now, pause batch being the one-command version of the rebuild incident mitigation that took frantic SQL at the time. Retired the placeholder priority ordering hack from the jitter fix session with a small satisfaction. Deferred consciously: more than two lanes (a proposed background-low for someday analytics felt speculative, two lanes solve every incident actually experienced), per-lane concurrency limits (the valve covers the present need with less machinery), and lane-aware metrics beyond a lane label added to the existing counters and histograms, which was nearly free and immediately makes the Grafana queue row filterable by lane. Next real test arrives with the next big rebuild, and the runbook pause-drain-dribble entry now has a one-line addendum, probably unnecessary now, kept until proven.

Quillbase search quality session in lib/search/rank.ts, the first pass at ranking since analyzer v2 landed, driven by a concrete complaint from actual use: searching for a half-remembered article surfaces old barely-relevant clips above the obviously right one, because ranking is currently raw ts_rank over the weighted tsvector with no other signal. Changes made: blended score combining text relevance with recency and personal engagement, specifically final score is ts_rank_cd (switched from ts_rank for its cover-density behavior which rewards query terms appearing near each other, noticeably better for multi-word memory queries) multiplied by a recency decay factor with a 90 day half-life on saved_at, plus a small boost for clips actually opened at least once, on the theory that a read-later app's search is usually memory retrieval and memory correlates with both recency and having actually read the thing. Tuned the blend weights against a hand-built evaluation set, 40 queries with known-correct target clips drawn from real usage of the personal instance, measuring mean reciprocal rank: raw ts_rank scored 0.61, ts_rank_cd alone 0.68, the full blend 0.83, with the engagement boost contributing least and the recency decay most, numbers now recorded in a comment above the scoring function so the next tuning session has a baseline. Along the way fixed a latent correctness issue, the query builder was websearch_to_tsquery in the API route but plainto_tsquery in the older command palette path, meaning quoted phrases behaved differently between the two search boxes, unified on websearch_to_tsquery everywhere with its more forgiving syntax. Query latency checked after the changes, p95 34ms on 34k clips including the decay computation done inline in SQL, fine, though the note for future scale is that the decay multiplication defeats any potential GIN index-only shortcuts and a materialized rank component would be the move past a few hundred thousand clips. Deferred with intent: typo tolerance (pg_trgm fuzzy fallback when tsquery yields nothing, sketched but the empty-result rate is only 4 percent of searches, measured tonight, so it is real but not urgent), snippet highlighting improvements, and any learning-to-rank ambitions which at two users would be tuning on noise. The evaluation set itself is the quiet win of the session, checked in under tests/search-eval with a tiny runner, turning future ranking arguments into measurements.

Bad day ferrite session: the duplicate execution signature is back. The nightly stress harness, the tripwire wired up after the race fix precisely because this class of bug regresses silently, went red for the first time in its six weeks of existence, two duplicate executions in 180k jobs, and the immediate sick feeling was that the uniform conditional UPDATE fix had a hole after all. Half a day of forensics later the truth is more annoying and less scary: the fix holds, the regression is new code violating the pattern the fix established. The lane column migration from the priority lanes work included a data backfill, and to make the backfill safe to run against a live queue it re-derived lane values for rows in ambiguous states, and that re-derivation was implemented as a read-then-write pair against jobs in claimable states, exactly the check-then-act shape the race postmortem banned from lease mutations, except this code touches jobs.state not leases, so the string-inspection guard test that enforces the three-column lease guard never looked at it. Under precisely wrong interleaving the backfill's write could resurrect a job row from claimed back to ready after observing it pre-claim, creating a second claimable copy of an already-running job, fence machinery never involved because the corruption happened upstream of any lease. The immediate fix was easy, the backfill re-derivation became a single conditional UPDATE with the state predicate inline, and the backfill is done anyway so the live risk window was the migration deploy itself, harness confirmed clean over 400k jobs tonight. The uncomfortable finding is the process one: the postmortem lesson was encoded as a checklist line and a guard test scoped to the lease table, and the very next substantial feature reintroduced the pattern one table over, which says the lesson was stored in the wrong layer. Spent the last hours acting on that properly rather than just patching: the guard test generalized into a lint-style test that scans every UPDATE in the crate touching jobs.state or leases and asserts single-statement conditional form with no preceding SELECT of the same row in the same function, implemented crudely via syn-based source walking, crude but it correctly flags tonight's bug when run against the pre-fix commit, which is the only credential a lint needs; and the code review checklist line got promoted into a short doc, docs/concurrency-rules.md, three rules with the incident links attached, referenced from CONTRIBUTING so it survives even when the checklist culture inevitably decays. Also re-examined every other UPDATE that lanes touched, the claim CTE reordering and the valve, both clean, both already covered by the deterministic race tests, and added the backfill scenario as a permanent deterministic test since stress-only coverage is what let it slip through. Confidence status at end of session: the original fix was never broken, the property that failed is that new code must inherit old lessons automatically, and that property now has enforcement with teeth. The nightly harness caught it within a day of the migration shipping, which is the system working exactly as designed, worth saying out loud because the day felt like failure while being evidence the safety net earns its 20 CI minutes.

Long, careful ferrite session closing out the second act of the race saga properly, because the syn-based lint from the regression session was honest about its own crudeness and the goal today was to replace crude with sound, plus resolve a lingering visibility question about SKIP LOCKED that the regression forensics surfaced but did not fully chase down. The SKIP LOCKED question first, since it turned into the deeper half of the day: while re-verifying the claim CTE during the regression audit, one interleaving in the logs looked like a claim observing a job in ready state that a concurrent backfill write had just moved out of ready, raising the ugly possibility that the claim path itself could act on a stale read under read committed even in single-statement form. Built a minimal reproduction attempt to settle it: two sessions, one running the claim CTE in a loop, the other flipping a target row's state, with statement-level logging of xmin and ctid to watch row versions, roughly 3 hours of increasingly precise experiments. Conclusion, written into docs/concurrency-rules.md with the experiment preserved under tests/experiments: the claim CTE is sound, because a single UPDATE re-evaluates its predicate against the newest committed version of a row after acquiring its lock (the standard read-committed recheck behavior), and SKIP LOCKED only skips rows whose locks are held, never delivering stale versions of unlocked rows; the suspicious log interleaving was the backfill bug itself viewed from the other side, the claim behaved correctly against a row the backfill had corrupted, case closed with the correction that the earlier incident write-up briefly speculated about claim-side staleness and now carries a strikethrough note pointing here, keeping the record honest matters when the record is what future debugging trusts. The second half was the lint rework: the syn-based source walker had two failure modes found within its first week, a false positive on a legitimate SELECT of a job row for read-only display in the same function as an unrelated UPDATE, and a blind spot for mutations composed through the query-builder helper where the SQL string is assembled across function boundaries. Replaced the approach entirely: instead of analyzing source, the rule is now enforced at the query layer, all state-mutating queries against jobs and leases must go through a new guarded_update module in ferrite-core that takes the predicate components as typed arguments (job id, expected state or fence, worker identity where applicable) and emits the single conditional UPDATE itself, raw sqlx access to those tables in the rest of the crate is denied by a clippy disallowed-methods configuration plus a CI grep for the table names in raw query strings outside the module, and the module is 200 lines with exhaustive tests including the three historical bug shapes replayed against it. This inverts the enforcement from detect-bad-patterns to make-bad-patterns-unwritable, which is the same design philosophy that made the lane parameter required at enqueue, and the migration of all existing call sites, 14 of them, was mechanical with two exceptions that genuinely needed new predicate combinations (the drain path's release-without-fence-bump and the archive mover's terminal-state-only guard), both of which forced clarifying thought that improved the call sites. The deterministic race test suite runs green through the new module, the nightly stress config unchanged, and perf of the claim and heartbeat paths is within noise since the module is compile-time composition not runtime indirection. Also spent an hour on the reclaim heuristic while inside the lease code, the poison-versus-infrastructure discriminator has accumulated three weeks of production data, 41 infrastructure reclaims (all deploy-correlated before the drain work landed, near zero after, which independently validates the drain), 2 poison classifications both genuinely poisonous (the 90MB HTML page made a return appearance before the parse cap caught it downstream), zero misclassifications found by hand-audit, so the heuristic is declared validated and its provisional-warning comment removed. End state of the whole saga after tonight: three incidents, one root cause pattern, and the pattern is now structurally unwritable rather than reviewably discouraged, the difference between those two being the actual lesson of the six weeks. Open threads going forward are all mercifully ordinary: the guarded_update module should eventually host the batch-claim variant when worker autoscaling work needs it, the experiments directory needs a README so the xmin methodology is reusable, and the concurrency rules doc deserves a diagram of the three historical interleavings while memory is fresh, assigned to a future documentation session.

Weekend tinkering session, personal: finally built the export pipeline for the bike computer data that has been accumulating unloved. The unit records rides as FIT files that only ever synced to the vendor cloud, and the goal was a local archive plus the ability to run my own analysis. Wrote a small Rust cli (the hammer at hand after months of ferrite) that pulls activities via the vendor API with OAuth, the token dance being the usual painful part, their refresh flow silently expires consent after 90 days which took an hour of confused 401 debugging to discover in a forum post. Once authenticated, the tool paginates the activity list, downloads original FIT files, and decodes them with the fit-rust crate into per-ride parquet files, one row per second sample, position, heart rate, cadence, power, temperature, chosen over CSV purely for size, 4 years of riding lands at 210MB parquet versus 1.9GB CSV. Wrote the whole history to the NAS with its freshly replaced disk, feeling like responsible data ownership. First analysis: a quick DuckDB session over the parquet answered a question the vendor dashboard never could, gross ascent per month across four years in one query, and confirmed the pandemic-year riding peak everyone claims they had. Rough edges accepted: incremental sync is a timestamp watermark file rather than anything clever, the decoder chokes on two corrupt files from a firmware crash in 2023 which are skipped with a warning, and there is no dashboard, DuckDB queries are the dashboard. Idea noted for someday, never: pushing rides into Quillbase as clips. Some things do not need to be clips.

Ferrite soak test session, the pre-release validation run for tagging v0.3 of the crates, everything from the race saga through priority lanes and the guarded_update module together under sustained realistic load for 72 hours over the long weekend. Configuration: 6 workers on Fly at production sizing, synthetic workload generator producing a realistic mix modeled from production traffic ratios, 70 percent interactive fetch-shaped jobs with real network calls to a controlled test origin (variable latency 50ms to 8s, 4 percent error injection), 25 percent batch index-shaped compute jobs, 5 percent poison and pathological cases including the beloved 90MB document, deploy simulation every 6 hours doing a full rolling restart through the drain path, and one deliberate chaos event per day, a Postgres restart, a Redis flush (which ferrite ignores but Quillbase-side code sharing the environment should tolerate), and a network partition of one worker via Fly firewall rules for 3 minutes. Headline results: 4.9 million jobs processed, zero lost, zero duplicated (the execution-log verifier ran the whole time), interactive queue_wait p95 held at 210ms except during the partition event where the partitioned worker's leased jobs correctly rode the reclaim path and p95 briefly hit 8 seconds, batch throughput satisfied the valve design with rebuild-scale bursts completing during interactive load exactly as the simulation predicted, and the fence and lease counters balanced perfectly against the execution log, the invariant that would have caught the original race in an afternoon had this test existed then. Findings worth fixing before the tag, three, all small: the archive mover fell behind during the batch bursts because its 5k batch size with sleep was tuned before lanes existed and batch bursts now legitimately complete 100k jobs in an hour, parameterized the batch size and made the sleep adaptive to hot-table depth; the partition event revealed that a worker cut off from Postgres logs a connection error every 50ms retry attempt, 3 minutes producing 3600 identical log lines, added exponential backoff with a cap to the connection retry and a once-per-minute summarized error; and the metrics endpoint on the partitioned worker kept serving its last-known gauge values as if fresh, which is how monitoring lies to you during exactly the incidents it exists for, added a staleness timestamp to the poller and the dashboard now greys out stale workers. No findings against the core invariants, which after the season this codebase has had reads as the soak earning its electricity. v0.3 tagged at the end of the session with the soak report checked in under docs/releases, and the workload generator promoted to a reusable tool with its config documented, future soaks are now a config file and a weekend rather than a bespoke build.

Quillbase API hardening session on app/api/clips/route.ts and its siblings, the kind of unglamorous pass that got scheduled after noticing during the search work that the clips route still trusted its inputs like it was a prototype, which it was, two architectural eras ago. Validation first: every route body and query param now goes through zod schemas colocated in a schemas.ts next to the routes, with the clip save schema enforcing URL well-formedness and scheme allowlist (http and https only, a data: URL made it into the queue last month and the fetch handler dutifully tried to fetch it), title length caps, and tag count and length limits, and the schema types are inferred and exported so the frontend fetch wrappers share the exact contract instead of drifting. The URL validation subsumes what the route did by hand and adds SSRF posture: hostnames resolving to private ranges are rejected at save time via a resolver check (with the check repeated in the ferrite fetch handler at fetch time since DNS can change between save and fetch, the rebinding window, and the handler check is the one that actually matters, the route check exists for immediate user feedback). Rate limiting second: a small sliding-window limiter on Redis, per-user rather than per-IP since everything requiring limits sits behind auth anyway, 60 saves per hour and 20 searches per minute as generous first numbers with headroom telemetry to tune from, returning 429 with retry-after, and the limiter module deliberately shared with the future public API in mind. Error shape third: routes previously leaked raw error messages including a memorable case of a full Postgres constraint violation reaching the client, now every route returns a stable error envelope with a machine code, human message, and request id, the request id also threading through to ferrite job payloads so a user-reported failure can be traced from support message to route log to job history in the cli show command, which was tested end to end with a deliberately broken save and is the sleeper feature of the session. Auth check consolidation last: three routes each did their own session lookup with subtly different handling of expired-but-present sessions, now one requireSession helper with explicit behavior, aligned with the clearharbor token rotation semantics landed recently, including the refresh-hint pass-through. Tests added at the route level with a schema round-trip suite and abuse cases, 429 behavior, oversized bodies, the data: URL regression. Not done, listed honestly: the household-sharing routes did not get the pass yet and are next, CSRF posture relies on SameSite alone and deserves an explicit review, and the rate limiter counts per user with no burst shaping, which will matter the day any client implements save-all-tabs.

Ferrite session delivering the dead letter queue, the sketch that has been sitting in the notes since the original backoff ladder work, promoted to real because the max_attempts-exhaustion-is-silent problem finally bit: a batch of 30 fetch jobs exhausted their ladders during an origin CDN outage last week and the failures were only noticed days later by a user asking where their clips went, the exact silent failure mode flagged as feeling wrong in the ladder session and then left to wait. Design: terminally failed jobs (Terminal errors and retryable exhaustion both) now land in a dead_letters table rather than merely a failed state row destined for the archive, carrying the full job payload, final error, complete attempt history serialized from the lease and retry records, and a denormalized job_type and lane for queryability, with the jobs row itself still archiving normally so the archive remains the complete historical record and the DLQ is strictly the actionable subset. The actionable part is the point: dead letters have exactly three exits, redrive (re-enqueue with a fresh ladder, original payload, and a redrive counter incrementing so a job cannot silently loop through the DLQ forever, capped at 3 redrives before requiring a force flag), discard (operator-acknowledged deletion with a reason string), and expire (90 day retention sweep for the ones nobody ever looks at, matching the archive retention decision). Redrive semantics got the careful thought: a redriven job is a new job row with a new id carrying a redrive_of reference, not a resurrection of the old row, which keeps the archive immutable, keeps every invariant the race saga hardened (no state transition backwards, exactly the class of thing guarded_update now makes unwritable anyway), and makes redrive lineage a queryable chain. Batch redrive in ferrite-cli accepts a filter (job type, error substring, time window) with mandatory dry-run first printing what would move, the CDN outage scenario replayed as the acceptance test, all 30 jobs redriven in one command and completing against the recovered origin. Notification finally exists too, in deliberately minimal form: a notify hook fires on DLQ arrivals, first consumer is a plain email digest batched hourly (not per-job, outages arrive in herds and 30 emails is spam) via the same SMTP setup clearharbor uses for billing mail, and the hook interface is a trait so the eventual proper alerting can subscribe without touching queue code. Explicitly rejected: auto-redrive on a schedule, which sounds helpful and is actually the system making unsupervised decisions about work that already failed ten times, the whole DLQ premise being that a human glances at the pattern before more compute is spent; if a genuine auto-redrive case emerges it can argue for itself later. Wired the Grafana outcomes row with dead_letters depth and arrival rate, added the DLQ to the cli stats summary, and backfilled the last 30 days of archived terminal failures into the DLQ as a one-time seed so the digest's first edition carries the true current state, 47 entries, 31 of them the CDN batch, 9 legitimately dead links, 7 the pathological documents already known to the parse-cap thread, a satisfying census of everything previously invisible.

Clearharbor session tightening webhook processing idempotency, the second pass on the pipeline built after the deploy-window incident, prompted by a shadow-mode audit that compared entitlement state derived from a full event replay against live state and found two customers whose entitlements had drifted, both traced to processing steps that were idempotent at the event level but not across event boundaries. The drift mechanism: the drainer applies events in per-customer timestamp order, but two Stripe events can carry the same timestamp second, and the tiebreak was insertion order into webhook_events, which for redelivered events reflects delivery order not occurrence order, so an invoice.paid and a subscription.updated in the same second could apply in either order across a redelivery, and one ordering wrote a plan tier the other then overwrote with staler data. Fix in two parts: ordering now tiebreaks on the Stripe event id after timestamp (stable across redeliveries, and Stripe ids being partially time-ordered makes it a reasonable occurrence proxy), and more fundamentally the application step for subscription state became a pure function of the Stripe subscription object snapshot carried in the event, taking the newest snapshot by the object's own updated field rather than folding event deltas, so ordering within a second stops mattering at all for the fields that drifted, the event stream now selects which snapshot wins instead of each event mutating state incrementally. The two drifted customers were corrected by replaying their full event history through the new logic, which is itself the recovery tool now, a replay-customer admin command in src/webhooks.ts that rebuilds one customer's entitlement state from their complete stored event log against a clean slate, run in shadow mode by default printing a diff, apply flag to commit, the audit that found the drift promoted from one-off script to a weekly scheduled shadow replay across all customers alerting on any diff, turning this whole class of bug from years-latent to week-latent. Also hardened the dedupe boundary: the unique constraint on event id protects ingestion, but a processing crash between marking processed and committing side effects could lose an application, so processing now marks and applies in one transaction, which was true for two of three event categories and is now true for the third, the invoice-triggered email sends, made transactional-outbox style with the send itself in a follow-on step, at-least-once with an idempotency key on the mail provider call. Remaining known gap, documented not fixed: events arriving during the weekly replay window can interleave with replay writes, the replay takes a per-customer advisory lock but the drainer does not respect it yet, one-line-ish fix queued for next session, low urgency since replay runs at 4am Sunday against a drainer that is usually idle.

Clearharbor webhook idempotency session, round two of the post-incident pipeline, driven by an audit finding: a shadow replay of all stored Stripe events against a clean slate disagreed with live entitlement state for two customers. Root cause was cross-event ordering, not per-event idempotency, the drainer orders per-customer by Stripe timestamp with second granularity, and same-second event pairs fell back to webhook_events insertion order for the tiebreak, which redeliveries scramble since insertion reflects when Stripe delivered rather than when the thing happened, so a same-second invoice.paid plus subscription.updated could apply in opposite orders on different delivery histories, and the losing order let a stale plan tier win. Two-layer fix: the cheap layer is a stable tiebreak, event id after timestamp, unchanged across redeliveries; the durable layer is a semantic change to how subscription events apply, previously incremental mutations per event type, now the drainer treats subscription-bearing events as carriers of full object snapshots and simply keeps the snapshot with the greatest updated timestamp on the Stripe object itself, making same-second ordering irrelevant for exactly the fields that drifted, last-snapshot-wins replacing fold-the-deltas. Built the recovery tooling in the same session because the fix needed it anyway: replay-customer rebuilds any single customer's entitlements from their stored event history, shadow mode printing a diff by default with an explicit apply flag, used to repair both drifted customers, and the weekly all-customers shadow replay is now a scheduled job that alerts on any diff, so drift detection latency drops from whenever-someone-notices to seven days. Transactionality got one hole closed too: event processing previously marked an event processed in a separate write from its side effects for the invoice email path, a crash between the two dropping the email invisibly, now mark-plus-apply share a transaction with the actual send moved to an outbox pattern carrying an idempotency key to the mail provider. Left open and written down: the drainer does not honor the replay's per-customer advisory lock, so a live event landing mid-replay for the same customer could interleave, acceptable for a 4am Sunday replay window but queued as the next small fix; and the snapshot-wins approach quietly assumes Stripe object updated timestamps are trustworthy monotonic, which held across the full event corpus when checked but earned a validation assertion in the drainer that logs loudly if it ever observes regression.

Ferrite metrics session of the humbling kind: Prometheus fell over Tuesday night, OOM-killed at 2GB on its small Fly machine, and the postmortem took half a day to conclude the wound was self-inflicted via label cardinality, the exact sin the original metrics session smugly recorded a deliberate decision against. The mechanism arrived sideways, as these always do: no per-job-id labels were ever added, the reviewed surface stayed clean, but the DLQ work's notify hook metrics included an error_class label derived by normalizing the final error string, and the normalizer, which was supposed to collapse errors into a small stable set, passed through anything it did not recognize, and fetch errors helpfully embed hostnames, so every unique failing origin domain minted a fresh label value, 11k series on that one metric family after the CDN-outage backfill seeded the DLQ with the long tail of the internet's broken hosts. Prometheus memory grew across two weeks then tipped. Fix layers: the normalizer allowlist inverted, unrecognized errors now map to other rather than passing through, with a log line preserving the raw string so information is lost from metrics but not from observability entirely, this being the correct division since logs are where unbounded cardinality belongs; a max-cardinality circuit breaker added to the metrics facade in ferrite-core that tracks label value counts per family and hard-caps at 100 values, folding overflow into a cardinality_overflow bucket and firing a warning metric about itself, so the next sideways cardinality arrival degrades gracefully instead of murdering the collector, the breaker being arguably the real deliverable since allowlists rot; and Prometheus itself got sample and series limits configured plus a bump to a 1GB memory alert threshold, monitoring for the monitoring. Recovery was clean, the series churned out past retention within the day, dashboards unaffected once the scrape recovered, and the only permanent loss is two nights of metrics during the outage window, logs covered the gap. The general lesson entered docs/observability alongside the dashboard JSON: label values must come from code-controlled enumerations, never from data, and any derivation from data must terminate in an allowlist with a closed default, phrased exactly because the original decision said the same thing about ids and the failure arrived through a string that nobody thought of as data. The cli stats command, which reads the same metrics, was checked for the same disease and found clean. Follow-up queued: the error_class allowlist deserves five minutes of curation now that other lumps 30 percent of DLQ arrivals together, the useful distinctions (dns, tls, http_4xx, http_5xx, timeout, parse) are known from the DLQ census and just need encoding.

Ferrite operations session on the interaction between crash recovery and Fly.io deploy mechanics, pulling together loose threads from the drain work, the torture testing, and two recent deploys that behaved worse than the drain design promised. The symptom: despite the drain path handing leases back explicitly, the last two deploys each produced a small burst of sweep-based reclaims, 4 and 7 jobs respectively, meaning some workers died hard without completing their drain, and the queue_wait spike the drain work eliminated made a small comeback. Investigation went through Fly deploy logs and the answer was a stack of platform details: Fly sends SIGINT not SIGTERM by default for the configured kill_signal on these machines (a config drift from an old fly.toml edit, half the fleet's config specified kill_signal SIGTERM and half inherited the SIGINT default after a machine rebuild), the drain handler listened only for SIGTERM, so half the workers on any deploy got a signal they ignored and then the kill_timeout expired into SIGKILL mid-job. On top of that, kill_timeout was still the default 5 seconds on the rebuilt machines against the drain deadline of 20, so even the SIGTERM-receiving workers could not finish a full drain when holding slow jobs, they just usually got lucky. Fixes: worker signal handling now treats SIGINT and SIGTERM identically (there is no world where either means anything but shut down cleanly here), fly.toml normalized across all machine configs with kill_signal SIGTERM and kill_timeout 30 to give the 20 second drain honest headroom, and a startup assertion logs the effective config so drift like the rebuild-inherited default becomes visible at boot instead of at deploy time. Then made the failure observable rather than trusting it fixed: the drain path now emits drain_started, drain_completed, and per-job drain_released events with timing, and a new deploy-health query in the cli summarizes the last deploy window, drains completed versus workers seen, sweep reclaims during window (should be zero), worst drain duration, which turns the previously vibes-based deploy went fine into a number, and the next three deploys after the fix scored clean, zero sweep reclaims, worst drain 6.1 seconds held by an index batch job. That worst-drain number reopened the checkpointable-handlers question from the drain session, since a long batch job can eat most of the drain budget, but the data also showed the valve keeps batch jobs short in practice except the archive-export type, so the pragmatic move recorded was capping archive-export chunk size to keep any single job under 10 seconds rather than building handler checkpointing, the big idea once again deferred with a smaller idea doing its job, a pattern that is either wisdom or debt and gets harder to tell apart each time. Also documented the whole Fly signal and timeout contract in docs/operations/deploys.md, including the machine-rebuild config inheritance gotcha, because this is the second time platform config drift produced application-looking symptoms (the first being the metrics port allocation collision months back) and the runbook is cheaper than the rediscovery. Deferred: blue-green deploys for the workers, which Fly supports and would make deploy windows overlap-free, considered and shelved since the drain path now demonstrably delivers a zero-reclaim deploy and blue-green adds a second fleet's worth of config surface to drift.

Quillbase parser session, the long-promised sanitizer rewrite in lib/ingest/parser.ts, scheduled after the parse-cap band-aid from the timeout classification work and finally forced to the top by the DLQ census showing the pathological-document bucket still feeding failures. The quadratic behavior found during that earlier profiling was confirmed and characterized precisely: the sanitizer walked every node's ancestor chain to compute effective styling context for the keep-or-strip decision, O(depth) per node with pathological documents nesting 60+ levels deep (auto-generated span soup from certain publishing tools), yielding the observed 20-plus-second parses on big documents. Rewrite approach: single-pass traversal threading the styling context down through recursion instead of re-deriving it upward per node, the textbook fix, plus the strip rules reorganized from a scattered if-chain into a declarative rule table evaluated against the threaded context, which incidentally made the rules unit-testable in isolation for the first time, 40 rule cases now covered directly versus the previous approach of testing rules only through whole-document snapshots. Results on the fixture corpus: the worst 12MB publisher fixture drops from 24s (pre-cap) to 1.4s full-document, meaning the 3MB truncation cap installed as a band-aid is no longer needed for latency and was reconsidered on its merits, decision being to keep a cap but raise it to 10MB and re-justify it as a resource bound rather than a latency bound, with the truncation marker finally surfaced in the reader UI as a subtle notice, closing that dangling thread from the timeout session honestly instead of silently. Re-ran the 7 DLQ pathological documents through the new parser via redrive, 6 now parse cleanly including the famous 90MB-page-generating origin (its page is 8MB of actual HTML, the 90MB was a redirect loop artifact fixed separately in the fetch layer when the final-URL plumbing landed), the seventh is genuinely malformed beyond rescue and was discarded with a reason per DLQ protocol. Snapshot test maintenance was the tax of the session, the rewrite changes whitespace normalization in ways that are strictly better but touched 60 of 200 snapshots, each diff reviewed rather than blanket-accepted, which caught one real regression, the new rule table dropped figure captions inside nested picture elements, fixed with a rule case added. Parse-phase p95 across the live corpus replayed on staging: 340ms to 95ms. Deferred with a clear conscience now that latency is boring: readability extraction quality improvements for paywalled-preview pages, and the eventual structured-content ambitions (code block and table preservation fidelity) that keep almost mattering.

Quillbase session building the archive export feature, first user-facing feature to ride entirely on ferrite batch lanes and a deliberate dogfooding of every queue capability shipped this quarter. The feature: a user can request a full export of their household's clips, content and metadata, delivered as a zip of clean HTML files plus a JSONL metadata manifest, the data-ownership story a self-hosted read-later app owes its users on principle. Pipeline design: an export request creates an exports row and enqueues a plan_export job (interactive lane, it runs in milliseconds) that partitions the household's clips into chunks of 200 and enqueues one export_chunk job per chunk in the batch lane, each chunk job rendering its clips to HTML files in a staging prefix on the persistent volume, and a finalize_export job enqueued with a dependency-counter pattern, each completing chunk decrements a remaining counter on the exports row via guarded-update-style conditional decrement, and the chunk that brings it to zero enqueues finalization, which zips the staging prefix, moves the artifact into place, records the download path, and emails the requester through the same digest-tested SMTP path. The counter pattern is the interesting part since ferrite has no native job dependencies, considered building real DAG support and rejected it, the counter idiom costs 15 lines at the application layer while DAG support in the queue is a genuinely large feature with its own failure modes, and one use case does not justify it, recorded in the decisions file with the counter idiom documented as the blessed pattern until a third use case argues otherwise (the second, index rebuild completion notification, was retrofitted to the same idiom in this session as proof of reuse). Chunk sizing at 200 clips keeps each job under 8 seconds even for content-heavy chunks, comfortably inside the drain budget per the deploy-health work, verified by exporting the production household, 34k clips, 171 chunk jobs, 12 minutes end to end with the valve trickling it during normal evening usage, interactive latency untouched per the dashboard. Failure semantics thought through rather than inherited: a chunk job failing terminally marks the export failed and cleans staging via a cleanup job, no partial zips ever delivered, and the finalize counter can never be stranded by a crashed chunk because reclaim-then-retry re-runs the chunk idempotently (chunks write deterministic filenames, re-render overwrites cleanly) and only successful completion decrements, all of which fell out of existing machinery rather than needing new invention, which was the point of the dogfooding and the quarter's best evidence the queue abstractions are earning their complexity. UI is a settings-page button, a progress bar fed by remaining-counter polling, and a download link with 7 day expiry enforced by a scheduled cleanup job, batch lane, naturally. Open items: exports include no reading annotations yet since the annotations schema is mid-flux, noted in the export manifest version field for forward compatibility, and a rate limit of one concurrent export per household exists but a malicious-user story for export abuse has not been thought through, flagged for the next hardening pass.

Evening hardware detour, personal: flashed new firmware onto the mechanical keyboard, the split ergonomic one, because the right half has been intermittently dropping its first keystroke after idle and the fix candidates were firmware-level. Backed up the existing keymap first by dumping the current firmware image, learned during the last flash scare to never trust that the layout lives anywhere but the board. The keymap repo (QMK fork, kept alongside the dotfiles) needed a rebase against upstream, 8 months of drift, which brought in the new deferred-execution API that conveniently turned out to be the intended fix for exactly the idle-drop symptom, the matrix scan was being throttled too aggressively by the old power saving code and the first scan after wake ate the keystroke, and the updated power handling with a faster wake path resolves it per the changelog and, after flashing, per an hour of testing with deliberate idle gaps, zero dropped strokes. Took the opportunity to finally fix the layer arrangement annoyance, moved the symbol layer toggle from a hold-tap that misfired during fast typing to a sticky one-shot on the outer thumb key, and added a volume knob mapping for the rotary encoder that has done nothing since the board was built. Flash process itself uneventful, dfu mode, both halves, though the left half needed the reset button because the bootloader keycombo was on the layer being modified, a small chicken-and-egg comedy. Keymap changes committed to the fork with actual commit messages this time. Remaining annoyance not chased tonight: bluetooth latency on the travel board, different hardware, different rabbit hole, resisted.

Ferrite session redesigning the lease heartbeat, an efficiency and correctness pass motivated by fleet growth math: heartbeats are per-lease, every worker heartbeats each held lease every 20 seconds with an individual guarded UPDATE, and with concurrency raised to 8 jobs per worker and 6 workers, steady state is around 2.4 lease writes per second climbing linearly with fleet size, individually trivial but the deploy-health and soak data show heartbeat writes as the single largest write category on the database, 60 percent of all statements, pure overhead. Redesign: batched heartbeats, one UPDATE per worker per interval covering all its held leases via unnest of (job_id, fence) pairs, still fully guarded per row by the same three-column predicate composed within the batch statement, returning the per-row match results so LeaseLost detection stays per-lease exact, a worker holding 8 leases now writes once per 20 seconds instead of 8 times, and the statement rides through guarded_update with a new batch variant added for the purpose, the variant the race-saga module work predicted would be wanted for autoscaling and which arrived one feature early. The correctness subtlety that consumed the middle of the session: the batch UPDATE returns matched rows, and the naive implementation treated absent rows as LeaseLost uniformly, but absence can also mean the job completed between snapshot and heartbeat on the worker's own other thread, a benign self-race the per-lease code never had because completion removed the lease from the heartbeat set synchronously, while batching introduced a window between assembling the batch and executing it; resolved by having the batch assembly and the completion path share the held-lease set under a mutex with completion removing entries, and any residual absence after that is genuine LeaseLost, plus a deterministic test manufacturing the self-race via a completion injected between assembly and execution, in the spirit of the deterministic race tests being the only kind trusted around here anymore. Results measured on the soak workload generator at production-plus sizing: total database statements down 41 percent, heartbeat-attributable writes down 87 percent, jobs table dead tuple churn down enough that the autovacuum cadence from the bloat work relaxed visibly on the leases table, and claim and completion latency unchanged, with one pleasant surprise, p99 heartbeat latency improved from 4.1ms to 1.9ms because one batched statement beats eight statements racing the connection pool. Fence semantics unchanged by construction, the batch composes the same per-row predicates, and the nightly stress plus full deterministic suite ran green before merge. Follow-through items: the heartbeat interval itself deserves revisiting now that heartbeats are cheap, halving it to 10 seconds would halve worst-case reclaim latency for genuinely dead workers, tension being more writes versus faster recovery and the math now favors faster recovery at current fleet size, decided to ship the batching alone first and change one variable at a time, interval revisit queued with the reclaim-latency data collection to justify it; and the workers registry heartbeat (the janitor's liveness signal, separate from lease heartbeats) could fold into the same batch statement, minor, noted.

Quillbase design session on the search architecture question that has been deferred through every ranking and indexing improvement: whether Postgres full-text search remains the right engine or whether an external search service (the usual suspects, a dedicated search server or an embedded library with its own index files) should take over, prompted freshly by two accumulating pressures, the rank.ts note that the recency-decay multiplication defeats index shortcuts past a few hundred thousand clips, and a slow drip of quality complaints that are really tokenization complaints, hyphenated compounds, code snippets in clips being unsearchable as symbols, CJK content from two saved articles tokenizing into garbage. Spent the session as a structured evaluation rather than vibes: assembled a 60-query benchmark extending the ranking eval set with the known tokenization failure cases, stood up a local instance of the leading external candidate and an embedded-library prototype behind a thin SearchBackend seam hacked into rank.ts for the test (a seam built for the experiment, not committed as architecture, the QueueBackend trait lesson from the ferrite backend debate applying loudly here), and indexed the full 36k clip corpus into all three. Results, recorded in docs/design-notes/search-engines.md with the raw numbers: on ranking quality the external engine wins the benchmark 0.87 MRR versus 0.83 for the current blended Postgres ranking, real but modest, and the win concentrates entirely in the tokenization cases, on pure English prose queries the two tie within noise; on latency all three are boringly fine at this scale, 34ms Postgres, 11ms external, 6ms embedded at p95, differences a user cannot feel; on operational cost the external engine is a new always-on service with its own memory appetite, upgrade cadence, and backup story, the embedded library moves indexing into the Next.js process with awkward multi-instance coherence questions that its documentation waves at unconvincingly, and Postgres is already run, backed up, and understood. Decision, recorded firmly: stay on Postgres FTS, and spend the quality budget on the specific tokenization gaps within it, because the benchmark localizes the entire quality gap to tokenization, and Postgres offers targeted remedies, a custom dictionary chain for the hyphenation cases, pg_trgm fallback for symbol-ish queries (finally promoting the typo-tolerance sketch from the ranking session, since the same mechanism serves both), and honest acceptance that CJK support is poor and out of scope for two saved articles until real demand exists, documented as a known limitation instead of a driver for a new service.
