The deeper reasoning also written down since this decision will be re-litigated someday: the external engine's genuine advantages compound at corpus sizes and query rates two orders of magnitude beyond current reality, and adopting a second stateful service now buys tomorrow's scaling problem with today's operational complexity, the same shape of argument that settled the ferrite backend debate, single-store depth over multi-store breadth, and if the decision ever flips the SearchBackend seam experiment proved the migration surface is tractable, three query paths and one indexing job type. Immediate follow-ups extracted as work items: the pg_trgm fallback wired behind the empty-result condition measured at 4 percent, the hyphenation dictionary chain prototyped against the benchmark cases, and index_version bumped to drive the re-index through the now-boring lane-aware rebuild machinery, which itself is a quiet marker of how much infrastructure has hardened since the rebuild that starved the queue.

Ferrite session on worker autoscaling, the natural next step now that deploys are clean, heartbeats are cheap, and queue depth is trustworthy: the fleet currently runs a fixed 6 workers sized for evening peak, idle most of the day, undersized during rebuild bursts, and Fly machines bill by the second while stopped machines cost storage only, an obvious fit for scale-to-load. Design intentionally modest: no control plane, no new service, the workers already can see everything needed for a distributed decision through the jobs table, so scaling is a cooperative protocol among the workers themselves plus Fly machine autostart. Scale-up path: Fly machines in stopped state are woken by connection pressure via the existing autostart mechanism on the metrics port being probed by a tiny scale-probe loop that any running worker executes when it observes interactive queue_wait p95 above 2 seconds or batch depth above 5k for over a minute, waking one stopped machine per observation window with a fleet-wide advisory lock preventing thundering wake, reusing the sweep lock pattern from the torture-test fix. Scale-down path is where the correctness lives: a worker considering shutdown (queue near-empty for 10 minutes, and not the last worker, minimum floor of 2 enforced by counting live registry heartbeats) drains itself through the exact SIGTERM drain path deploys use, which was the design's best decision since it means scale-down inherits every hard-won property of the deploy work, explicit lease release, zero sweep reclaims, deploy-health observability, all for free, and then exits with a code Fly interprets as do-not-restart, machine returning to stopped state eligible for future wake. The floor-of-2 rather than scale-to-zero was debated and settled by the DLQ email digest incident class, some ferrite work (digest sending, archive moving, retention sweeps) is scheduled rather than queue-driven and a zero-worker fleet executes no schedules, revisitable if scheduled work ever moves to Fly machines cron. Simulation before deployment, replaying two weeks of production load traces against the policy in the workload generator: fleet averages 2.6 workers versus the fixed 6, evening peaks scale to 5 within 90 seconds of the wait threshold breaching, the rebuild-burst trace wakes all 8 configured machines and drains back within 20 minutes of burst end, and compute-hours drop 58 percent, at a latency cost measured as interactive p95 briefly reaching 2.8 seconds during the sharpest wake ramp versus 210ms steady state, judged acceptable since the threshold itself is 2 seconds and the excursion is the policy working. Live rollout behind a fleet config flag, first three days watched via a new autoscale row on the dashboard (wake events, drain-down events, worker count over depth), one issue found and fixed, the scale-probe evaluated its thresholds against lane-blind depth on day one, waking machines for deep batch backlogs the valve was intentionally trickling, exactly the lane confusion the lanes work was meant to prevent, probe made lane-aware, batch depth threshold separated with a much higher bar. Deferred: predictive scaling on the daily pattern (the traces show a clean evening ridge a cron pre-warm could anticipate, but reactive is currently fast enough at 90 seconds to threshold), and any scaling of the Quillbase web tier which is a different problem owned by different constraints.

Clearharbor session on an entitlement caching bug with a lesson attached: a customer downgraded from the household plan to solo, kept full household features for 34 minutes, and the mystery is that the cache TTL is 60 seconds, so staleness should have capped at a minute, not half an hour. Root cause hunt traced it to the interaction between the soft-TTL refresh scheme and the failure posture from the original caching session: the background refresh triggered at the 45 second refresh_after mark calls clearharbor, and during the incident window clearharbor was mid-deploy returning connection resets for 40 seconds, the async refresh failed, and the failure path in src/entitlements.ts logged and left the stale entry in place, correct per the serve-stale-on-outage posture, but the refresh_after timestamp was never re-armed after the failed refresh, so the entry stopped being eligible for background refresh at all and only a hard TTL expiry would evict it, except the hard TTL check had been effectively neutered for warm entries by the 10-minute stale-serving window, and the per-key in-flight guard had a bug where a failed refresh left the guard locked, blocking every subsequent refresh attempt for that key until process restart, which on the quiet weekday in question was 34 minutes away when a deploy recycled the process. Three small bugs conspiring, none visible alone: failed refresh does not re-arm, stale window slow-walks eviction, poisoned in-flight guard, the third being the actual severity multiplier. Fixes: the in-flight guard now clears in a finally block (the one-line fix that matters most), failed refreshes re-arm refresh_after with backoff so retry pressure is bounded but continuous, and the stale-serving window now applies only when the last refresh attempt failed with a connectivity-class error, a genuine outage signal, rather than any failure, so application-level errors from clearharbor (customer deleted, plan unknown) evict immediately instead of serving ghosts. Then the part that makes it stick, the downgrade path got the active invalidation the original session explicitly deferred as a policy choice: the webhook drainer now deletes cache keys on entitlement-reducing events exactly as it does for upgrades, ending the asymmetry, because the incident demonstrated the deferred case compounding with unrelated bugs into a half-hour exposure, and the honest reading of the original trade-off is that it priced the staleness alone and not the staleness multiplied by everything else that can go wrong; the served_stale counter also finally got its promised dashboard panel, split by reason, and an alert at sustained elevation. Verification: replayed the incident timeline in a test harness with a fake clearharbor made to reset connections on cue, pre-fix reproduces the 34 minute pin, post-fix caps exposure at 4 seconds (one backoff-armed retry after connectivity recovery), and the downgrade invalidation path measured end to end at under a second from webhook receipt to cache clear. Recorded in the incident log with the compound-failure framing since the pattern, deferred edge case times unrelated bug equals incident, is the one this system keeps teaching.

Small Quillbase session shipping reading progress sync, a long-requested small feature: scroll position in the reader now persists per clip per user, so returning to a half-read article resumes where you left off across devices. Implementation kept deliberately light, a reading_positions table keyed by user and clip storing a content-relative anchor (paragraph index plus offset fraction, resilient to font and viewport changes, chosen over raw scroll pixels which break on any reflow and over character offsets which break on any parser improvement, the analyzer v2 experience informing that choice), written by a debounced beacon from the reader at most every 5 seconds of active scrolling and on visibilitychange, read on clip open with a subtle resume marker rather than an automatic jump, the auto-jump variant tested and rejected as disorienting when the anchor lands mid-viewport. The sync conflict story is last-write-wins on a served_at timestamp, two devices genuinely reading the same article simultaneously is a corner case where any resolution is defensible and LWW is free. One small piece of infrastructure fallout: the beacon endpoint is the first genuinely high-frequency write path in the app, and rather than let it write Postgres per beacon it batches through a short Redis buffer flushed every 30 seconds by, naturally, a ferrite batch-lane job, which felt like overkill until the math showed a heavy reading session generating 200 writes an hour per user for data whose loss tolerance is measured in scroll-seconds, the buffer collapsing that to 2 writes with no perceptible behavior change. Tested across the phone and desktop, the resume marker does its job, and the feature shipped behind no flag because its failure mode is a lost scroll position, the rare bug severity where doing nothing is a fine fallback. Noted for the annotations work looming on the roadmap: the paragraph-anchor scheme built here is exactly the anchoring primitive annotations need, extract it into a shared module before building twice.

Quarter-closing ferrite session, part retro and part roadmap, written up deliberately as a state-of-the-queue document since the next stretch of work shifts toward Quillbase features and this is the natural bookmark. Where things stand: the queue that started the quarter losing orphaned jobs to worker crashes now has leases with fencing, uniform guarded mutations enforced at the query layer, a drain path that survives deploys and powers autoscaling, priority lanes with an anti-starvation valve, a DLQ with redrive lineage, batched heartbeats, archive separation with bloat under control, and an observability stack that caught its own cardinality incident, with the invariant record standing at 4.9 million soak jobs and six weeks of nightly stress with zero lost and zero duplicated since the guarded_update migration. The race saga remains the quarter's defining arc and its final shape is worth restating: three incidents, one underlying pattern (check-then-act across statement boundaries under read committed), and the durable fix was not any single patch but moving enforcement into a layer where the pattern cannot be expressed, a lesson that has since been applied twice more by instinct (mandatory lane parameter, snapshot-wins webhook application on the clearharbor side) and belongs in the permanent engineering vocabulary. Numbers for the record, current production steady state: 41k jobs per day, interactive queue_wait p95 210ms, fleet averaging 2.6 workers under autoscaling at 58 percent lower compute spend than the fixed fleet, dequeue p95 1.05ms, zero sweep reclaims across the last eleven deploys. The open threads carried forward, ranked by likely next-touch: checkpointable handlers stays deferred with its two workarounds (chunk sizing, archive-export caps) holding, and the honest note from the deploy session about deferral-versus-debt stands; the heartbeat interval halving awaits its reclaim-latency data collection; scheduled-work-on-zero-workers blocks true scale-to-zero and probably resolves via Fly cron eventually; DAG support stays rejected with the counter idiom at two use cases and a third would reopen it; and the SQLite backend question stays closed but the open source packaging of ferrite, which motivated it, is unstarted and will resurface the moment external users exist, at which point the Postgres-only decision, the metrics flag gating, and the docs debt all get stress-tested by strangers. Biggest known risk going into the feature-focused stretch is attention, the queue is now reliable enough to be forgotten, and the nightly stress run plus the deploy-health check plus the weekly clearharbor shadow replay are the three tripwires that watch while attention is elsewhere, all three having fired usefully at least once this quarter, which is the best available evidence the system can be safely ignored, and the reason the retro ends on it.

Spent the session standing up the first production-grade Stripe webhook receiver in clearharbor. The naive handler Marek sketched last week fell over immediately in staging: stripe.webhooks.constructEvent threw Webhook signature verification failed, no signatures found matching the expected signature for payload, because the Express json middleware was consuming and re-serializing the body before the handler saw it, which changes byte ordering and kills the HMAC check. Fixed it by mounting express.raw with type application/json only on the /stripe/webhooks route in src/webhooks.ts and keeping the parsed-body middleware everywhere else; the raw Buffer now goes straight into constructEvent along with the stripe-signature header and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, which we now inject per environment through Fly.io secrets instead of the shared .env file that had been floating around between our laptops. Decided to whitelist the event types we actually handle — checkout.session.completed, invoice.payment_succeeded, invoice.payment_failed, customer.subscription.updated, customer.subscription.deleted — and return 200 immediately for everything else so Stripe stops retrying events we do not care about. Also decided to persist every received event verbatim into a new webhook_events table (columns id, type, payload jsonb, received_at, processed_at, error) before doing any business logic, partly for debugging and partly so we can replay locally; put a 30 day retention job on it since payloads carry customer email addresses and an unbounded PII archive is a liability we do not want. Wrote the first two handlers as thin translation functions on the theory that webhooks.ts should stay a routing layer and the real logic belongs in entitlements.ts and the subscription module. Pinned the Stripe API version explicitly in the client constructor rather than floating on the account default, after reading that webhook payload shapes follow the account version and an implicit upgrade could silently rename fields under us; left a comment in src/webhooks.ts documenting the pinned version and added a checklist item for upgrading deliberately. Wrote an integration test that signs a canned invoice.payment_succeeded fixture with stripe.webhooks.generateTestHeaderString and asserts the route accepts it and rejects a tampered body, wired into the GitHub Actions job so signature handling cannot regress quietly. Tested end to end with stripe listen forwarding to localhost and a test-mode checkout for the $8 monthly Pro plan; the full loop from checkout completion to the plan row flipping to pro took about three seconds. Two open threads for next time: there is no idempotency at all yet, and Stripe explicitly delivers at least once, so a retried event would double-apply whatever it touches; and we have not decided what a throwing handler should return — for now we 500 so Stripe retries, but that means a poison event hammers us for three days, which argues for routing webhook processing through ferrite and a dead-letter path rather than anything bespoke in clearharbor.

Designed and implemented webhook idempotency for clearharbor, the missing piece flagged at the end of the last session. The core decision: a processed_events table keyed by the Stripe event id with a unique constraint, and every handler runs inside a single Postgres transaction that begins by inserting that id. If the insert hits the unique violation we know the event was already handled and the whole transaction rolls back into a no-op; if the business logic throws, the insert rolls back too, so a retry gets a clean slate. This makes handler execution exactly-once-per-effect even though delivery is at-least-once, provided every side effect lives inside the same transaction — which forced a small refactor, because the old grantEntitlement helper in src/entitlements.ts opened its own connection instead of accepting a transaction handle. Threaded a tx parameter through grantEntitlement, revokeEntitlement, and recordInvoice so callers control the transaction boundary; internal helpers no longer touch the pool directly. The second and thornier problem is ordering. Stripe does not guarantee event order, and we saw it concretely in staging: a customer.subscription.updated arriving before the customer.subscription.created it logically follows, and an invoice.payment_succeeded landing before checkout.session.completed had even created our local subscription row. Considered building a sequencing buffer that holds events until their prerequisites arrive, and rejected it as a distributed-systems science project neither of us wants to maintain. Adopted the convergent-handler pattern instead: treat every webhook as a hint that something changed, and have the handler re-fetch the authoritative object from the Stripe API — stripe.subscriptions.retrieve for subscription events — then upsert our local state to match, keyed on the Stripe object id. With upserts, applying events in any order converges to the same final state, and a stale event simply rewrites the row to values that the fresher event already wrote or will write. The cost is one extra API read per event, which at our volume of maybe two hundred events a day is nothing against the rate limit. Handlers that cannot be made convergent — the ones that send email or enqueue ferrite jobs — get their effects deduplicated separately by carrying the event id as a dedupe key into the jobs table, so even a bug in processed_events cannot double-send a receipt. Also tightened error semantics: handlers now classify failures as transient (database timeout, Stripe API 500) which return 500 so Stripe retries, or permanent (unrecognized price id, malformed payload) which get recorded in webhook_events.error with processed_at set, return 200, and fire an alert to the internal alerts webhook, because retrying a permanent failure for 72 hours accomplishes nothing except noise. Backfilled processed_events from the webhook_events archive so replays of old events are recognized. Wrote a replay script that re-posts archived payloads through the full pipeline with signatures regenerated from the test secret, and used it to run the last 300 staging events through twice back to back — zero duplicate grants, zero duplicate emails, and the mirror rows matched Stripe exactly afterward. Remaining doubt: the convergent re-fetch means a webhook for a deleted object can 404, and I have not decided whether that should be treated as permanent (object gone, converge to deleted locally) or transient; leaning permanent-with-local-tombstone but want to think about the account deletion flow first, since that will produce exactly this shape of late event.

Cleanup session dealing with the damage from the pre-idempotency era. Before processed_events landed, at least one burst of Stripe retries got double-applied, and the symptom finally surfaced: a user emailed asking why their account showed a Pro period ending fourteen months out when they had paid for twelve. Queried entitlement_grants with a window function partitioned by user_id and source reference and found 14 duplicate rows across 9 users, all clustered in a two-day window in which Fly.io had been restarting the clearharbor instance repeatedly and Stripe retried into the gaps. The bug compounded because grantEntitlement extended current_period_end additively instead of setting it from the subscription object — each duplicate invoice.payment_succeeded stacked another month on. Fixed the root cause first: grants now carry a source_event_id column, backfilled where recoverable from the webhook_events archive, with a unique index on (user_id, source_event_id) so even a code regression cannot stack duplicates again. Then wrote scripts/reconcile_grants.ts, which walks every user with an active subscription, fetches the authoritative subscription from Stripe, and compares current_period_end against our local value; it has a dry-run mode that prints a diff table and a commit mode that rewrites local state to match Stripe inside a transaction with an audit row. Dry run found the expected 9 users plus 2 more with drift in the opposite direction from a manual dashboard edit months ago. Ran commit mode, verified the diff table came back empty on a second pass, and emailed the affected user an apology with an extra month comped — decided comping beats clawing back a month someone was told they had, and the cost is roughly $8 against the goodwill. Standing decision recorded in the repo docs: every webhook-driven mutation must carry source_event_id from now on, no exceptions, and reconcile_grants runs weekly in CI as a drift alarm rather than waiting for the next confused customer email.

Short ferrite session to give clearharbor a way to send billing email without blocking a request or a webhook handler. Added a billing_email job kind to ferrite-core: clearharbor inserts a row into the shared jobs table with kind billing_email and a payload containing template name, recipient, and a variables map, and the dispatch match in src/worker.rs routes it to a new handler that renders the template with minijinja and sends through the SMTP relay. Decided rendering belongs in the worker rather than shipping pre-rendered HTML in the payload — keeps job rows small and means a template fix applies to queued jobs, not just future ones. Versioned the payload with a schema_version field set to 1 so we can evolve the shape without guessing later. Payloads are validated with serde into a typed struct at dequeue time; a payload that fails to deserialize is a permanent failure, no retries. Added max_attempts 5 with exponential backoff for SMTP transients in src/queue.rs, honoring the existing lease semantics from src/lease.rs. First real consumer will be payment receipts, then the dunning sequence once that gets designed. Left a TODO on dedupe keys — the jobs table needs a unique dedupe_key column before anything retry-adjacent enqueues email, or a webhook replay could send a customer the same receipt twice.

Built the upgrade path from monthly to annual Pro in clearharbor. Pricing is $8 a month or $80 a year, and the whole point of the annual push is cash up front, so the first decision was proration_behavior: with the default create_prorations, the credit and the new charge just sit on the subscription as pending invoice items until the next billing cycle, meaning someone could switch to annual and not pay for three weeks. Went with always_invoice instead, which finalizes and charges immediately — user clicks upgrade, card is charged, done. Verified the arithmetic in test mode: upgrading 10 days into a monthly cycle produced an invoice with a -$5.33 credit line for unused time on the $8 plan and the full $80 annual charge, netting $74.67, which matches what the marketing page promises. Second decision was the preview. Showing a user Upgrade for $80 and then charging $74.67 is fine; the reverse would be a support ticket, and the exact credit drifts by the hour. Used the upcoming invoice preview endpoint with subscription_details and a pinned proration_date generated at the moment the confirmation modal renders, then passed that same proration_date into the actual update call, so the number the user confirms is the number the card sees even if they sit on the modal for ten minutes. The preview endpoint returns line items in cents with the proration flag set on the credit lines, and the modal sums them rather than trusting any single field, after a test-mode case where a leftover discount produced a third line I had not accounted for. Wired the flow as POST /billing/upgrade in clearharbor which validates the session, fetches the subscription, refuses if the subscription is not active or already annual, and returns the finalized invoice id; Quillbase just renders. Recorded the direction decision explicitly in the code comments: upgrades take effect immediately with always_invoice, and downgrades will NOT reuse this path — deferring plan decreases to period end needs subscription schedules, which is its own session. Open thread: the webhook side sees the proration invoice as a normal invoice.payment_succeeded, and the receipt email template reads slightly absurd for a $74.67 partial — need a proration-aware receipt template before pushing annual hard in the UI.

Downgrade session, the deferred half of the proration work. The rule we want: upgrades are immediate (shipped with always_invoice last time), downgrades take effect at period end — nobody gets money back mid-cycle and nobody loses paid-for time. First attempt used cancel_at_period_end plus a scheduled re-subscribe, which is obviously wrong the moment you say it out loud (a cancellation email fires, the card requires re-authorization, involuntary churn risk for a voluntary downgrade), so that got deleted within the hour. The correct tool is subscription schedules: stripe.subscriptionSchedules.create with from_subscription to adopt the live subscription, then two phases — the current phase pinned to its existing end date, and a second phase starting at period end with the target price. Immediately hit the classic footgun on the very next unrelated code path: once a subscription is managed by a schedule, a plain stripe.subscriptions.update throws You cannot update a subscription that is managed by a subscription schedule, which broke the upgrade endpoint for any user who had a pending downgrade. Wrote a helper releaseScheduleIfPending that checks subscription.schedule, and if the schedule exists only to serve a pending downgrade, releases it (releasing keeps the subscription intact, cancelling the schedule would cancel the subscription — the naming is a trap and I wrote a comment saying so in blunt terms). So the interaction matrix now works: downgrade then re-upgrade before period end releases the schedule and applies the upgrade immediately; downgrade twice just rewrites phase two. Second bug was on our webhook side. The phase transition at period end emits invoice events whose line items include proration lines, and the invoice.payment_succeeded handler in src/webhooks.ts was treating any successful invoice as a signal to extend entitlements, which double-counted when a schedule transition and a renewal landed together in test-clock simulation. Resolved it with a clean division of responsibility, now written at the top of webhooks.ts: subscription state and entitlements change ONLY in response to customer.subscription.updated and customer.subscription.deleted, which carry the authoritative status and period; invoice events drive ONLY receipts, dunning, and revenue records. Reran the whole matrix under a Stripe test clock — monthly to annual immediate, annual to monthly at period end, downgrade then upgrade, downgrade then cancel — and the mirror table tracked correctly through all four. The remaining ugliness is display: between scheduling a downgrade and period end, Stripe reports the subscription on the old price while our UI needs to say Annual until March 4, then monthly, so /billing/subscription now returns a pending_change object derived from the schedule phases, and Quillbase renders it as a banner with an undo button wired to the release helper. Undo tested, works, feels genuinely good. Note for the future: the customer portal has its own proration settings and will happily let users do plan switches with different behavior than ours — when we adopt the portal we either align its config or disable plan switches there entirely.

Personal session, nothing to do with work. Finally wrote the photo library dedupe script that has been on the someday list since the last laptop migration left three overlapping copies of everything. Python, using perceptual hashing rather than byte hashing since half the duplicates are re-exports with different JPEG quality or stripped EXIF: phash at 16 bytes per image, walk the 48,000-file library, bucket by hash, then within buckets compare hamming distance with a threshold of 6, which testing on a known-duplicate folder showed catches quality-variant copies without false-positiving burst shots. Burst shots were the surprise problem — sequential frames of the same scene sit at distance 4 to 8, so the threshold alone was not enough, and the script now also requires matching capture timestamps within two seconds when EXIF survives, or falls back to exact dimension match plus distance 3 or less when it does not. Keeps the copy with the earliest file mtime and the most EXIF fields, moves the rest to a quarantine directory rather than deleting, prints a decision log. First full run found 9,412 duplicates reclaiming 62 GB, and spot-checking 50 quarantined files found zero mistakes. Letting the quarantine sit for a month before emptying it, because confidence is not the same thing as having your wedding photos.

Design session for session-token rotation in clearharbor, since the current implementation — a random token in a cookie that lives for 90 days and dies only on explicit logout — is the kind of thing you write in week one and regret in an incident. Decisions, with reasoning. Tokens stay opaque, not JWTs: revocation has to be instant when we suspect theft, and a stateless JWT cannot be revoked without rebuilding the state we were trying to avoid; clearharbor sits next to its Postgres anyway, so the lookup is a non-problem, and a small Redis cache in front absorbs the hot path. Two-token model in src/session.ts: a 15-minute access token checked from Redis, and a single-use refresh token that rotates on every use. Each refresh issues a new refresh token and marks the old one used, and all tokens issued from one login share a family id. The family is the security primitive: if a refresh token that was already rotated gets presented again, someone is replaying a stolen token — either the attacker or the victim holds the stale one, and we cannot tell which — so the whole family is revoked and both parties get logged out to re-authenticate. That reuse-detection rule comes straight from the OAuth security best-current-practice guidance and is the single biggest win of the design. Lifetimes: 30 days absolute from login, 14 days idle — a refresh inside the idle window slides expiry, but nothing extends past the absolute cap. Storage is sha256 hashes only, never raw tokens, so a database leak does not hand out live sessions. Cookie is __Host-ch_session, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite Lax — Lax and not Strict because Strict breaks landing on the app from an email link, and the state-changing routes all have CSRF protection anyway. Sketched the sessions table migration (family_id, token_hash, used_at, expires_at, absolute_expires_at, last_ip, last_user_agent) and stubbed rotateSession and revokeFamily. Implementation and the inevitable concurrency fun are next session; flagged in the notes that two tabs refreshing simultaneously is going to trip reuse detection and needs an answer before this ships.

Worked through the redesign of clearharbor session handling today — pure design, no production code yet beyond stubs. The existing scheme (one long-lived random cookie token, 90 days, revoked only on manual logout) has no way to notice a stolen token, which is the actual threat worth engineering against. Landed on rotating refresh-token families, implemented in src/session.ts. Shape of it: short-lived access tokens, 15 minutes, validated against Redis; refresh tokens that are strictly single-use, where every refresh call retires the presented token and mints a successor; and a family id stamped on every token descended from the same login. The family exists for one reason — theft detection. Present an already-retired refresh token and the server concludes the token leaked (no way to know if the presenter is the thief or the victim), kills every token in the family, and forces a fresh login on both ends. This mirrors the recommendation in the OAuth security BCP and turns a silent compromise into a visible logout event. Chose opaque database-backed tokens over JWTs deliberately: instant revocation matters more to us than statelessness, the verification hop is a local Postgres or Redis hit, and we avoid the entire key-rotation and algorithm-confusion surface. Expiry policy: 14-day sliding idle window, 30-day hard ceiling from initial login regardless of activity. At rest we keep only sha256 digests of tokens, so a leaked backup or a read-only SQL injection yields nothing replayable. Cookie hardening rides along: renamed to __Host-ch_session to get the prefix guarantees, HttpOnly and Secure of course, SameSite Lax rather than Strict since Strict eats top-level navigations from external links and our CSRF tokens already cover the mutating endpoints. Wrote the migration draft for the sessions table with family_id, token_hash, used_at, both expiry columns, and last-seen metadata for an eventual active-sessions screen. Known open problem going into implementation: concurrent refreshes from multiple tabs will make the second tab present a just-retired token and false-trigger family revocation — needs a grace mechanism or idempotent rotation, deciding next session.

Implementation session for the session-rotation design, and the concurrency problem flagged last time showed up exactly on schedule. Built rotateSession in src/session.ts: transaction marks the presented refresh token used, inserts the successor with the same family_id, updates Redis for the new access token, returns the pair. Built revokeFamily. Wired reuse detection: presenting a token with used_at set logs token reuse detected for family with the family id and revokes everything. Shipped it to staging, and within an hour the log was full of exactly that line — not from attackers, from me, because Quillbase open in two tabs fires two refreshes with the same token when both tabs wake from a laptop sleep, the first wins the rotation, and the second presents what is now a used token. In production this would have force-logged-out every multi-tab user roughly daily; the staging extrapolation was something like 40 forced logouts a day against maybe 2 genuine thefts a year, which is a terrible trade. Considered a per-family mutex so the second refresh blocks and then succeeds with a fresh token of its own — rejected because the second tab still holds the pre-rotation token it sent, so serialization alone does not save it. The fix that works is idempotent rotation with a grace window: when a token is rotated we store successor_id on the used token, and a re-presentation of that token within 10 seconds of its used_at timestamp returns the SAME successor pair instead of triggering revocation, so both tabs converge on one live token. Re-presentation after the grace window is treated as genuine reuse and burns the family. Ten seconds came from measuring tab-wake refresh spreads in staging (worst observed was 3.1 seconds, so 10 gives margin without leaving a meaningful theft window — a thief replaying within 10 seconds of the victim gets the same successor the victim already holds, and the victim's next refresh still trips detection). Serialized concurrent rotations per family with a short Redis lock so the two requests cannot both think they performed the rotation, with the lock keyed on family id and a 2 second TTL as deadlock insurance. Rewrote the tests around a simulated two-tab race using two parallel requests against one token and asserting both receive the identical successor and the family survives; also a test that a third presentation at 11 seconds kills the family. Forced logouts in staging dropped to zero over the following two days, and the one deliberate replay I ran from a second machine outside the window revoked the family exactly as designed. Also added last_ip and last_user_agent updates on rotation, which makes the future active-sessions screen nearly free. Migration ran clean in production with the old 90-day tokens honored until natural expiry via a compatibility branch that treats legacy tokens as their own single-member families — no forced logout wave, which Marek specifically asked for since the last thing a two-person company needs is every user emailing at once.

Session on the Quillbase side of entitlements — the consumer half of what clearharbor serves. Added lib/billing/entitlements.ts in the Quillbase repo (deliberately mirroring the clearharbor filename so grepping either repo tells the same story) exposing getEntitlements(userId) which calls clearharbor at GET /internal/entitlements/:userId authenticated with a shared service token over the private Fly.io network. The interesting decisions were all about failure. Every page render calling across to clearharbor would couple Quillbase uptime to clearharbor uptime, so there is a 60-second in-memory cache with stale-while-revalidate: serve the cached value immediately, refresh in the background once it is older than 60 seconds, and only block on the network when there is no cached value at all. On clearharbor being unreachable, the policy took some arguing with myself: fail-open for everything except explicit Pro-only features. Read paths never gate — nobody should be unable to see their own clips because the billing service is down. Clip creation over the free limit technically should block, but blocking saves during an outage punishes paying intent with data loss (the clip they tried to save is gone), so creation fails open with a structured log line entitlements_unavailable_fail_open and an alert, accepting that an outage window lets some free users exceed 200 clips — the blast radius is a few free clips, versus the alternative blast radius of lost user data. Pro-only features like partner sync fail closed because the failure mode there is showing a feature that then errors deeper in the stack, which is worse than a clear upgrade prompt. Response shape from clearharbor is the versioned v1 envelope with plan, features map, and a generated_at timestamp; the client refuses to cache a response older than five minutes by that timestamp, which protects against a misbehaving proxy cache someday. Wrote contract tests against a recorded fixture of the clearharbor response so either repo changing the shape breaks CI rather than production. Next session: actually enforcing clip_limit in the clips route, which is deliberately a one-liner now that this layer exists.

Fleshed out src/entitlements.ts in clearharbor into an actual service instead of the two hardcoded functions it was. The model: a plans table mapping plan ids to a features jsonb, currently free with clip_limit 200, and pro with clip_limit null meaning unlimited, plus partner_sync true and priority_fetch true. Kept features as data rather than code after going back and forth — the code version type-checks better, but comping a friend a custom limit or grandfathering a cohort becomes a migration instead of an insert, and with two of us the flexibility wins. There is also a feature_overrides jsonb column on users that merges over the plan features, which is how one-off arrangements happen without inventing fake plans. The endpoint GET /internal/entitlements/:userId resolves user, subscription status, plan, and overrides into the flat v1 envelope Quillbase consumes: plan, features, status, and generated_at. Decided firmly that this endpoint reads ONLY our local subscriptions mirror and never calls Stripe inline — it sits on every Quillbase page render, and putting a third-party API in that path would be a self-inflicted outage waiting to happen; the mirror is kept honest by the webhook pipeline and that is the deal. Statuses map conservatively: active and trialing resolve to the plan's features, past_due keeps them temporarily (grace handling is its own upcoming session), everything else resolves to free. Added an ETag derived from a hash of the envelope so Quillbase's refresh calls mostly return 304 and the whole exchange costs almost nothing. Wrote table-driven tests across the status times override matrix, 14 cases, including the one that already caught a bug: a canceled subscription with a leftover feature_overrides entry was resolving to pro features because the merge ran before the status check instead of after. Merge now applies only to the status-resolved base. Remaining thread: nothing invalidates the Quillbase-side 60-second cache when an upgrade lands, so a user who pays can stare at a free-tier banner for up to a minute — fine for now, but the paywall session should add a poke.

Quick session wiring the actual enforcement into Quillbase. POST in app/api/clips/route.ts now consults getEntitlements before insert, and over-limit free users get a 402 with a machine-readable body: code clip_limit_reached, current count, the limit, and an upgradeUrl pointing at the billing page with a context parameter for attribution. Chose 402 over 403 deliberately — it is the semantically honest status and it gives the frontend one unambiguous thing to switch on. Counting clips was the only real work: count(*) per save is a table scan waiting to get slow, so users now carry a denormalized clip_count maintained in the same transaction as the insert and delete paths. Considered a trigger for it but kept it in application code where it is visible and testable; there are exactly two write paths and both live in this route file. Backfilled the counter from a one-off script and added a nightly drift check that recounts and alerts on mismatch rather than silently fixing, since a mismatch means a write path I forgot. Deletes decrement, so a user at the limit can delete two clips and save one, which is the behavior that feels fair. The GET and search paths remain deliberately ungated per the fail-open policy decided in the entitlements client session — limits stop accumulation, never access to what you already saved. Frontend work to catch the 402 and render something better than a toast is next.

Built the Quillbase paywall proper — the thing users actually see when they hit the 402 from the clips route. An upgrade modal component that catches clip_limit_reached, shows current usage against the 200-clip free limit, offers monthly at $8 and annual at $80, and hands off to Stripe Checkout via a new clearharbor endpoint POST /billing/checkout that creates the session server-side with the right price id, the user's existing Stripe customer if one exists, and success and cancel URLs back into Quillbase. Decided against embedding a payment form and for hosted Checkout without much agonizing: two-person company, PCI scope of nothing, conversion-optimized payment UI for free, and the cost is only that the user leaves our domain for a minute. The genuinely tricky part was the return trip. The success URL lands the user back on /clips?upgraded=1 but the entitlement flip happens when the checkout.session.completed webhook processes, and there is a real race: in testing, the redirect beat the webhook by two to nine seconds routinely, and once by forty when I had stripe listen paused. First instinct was to just trust the upgraded=1 parameter and render Pro immediately, which is wrong twice over — the parameter is spoofable by anyone who can type a query string, and optimistically showing unlimited saves that then 402 again is a support nightmare. Went with honest optimism instead: the redirect param triggers only a processing banner (Payment received, activating your plan) and the client polls the entitlements endpoint every two seconds for up to fifteen, flipping the UI the moment the real entitlement lands. If fifteen seconds pass without the flip, the banner degrades to a message saying activation is taking longer than usual with a support link — in staging that path has fired only when I deliberately broke the webhook worker, but the incident-shaped part of my brain wanted it there. Also handled the cancel path: cancel_url lands on /clips?checkout=canceled which logs an analytics event and reopens nothing, on the theory that re-shoving the modal at someone who just backed out is hostile. Instrumented the funnel with our self-hosted analytics: paywall_view, plan_selected with the interval, checkout_started, checkout_completed, and the delta between the last two is the number Marek cares about weekly. One deliberate scope cut, recorded here so it does not look like an oversight later: no coupon field and no plan comparison table in the modal — the modal sells the one thing it can sell at the moment of highest intent, and the marketing page can do the rest. Open threads: the receipt email for the initial charge still uses the generic template flagged back in the proration session, and the entitlements cache poke from clearharbor to Quillbase still does not exist, so the two-second poll is doing load-bearing work the cache invalidation should be doing.

Dunning session — what happens after invoice.payment_failed, on the email side. Designed a three-step sequence driven entirely by ferrite billing_email jobs enqueued from the clearharbor webhook handler: day 0 a soft heads-up (card declined, we will retry automatically, here is a portal link to update payment), day 3 a firmer note with the retry date, day 7 a final notice stating the date access drops to the free tier. Tone decisions written into the templates themselves: no red banners, no ALL CAPS urgency, the working theory being that people whose cards expired are customers having a minor administrative moment, not adversaries. All three jobs are enqueued at once with scheduled_at offsets rather than each email scheduling the next — a chain where step two enqueues step three has a single point of failure per link, while enqueue-all-up-front means one webhook handler owns the whole plan. That required cancellation to be first-class: when invoice.payment_succeeded or customer.subscription.updated shows recovery, the handler deletes pending jobs by dedupe-key prefix dunning:invoiceId: so a recovered customer never gets a stale final notice, and there is a test that walks exactly that recovery-between-steps timeline. Dedupe keys are dunning:invoiceId:step with the unique constraint on jobs.dedupe_key doing enforcement, so webhook replays cannot double-enqueue — this leaned directly on the dedupe column TODO from the original billing_email session, which got built here. Each send also records into a sent_emails ledger keyed by the same dedupe key, belt and suspenders so even a replayed job cannot re-send. Copy for all three templates written and reviewed with Marek over a call; he cut my favorite sentence and he was right. Not yet handled: customers with no portal-reachable payment method at all (card removed entirely), who currently get the same emails with a link that cannot help them — logged as a follow-up rather than blocking, since the population is currently zero people.

Worked out the full failed-payment lifecycle in clearharbor, the state-machine half that the dunning emails hang off. Stripe's smart retries are configured to four attempts over three weeks, and the subscription sits in past_due throughout, so the question was what past_due means for entitlements. Decided on a 14-day grace window: a grace_until timestamp set by the invoice.payment_failed handler, during which entitlements.ts continues resolving Pro features; past grace_until, resolution falls to free even though the subscription object still says past_due. Fourteen days covers the realistic card-fix latency (new card in the mail takes a week to ten days) without letting the effectively-unpaying ride for the full retry window. Deliberately did NOT immediately downgrade on first failure — the most common cause is an expired card on an annual renewal, and yanking access on day zero for someone 51 weeks into paying is how you convert a card expiry into a cancellation. The state transitions are all driven by customer.subscription.updated per the division of responsibility decided during the schedules session: recovery clears grace_until and cancels pending dunning jobs, transition to canceled or unpaid at the end of Stripe's retry ladder clears entitlements and stamps the row. Also decided Stripe's setting for what happens after final retry should be mark canceled rather than leave unpaid, because unpaid subscriptions accrue invoices for service the user is not receiving, which is both rude and an accounting mess; cancellation is honest and the user can re-subscribe cleanly. Edge case that cost an hour: a user who fixes their card via the portal mid-grace triggers invoice.payment_succeeded on the RETRY invoice, not a new one, and my grace-clearing logic was keyed to the wrong invoice id — caught by a test-clock run of the full decline-then-recover timeline, fixed by keying on subscription id instead. Wrote the whole lifecycle as a state diagram comment at the top of the subscription module because in six months neither of us will remember why grace_until exists. Follow-up thread: the account page should surface grace state (your card failed, N days of Pro remain, fix it here) instead of leaving the UI silent until features vanish.

Weekend interlude, logged for honesty. Spent four hours on my parents' printer, which had stopped being discoverable from either of their laptops after their ISP swapped the router. Diagnosis meandered through every layer: the printer had wifi, could print a test page from its own panel, but neither macOS nor Windows could see it. Root cause was the new router shipping with AP isolation enabled by default on the 2.4GHz band — every wireless client walled off from every other, which is a fine default for a coffee shop and a bewildering one for a home network, and it silently breaks the mDNS discovery that everything consumer depends on. Turned AP isolation off, and discovery came back on the Mac immediately. Windows took another hour because it had cached three ghost copies of the old printer queue, all pointing at a DHCP address the printer no longer held; deleted all three, and rather than trust discovery twice, gave the printer a DHCP reservation on the router and added the queue by IP with the driverless IPP path. Printed test pages from both laptops, then documented everything in a note taped inside the router cabinet: the reservation address, the admin password location, and the sentence do not factory reset the router before calling me. The recurring lesson from every visit home is that the fix is thirty minutes and the diagnosis is three and a half hours, and that consumer networking gear changes one invisible default per generation specifically to keep adult children humble.

Big session kicking off the partner OAuth work. Context for the record: Otterworks, the e-ink reader company, wants their device to sync a user's Quillbase clips — their firmware would pull unread clips and push read-state back — and they are exactly the kind of partner that makes the annual plan sticky, so this got prioritized over the billing portal work. That means clearharbor grows a real OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and today was protocol decisions plus the first third of the implementation. Flow selection first. Authorization code flow, full stop: the user must consent in our UI, tokens must never transit the browser fragment, and the device itself never sees Quillbase credentials. Implicit flow is dead per current guidance and was never considered; client credentials is wrong because this is user-scoped data; device authorization flow is tempting given they ship hardware, but Otterworks confirmed their onboarding runs through their phone app which can hold a proper browser session, so standard authorization code with the phone as the user agent works and keeps our surface smaller — device flow can come later if their UX changes. PKCE with S256 is mandatory even though Otterworks is a confidential client with a secret; it costs them ten lines of code and closes the authorization-code-injection class outright, and making it mandatory now means we never ship the flag that lets someone forget it. Token format was the meatiest decision. JWTs are seductive for a resource server split like ours — Quillbase could verify locally without calling clearharbor — but revocation reality won: when a user disconnects Otterworks or we kill a compromised client, access has to end within seconds, not at token expiry, and the moment you add the revocation list you have rebuilt statefulness with extra steps and a key-rotation liability on top. So access tokens are opaque random strings, sha256-hashed at rest exactly like session tokens, and Quillbase validates them against a new clearharbor introspection endpoint POST /oauth/introspect (RFC 7662 shape: active, scope, sub, client_id, exp), with Quillbase allowed to cache a positive introspection for at most 60 seconds — the compromise number where revocation latency stays bounded by a minute and steady-state sync traffic amortizes to one introspection per device per minute. Consistency with the session-token philosophy was itself an argument: one revocation model in the codebase, not two. Schema landed as three tables. oauth_clients: client_id, client_secret hashed with the same KDF as passwords, redirect_uris as a strict array with exact-match-only comparison (no wildcards, no substring matching, the comment cites the classic open-redirect-to-token-theft chain), scopes allowed, and a suspended flag for the kill switch. oauth_codes lives in Redis, not Postgres: 60-second TTL, single-use enforced by an atomic GETDEL, stores the PKCE challenge, user id, client id, scope, and redirect_uri for the token-exchange comparison. oauth_grants: the durable record of user-approved-client-with-scopes that consent checks read, one row per user-client pair, updated on scope expansion. Scopes defined so far are deliberately few: read:clips, write:clips (read covers pull-to-device, write covers pushing read-state and archiving), and offline which gates refresh token issuance following the convention everyone recognizes. Otterworks asked for a read:highlights scope for a feature their next firmware wants; said yes in principle but not until highlights are actually a first-class object in Quillbase, and wrote that in the shared doc so it does not become a verbal commitment with a phantom deadline. Implemented the authorize endpoint in a new src/oauth/authorize.ts (webhooks.ts and session.ts stay untouched; auth server code gets its own directory): validates client_id exists and is not suspended, redirect_uri exact-matches registration, scope is a subset of the client's allowance, response_type is code, state is present and echoed back verbatim — state is required, not optional, and the error page for a bad redirect_uri deliberately does NOT redirect (you never redirect to an unvalidated URI, even to report an error; the RFC is explicit and people get it wrong constantly). If the user has a live clearharbor session and an existing grant covering the requested scopes, the flow can skip straight to code issuance; any scope expansion re-prompts. The consent screen itself is stubbed to auto-approve in the dev environment only, real UI next session. Token endpoint POST /oauth/token handles grant_type authorization_code: authenticates the client with basic auth against the hashed secret, GETDELs the code so a second exchange attempt finds nothing, verifies the PKCE verifier hashes to the stored challenge, verifies redirect_uri matches the one bound at authorization time, then mints an access token with a 30-minute TTL and, when offline was granted, a refresh token wired into a partner-token variant of the existing family-rotation machinery. Deferred deliberately: refresh rotation for partner tokens needs the session rotation code generalized rather than copy-pasted, and that refactor deserves its own session instead of being rushed at hour six; rate limiting per client; the grant revocation UI. Tested the happy path and eleven deliberately hostile variants with a script that speaks raw HTTP — wrong verifier, reused code, expired code, mismatched redirect_uri, scope escalation at the token endpoint, suspended client — all rejected with the correct RFC 6749 error codes. The suspended-client test caught a real bug: suspension was checked at authorize time but not at token time, so a client suspended mid-flow could still redeem an outstanding code. Fixed, test locked in. Sent Otterworks their staging client_id today; their sandbox hits our staging next week, which is the real test of whether the error responses are as self-explanatory as I think they are.

Follow-through session on partner OAuth: refresh rotation and scope enforcement, the two deliberate deferrals. The refactor first. Session refresh tokens and partner refresh tokens want identical mechanics — single-use, family id, reuse detection burns the family, grace-window idempotent rotation for concurrent presenters — and the wrong move was copy-pasting session.ts into the oauth directory to drift independently forever. Extracted the machinery into src/tokens.ts as a TokenStore parameterized by table and lifetime policy: session.ts now instantiates it over the sessions table with 14-day idle and 30-day absolute, and the oauth module instantiates it over oauth_tokens with 90-day absolute and no idle window (a reader device that sits in a drawer for a month should not force re-linking; the 90-day cap plus rotation-on-use is the theft bound, and reuse detection still applies in full). The extraction immediately paid for itself by catching a latent bug: the partner path was looking up presented refresh tokens in the SESSIONS table — the copy-paste error I almost shipped — which surfaced in staging as invalid_grant on every single Otterworks refresh. The Otterworks sandbox engineer reported it within an hour of getting staging access, with a beautifully precise reproduction; fixed by the parameterization itself, since there is no longer a hardcoded table name to get wrong. Their sandbox then completed link, sync, unlink, relink, and a 26-hour soak with hourly refreshes overnight — zero errors. Scope enforcement second. Quillbase partner routes live under app/api/partner/ and now pass through a requireScope middleware that introspects the bearer token against clearharbor (60-second positive cache per the introspection decision) and asserts the required scope: read:clips on the pull endpoints, write:clips on the read-state push. Wrote the middleware to attach sub and client_id to the request context so downstream handlers never parse the token themselves, and added the insufficient_scope error response with the WWW-Authenticate header per RFC 6750, which the Otterworks client library apparently parses natively — their engineer was pleased, which I am counting as an integration test of the spec-compliance bet. Rate limiting went in as a Redis sliding window per client_id: 60 requests a minute on the data routes, 10 a minute on the token endpoint, the latter mostly as brute-force insurance since client secrets are long random strings. Chose per-client rather than per-token limits so a partner cannot widen their budget by minting sessions. 429s carry Retry-After. Remaining before this is GA rather than staging-only: the consent screen is still the dev auto-approve stub, there is no way for a user to see or revoke the Otterworks grant, and no audit trail of grant events — all one session of work, and it is the next one.

Closed out the user-facing third of the OAuth work. Built the real consent screen in clearharbor: client display name and logo (served from our own storage, uploaded at client registration — never hotlinked from the partner, both for privacy and because a partner controlling an image on our consent page is a phishing canvas), the requesting scopes rendered in human language from a scope-to-description map (read:clips becomes See your saved articles, write:clips becomes Mark articles as read and archive them), and Approve and Deny with no dark patterns — Deny is the same size and weight as Approve, which took exactly one line of argument with myself and zero with Marek. Approval writes the oauth_grants row and redirects with the code; denial redirects with error access_denied per spec so the partner app can handle it gracefully. Scope expansion on an existing grant renders a differential consent screen showing only the NEW permissions with the existing ones listed as already granted, because re-consenting to everything trains people to click approve without reading. Added the grants management view to the account page: each connected app with its scopes in the same human language, connected date, last-used timestamp (bumped by introspection at most hourly to keep write traffic sane), and a Disconnect button that deletes the grant and revokes every live token for that user-client pair through the TokenStore in one transaction. Disconnect is immediate — within the 60-second introspection cache bound — and the Otterworks device's next sync gets invalid_token, which their firmware handles by prompting to relink; verified against their sandbox. Backing all of it is a new append-only auth_events table recording grant created, scopes expanded, grant revoked, family-reuse detections, and client suspensions, with actor, timestamps, ip, and user agent — the table the future security page and any incident response will read from. Decided grants survive password changes (changing a password is not evidence you distrust your e-reader) but the revoke-all-sessions panic button now also kills partner tokens, because the person hitting the panic button means everything and partial panic is a support ticket plus a worse incident. OAuth GA checklist is now: rotate the Otterworks client to a production client_id, and done.

Started the account deletion flow for Quillbase, design-first because deletion is the one feature where a bug is unrecoverable by definition. Core decision: soft delete with a 30-day grace window, not immediate destruction. The horror scenario driving it is account takeover — someone phishes a session, hits delete, and a real user loses years of saved reading with no recourse; 30 days converts that from catastrophe to inconvenience. Requesting deletion requires a fresh password confirmation (not just a live session) and then sets deleted_at, which immediately: revokes all session families and partner token families through the TokenStore, hides all clips from every read path via a global deleted_at guard in the query helpers rather than per-route filters (one choke point, impossible to forget on a new route), removes the account from search indexing, and sends a confirmation email stating the purge date with a single-click restore link. Logging in during grace shows exactly one screen: your account is scheduled for deletion on date X, restore or leave. Restore clears deleted_at and reindexes; nothing else needed because nothing was destroyed. Deliberately decided against the pattern where the confirmation email link performs the deletion (email links that destroy things get clicked by scanners and forwarded by confused people) — email confirms identity for the restore path, never the destructive path. Also decided the grace period is non-negotiable even when users ask for immediate erasure; support can shorten it manually after an identity check if someone has a genuine urgent reason, but the self-serve path always gets the safety margin, and the deletion screen says so plainly. The hard purge itself — cascade order, blob storage, billing interplay, what survives for legal retention — is designed on paper but unimplemented; it will run as a ferrite job and it is the next session. Open question flagged for that session: what happens when a deletion request arrives while a Stripe subscription is active, which touches refund policy and cannot be answered by engineering preference alone.

Implemented the hard-purge half of account deletion. It runs as a ferrite job kind account_purge, enqueued at deletion request time with scheduled_at set to deleted_at plus 30 days, and the job re-checks deleted_at is still set at execution — a restore during grace leaves a scheduled job that must become a no-op, and making the job self-verifying is sturdier than trying to cancel it from the restore path (though restore also cancels by dedupe key as a courtesy; the re-check is the guarantee, the cancel is an optimization). Purge order took real thought because every ordering mistake is either an FK violation or an orphan. First attempt deleted the user row first and Postgres immediately taught me the lesson: update or delete on table users violates foreign key constraint clips_user_id_fkey on table clips. Rather than switching everything to ON DELETE CASCADE — which makes the database silently do in one opaque step the thing I specifically want to be explicit, logged, and resumable — the job deletes in dependency order with progress markers: search index entries for the user's clips, then clip full-text rows, then clips in batches of 500 with a progress cursor so a crash mid-purge resumes instead of restarting, then stored article snapshots in blob storage (the step most likely to partially fail, hence early progress persistence), then oauth grants and token families, then sessions, then finally the user row. Each step writes to a purge_log so we can answer what was destroyed and when, without retaining any of the destroyed content. Blob deletion gets verified with a follow-up existence check because storage deletes are the classic silent-failure. The billing interplay resolved partially: the Stripe customer object is NOT deleted — invoices and dispute history have legitimate retention requirements measured in years — but we redact what we control: customer email replaced with a tombstone address, name and metadata cleared, default payment method detached. Local invoice mirror rows survive with amounts and dates but their user_id now points at a purged-users tombstone table entry (id and purge date only), which keeps accounting queries working while making re-identification impossible from our side. The active-subscription question from last session is still parked: current behavior refuses self-serve deletion while a subscription is active, with copy telling the user to cancel first — honest but clunky, and Marek thinks it will cost us goodwill with exactly the users who are leaving, so resolving that properly (probably cancel-at-period-end with purge deferred to period end) is an explicitly open thread. Tested the whole thing in staging with a seeded account carrying 1,400 clips, 3 sessions, an Otterworks grant, and a canceled subscription: purge completed in 40 seconds, purge_log showed all eight steps, the tombstone renders where the user did in old billing rows, and a deliberately crashed run at the blob step resumed from its cursor cleanly on retry.

Short ferrite session adding the dead-letter path that has been implicitly promised since the first billing email shipped. Jobs in src/queue.rs that exhaust max_attempts (5, exponential backoff) no longer sit in the main table as permanently-failed rows that every poll skips over; they move to a dead_jobs table carrying the full original row plus last_error, attempt timestamps, and the worker id that made the final attempt. The move happens in the same transaction as the final failure record, so a job is always in exactly one of the two tables — no window where a crash duplicates or drops it. A mover that loses jobs is the one unforgivable version of this feature, so that transactional invariant got its own test with an injected panic between the insert and delete. Dead-lettering fires an alert to the internal webhook with kind, dedupe key, and last error, throttled to one alert per job kind per hour because the likely failure mode is fifty SMTP jobs dying together and fifty pages teach people to ignore pages. First real tenants arrived within a day of deploying: two billing_email jobs that had been failing on a transient DNS resolution error against the SMTP relay, retried five times across 40 minutes, correctly parked. Inspection and replay tooling is deliberately absent — read the table with psql for now; ferrite-cli subcommands for list and replay are designed in my head and getting their own session rather than being bolted on at 6pm.

Iteration session on the paywall modal, driven by two weeks of funnel numbers from the analytics events. The paywall_view to checkout_started conversion sat at 4.1 percent, and the plan split was 80 percent monthly — bad for us, since annual is the cash-flow play. Two changes. First, the annual option is now preselected, with the framing changed from $80 per year to $6.67 per month, billed annually next to the monthly option's $8 per month; the per-month equivalent framing makes the comparison legible in one glance instead of asking the user to do division inside a purchase decision. Kept a small two months free badge as reinforcement but demoted it from the headline, where it had been reading like a coupon-site banner. Second, rewrote the headline copy from You have reached your free limit (states the user's problem as a wall) to Keep everything you save (states what the money buys); the old copy was accusatory in a way I only heard after reading it aloud. Considered and rejected hiding the monthly option entirely to force annual — short-term revenue, long-term resentment, and the users who genuinely want monthly would read it as a trick the moment they found the real pricing page. Instrumented the change with a variant field on the existing paywall events rather than building an A/B framework: with our traffic, a proper split test needs a month per arm to reach significance anyway, so we are doing sequential comparison against the two-week baseline and accepting the confound, which is the honest version of what a two-person company can measure. Also fixed a real bug the funnel data surfaced: paywall_view was firing on every 402 including background retry attempts from the extension, inflating views by roughly 30 percent and understating true conversion — views are now deduplicated per user per hour client-side. Next check-in on the numbers in two weeks; if annual share moves past 40 percent of checkouts the preselection stays.

Paywall tuning session, working from the first two weeks of real funnel data. Headline numbers going in: 4.1 percent of paywall views started checkout, and four in five buyers picked monthly over annual — the wrong plan mix for a company that wants cash up front. Shipped two deliberate changes. The annual plan is now the default selection, reframed as $6.67 per month, billed annually and placed directly against monthly's $8 per month, so the saving is visible without the user doing arithmetic mid-decision; the two months free badge survives but smaller and below the price, having previously dominated the header like a discount-mall sticker. And the headline changed from limit-reached phrasing, which frames the moment as the user hitting a wall we built, to Keep everything you save, which frames it as what upgrading actually gets them — the difference was obvious the moment I read both versions out loud, which is apparently my entire copywriting methodology. Explicitly decided against removing the monthly option to strong-arm annual: it would juice this quarter and poison the well, and anyone comparing against the pricing page would correctly conclude we were hiding the cheaper choice. Measurement stays deliberately crude: a variant tag on the existing self-hosted analytics events and a before-after comparison against the baseline fortnight, because real A/B significance at our volume means months of waiting for an answer we need directionally now — wrote that reasoning down so future-us does not mistake pragmatism for ignorance. The data spelunking also turned up an instrumentation bug worth the whole session: the browser extension's silent background retries were each logging a paywall_view, inflating the denominator about 30 percent, so true conversion was meaningfully better than reported; views now dedupe per user per hour before sending. Review scheduled in two weeks — the decision rule agreed with Marek is that annual preselection is permanent if annual share of completed checkouts clears 40 percent.

First chargeback arrived today, so this session was half handling it and half building the machinery I should have built before it existed. The dispute: an $80 annual Pro charge from six weeks ago, reason code fraudulent, and the dispute fee is $15 on top of the contested amount, non-refundable in most outcomes, which changes the economics of fighting anything small. Stripe notified via charge.dispute.created, which we were not even subscribed to — first change was adding the dispute event family (created, updated, closed) to the webhook whitelist in src/webhooks.ts, with a handler writing to a new disputes table: dispute id, charge, customer, amount, reason, status, evidence_due_by, and a state timeline. Alert wired to the internal channel with the due date front and center, because dispute deadlines are hard cutoffs measured in days and missing one is an automatic loss. Then the actual investigation. Pulled the account: created six weeks ago, verified email on a consumer domain, 247 clips saved across 41 sessions from two device fingerprints, an Otterworks device linked for a month, TOS acceptance logged at signup with IP matching the payment IP's city. This is not fraud; this is someone who forgot what quillbase means on a card statement, or a partner on the account disputing an unrecognized charge. Assembled evidence accordingly: the activity timeline, signup and usage IP correlation, TOS acceptance record, the receipt email delivery log, and a screenshot of their still-active reading queue, submitted through the dashboard with a cover narrative keeping it factual and short. Odds are still poor — issuing banks side with cardholders on fraudulent claims overwhelmingly — but an active-usage evidence pack is the one profile that sometimes wins. Structural fixes that came out of it: the statement descriptor was the legal entity name LARKSPUR LABS LLC, which explains the confusion; changed to QUILLBASE.APP which is what the customer actually sees in their browser every day. And receipts now include a manage-or-cancel link plus a reply-to that reaches us, since every support email we get is a dispute that did not happen. Refund-versus-fight policy question — when the math says eat it — is deliberately deferred until there is more than a sample size of one.

The chargeback was not a sample size of one. Eleven disputes landed across nine days, and this session was pattern analysis. All eleven: annual $80 charges, accounts created inside the same eight-day window five to six weeks ago, email addresses on two domains I had never heard of — mailfoglio.com and inkdrop.click, both of which turn out to be disposable-address services — and card BINs that the Stripe dashboard identifies as prepaid, spread across three issuers. Usage profiles are the tell: median 4 clips saved, single session, no Otterworks linkage, several accounts sharing overlapping IP ranges out of a single hosting provider ASN. This is a batch, not eleven coincidences — almost certainly stolen or churned prepaid cards being tested or cashed through us, with the disputes arriving as the cards' real state caught up. Exposure math: 11 times $80 is $880 in contested revenue, plus 11 times $15 in dispute fees is $165 that is gone regardless of outcomes, and a dispute RATE problem on top — the processors care about ratio, and at our volume eleven disputes moves the ratio in ways that get accounts reviewed. Immediate actions taken tonight. Radar rule blocking payments where the card funding type is prepaid AND the amount is the annual price — prepaid plus our biggest ticket is the entire fraud profile, and the collateral damage is legitimate prepaid users buying annual, who can still buy monthly (rule and reasoning documented in the repo). Second Radar rule routing elevated-risk-score payments to review rather than block, so a human (me) looks before the charge exists. Signup-side: both disposable domains blocked at registration, with the obvious note that this is whack-a-mole and a real disposable-domain list is the durable answer. Marked the remaining not-yet-disputed accounts from the same cohort — there are three more matching the exact profile — for the next session, because there is a real question about proactively refunding them before they convert into $15 fees plus near-certain losses. Evidence submission for the eleven is also pending; given the usage profiles there is close to nothing to submit on most of them, which itself informs the fight-or-fold policy taking shape.

Full-day forensic session on the chargeback ring, because the eleven disputes turned out to be the visible fraction of something with more moving parts, and the goal today was understanding the actual scheme before hardening against the wrong one. Started from the three flagged-but-undisputed accounts matching the cohort profile and widened the query: any account created in the same eight-day window, paying annual, with either a disposable email domain, a prepaid BIN, or signup IP in the hosting ASN the earlier analysis surfaced. That net caught 14 accounts total — the 11 disputed, the 3 flagged, and zero others, which was itself informative: the cohort is bounded, this was one operation, not a persistent leak. Then looked at what the accounts actually DID, which nobody had done yet because the dispute view only shows billing. The answer was surprising: the median-4-clips profile from the dispute batch was misleading, because the three undisputed accounts plus two of the disputed ones had enormous ferrite fetch volume — between them roughly 40,000 fetch jobs over three weeks, hammering three specific news sites through our article-snapshot pipeline, with clips created and deleted in batches so the visible clip count stayed low while the fetcher kept working. So the scheme has two layers: stolen or churned prepaid cards buying annual plans (the carding layer, which produced the disputes as the cards' owners noticed), and the purchased accounts then being used as a scraping proxy — our fetch infrastructure, our IPs, laundering their crawl traffic against sites that would have blocked them directly. We were selling proxy access for $80 a year and eating the chargebacks for it. Found what looks like the distribution side too: searching one of the disposable domains led to a public forum listing selling aged reader-app accounts with unlimited article fetching, at a price that only makes sense if the cards were free. Actions, in the order taken. Fetch-side abuse controls in ferrite, which should have existed regardless: per-account token-bucket rate caps in src/worker.rs on fetch job execution (burst 30, refill 200 per day for free, 1000 per day for Pro — generous multiples of the p99 legitimate user, who fetches 40 a day), plus a per-destination-domain circuit breaker so no single account can direct sustained volume at one target site, with breaker trips logged and alerted since a trip IS the abuse signature.
