Terminated the 14 accounts under the TOS abuse clause, tokens revoked through the family machinery, purge scheduled. Proactively refunded the three undisputed accounts before termination — $240 refunded voluntarily versus the alternative of three more near-certain disputes at $80 plus $15 each, so the refund is $45 cheaper than losing, protects the dispute ratio, and Stripe's guidance explicitly favors refunding suspected-fraud charges before they convert; recorded the reasoning in the disputes doc since refunding fraudsters feels wrong until you do the arithmetic. Radar hardening beyond last session's rules: enabled the rule requesting 3D Secure on elevated-risk annual charges, which shifts liability to the issuer precisely on the population most likely to dispute — 3DS friction on the highest-risk slice only, not on every checkout, since blanket 3DS measurably kills conversion. Registration hardening: swapped the two-domain blocklist for a maintained disposable-domain list refreshed weekly by a ferrite job, matched at signup AND retroactively flagged (not blocked) on existing accounts for review-listing. Considered requiring a card before the trial as a fraud gate and rejected it again — the no-card trial decision stands because trial accounts were not the vector, purchased annual plans were; writing that down so the trial does not get blamed by future-us misremembering. Also considered IP-reputation blocking of hosting ASNs at signup and rejected it: VPN users are a real and legitimate slice of a privacy-adjacent product's audience, and the fetch-side caps now bound the damage regardless of who signs up. What is left open: the three sites that got scraped through us have grounds to be annoyed and one has already tightened rate limits against our fetcher's user agent, degrading snapshots for legitimate users — deciding whether to reach out proactively is a judgment call parked for discussion with Marek; and the evidence packs for the eleven live disputes are still owed, though today's findings mostly write the fold half of the fight-or-fold policy for us: on accounts with this profile there is nothing to fight WITH, and the fee math says accept quickly and spend the effort on prevention, which after today actually exists.

Closing session on the chargeback arc — outcomes are in and the policy is now written. Final tally on the eleven disputes: submitted evidence on all eleven despite knowing most were hopeless (partly to test the process end to end, partly because the two with real usage deserved the effort), won 2, lost 9. The two wins were exactly the two with genuine activity profiles — the original 247-clip account from the first dispute and one other with weeks of real usage — which confirms the pattern: evidence wins when there is a person who plainly used the thing, and never otherwise. Money: 9 times $80 lost is $720 in reversed revenue, dispute fees ran $135 net (the $15 fee came back on the two wins in our processor configuration, 9 times $15 kept), against $240 in proactive refunds from the forensic session that avoided three more fees and three more ratio hits. Time was the eye-opener: reconstructing each evidence pack averaged 40 minutes even with the disputes table timeline, call it seven hours across the batch for $160 recovered. The standing policy, now in the repo docs as dispute-playbook: disputes under $100 with a thin-usage profile are accepted immediately, no evidence, no agonizing — the expected value is negative before the first minute of effort; disputes with a real-usage profile get the evidence template regardless of amount, because those win and because letting real usage go undefended trains nothing good; anything at pattern scale (3 or more in a rolling week, or shared cohort markers) skips straight to the forensic checklist from the ring investigation rather than being handled one-by-one. Built the evidence pack template while the memory was fresh: activity timeline query, IP correlation, TOS acceptance, receipt delivery log, Otterworks linkage if present — assembling one is now maybe ten minutes. Added a monthly recurring review of the disputes table and Radar performance to the calendar, and a dashboard tile showing rolling dispute rate against the ratio thresholds that matter to the processor. Dispute rate since the Radar rules and fetch caps went live: zero new disputes in three weeks, which proves nothing yet but is the right direction. Arc closed unless the ring reconstitutes.

Non-work session, small and satisfying. Volunteered (was volunteered by marriage, technically) to fix the HOA newsletter, which has been a Word document mangled differently by every board member who touches it, emailed as a 40 MB attachment because of embedded phone photos. Requirements gathered from the board president in one phone call: two pages, a masthead, three to five short articles, a calendar sidebar, large print because the readership skews retired, and it must be producible by someone who is not me after I inevitably rotate off this duty. Considered a Word template with locked styles (they will unlock them), a Google Doc (half the board refuses accounts on principle), and LaTeX (I want to remain married), then landed on a single-file HTML template styled for print: fixed page-size layout with print CSS, system fonts only, a two-column grid that degrades to one column for the web version, and image slots that constrain photos to sane dimensions no matter what 12-megapixel original gets dropped in. Anyone can open it in a browser, edit text in any editor with the four commented regions I marked EDIT ARTICLE ONE through FOUR, and print to PDF; the print dialog does the compression that nobody was doing manually. Produced this month's issue as the proof: 380 KB PDF versus last month's 40 MB, and the president reported it looks fancy, which is the highest available rating. Total time two evenings, most of it spent making the instructions idiot-adjacent-proof rather than on the layout itself, which is the correct ratio for anything handed to a committee.

Debugged a genuinely instructive ferrite failure today. Symptom: a customer received the same day-3 dunning email twice, eleven minutes apart, despite the dedupe key design that was supposed to make that impossible. Trace: the jobs table showed job 8841 attempted twice by two different workers, and the worker logs showed the first attempt never failed — it succeeded, slowly. Root cause chain: the SMTP relay was having a bad afternoon and the send call blocked for 96 seconds; leases in src/lease.rs default to 60 seconds with a heartbeat every 20; but the heartbeat was being driven from the same task that runs the job handler, and the SMTP client call is blocking I/O sitting inside the async runtime, so the task could not yield to send heartbeats while inside the send — the lease expired at 60 seconds with the log line lease expired for job 8841 while handler still running, worker two legitimately claimed it, sent the email, and then worker one's send ALSO completed. Two fixes, both necessary. The structural one: blocking calls have no business inside the async workers, so the SMTP send moved into spawn_blocking, which frees the runtime to keep heartbeating — and an audit of the other handlers found one more offender, the blob-storage delete in the purge handler, moved likewise. The defense-in-depth one: enqueue-time dedupe cannot prevent double-SEND when the same job legitimately runs twice under lease expiry, so sends now write to the sent_emails ledger keyed by dedupe_key BEFORE the SMTP call, inside a transaction that makes the second runner's insert fail and skip — at-most-once on the send side, complementing at-least-once execution. Chose write-ledger-then-send over send-then-write deliberately: the failure mode of ledger-then-crash-before-send is a missing email that retries can be reasoned about, while send-then-crash-before-ledger is a duplicate that nothing can prevent; missing beats duplicate for dunning specifically since a later step in the sequence covers the gap. Also bumped the default lease to 120 seconds — 60 was tight for anything touching third-party services even with correct heartbeating — and added a metric on lease-expiry-while-running so this failure class pages instead of being discovered by an annoyed customer. Wrote the incident up in the repo docs with the full timeline; apologized to the affected customer, who replied that they had assumed it was just email being email.

Decoupling session: moved Stripe webhook processing out of the request path and into ferrite, which has been the standing intention since the very first webhook session flagged the poison-event problem. The clearharbor endpoint in src/webhooks.ts now does exactly four things: verify signature, insert the raw event into webhook_events, enqueue a ferrite job process_stripe_event with the event id, and return 200 — measured p95 response time dropped from 1.8 seconds (the convergent handlers re-fetching from the Stripe API inline) to 41 milliseconds, which matters because Stripe times out webhook deliveries and counts slow endpoints against delivery health. All actual processing — the transaction, the idempotency insert, the convergent re-fetch, entitlement effects — moved unchanged into the ferrite handler, which just made the existing dead-letter machinery apply to webhook processing for free: a poison event now retries five times with backoff and parks in dead_jobs with an alert, instead of hammering the endpoint for 72 hours, closing the oldest open thread in these notes. Ordering was the design question worth thinking hardest about. In-request processing had accidental serialization per Stripe's delivery patterns; a concurrent worker pool destroys that, and while the convergent handlers are order-tolerant by design, two workers processing two events for the SAME customer concurrently can interleave their re-fetch-then-upsert sequences badly — worker A fetches state, worker B fetches state, B writes newer, A writes staler on top. Solution: added a group_key column to the ferrite jobs table, set to the Stripe customer id for these jobs, with queue.rs guaranteeing at most one running job per group_key — implemented in the claim query itself, which skips any job whose group_key has a running claim, using the existing SKIP LOCKED scan plus a partial index on running jobs by group key so the check is cheap. Cross-customer parallelism preserved, per-customer serialization guaranteed, and the mechanism is generic enough that the purge and dunning jobs adopted group keys in the same commit (user id and invoice id respectively) to kill their own theoretical interleavings. Tested by replaying the full webhook_events archive through the new path with eight workers — the reconciliation script came back clean against Stripe afterward, same as the serial baseline. One eventual-consistency consequence acknowledged and accepted: checkout completion now flips entitlements a few hundred milliseconds later than before, but the paywall's polling banner already treats activation as async, so the UX contract does not change at all — the polling design bought headroom it did not know it was buying. Follow-ups: dashboard tile for queue depth and oldest-unprocessed age on the webhook job kind, and the webhook_events retention job should now also verify a row's job completed before deletion.

Grandfathering session, the last thing between us and turning the paywall on for everyone. The problem: about 60 existing users are already over the 200-clip free limit — they signed up when there was no limit, and enforcing one on them retroactively converts our earliest supporters into our angriest emails. Considered three shapes. Hard grandfather (existing users exempt forever): simplest, but the free tier never converges and the earliest users — the likeliest payers — never see a reason to upgrade. Soft cap (over-limit users keep existing clips but cannot add): technically the same enforcement everyone gets, but it lands as a retroactive punishment for having trusted us early. Landed on the middle: every account created before the paywall launch date gets a legacy window — twelve months of unlimited saves, flagged via a feature_overrides entry legacy_unlimited with an expires_at, after which they get the standard limit but with their existing count honored as a floor (they can always keep what they have and delete-to-make-room, never forced to purge down to 200). The override machinery from the entitlements service handles this without schema changes, which is exactly the flexibility that data-not-code features decision was betting on. Implementation was accordingly small: a backfill script stamping the override on the pre-launch cohort, an expires_at check in the override merge in src/entitlements.ts (overrides now support expiry generally, which future comps will want too), and copy — an email to the cohort explaining the year of unlimited as a thank-you, written to be forwarded, plus a banner in-app for over-limit legacy users showing the countdown honestly starting at month nine rather than day one, since a twelve-month-early warning is noise. Decided against making the legacy window silent: users finding out about grandfathering only when it expires reads as a rug-pull, while a named thank-you with a date reads as a gift, and the difference is entirely in the telling. Marek reviewed the email, cut two sentences, right both times.

Tax session, overdue and about as fun as expected. Enabled Stripe Tax on all checkout sessions and the billing portal config, which required customer address collection at checkout — a field we had proudly not been collecting, and the conversion-instinct wince at adding a form field lost to the alternative of hand-maintaining tax logic across jurisdictions forever. The pricing decision was the real content: tax-inclusive versus tax-exclusive presentation. Went with tax_behavior inclusive for the EU-facing prices and exclusive for the US — EU consumers expect the sticker price to be the charged price and VAT-on-top at checkout reads as a bait-and-switch there, while US customers expect sales tax added and inclusive pricing would mean our margin varies by state invisibly. Mechanically that meant splitting the single price objects into a small price set per presentation currency with the behavior flag set appropriately, and teaching the checkout endpoint to select by the customer's inferred region with a fallback to exclusive USD; the subscription mirror needed a new column for the price variant so entitlement resolution stays price-id-agnostic. On the $8 monthly EU price, inclusive VAT at typical rates means we net roughly $6.55 — margin eaten deliberately in exchange for a clean customer experience, and the annual math still works. Registration thresholds are the part that actually matters legally: Stripe Tax monitors exposure per jurisdiction and we are currently below every registration threshold it tracks, so the decision — recorded explicitly — is to collect-and-monitor but defer registrations until the dashboard shows a jurisdiction approaching threshold, tracked in a recurring monthly calendar check rather than a spreadsheet I will forget. Existing subscribers keep their current pricing untouched; the tax treatment applies at their next natural renewal per Stripe's handling, and nobody gets a surprise mid-cycle price change. Verified the checkout flows in test mode across a US, German, and UK address: line items, receipts, and the mirror all record what they should. Follow-up: receipts for inclusive-tax charges show the VAT breakdown, which makes the proration receipt template situation from weeks ago even more overdue — that template debt is now three sessions old and getting flagged in bold this time.

Short operational session prompted by a near-miss: last week a debugging printf in the GitHub Actions workflow briefly echoed environment variables into a CI log, and while the log was private and got scrubbed within the hour, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET was in the blast radius and the honest move is to rotate it rather than reason about who could have seen a private log. Rotation with zero webhook downtime needs an overlap window, so verifySignature in src/webhooks.ts now tries STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET first and falls back to STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET_OLD when present — roll the secret in the Stripe dashboard, set OLD to the outgoing value, deploy, confirm deliveries verify against the new secret in the logs, unset OLD within 24 hours. Executed the whole dance today: total gap of zero failed deliveries per the Stripe dashboard. Wrote it up as a runbook in the repo docs with the exact dashboard clicks and the verification query, because secret rotation is the kind of procedure that gets invented from scratch in a panic if it is not written down calmly first. Also added a CI lint that fails any workflow step containing env dumps, so the class of near-miss that started this gets caught by a robot instead of by me reading logs at 11pm.

Trial design session — the last big conversion lever before we call the billing stack feature-complete for the quarter. Decided on a 14-day Pro trial with NO card required, which was genuinely contested internally (both voices being mine, with Marek as tiebreaker). Card-upfront converts the people who forget to cancel, which is revenue with a resentment flavor and generates exactly the unrecognized-charge disputes we just spent a month learning to hate; no-card means everyone who converts chose to pay, and given the chargeback arc's lesson that our fraud exposure came from PURCHASED plans rather than trials, the abuse argument for card-gating evaporated on inspection — reasoning recorded so the trial does not get relitigated every time something unrelated goes wrong. Implementation deliberately avoids Stripe entirely for the trial itself: no subscription object exists until actual conversion, the trial is a local trial_ends_at timestamp on the user plus a trialing pseudo-status resolved by src/entitlements.ts into full Pro features. This keeps the Stripe mirror meaning what it says (every row is real money) and makes the trial a pure entitlements concern — the resolution order in entitlements.ts now reads paid subscription first, then live trial, then overrides merge, then free, with the ordering test matrix extended to cover a trialing user who also has a legacy override, which resolves to whichever grants more (fixed a case where trial expiry was clawing back legacy unlimited a month early). Trial starts implicitly at the moment a user would first hit a Pro gate, not at signup — starting the clock at signup burns trial days while the user is still figuring out what Quillbase is, whereas starting at first gate-touch means all 14 days apply to actually experiencing the feature they wanted; this also means most users never technically start a trial, which keeps the funnel numbers meaningful. The day-11 nudge email runs as a ferrite billing_email job enqueued at trial start with the established dedupe machinery, canceled by conversion through the same key-prefix mechanism dunning uses; conversion at trial end is just the normal paywall with copy acknowledging the trial ending, and expiry without conversion degrades to free silently — no guilt email, decided deliberately, since the day-11 note already asked once and twice is nagging. Instrumented trial_started, trial_converted, trial_expired events with the gate that triggered the start attached, so in a month we will know WHICH Pro feature actually sells subscriptions rather than guessing. Open question parked: whether trial users should get partner sync (currently yes, since an Otterworks device link during trial is probably the strongest retention hook we own, but it is also the costliest feature to serve free — revisit with data).

Quillbase frontend session cleaning up the upgrade page, which had drifted into a mess of client-side fetches and loading spinners layered over three sessions of billing changes. Rebuilt it as a Next.js 15 server component: plan state, trial state, pending downgrade banner, and grace-period warnings all resolved server-side in one entitlements fetch during render, so the page arrives complete instead of assembling itself in front of the user. The interesting problem was cache invalidation. The server component result is cached with a per-user cache tag, and the stale case that matters is upgrade-just-happened: user pays, webhook processes, and their next page load must show Pro — a 60-second stale window here undoes all the careful polling work in the paywall modal. Wired event-driven invalidation: clearharbor now pings a Quillbase internal endpoint after entitlement-changing webhook effects commit, and that endpoint calls revalidateTag on the user's billing tag — decided event-driven over short TTL because the upgrade moment is the one time staleness is unacceptable, while every other moment tolerates minutes of it happily; a short TTL would buy worst-case freshness by paying render cost constantly, invalidation pays only when something actually changed. The ping is fire-and-forget with a retry, and the fallback if it is ever lost is the old 60-second staleness, which is a graceful floor. Also finally consolidated the four scattered plan-state badge components into one PlanBadge that renders from the single entitlements envelope, deleting three subtly different definitions of what counts as Pro that had already disagreed once in production (the header said Pro while the settings page said Free for a grace-period user — that class of bug is now structurally gone). Screenshot-tested the page across the six states that matter: free, trialing, pro monthly, pro annual with pending downgrade, past-due in grace, legacy override. Small session, but the billing UI now has one source of truth and zero spinners, which is how it should have been from the start.

Security-hardening pass on clearharbor sessions, prompted by finally doing the cookie audit that has been a checklist item since the rotation work. Findings and fixes. The session cookie was still being set with SameSite None — an artifact of a long-abandoned experiment embedding a Quillbase widget cross-site — which had been silently converting every cross-site request into a credentialed one and leaning entirely on CSRF tokens for safety. Moved to SameSite Lax, which killed nothing in testing except a prototype iframe page that deserved to die. Evaluated Strict and rejected it concretely rather than vibes-based: Strict strips the cookie from top-level navigations arriving from external sites, which breaks the logged-in landing from magic-link emails and from the Otterworks post-consent redirect — both real flows we ship, so Lax plus CSRF discipline is the right point on the curve, and the reasoning is now a comment above the cookie config in src/session.ts rather than tribal knowledge. Confirmed the __Host- prefix, Secure, and HttpOnly settings from the rotation session survived intact. CSRF: kept the double-submit token on state-changing form posts, and added Sec-Fetch-Site checking as a second layer — requests bearing cross-site on mutating routes get rejected before the token check even runs; belt and suspenders, and the belt is free since every modern browser sends the header. Session fixation: login and privilege-elevation paths (password change, the upcoming email change) now unconditionally mint a fresh session family and retire the presenting one, so a session id planted pre-authentication is worthless post-authentication — this was PROBABLY already safe given rotation mechanics, but probably is not a security posture, and now it is explicit with a test. Also added login notification plumbing (new family created from a never-seen device fingerprint records an auth_events row; the email itself is stubbed pending copy) and rate limiting on the login endpoint keyed by account and by IP separately, sliding window via the same Redis pattern the OAuth endpoints use. Nothing here was on fire; all of it is the kind of thing that is cheap on a calm Tuesday and expensive during an incident.

Evening experiment, unrelated to work: built a tiny chess opening trainer because my Caro-Kann keeps falling apart at move eight against the Advance variation and flashcard apps do not understand trees. The shape of it: a CLI tool that ingests annotated PGN lines into SQLite as a position tree keyed by FEN, then quizzes with spaced repetition — show a position, demand the move, grade instantly. Scheduling is SM-2 with the standard interval progression, but applied per POSITION rather than per line, which is the whole reason existing apps frustrated me: transpositions mean the same position arrives via multiple move orders, and a card system that treats each line as a flat sequence quizzes you on positions you already know while starving the novel branch points. Keying by FEN collapses transpositions automatically, and the scheduler naturally concentrates on exactly the positions I actually miss, which after three evenings of data is a brutally honest list of four squares I apparently refuse to see. Grading forgives move-order alternatives when both moves are in the tree as sound. Content is 31 lines of the Advance Caro deep enough to cover the plans I keep botching, entered by hand, which was itself half the study value. Considered adding an engine to evaluate deviations and decided firmly against — the tool trains recall of PREPARED lines, and an engine turns every session into analysis paralysis; when I want analysis I have analysis tools. It is 400 lines of code, it is ugly, and my quiz accuracy on the problem positions went from 55 to 85 percent in a week, which is a better outcome than most things I build on purpose.

Billing portal session, resolving the customer-portal thread that has been dangling since the schedules work predicted it would be trouble. Decision: adopt the Stripe hosted customer portal, but scoped narrowly — payment method updates, invoice history, and cancel-at-period-end only. Plan switching stays in OUR UI exclusively, and the portal configuration has plan changes disabled outright. The reasoning is the prediction coming true: the portal's plan-change behavior is configured with a single proration policy for all switches, while our model is asymmetric by explicit decision — upgrades immediate with always_invoice, downgrades deferred via subscription schedules — and the portal has no concept of the schedule-based deferral at all, so enabling portal plan switches would create a second, contradictory way to change plans that bypasses the pending_change machinery, the release-schedule-on-upgrade helper, and the paywall analytics in one stroke. Rather than degrade our model to what the portal can express, the portal gets the jobs it does perfectly (card updates are exactly the thing we never want to build) and none of the jobs it would do wrongly. Implementation: a portal configuration object created via the API and pinned by id in config rather than clicked together in the dashboard — dashboard-configured portals drift, API-configured ones are code-reviewed; a POST /billing/portal endpoint in clearharbor that mints a portal session for the authenticated user with return_url back to the account page; and the account page linking to it for the three sanctioned tasks. Cancellation through the portal flows back as customer.subscription.updated with cancel_at_period_end true, which the webhook pipeline already handles from the schedules era — verified in test mode, including the un-cancel case where a user resubscribes through the portal before period end, which produced a state transition I had a test for but had never seen live. One genuine surprise cost an hour: the portal's payment-method update fires payment_method.attached and detached events we were not whitelisting, harmless to ignore for state purposes, but the dunning flow WANTS to know — a past-due customer updating their card through the portal should trigger an immediate retry rather than waiting for the next scheduled attempt, so payment_method.attached on a past-due customer now enqueues an invoice pay attempt, closing the loop that previously left a fixed card idle for up to a week. Grace-period copy on the account page now points at the portal link directly. The proration receipt template — flagged bold last session — remains unbuilt, a debt now four sessions old; writing it at the top of next session's plan before anything else gets touched.

Built the DLQ tooling for ferrite that the dead_jobs table has been waiting on. ferrite-cli grew a dlq subcommand family: dlq list with filters by kind, error substring, and age, rendering a compact table with id, kind, dedupe key, attempts, and the tail of last_error; dlq show for the full payload and complete attempt timeline of one job; dlq replay taking either an explicit id or a filter (kind plus error-hash) with a mandatory count confirmation before mass replay, so fat-fingering a filter cannot silently resurrect three hundred jobs; and dlq discard with the same confirmation gate for jobs that should never run again. Replay re-inserts into the live jobs table with attempts reset to zero but a replay_of column pointing at the dead row, preserving provenance, and the dead row is marked replayed rather than deleted — history stays inspectable. The design decision worth recording is poison-pill quarantine: a job that gets replayed and dead-letters AGAIN with the same error hash three times total moves to quarantined status, which dlq replay refuses to touch without an explicit force flag; the pattern this prevents is the reflexive replay-all after an outage repeatedly resurrecting the one genuinely broken job in a batch of transient failures, burning five retries times SMTP calls each cycle. Error hashing is a normalized digest of the error message with ids and timestamps stripped, so the same failure shape matches across instances. First production use came the same week, which is the best kind of tool validation: the SMTP relay credentials expired (rotation email went to an unwatched inbox — separate lesson, forwarded now), and 47 dunning and receipt emails dead-lettered over six hours before the alert throttle woke me up. After fixing the credentials, dlq list confirmed all 47 shared one error hash, dlq replay with the filter resurrected them in one command, and the sent_emails ledger from the lease-expiry incident quietly proved its worth — 12 of the 47 had actually completed their SMTP handoff before the connection died and were sitting in the ledger, so their replays skipped as already-sent and zero customers got duplicates. The remaining 35 delivered clean. Not built on purpose: automatic replay on a timer, which everyone wants until the quarantine scenario plays out unattended; the alert now includes the suggested replay command with the filter pre-filled, which is the right amount of automation — a human runs it, but running it is one paste.

Session on ferrite dead-letter operations — the dead_jobs table finally has tooling instead of raw psql. Shipped a dlq command family in ferrite-cli. Listing supports kind, age, and error-substring filters and prints the essentials per row (id, kind, dedupe key, attempt count, truncated last error); show dumps one job completely, payload and attempt-by-attempt timeline; replay accepts an id or a kind-plus-error-hash filter and always states how many jobs match before asking for confirmation, because a mistyped filter on a mass replay is how you accidentally re-run everything that ever failed; discard exists for the truly dead, same confirmation ritual. Replays keep full lineage — new live row with attempts zeroed and replay_of linking back, dead row flagged replayed instead of removed — so the question what happened to job X always has an answer. The idea I most wanted to get right: quarantine for poison pills. Any job whose replays produce the same normalized error hash three times over its lifetime flips to quarantined and becomes invisible to normal replay, force flag required — the scenario being guarded against is the post-outage replay-everything reflex endlessly reviving one structurally broken job amid a crowd of legitimately transient failures. The error hash normalizes messages by stripping identifiers and timestamps so recurrence detection works across workers and days. Validation arrived unreasonably fast: expired SMTP relay credentials (the provider's rotation notice had been landing in an inbox nobody reads — that forwarding rule now exists) dead-lettered 47 billing emails across an evening. Post-fix, the filtered replay restored the batch in a single confirmed command, and the send-side ledger caught that 12 of them had already made it out before the credential failure — those replays no-opped as already-sent, so the incident ended with 35 late emails and zero duplicates, exactly the guarantee the ledger was built to make. Deliberately did NOT add scheduled auto-replay: an unattended replay loop plus one quarantine-worthy job is a machine for converting one bug into recurring load, and the compromise shipped instead is that the dead-letter alert embeds a ready-to-paste replay command with the filter filled in. Human judgment, one paste of friction.

Resolved the deletion-while-subscribed question that has been parked since the purge session, and it took a real bug with it. The policy, settled with Marek over an hour of talking through cases: a user with an active subscription who requests deletion gets cancel-at-period-end applied automatically as part of the deletion request — they keep the Pro features they paid for through the period they paid for, no automatic refund, and the purge job's scheduled_at becomes the LATER of deletion-plus-30-days or the period end, so the account is never destroyed while a paid period is still running. Refunds stay a manual support action with one standing rule: a pro-rata refund is granted on request within 14 days of an ANNUAL renewal charge, because the person who forgot an annual renewal and immediately wants out is a real and sympathetic case, while mid-cycle monthly refunds round to zero dollars of goodwill for real accounting friction. The refuse-until-canceled screen is gone; deletion now says plainly what will happen and when, with the period end date rendered in the confirmation. Implementing this surfaced the bug: in staging, purging a test account whose subscription was mid-cancellation produced a crash in the webhook worker when the eventual customer.subscription.deleted event arrived AFTER the user row was purged — the handler resolved the Stripe customer id to a local user, got nothing, and threw user not found for stripe customer, which dead-lettered the job and would have alerted at 3am in production. The fix leaned on the tombstone design from the purge work: the purge job now writes the Stripe customer id into the purged-users tombstone row, and the webhook pipeline checks the tombstone table on user-resolution failure — a tombstone match means the event refers to a deliberately destroyed account, and the handler acknowledges cleanly as a no-op with a log line instead of dead-lettering. Wrote the test as a full timeline: subscribe, request deletion, simulate period end, purge, then deliver the late subscription.deleted — green. Also covered the nastier sibling: a REFUND or dispute event arriving after purge (chargebacks have month-long windows and outlive accounts by design) resolves through the same tombstone path, and the redacted-but-retained billing mirror rows mean we can still respond to a dispute on a purged account with charge metadata even though the content and identity are gone — checked that the dispute evidence template degrades gracefully when the account behind it is a tombstone, which it now does, stating account deleted by user on date X as its own kind of evidence. The deletion flow is now, as far as either of us can construct cases, complete: grace, restore, purge, billing interplay, and late-event hygiene all specified and tested. Closing the arc unless reality invents a case we did not.

Metrics session — Marek asked the reasonable question how is revenue actually doing and the honest answer was a shrug plus the Stripe dashboard, which conflates test refunds, does not know about grace periods, and cannot segment by any dimension we care about. Built the first version of internal billing metrics. Core decision: all metrics compute from OUR mirror tables (subscriptions_mirror, invoices_mirror, the disputes table) and never from live Stripe API calls — the API is rate-limited, slow to paginate, and gives answers about NOW that quietly rewrite history, whereas the mirror plus webhook archive is a stable substrate that yields the same answer for last March every time you ask. A nightly ferrite job billing_metrics_rollup writes one row per day into daily_metrics: MRR, active subscriber count by plan and interval, new-trial count, trial conversions, churn events split voluntary versus payment-failure, and dispute count. MRR normalization decided explicitly and documented in the job: annual subscriptions contribute one-twelfth of their price per month ($6.67 for the $80 plan), trials contribute zero until real money exists, past-due-in-grace contributes normally until grace expires (they are still probably-customers) and zero after. Churn gets tracked BOTH ways after reading one too many arguments about it: logo churn (subscriber count) and revenue churn (MRR lost), because a month where two annual customers leave and five monthlies join looks like growth by logo count and shrinkage by revenue, and pretending one number tells the story is how startups surprise themselves. Current snapshot for the record: MRR $1,720, 289 paying accounts, 61 percent monthly by count but only 44 percent of MRR — the annual push is working. Backfilled daily_metrics from the webhook archive back to the first paid month, which the replay infrastructure made almost embarrassingly easy — the archive-everything decision from the very first webhook session keeps paying dividends nobody predicted. Simple dashboard page in the internal tools area renders the series with the dispute-rate tile from the chargeback arc alongside. Deliberately no forecasting, no cohort curves yet — first month of just LOOKING at real numbers before deciding which sophisticated questions are worth building answers to.

Reconciliation session, closing the loop on a quiet anxiety: the subscriptions and invoices mirrors are maintained entirely by the webhook pipeline, and the pipeline is good now, but good is not proven, and the metrics job just made the mirrors load-bearing for business decisions. Built drift detection as a weekly ferrite job stripe_reconcile: pages through every subscription and the trailing 90 days of invoices via the Stripe list APIs, compares field-by-field against the mirrors (status, price, period boundaries, cancel flags, amounts), and writes a drift report — matched counts, mismatched rows with field-level diffs, and rows present on one side only. Ran the first full pass expecting vindication and got education instead: 3 drifted rows out of 312 subscriptions. First was a fossil from the outage era before per-customer serialization, a subscription whose mirror status stuck in past_due while Stripe said active — the exact interleaving bug the group_key work fixed, confirming both the bug's reality and the fix's value. The other two were more interesting: both traced to manual edits in the Stripe dashboard, one where Marek comped a friend two free months by editing the subscription directly, and one where I extended a trial-adjacent discount the same way months ago and forgot. Dashboard edits DO emit webhooks and the mirror had actually followed them correctly — the drift was in our SUBSIDIARY state, the entitlements-adjacent columns the webhook handler derives, because manual edits produce state combinations (a discount with no checkout provenance) the derivation never anticipated. Two responses. Structural: manual dashboard edits are now banned by team agreement — comps and extensions go through a small admin endpoint that writes local intent FIRST and then updates Stripe, so provenance always exists; the endpoint took an hour to build and covers both real cases we have ever had. Detective: the reconcile job now also alerts on any subscription whose recent webhook events include a modification with no corresponding admin-endpoint intent record — catching future dashboard temptation within a week rather than at the next drift report. Fixed the three rows (auto-heal adopts Stripe as truth for object state, with an audit row; subsidiary state re-derives), re-ran the job, clean pass. The remaining philosophical wrinkle, noted for honesty: reconciliation trusts Stripe as ground truth, which is correct for Stripe-owned objects but circular for our derived state — the real invariant is that derived state is a pure function of mirror plus local intent, and the derivation being deterministic is what the test suite owns. Wrote that sentence into the reconcile job's header comment because it took an embarrassing amount of thinking to say that simply.

Small Quillbase session fixing the worst edge of the paywall rollout: the browser extension and bookmarklet clip path. When an over-limit free user clipped from the extension, the 402 from app/api/clips/route.ts was being swallowed by the extension's generic error handler, which showed Could not save clip — a message indistinguishable from a server outage, and the analytics showed users retrying four and five times against the limit, each retry logging another failure. The user experience was a wall pretending to be a bug. The extension now recognizes the clip_limit_reached code specifically and shows an honest state: You have used all 200 free saves, with the count, and a button that deep-links into Quillbase at /clips with a context parameter that opens the paywall modal directly — the moment of blocked intent lands on the purchase decision with one click, which is both better selling and better manners than the ambiguous failure. The deep link carries the URL the user was trying to clip, and after a successful upgrade the modal offers to complete that save, so the original intent survives the detour — small touch, disproportionate goodwill. Also stopped the background retry loop from re-attempting 402s at all (retries are for transient failures; a limit is not transient), which cleans up the inflated failure metrics the paywall-tuning session had to dedupe around. Tested across the extension and the bookmarklet on the three states: under limit, at limit, and upgraded-mid-session, where the entitlements cache poke means the very next clip after upgrading succeeds without a reload. Shipped in an afternoon; should have been in the original paywall scope, and the lesson recorded is that the paywall's surface area is every path that can create a clip, not just the app UI.

Incident session, written up while the adrenaline is still informative. Timeline first. At roughly 23:40 last night a routine clearharbor deploy went out with a subtly wrong health check path in fly.toml — the check pointed at /healthz which the app serves on the internal port, but the deploy also changed the internal port assignment and the two changes composed into every instance reporting unhealthy; Fly kept the old instances draining and the new ones out of rotation, and from about 23:45 the public clearharbor endpoints, including /stripe/webhooks, returned 502 on most requests. Neither of us noticed until morning because the only alerting on clearharbor was the dead-letter throttle inside ferrite, and ferrite was fine — the jobs simply were not arriving. Stripe, meanwhile, did exactly what its documentation says: retried every failed delivery with exponential backoff and kept the events queued. By the time I shipped the fix at 05:50 (health check path corrected, one-line diff, deploy verified green), the dashboard showed roughly 3,100 events pending retry against our endpoint. The recovery is where the last three months of architecture decisions got their real exam. The burst came in fast once deliveries resumed — hundreds of events inside the first minutes, far beyond the steady-state pace the system had ever seen. The thin-endpoint design held beautifully: verify, archive, enqueue, 200, so ingestion itself never buckled. What DID buckle, for about ten minutes, was Postgres connections: the ferrite workers processing the backlog plus the archive inserts plus normal app traffic exhausted the pool, and the log filled with FATAL 53300 remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections — the first time we have ever seen that error. Triaged in the moment by dropping ferrite worker concurrency for the webhook job kind from 8 to 3, which throttled backlog processing to a pace the pool tolerated; the backlog cleared completely in 38 minutes and the pool never faulted again. Then the accounting. The idempotency layer processed all ~3,100 events with zero duplicate effects — the processed_events table shows exactly one processing per event id, and the reconciliation job run manually after cleanup came back with zero drift against Stripe, which after the earlier drift-hunting session I am prepared to call proof. Per-customer serialization via group_key meant the burst's internal ordering chaos — six hours of events for the same customers arriving interleaved across minutes — converged correctly everywhere; the convergent-handler re-fetch design was built for exactly this and it delivered. Four accounts did hit a transient wrong state visible to users during the recovery window: subscriptions created during the outage whose entitlements resolved as free until their event batch processed, one of whom emailed support; all four self-corrected within the backlog window and the support reply was honest about the outage. Dunning emails were the one place I intervened manually: 9 dunning jobs enqueued during recovery for invoices whose payment had ALSO succeeded during the outage window — the cancel-on-recovery logic works off event arrival order and the outage compressed six hours of cause and effect into interleaved minutes — caught them in the queue by searching pending dunning keys against just-succeeded invoices and cancelled them by hand before send; zero customers got a wrong email, but only because I thought to look, and that gap is now item one on the hardening list since the ledger would not have caught these (they were legitimate enqueues by the logic that made them, just wrong about the world). Lessons, filed as the postmortem action list. One: the outage was invisible for six hours because our alerting watches job failures, not job ABSENCE — an alert on webhook_events ingestion silence longer than 30 minutes would have paged at half past midnight; building it this week along with an endpoint uptime check from outside Fly's own network. Two: pool exhaustion under backlog was predictable and the concurrency knob that saved us was a lucky manual lever — the webhook job kind now gets a permanent concurrency ceiling sized against pool arithmetic, and pgbouncer moves up the list. Three: deploy health checks are themselves code and the composing-changes failure mode means the deploy checklist now includes watching one real request succeed post-deploy, not just trusting green checks. Four, the meta-lesson: every safety mechanism that mattered tonight — archive-first ingestion, idempotency, convergent handlers, group keys, the reconcile job — was built calmly over months for reasons that felt slightly paranoid at the time, and the incident consumed all of them at once; the system earned its keep, and the parts that failed were the parts nobody had built yet, not the parts built wrong. Total customer-visible damage: one six-hour signup-to-activation delay window affecting four accounts, one honest support email, zero money wrong, zero duplicate effects. Could have been so much worse.

Hardening session, executing the incident postmortem list before the urgency evaporates — the half-life on post-incident motivation is about a week and I intend to spend it. Item one, the silence alarm: a scheduled ferrite job now checks the age of the newest webhook_events row every ten minutes, and raises an alert when ingestion has been silent for more than 30 minutes during hours when silence is statistically abnormal — the threshold uses a per-hour-of-day baseline from the archive rather than a flat number, since 3am Sunday silence is normal and 2pm Tuesday silence means the endpoint is down; the incident's six invisible hours would have been forty-one visible minutes under this rule. Paired it with an external uptime check hitting a dedicated /stripe/webhooks/health path from outside the Fly network entirely, because the incident's specific shape — infrastructure-level unhealthiness with the app code fine — is invisible to any check that runs inside the same infrastructure. Item two, pool arithmetic: the webhook job kind now carries a permanent per-kind concurrency ceiling in ferrite config, derived from actual connection budget math written out in a comment (pool size, minus app baseline, minus archive insert headroom, divided by connections per worker) rather than the vibes-based 8 that exhausted the pool; and pgbouncer went in front of Postgres in transaction mode, which the connection-count math shows buys roughly 4x headroom before the next ceiling. Load-tested the whole path by replaying the incident's own 3,100-event archive through staging at full speed — cleared in 11 minutes with zero pool faults and zero drift on reconcile, which turns the incident from a scar into a benchmark. Item three, the dunning race: recovery-window dunning enqueues now pass through a pre-send world-check — the send handler re-verifies the invoice is STILL unpaid at send time, not just at enqueue time, closing the compressed-causality gap that required manual queue surgery during the incident; the check is a single indexed read per send and turns a class of wrong-email into a no-op. Item four: deploy checklist updated with the watch-one-real-request rule, and the health check config in fly.toml now has a comment block explaining exactly how it composed with the port change to take the site down, because config files are where context goes to die. Everything on the list shipped except the daily synthetic canary event, which needs a small signing harness to post through the real public endpoint — sketched, next session. The meta-note for the record: this entire session was cheap, roughly a day, and every item was cheap BEFORE the incident too; the difference is that now each one has a story attached, and stories are apparently what converts known-good practice into shipped practice.

Product-decision session on the free tier, prompted by Marek floating the idea of limiting full-text search to the last 90 days for free accounts as a second upgrade lever alongside the clip limit. Spent the morning genuinely considering it — the mechanics are easy, a date filter in lib/search/rank.ts and a features entry, maybe two hours of work — and then argued myself and eventually both of us out of it. The case against, now recorded as a standing decision: search over your OWN saved reading is the core promise of the product, and its value is precisely that it reaches the thing you saved two years ago and half-remember; a 90-day window guts the feature exactly where it demonstrates worth, so the crippled version does not advertise the full version, it teaches free users the product cannot do the thing they came for. The clip limit works as a paywall because it caps ACCUMULATION while leaving every saved clip fully useful, so the value of upgrading is legible: more of the good thing. A search window would degrade the good thing itself, and the user who hits it is mid-search, mid-need — the worst possible moment to demonstrate untrustworthiness. Differentiation stays on the additive axis: Pro gets priority fetch, partner sync, and unlimited saves; free gets a bounded but honest product. While in rank.ts anyway, fixed a real bug found while reading the code to estimate the rejected feature: the ts_rank weight vector was applying the title weight to the URL tokens column because the setweight labels in the indexing path (lib/ingest/parser.ts stamps them at ingest) and the rank expression disagreed on which label meant what — titles were ranked as body text and URL slugs as titles, which quietly explains a handful of odd-relevance reports that had been shrugged off as fuzzy-search-being-fuzzy. Fixed the label mapping, reindexed staging, and the three saved example searches from those old reports now surface the expected clip first. Scheduled a full production reindex for the weekend.

Quarter wrap-up session — closed the books on the billing and auth push with a review of where everything landed, written deliberately as the note future-us reads first. The numbers: MRR $1,940 at close against $1,720 at the metrics baseline six weeks ago, 312 paying accounts, annual now 41 percent of completed checkouts since the paywall preselection change (just under the 40 percent bar we set, but trending up, so preselection stays), trial-to-paid conversion at 11 percent in its first partial month with the gate-attribution data showing partner sync as the top trigger, dispute rate flat at zero since the Radar rules and fetch caps — the ring never reconstituted. Otterworks went GA quietly: production client rotated, 90 linked accounts in the first two weeks, their sandbox soak and the RFC-compliant error handling meant integration support amounted to two emails. The architecture that this quarter built, named for the record because the notes tell it in fragments: thin webhook ingestion with archive-first and idempotent convergent processing, per-customer serialization through ferrite group keys, dead-letter with quarantine and one-paste replay, rotating token families unified across sessions and partner OAuth, entitlements as a versioned envelope with overrides and expiry, mirrors reconciled weekly against Stripe with manual-edit detection, and a deletion flow that survives late webhooks via tombstones. The incident validated the stack better than any test could have, and the postmortem hardening is fully shipped except the synthetic canary, which remains the oldest small debt. Open threads carried into next quarter, ranked: the proration-aware receipt template, now legendarily five sessions overdue and finally embarrassing enough to be item one; the synthetic canary harness; EU VAT registration watch as thresholds approach (Germany closest per the Stripe Tax dashboard); the trial partner-sync question once a full month of gate data exists; whether the scraped news sites deserve proactive outreach, still parked with Marek; and the grace-period UI surfacing card-failure state, designed but unbuilt. Deliberate non-goals reaffirmed so they stay decided: no card-upfront trial, no free-tier search window, no portal plan-switching, no auto-replay on the DLQ. The quarter's meta-lesson, same one the incident taught but generalized: almost everything that worked was boring, written down, and built slightly before it was needed — the notes themselves turned out to be infrastructure, since at least four sessions this quarter started by rereading an old decision instead of re-deriving it. Next quarter's theme is growth mechanics on top of this foundation; the foundation itself is, for the first time, not the risk.

Worked the Redis eviction outage end to end today, from first page to stable mitigation. Timeline as reconstructed: at 09:12 UTC the Quillbase save endpoint in app/api/clips/route.ts started returning 500s, and by 09:14 the ferrite workers were logging missing-key errors from the rate limiter, which was the first clue that Redis itself was the problem rather than either app. The shared Redis on Fly had crossed its 256mb maxmemory around 08:50 and, because it ran with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, it silently evicted whatever was least recently used, which turned out to include the per-domain politeness tokens and the dedup keys that lib/ingest/parser.ts consults before fetching, plus a slab of clearharbor session cache entries. INFO stats showed evicted_keys at 412,806 by the time we looked. The nasty part is that nothing crashed: Redis stayed up and healthy on the surface, ferrite kept claiming jobs from Postgres just fine since the durable queue lives in queue.rs on Postgres, but every fetch immediately failed its rate-limit check with an eviction-shaped nil, and the retry logic in worker.rs treated that as transient and requeued with backoff, so queue depth climbed from about 400 to 31,000 in forty minutes. Meanwhile clearharbor session lookups in src/session.ts fell through the missing cache entries to Postgres, tripling connection usage and pushing p95 auth latency from 40ms to 900ms, which is what actually made the Quillbase UI feel down. Mitigation and decisions: first, scaled Redis to a 1gb machine and drained the retry storm by pausing the ferrite fetch lane via ferrite-cli. Second, we made the call we should have made months ago and split Redis into two logical roles, a cache instance that keeps allkeys-lru and a state instance for rate-limit tokens and dedup keys that runs maxmemory-policy noeviction, so overload becomes a loud OOM command not allowed when used memory over maxmemory error instead of silent data loss; the reasoning is that we can page on a hard error but we cannot page on quietly wrong behavior. Third, the eviction-shaped nil is now distinguishable: the limiter treats a missing token bucket as fail-open with a logged warning, on the theory that briefly over-fetching a domain is a better failure mode than stalling the whole pipeline, and that tradeoff is documented in a comment block at the top of the limiter module so future us does not helpfully flip it back. Fourth, added a used_memory alert at 75 percent and an evicted_keys alert on any nonzero delta, wired through the same small alert script that watches the webhook queue. We also verified that entitlements were never touched, since src/entitlements.ts reads Postgres directly and only uses Redis as a look-aside, which was a deliberate choice from the original clearharbor design and paid for itself today. Open threads: the lost dedup keys mean roughly six hours of duplicate refetches will bleed in over the coming week as articles cycle back around, and we decided to absorb that rather than rebuild the keys from the Postgres side because the rebuild script would take longer to write than the waste it prevents; the session cache should move to the cache instance explicitly rather than by default; and the real postmortem write-up is owed tomorrow. Cost note: the extra Redis machine is about 11 dollars a month, which is noise next to seventy minutes of downtime. Lesson recorded for the postmortem: allkeys-lru on a Redis that holds anything you cannot recompute is a standing incident waiting for a busy morning, and we knew that in the abstract and shipped the default anyway.

Follow-up session on yesterday's Redis eviction outage, mostly hardening and paperwork. Finished splitting the two Redis roles for real: the state instance now runs with maxmemory-policy noeviction and appendonly yes, and both ferrite and clearharbor read the new REDIS_STATE_URL and REDIS_CACHE_URL env vars instead of the old single REDIS_URL, which took touching src/session.ts, src/entitlements.ts, and the limiter setup in ferrite-core. Found one landmine while doing it: the maxmemory and policy settings had been applied on the old instance via CONFIG SET during some long-forgotten debugging session, so they lived only in memory and would not have survived a restart; both instances now get their config from the command line in fly.toml so the settings are declarative and versioned. Wrote the postmortem doc with the timeline from the session notes, five contributing causes, and six action items, of which four are already done: the split, the declarative config, the fail-open limiter behavior, and the used_memory plus evicted_keys alerts. The remaining two are moving the clearharbor session cache explicitly onto the cache instance, which is scheduled for this week, and adding a synthetic canary that saves a clip end to end every five minutes so we detect ingestion stalls from the outside instead of waiting for a user report; the outage ran 22 minutes before either of us noticed, and that detection gap embarrassed us more than the root cause did. One decision worth recording: we considered moving the rate-limit state into Postgres to get rid of the Redis dependency entirely, and decided against it because the token buckets take roughly 4,000 writes a minute at current crawl volume and we do not want that churn in the same database that serves reads for Quillbase; Redis with noeviction and AOF is the right tool, we were just holding it wrong. Also tightened the ferrite reconnect behavior in worker.rs while in there: the redis client now uses exponential backoff with jitter capped at 30 seconds instead of the old fixed 500ms retry, because during the incident sixty workers hammering reconnects added measurable load at exactly the wrong time. Verified the fix by running a controlled eviction drill against a scratch Redis on my machine, filling it with junk keys until eviction kicked in, and confirming the limiter logs the warning and fails open while the dedup layer treats a missing key as fetch-needed, which is correct and safe. Queue depth is back under 300 and refetch waste from the lost dedup keys is tracking at about 2 percent of fetches, lower than the 5 percent we budgeted. Next session should close out the canary work and then get back to the search ranking backlog that this outage interrupted.

Today was the Postgres migration incident, which is now the second-worst self-inflicted outage in Larkspur history and the first one where we took ourselves down with a single line of SQL. Context: as part of the Drizzle schema cleanup we wanted a read_state column on the clips table, non-null with a default of unread. Drizzle-kit generated a straightforward ALTER TABLE clips ADD COLUMN read_state text NOT NULL DEFAULT unread, and on Postgres 16 that is normally fine because the default is stored in the catalog and the table does not get rewritten. What we forgot is that ALTER TABLE still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, however briefly, and at 14:03 UTC when the migration ran, there was a long analytics query from my scratch tooling holding an AccessShare on clips inside an idle-in-transaction psql session I had abandoned before lunch. The ALTER queued behind it, and because ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queues ahead of everything else, every subsequent read and write on clips queued behind the ALTER. Within ninety seconds the Quillbase API drained its connection pool, app/api/clips/route.ts started throwing timeouts, ferrite workers blocked in queue.rs trying to mark jobs complete because the completion update joins against clips, and the whole system seized in a way that looked at first like a database crash rather than a lock convoy. Diagnosis took eleven minutes, mostly because we looked at CPU and memory graphs first when we should have gone straight to pg_stat_activity, where the picture was instantly obvious: one idle in transaction session from 11:40, one ALTER TABLE waiting, and 47 sessions waiting behind it. Killed my zombie session with pg_terminate_backend, the ALTER completed in 300 milliseconds, and everything unwound on its own within a minute. Total user-facing damage: about 14 minutes of full write unavailability and a burst of failed saves. Decisions coming out of this, all recorded in the migration runbook doc that now exists: one, every migration session sets lock_timeout to 5 seconds and statement_timeout to 30 seconds so that a blocked DDL statement gives up quickly and loudly instead of holding the front of the lock queue while traffic piles up behind it; drizzle-kit does not do this for us, so the deploy script wraps psql with the settings applied at session level. Two, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is now set globally to 10 minutes, because an abandoned transaction should die on its own rather than lurk until it ambushes a migration; we debated 2 minutes but some legitimate ferrite batch commits can run long during backfills, so 10 is the compromise. Three, migrations that touch hot tables run through a checklist: check pg_stat_activity for long transactions first, run during the morning low-traffic window, and never combine multiple ALTERs on different hot tables in one transaction because that multiplies deadlock surface. Four, big structural changes get the expand-and-contract treatment going forward: add the column nullable, backfill in batches of 10,000 with a small script that sleeps 100ms between batches, add a CHECK constraint as NOT VALID and then VALIDATE it, and only then flip the column to NOT NULL, since VALIDATE CONSTRAINT takes only a ShareUpdateExclusive lock and does not block writes. That choreography is overkill for a catalog-only default like today, but the postmortem point is that we should not be doing lock analysis under adrenaline on a per-migration basis; the safe pattern should be the default pattern and the fast path should be the exception we consciously opt into. Five, my analytics scratch queries move off the primary entirely; that was already the intention when we talked about a read replica during the Fly region planning, and today converted it from nice-to-have to action item. One more find during cleanup: the deploy pipeline runs migrations before the new app version rolls, which is correct for additive changes but means an old app version briefly sees the new column; harmless here, but we noted that destructive changes need the reverse order plus a compatibility window, and that note went in the runbook too. Open threads: the batched backfill helper does not exist yet as a reusable script, the runbook needs the pg_stat_activity one-liners pasted in so we are not composing them mid-incident, and we owe a test that asserts every generated migration file contains the lock_timeout preamble, which should be a twenty-line CI check on the drizzle output directory. Feeling: annoyed at the abandoned psql session, but genuinely glad this happened on a 45,000-row-per-day system and not two years from now.

Stripe webhook storm today, the kind of incident that is really two bugs wearing a trenchcoat. Sequence: we deployed clearharbor at 15:20 UTC with a broken import in src/entitlements.ts, a rename that half-landed, so every webhook handler invocation threw at module load and Stripe got 500s for everything. We caught the deploy within twelve minutes and rolled back, but by then Stripe had queued retries for roughly 40,000 events, and its retry schedule delivered them in compressed bursts once we started returning 200s again. The second bug: src/webhooks.ts processed each event synchronously inside the request handler, verify signature, update Postgres, recompute entitlements, all before responding, at about 120ms per event. The replay burst arrived at ten times our normal event rate, request handlers piled up, the Postgres pool hit its cap of 20 connections, and latency on the events endpoint climbed past the point where Stripe times out and marks delivery failed, which requeues the event and makes the storm feed itself. We stabilized by scaling clearharbor to three machines temporarily and letting the burst drain, which took about 50 minutes. The real fix, decided and half-built tonight: webhook handling becomes acknowledge-then-process. The endpoint now verifies the signature, inserts the raw event into a webhook_events table with a unique constraint on the Stripe event id, and returns 200 immediately, target under 10ms of work. A ferrite job lane consumes the table and does the actual entitlement work, which gives us ordering control, retry control, and a natural idempotency barrier since a replayed event violates the unique constraint and is dropped as already-seen. We debated processing events strictly in order versus accepting Stripe ordering as-is, and decided per-customer ordering is what matters, so the consumer keys work by customer id and processes each customer serially while different customers proceed in parallel. Remaining work for tomorrow: the consumer loop itself in the ferrite lane, backfill of the 212 events that landed during the worst of it and may have been processed twice, and a reconciliation pass against the Stripe API to make sure entitlements match reality before we trust the new path.

Wrote up today's Stripe webhook incident while it is fresh. What happened: a clearharbor deploy at 15:20 UTC shipped a half-finished rename in src/entitlements.ts that made module load throw, so the webhook endpoint returned 500 for every delivery until we rolled back twelve minutes later. Stripe had accumulated around 40k retryable events by then, and its retry backoff delivered them back to us in dense bursts. That exposed the second, older problem: src/webhooks.ts did all of its work inline in the request, signature verification then Postgres writes then entitlement recomputation, about 120ms per event, which was fine at normal trickle rates and hopeless at replay rates. Handlers stacked up, the 20-connection Postgres pool saturated, response times crossed the Stripe delivery timeout, failed deliveries got requeued, and the storm sustained itself for the better part of an hour until we added two temporary machines and let it drain. Decisions made tonight: switch to an ack-first design where the endpoint verifies the signature, writes the raw payload into a new webhook_events table, and returns 200 in under 10ms, with a unique index on the Stripe event id so replays collapse into no-ops at insert time. Processing moves into a ferrite consumer lane reading from that table, because ferrite already gives us retries with backoff, dead-lettering, and visibility, and building a second bespoke retry system inside clearharbor would be a mistake. On ordering we agreed that global order is a non-goal and per-customer order is the real requirement, so the consumer serializes by customer id and parallelizes across customers. Still open as of end of session: writing the consumer itself, auditing the roughly 200 events that were handled during the chaos window for double-processing, and running a full reconciliation of entitlements against Stripe before declaring the incident closed. Also noted for the postmortem: the broken deploy should have been caught by a smoke test that simply imports every module, which is trivial to add to CI and would have turned this whole evening into a red check mark.

Chased the ferrite worker memory leak that has been forcing a restart of the job runner every two days, and finally have a root cause with receipts. Symptom: resident memory on the ferrite machine climbed roughly 40mb per hour under normal load, flat when the queue was paused, and the climb rate scaled with job throughput, which pointed at something allocated per job and never freed. First theory was the HTML buffers in the fetch lane sticking around via some cache, but heap growth persisted even with the fetch lane paused and only the index lane running, so that theory died. Second theory was tokio task leakage, and tokio-console confirmed it in about ten minutes: the task count grew monotonically, and the leaked tasks were all parked in the heartbeat loop. The actual bug lives in worker.rs: when a worker claims a job it spawns a companion heartbeat task that renews the lease in lease.rs every 15 seconds, and on the happy path the main task sends a shutdown signal over a oneshot channel when the job completes. But when the job future panicked, or when it was cancelled by the timeout wrapper we added during the batching work, the completion path that sends the shutdown signal never ran, and the heartbeat task lived forever, holding its interval timer, its cloned Postgres pool handle, and its job metadata struct, which for index jobs includes a copy of the extracted document text, hence the 40mb per hour. Roughly 900 orphaned heartbeat tasks had accumulated on the prod instance at the time of diagnosis, each renewing a lease for a job that no longer existed, which also explains the mystery lease renewals we noticed in the queue stats last week and wrongly dismissed as a metrics bug. The fix is structural rather than a patch: the heartbeat handle now lives inside a guard struct whose Drop impl calls abort on the JoinHandle, and the guard is owned by the job execution scope, so any exit path, completion, panic, cancellation, or early return, tears the heartbeat down deterministically. Rust makes this pattern pleasant, and it removes the whole class rather than the instance; the oneshot channel is gone entirely. Also fixed the secondary damage: lease renewal for a dead job means a crashed job looks alive and is never reclaimed by the reaper in lease.rs, so three jobs from last month were stuck in a permanent running state; wrote a one-off cleanup that reset them and added a sanity check to the reaper that flags any lease older than 24 hours regardless of renewal, on the reasoning that no legitimate job runs that long in our system and a loud flag beats silent immortality. Verification: ran the panic-injection test we now have, a job type that panics 10 percent of the time under load for an hour on staging, task count stayed flat at the worker pool size, memory flat at 140mb. Deployed to prod at 21:40, will watch the graphs for 48 hours before calling it closed. Open threads: the timeout wrapper that widened this hole was added without a test for the cancellation path, worth a retro comment in the PR; and tokio-console proved valuable enough tonight that it should be compiled into the prod build behind a flag rather than requiring a special debug build, decided yes, the overhead is acceptable at our scale.

Closed out the ferrite leak work from Tuesday. The 48-hour observation window ended this morning with memory dead flat at 142mb through two deploy cycles and one queue spike of 12k jobs, so the Drop-guard fix is confirmed and the every-two-days restart cron is deleted with pleasure. Spent the rest of the session turning the incident into permanent guardrails rather than moving straight on. Added a task-count gauge to the ferrite metrics endpoint, sampled from the tokio runtime metrics API, with an alert if the count exceeds worker pool size plus 20 percent for more than ten minutes; that alert would have caught this leak within hours of introduction instead of weeks. Promoted the panic-injection job type from a scratch script into a permanent fixture in the ferrite-core test suite, and added a second chaos variant that gets cancelled by timeout mid-execution, since the cancellation path was exactly the one we never tested and both variants now assert task count and lease count return to baseline. While in the test suite, noticed the lease reaper had no test coverage at all, which is alarming for the component responsible for crash recovery, so wrote three: reaper reclaims an expired lease, reaper leaves a renewed lease alone, and the new one, reaper flags any lease older than 24 hours regardless of renewal state. That last behavior triggered a small design argument we resolved in favor of flag-and-alert rather than flag-and-kill: automatically killing a long-lease job felt like the kind of automation that turns one incident into two, so a human decides, and the decision is recorded as a comment on the reaper function. Also cleaned up the one-off script that reset the three zombie jobs and folded its logic into ferrite-cli as a jobs doctor subcommand that lists anomalies, stuck leases, jobs with no lease, retry counts over threshold, without mutating anything unless given an explicit apply flag; read-only by default felt like the right posture for a tool we will next use during some future 2am incident. Remaining thread: the metrics endpoint now exposes enough gauges that our hand-rolled alert script is getting unwieldy at 200 lines of bash, and we should decide whether to adopt a real alerting stack or keep growing the script; parked that question deliberately since the script works and the week has had enough infrastructure adventures.

Finally attacked the N plus one problem in the Quillbase clips listing, which has been the slowest page in the app since roughly forever. The symptom: loading the main library view with 50 clips per page fired one query for the page of clips, then for each clip a query for its tags, a query for its highlight count, and a query for the folder name, so 151 queries for a single page render, all sequential because they were awaited in a map inside the server component. Local dev hid this because Postgres round trips on localhost are 300 microseconds, but production round trips from the Fly app to the database run about 1ms, so p95 page latency sat at 780ms and users with big libraries felt every bit of it. The fix came in three layers. First, restructured the data access in app/api/clips/route.ts and the library server component to use a single query with Drizzle relational queries, pulling clips with their tags via the with clause, which Drizzle compiles to a lateral join rather than N selects. Second, the highlight counts could not ride along that way without dragging every highlight row over the wire, so those became a grouped subquery, count star grouped by clip id over the page of clip ids, joined in as a derived table; Drizzle needed the sql template escape hatch for the lateral piece but the result is still typed at the edges. Third, folder names were the easy one, folders are small and stable, so the folder list is now fetched once per request and joined in memory, and honestly it should become a cached lookup eventually but per-request is already fine. Results measured against production data volume restored into staging: 151 queries down to 3, page p95 from 780ms to 95ms, p50 from 420ms to 38ms. While profiling, found a bonus offender: the sidebar badge that shows unread count was issuing its own count query per folder, 12 more queries, which collapsed into the same grouped-count pattern, one query for all folders. Decisions worth recording: we standardized on the rule that any list endpoint must be constant-query, meaning the number of queries does not depend on result count, and added a lightweight query counter to the dev-mode request logger that prints the count per request and screams in red when a request exceeds 10, which is a tripwire rather than enforcement but matches our size; a real CI enforcement mechanism felt heavier than a two-person team needs. Also deliberately did not add a caching layer here, because correct invalidation on tag edits and highlight changes is real work, and the honest fix was always fewer queries rather than hiding query storms behind a cache; recording the reasoning so future us does not read this as an oversight.
