Open threads: the search results page almost certainly has the same shape of problem since it renders the same clip cards, needs the same treatment against lib/search/rank.ts result hydration; and the Drizzle sql escape hatch usage deserves a comment block explaining the lateral join, written but should be expanded if we touch it again. Marked the query-counter tripwire as an experiment; if it annoys us within a month we will demote it to a plain log line.

Refactored the scoring hot path in lib/search/rank.ts after the profiler showed search spending 60 percent of its time recomputing things that never change within a request. The old shape: for each candidate document we recomputed the inverse document frequency for every query term by hitting the term stats map with per-call normalization, re-lowercased and re-tokenized the query, and rebuilt the field weight table, all inside the per-candidate loop. With 4,000 candidates and a three-term query that was 12,000 redundant idf computations and 4,000 redundant tokenizations per search. The refactor hoists everything query-invariant into a prepared scorer: tokenize once, resolve idf per term once, precompute the weight table once, and return a closure that scores a candidate with nothing but multiply-adds and a length normalization. Benchmarked with the saved-query corpus we captured last month: mean scoring time for a 4,000 candidate set dropped from 48ms to 9ms, and end-to-end search p95 from 210ms to 160ms, the residual being Postgres candidate retrieval which is a separate fight. Two decisions along the way. First, we kept the scoring function pure and synchronous rather than making it async to interleave with retrieval, because the profiler shows overlap would save at most 15ms and the readability cost of async scoring plumbing is real; noted in the file header. Second, we resisted the temptation to cache prepared scorers across requests keyed by query string, because term stats drift as documents are ingested and a stale idf table produces subtly wrong rankings, the kind of bug we would never notice without a relevance harness; the prepare step is 0.3ms, there is nothing worth caching. Also fixed an actual correctness bug found while reading: the tokenizer treated hyphenated terms inconsistently between indexing in lib/ingest/parser.ts and querying in rank.ts, split on hyphens at index time but kept them whole at query time, so a search for a hyphenated word matched nothing unless the user happened to type the fragment. Unified both paths on the same shared tokenize function and added a round-trip test asserting index tokens and query tokens agree on a nasty fixture list, hyphens, apostrophes, unicode dashes, numbers with units. That bug has probably been silently degrading search since the beginning; slightly haunted by how invisible it was. Open thread: the candidate retrieval query is now the dominant term and wants the GIN index treatment, scheduled next.

Personal session, nothing to do with the company. Built out the marathon training spreadsheet for the spring race, sixteen weeks back-planned from race day with three build cycles and a taper. Wrote a small script that generates the week rows from a target weekly mileage curve rather than typing eighty cells by hand: peak week 52 miles, 10 percent down weeks every fourth week, long run capped at 20 miles three weeks out. Added pace zone columns computed from my recent 10k time using the usual threshold-derived formulas, easy pace band, marathon pace, threshold repeats, and conditional formatting that turns a cell red if the week-over-week mileage jump exceeds 12 percent, since ignoring exactly that rule is how the last training block ended in a sulking posterior tibialis. The script spits out CSV and I paste into the sheet; considered wiring the watch export API in so actual miles fill automatically next to planned miles, but decided the manual Sunday entry ritual is a feature, it forces a weekly review of how the body actually feels versus what the plan says. Open item: decide whether the second build cycle keeps two quality sessions a week or drops to one when work weeks get ugly; provisionally penciled in the honest answer, which is one.

Started the Next.js 15 to 16 migration for Quillbase, the first of two planned sessions. Ran the official codemod first, which handled the mechanical part: 61 files touched, mostly the async request API changes where params and searchParams are now promises everywhere, and the last stragglers of cookies and headers call sites that we had partially migrated during the 15 cycle. The codemod got 90 percent; the remaining 10 percent was the interesting part. Three clusters of manual work. First, our clip detail page did the old trick of reading params synchronously in a client component via props drilled from the server layout, and with promised params the drilling chain needed rethinking; restructured so the server page awaits params once and passes plain values down, which is what we should have done originally. Second, the fetch caching defaults moved again, and two internal API calls in the library view that silently relied on the old default caching became explicitly cache no-store, which is what they always should have been since they read per-user data; the migration is forcing overdue honesty about which fetches are actually cacheable, and we decided every internal fetch now declares its cache behavior explicitly, no defaults, enforced by a grep-based lint rule in CI that fails on a bare fetch to internal routes. Third, the middleware signature changes: our auth guard middleware that validates the clearharbor session cookie needed updating for the new request context shape, and while in there we discovered it was running on prefetch requests and doing a full session validation round trip to clearharbor for link hovers, which is a performance bug we shipped months ago and never noticed; added the purpose header check to skip validation on prefetches, which alone cut clearharbor session validation traffic by roughly 30 percent in staging. Turbopack is now the default bundler and our custom webpack config for the reader-mode CSS extraction no longer applies; ported the one thing we genuinely needed to the new config format and deleted 40 lines of cargo-culted webpack settings whose purpose nobody remembered, with a note that if something visual breaks in reader mode this deletion is suspect number one. Build currently green locally, typecheck green, 14 of 340 tests failing, all in the page-param test helpers that still construct synchronous params objects; fixing the helpers is tomorrow's first task, then a staging soak with the visual regression pass before we let it near production, then the Tailwind and Drizzle upgrades queue up behind it. Deliberately resisting the urge to bundle those into this branch; one major migration per deploy, we have re-learned that rule enough times.

Second and final session of the Next.js 16 bump. Fixed the 14 failing tests by rewriting the page test helpers to construct promised params the way the framework now delivers them, and extracted a makePageProps test utility so the next signature change is a one-file fix instead of a fourteen-file fix. Then the staging soak found two real issues the type system could not see. One: the reader mode page went visually wrong, exactly as predicted in yesterday's note about deleting the webpack CSS extraction config, the fonts loaded but the print stylesheet was being bundled into the main stylesheet and grayscaling images on screen; the fix was moving the print styles to a proper media-scoped import that Turbopack handles natively, and honestly the new setup is cleaner than the deleted config ever was. Two: the streaming metadata behavior changed and our clip share pages, which generate open graph tags from clip content, were emitting metadata after first paint on slow connections, so link unfurls in chat apps intermittently grabbed the fallback title; pinned those routes to blocking metadata generation since unfurl correctness matters more than 80ms of first paint on share pages specifically, and left the rest of the app on streaming metadata, recording the split as a deliberate per-route decision rather than a global setting. Ran the visual regression pass over the 18 screenshot fixtures, one intended diff from the reader mode fix, zero unintended. Deployed to production at 16:10 with the instant rollback tag prepared, watched error rates and web vitals for two hours: errors flat, LCP on the library page actually improved from 1.9s to 1.6s, presumably Turbopack chunking, and the prefetch middleware fix from yesterday is showing a 28 percent drop in clearharbor session validation calls in production, close to the staging estimate. Total migration cost: two sessions, one deploy, zero user-visible incidents, which redeems the somewhat bruising 14-to-15 migration experience. Follow-ups queued rather than done: the grep-based fetch cache lint should graduate to a real eslint rule because the grep version cannot see dynamic fetch wrappers, the Tailwind 4 migration is now unblocked and next in the upgrade train, and there is a deprecation warning from one image loader dependency that will block Next 17 someday and got a backlog entry now while the context is fresh.

Big ferrite performance session: moved job claiming from one-at-a-time to batched, which has been the known ceiling on pipeline throughput since spring. The old loop in queue.rs did SELECT one job FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, claim it, hand it to a worker, repeat, which means every job costs a full round trip plus a transaction, and with the database now a couple of milliseconds away in the new region the claim path capped effective throughput around 220 jobs a second no matter how many workers we ran; workers sat idle waiting on claims while the queue backed up, the worst kind of idle. The change: claim in batches of up to 32, single statement, UPDATE jobs SET state running, lease fields, worker id, WHERE id IN a subselect with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and LIMIT 32, RETURNING everything the worker needs, so one round trip and one transaction amortize across 32 claims. Two subtleties ate most of the session. First, lease semantics: each job in the batch still gets its own lease row and its own heartbeat timing under the Drop-guard scheme from the leak fix, because batching claims must not create batch-level failure coupling, one panicking job should not endanger the leases of its 31 batchmates; this required threading per-job lease state through code that briefly wanted to share one timer, resisted the temptation, kept them independent. Second, fairness across lanes: a naive batch claim drains whichever lane has the oldest jobs, and during backfills the bulk lane would starve the interactive fetch lane that user-facing saves depend on; solved with weighted lane sampling in the claim query, the subselect unions a slice per lane with per-lane limits proportional to configured weights, interactive lane weight 4, index lane 2, bulk lane 1, so a full bulk queue slows but never starves user-facing work. Wrote a queue simulation harness in ferrite-cli, seed 50k synthetic jobs with configurable lane mix, run against a local Postgres, and measured: sustained claim throughput went from 220 per second to 1,900 per second at batch 32, and interactive lane p95 wait during a simulated 40k bulk backfill dropped from 90 seconds under the old fairness-free prototype to 1.1 seconds with weights. Diminishing returns above batch 32, and batch 64 raised the variance of interactive wait, so 32 is the setting and the reasoning is recorded in the config comment. Also fixed an adjacent wart while in the claim path: the retry backoff calculation was recomputed per poll for every eligible job, moved to a stored next_attempt_at column computed at failure time, indexed, so the claim subselect is a pure index range scan; EXPLAIN confirms index-only. Open threads: the completion path is still one round trip per job and could batch the same way, probably worth another 2x on index-heavy workloads; the lane weights are static config and someday want to be adaptive to queue age, deliberately deferred, static weights are predictable and debuggable and we are two people; and the simulation harness deserves promotion from scratch tool to committed fixture, done for the claim tests, still owed for the fairness tests.

Tuning session on the ferrite batch claiming that landed Tuesday. Production told a slightly different story than the simulation harness, which is why we watch. Throughput was as predicted, sitting comfortably above demand, but the interactive lane wait showed a periodic sawtooth, p95 spiking to 4 seconds every ten minutes, which the simulation never showed. Cause: the scheduled dedup sweep enqueues its jobs in one burst of about 3,000, and the weighted lane sampling only enforces proportions when multiple lanes have eligible work; the burst lands, bulk momentarily dominates eligibility, and the first few batch claims after the burst are nearly all bulk before interactive jobs arrive to claim their weighted share. Two candidate fixes considered: reserve guaranteed slots per batch for the interactive lane even when it is empty at claim time, or smear the sweep enqueue over five minutes instead of one burst. Chose both, because they solve different layers: reserved slots, 8 of 32 held for interactive with unused reservations released to other lanes within the same query, makes the claimer robust to any future bursty producer, and smearing the sweep stops the largest known burst at its source; the second alone would leave the structural weakness for the next bursty producer we write. Implementation was mostly careful SQL in queue.rs, the reservation is another union branch with its own limit and a coalescing outer select, EXPLAIN still shows index usage, claim latency unchanged at about 3ms per batch. Re-ran the simulation with a burst scenario added to the harness, reproduced the sawtooth against the old code, confirmed flat 1.2 second p95 with reservations on, and the burst scenario is now a committed regression fixture alongside the fairness tests, which pays down the promotion debt noted in Tuesday's session. Production after deploy shows the ten-minute sawtooth gone, interactive p95 wait steady at 900ms through two sweep cycles. One more small decision: the sweep smear interval is jittered rather than fixed so it cannot accidentally synchronize with other periodic producers, cheap insurance recorded in a comment. Parked thread: batching the completion path remains open from Tuesday, and after watching production this week it is genuinely next, the completion round trips are now the largest queue-side cost on index backfills.

Postmortem completion session for the Redis eviction outage, closing the last two action items and writing the final doc. The synthetic canary is live: a scheduled job saves a clip through the real Quillbase API into a dedicated canary account every five minutes, waits for it to appear in search results, then deletes it, exercising app/api/clips/route.ts, the ferrite fetch and index lanes, and the read path in one loop; alerting fires if two consecutive canary runs fail, tuned to two to avoid paging on a single transient. Building it surfaced a small real bug as canaries tend to: the delete endpoint left the search index entry behind and search showed ghost results until the next reindex sweep, up to six hours; fixed by having the delete handler enqueue an immediate index removal job rather than waiting for the sweep, which also fixes real user deletes, so the canary paid for itself before its first alert. Session cache migration also done: clearharbor session entries now live explicitly on the cache Redis instance with allkeys-lru where eviction is a performance event, not a correctness event, while the state instance holds only rate-limit buckets and dedup keys under noeviction. Load-tested the split by artificially filling the cache instance and confirming evictions cause only a Postgres fallback latency bump, 40ms to 70ms p95 on session validation, no errors. The final postmortem doc records the five contributing causes: shared Redis across correctness and cache workloads, allkeys-lru applied to non-recomputable state, config applied via CONFIG SET and never persisted, retry logic that amplified rather than dampened, and no external detection giving the 22-minute discovery gap. All six action items now closed. Also recorded the counterfactual we keep bumping into: the pull toward moving rate-limit state into Postgres to delete the Redis dependency entirely, rejected again for the same write-rate reasons as before, roughly 4,000 bucket writes per minute does not belong on the primary; recording the rejection twice is fine, it means the reasoning is stable. Declared the incident closed and moved the postmortem into the incidents directory next to the migration lock writeup, which now makes two documents in a pattern that suggests we should template the format; did exactly that with a five-section skeleton, timeline, causes, damage, actions, lessons, so the next incident starts from structure instead of a blank page.

Marathon session on the Drizzle schema refactor, the one we have been deferring since the clips table grew its fourteenth ad hoc column. Goal: reorganize the schema from one 900-line lib/db/schema.ts into per-domain modules, clips, folders, tags, users, jobs-adjacent read models, fix the naming inconsistencies that accreted across three naming eras, snake case here, camel case there, a tag_id column pointing at a table named labels for historical reasons nobody defends, and get the relational query layer onto explicit relations definitions so the N plus one fixes from last month stop relying on inference. Executed in four movements. Movement one, pure reorganization: split schema.ts into schema/clips.ts, schema/folders.ts, schema/tags.ts, schema/users.ts with a barrel export, zero SQL changes, drizzle-kit diff confirmed an empty migration, committed separately so the noisy-but-safe change is isolated in history from the risky ones; this discipline saved us within the hour when movement two got interesting. Movement two, the renames: labels table to tags, tag_id stays, three column renames on clips including the read flag becoming read_state to match the enum introduced during the migration incident, and here drizzle-kit generated DROP TABLE plus CREATE TABLE instead of ALTER TABLE RENAME for the table rename, which would have been a spectacular data loss event if applied blind. This is a known sharp edge, the diff tool cannot always distinguish rename from drop-and-create, so the migration SQL was hand-edited to explicit ALTER TABLE labels RENAME TO tags and ALTER TABLE renames for columns, then drizzle-kit was re-pointed at the corrected state; recorded a standing rule in the runbook, every generated migration containing a DROP gets a human read before it merges, and the CI check from the incident postmortem now also greps generated migrations for DROP TABLE and requires an explicit acknowledged-destructive marker comment to pass. Movement three, explicit relations: wrote the relations definitions for all four domains so the with-clause queries in app/api/clips/route.ts and the library components resolve through declared relations instead of foreign key inference, which matters because two of our foreign keys are soft, enforced in app code only, the clip to latest-fetch-job link crosses into ferrite-owned tables that Drizzle should describe but never migrate, and inference cannot see policy like that. Declared those cross-service tables in a schema/external.ts with a loud comment that clearharbor and ferrite own their migrations, we only read; the alternative of importing their schema packages was considered and rejected because version-coupling three deploy cycles through a shared schema package is exactly the coupling the service split exists to avoid. Movement four, type propagation: switched the app to the inferred select and insert types from the new schema modules, deleting the hand-written interface duplicates in six files, and the compiler found two genuine drift bugs, a nullable folder reference typed as required in the folder-move dialog, and the highlight count typed as string in one component because an old raw query returned it uncast, both real, both fixed, both the kind of thing hand-maintained types exist to hide. Applied everything to staging against a production snapshot: migration runs in 1.8 seconds, the renames are metadata-only, all 340 tests green, the query counter tripwire shows no regressions in query counts. Production application is deliberately scheduled for tomorrow morning in the low-traffic window with the lock_timeout preamble from the incident runbook, because the renames take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE briefly and we now respect brief. Open threads: the enum for read_state exists in Postgres but two call sites still compare raw strings, fine but worth a cleanup pass; the barrel export tempts circular imports between clips and tags relations, currently resolved by a careful import order that deserves a lint rule instead of vigilance; and schema/external.ts wants a drift check, a weekly CI job that introspects the live database and diffs against the declared external tables so we learn when ferrite or clearharbor change shape under us, sketched, not built. Tired, but this pays down the oldest structural debt in the codebase and the diff is minus 400 lines net.

Attacked clearharbor cold starts, which have been quietly taxing every first-login of the day since we moved it to scale-to-zero on Fly. Measured before touching anything: machine start to first successful response was 6.2 to 8.9 seconds across ten cold starts, which users experience as a hung login page since the Quillbase auth redirect waits on it. Broke the time down with boot-phase logging: 1.1s machine and runtime start, 2.8s module graph load, 1.9s of eager initialization in our own code, and the remainder TLS plus first Postgres connection establishment. The module graph number was the shock, and the profile pointed at two offenders: the Stripe SDK, which we import at top level in src/webhooks.ts and src/entitlements.ts and which pulls a large dependency graph, and our own barrel imports, where importing one session helper dragged the entire src tree including the webhook machinery into every entry point. Fixes in order of impact. First, lazy Stripe initialization: the client is now constructed on first use behind a memoized getter, and the webhook route imports Stripe types only as types, so the login path never loads Stripe at all; module load drops to 1.0s on the login-only path. Second, broke the barrel imports so each route imports exactly what it uses, mechanical work across 23 files, and the entry graph for session validation shrank from 410 modules to 96. Third, the 1.9s of eager init was mostly synchronous JWKS fetch and entitlement table preload; the JWKS fetch became a cached-on-disk copy with background refresh since the signing keys rotate rarely and a stale-by-hours key set is checked against the kid header anyway, and the preload became lazy with a 30-second TTL cache, which we can afford because entitlement reads tolerate that staleness by design, a decision from the original architecture that keeps paying dividends. Fourth, Postgres connection establishment moved to boot-time-concurrent, started as soon as the process starts rather than awaited on first request. After all four: cold start to first response 1.6 to 2.1 seconds across ten trials, a 4x improvement, and warm path unchanged. Then the policy question, is 2 seconds acceptable for first-login-of-the-day, and we decided no for weekday business hours, so min_machines_running is now 1 during 06:00 to 22:00 UTC via two scheduled scale commands, and scale-to-zero applies only overnight; marginal cost about 4 dollars a month, obviously worth it against the single worst-feeling latency in the product. Open threads: boot-phase logging should stay permanently, it cost nothing and turned a vague complaint into a ranked list; the barrel-import regression risk needs a lint rule limiting entry point graph size, sketched as a CI check that counts modules via the bundler stats output and fails over 150 for the session entry; and the disk-cached JWKS wants a metric on staleness age so a stuck refresh loop cannot go unnoticed for weeks.

Postgres 15 to 16 upgrade session, the planning and rehearsal half. Decided on logical replication for the cutover rather than pg_upgrade in place, reasoning: logical replication lets the 16 instance build and settle while 15 keeps serving, gives us a rehearsable cutover measured in seconds, and leaves the old primary intact as an instant rollback target, whereas in-place pg_upgrade is faster in wall time but all-or-nothing on the shared history. Stood up the 16 machine on Fly, created the publication on 15 covering all tables in the quillbase and clearharbor databases, subscription on 16, initial sync of the 38gb took 2 hours 10 minutes and replication lag settled under one second. Two gotchas surfaced in rehearsal, which is what rehearsal is for. First, sequences do not replicate logically, so the cutover script snapshots every sequence with a generated setval statement batch and applies it on the target during the write freeze, otherwise the first insert after cutover collides with an existing id; tested this failure deliberately on the scratch copy and watched the duplicate key violation happen before writing the fix. Second, collation: the 16 image carries a newer glibc, and index ordering for text columns can silently differ, so the plan includes REINDEX on the five text-keyed indexes immediately after cutover, verified by running amcheck on the rehearsal target, which flagged exactly the two indexes we expected on the tags name column and the clips url column. Rehearsed the full cutover on scratch copies twice: freeze writes by pausing ferrite lanes and putting clearharbor and the Quillbase API in a brief maintenance mode, wait for lag zero, apply sequence sync, flip the connection strings via Fly secrets, unfreeze; second rehearsal came in at 41 seconds of write freeze end to end. Set the real cutover for tomorrow 07:00 UTC in the low-traffic window. Rollback plan documented: if anything looks wrong within the first hour, flip connection strings back to the untouched 15 primary and accept the loss of the few minutes of post-cutover writes, with the webhook_events table replayable from Stripe and ferrite jobs re-enqueueable, which bounds the real loss to nearly nothing. Remaining risk acknowledged in the doc: extensions, we run only pg_trgm and it is version-compatible, checked explicitly.

Wrote up the Postgres 16 upgrade prep that we finished today ahead of tomorrow's cutover. Method chosen: logical replication into a fresh 16 machine, not in-place pg_upgrade; the deciding arguments were the seconds-scale rehearsable cutover, the ability to let the new instance settle under replication while the 15 primary keeps serving untouched, and the free rollback story of simply pointing connection strings back at the old machine, which pg_upgrade cannot offer once it has run. Mechanics done today: publication created on the 15 primary for both the quillbase and clearharbor schemas, subscription on the new 16 instance, initial copy of 38gb completed in a bit over two hours, steady-state lag under a second. Rehearsal on scratch copies caught the two classic traps before they could catch us. Sequences are not carried by logical replication, so without intervention the first post-cutover insert would hit a duplicate key error on an id already used; the cutover script now snapshots all sequence values into setval statements and applies them on the target while writes are frozen, and we proved the failure mode first by cutting over a scratch copy without the fix and watching it break exactly as predicted. And the glibc collation difference on the new image means text index order can be subtly wrong after cutover, so the script runs REINDEX on the five indexes over text keys, with amcheck used on the rehearsal target to confirm which ones actually misordered, the tags name index and the clips url index, matching prediction. Full dress rehearsal twice, freeze via ferrite lane pause plus maintenance mode on both app-facing services, lag drain, sequence sync, connection string flip through Fly secrets, unfreeze, 41 seconds of write freeze on the second run. Cutover scheduled 07:00 UTC tomorrow. Rollback is the untouched 15 primary; the accepted worst case is losing the trickle of writes made after cutover, bounded because webhook events can be replayed from Stripe and ferrite work can be re-enqueued. Extension audit done, pg_trgm only, compatible. The one thing left deliberately unautomated is the go or no-go decision after the smoke checks, which stays human.

Closed out the Stripe webhook storm remediation today, the last incident from that bad fortnight still carrying open items. The ferrite consumer lane for webhook_events has now been in production for a week: endpoint acks in a median 6ms, consumer keys work by customer id with per-customer serial ordering, cross-customer parallelism at 8, steady state consumer lag under two seconds even through the Tuesday invoice cycle, which is the weekly worst case at roughly 4x baseline event rate. Today was reconciliation, verifying the state Stripe believes against the state clearharbor believes. Wrote reconcile.ts as a standing script rather than a one-off, deliberate decision, because a billing system without a reconciliation loop is a billing system quietly accumulating drift, and this incident proved it: the audit walked every Stripe subscription via the list API, compared status and plan and period end against src/entitlements.ts state, and found 87 mismatches out of 3,912 subscriptions. Categorized before fixing anything: 61 were entitlements more generous than Stripe, customers keeping pro features after cancellation, all traceable to deleted-subscription events that arrived during the storm window and were double-marked as processed by the messy manual handling that day; 22 were the opposite direction, paying customers missing entitlements, which is the category that actually hurts and got fixed within the hour; 4 were test-mode artifacts from our own debugging. The fix path applied the Stripe state as truth in all 83 real cases, on the principle that Stripe is the system of record for money and entitlements are a projection, a principle now written at the top of entitlements.ts where it can argue with future clever ideas. Decisions recorded: the reconciler runs nightly via a ferrite scheduled job, alerting only on mismatch counts above a threshold of 5 or any mismatch in the paying-but-unentitled category, which alerts at any count because silently shorting paying customers is intolerable; drift below threshold logs quietly for trend-watching, since some drift is inherent to eventual consistency between the two systems and paging on every singleton would train us to ignore the alert. The 61 over-entitled accounts got a seven-day grace flag rather than an instant cutoff, both for decency and because a few might have re-subscribed through channels the comparison missed; the flag expires on its own and downgrades. Postmortem doc finished using the template from the Redis incident, five causes: no import smoke test allowed the broken deploy, synchronous processing in the webhook path amplified the replay burst, no idempotency barrier existed before the unique constraint, no reconciliation existed to bound damage duration, and alerting watched error rate but not delivery success rate, so Stripe seeing failures while we saw silence was invisible. All five have closed action items as of tonight, the smoke test being the cheapest and most embarrassing, eight lines of CI that just imports every module and would have prevented the entire cascade. Open thread carried forward: the reconciler covers subscriptions only, and invoices with metered usage will need the same treatment when usage-based pricing ships next quarter, noted in the pricing project doc so it is a launch requirement rather than a future incident.

Search latency session, picking up the thread from the rank.ts refactor where candidate retrieval became the dominant cost. The retrieval query does full-text matching over the clips corpus to produce the candidate set that rank.ts scores, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed it sequential-scanning 480k rows and computing tsvector on the fly for every row, 140ms of the 160ms search p95, because the to_tsvector call was in the WHERE clause against the raw content column with no index able to serve it. Fix was the standard one done properly: added a generated stored column search_vector as to_tsvector over title, extracted content, and tag names concatenated with weights, title weight A, content C, tags B, then a GIN index on it, built CONCURRENTLY per the migration runbook rules so no lock drama, took 6 minutes on production during the quiet window. Rewrote the retrieval in lib/search/rank.ts to match against the indexed column and pushed the first-stage cut into the database with ts_rank on the weighted vector, limit 1,000 candidates, so our custom scorer ranks a bounded set instead of everything that matches; the two-stage split, cheap recall in Postgres then expensive precision in application code, is now the documented architecture of search and the note explains why neither stage should absorb the other, the database stage cannot express our recency and folder-affinity signals, and the application stage must not scan unbounded matches. Numbers: retrieval 140ms to 4ms on the indexed path, end-to-end search p95 from 160ms to 28ms, and the index adds 210mb of disk which is nothing. One behavioral change shipped alongside deliberately: prefix matching for the search-as-you-type case via ts_query with prefix flags on the last term only, which the GIN index serves fine and which makes the type-ahead feel dramatically better, previously it only matched complete words and users assumed search was broken mid-word. Verified relevance did not regress using the saved-query corpus, top-5 overlap with pre-change results at 94 percent, and the diffs eyeballed were all improvements from prefix matching. Open threads: the weighted vector bakes in weight decisions that rank.ts then partially re-weights, slightly redundant, harmless, but worth unifying when we next touch scoring; and highlight snippets still come from a separate ts_headline call per result, 8 results times 2ms, acceptable, noted only so future profiling does not rediscover it.

Weekend tinkering, not work. Finished the smart thermostat script for the house. The bones: a Python daemon on the hallway Pi polling three zigbee temperature sensors, kitchen, office, bedroom, and driving the heat pump through its local API, replacing the vendor scheduling app that insists on cloud round trips for a device ten feet away. Core logic is a simple state machine with hysteresis, half-degree band around target, minimum 15-minute compressor rest between state changes to stop the short-cycling the vendor app happily inflicted, and a schedule table in a yaml file, weekday and weekend variants, with an away override toggled by whether either phone is on the home network. The interesting fiddly bit was sensor fusion: the office sensor sits near the window and reads a degree low on windy days, so target evaluation uses a weighted median across the three sensors instead of any single reading, and the weights live in the yaml too. Logged everything to a sqlite file for a week and the compressor now runs 2 to 3 long cycles per evening instead of 9 short ones, and the bedroom overshoot that used to hit 1.5 degrees is under half a degree. Remaining itch: a tiny web page with the current state and a temporary hold button, because explaining ssh to houseguests is not a heating strategy.

Planning session for the Fly region move, deciding rather than doing. Motivation is accumulated evidence: 68 percent of active users now sit in Europe per the session geography stats, and the primary region being US east coast means their every interaction eats 90 to 110ms of Atlantic round trip, which compounds badly on pages that chain a clearharbor session check before data fetch; measured from a Frankfurt probe, library page load p50 is 610ms versus 280ms from a Virginia probe, and that gap is pure geography. Decision made: move the primary region for all three services and the Postgres primary to Amsterdam, chosen over Frankfurt and Paris on Fly capacity reputation and equivalent latency, since the difference among the three for our user base is inside measurement noise. The consequential sub-decisions: Postgres primary moves with the apps, not before and not after, because a split where apps sit in ams and the database in iad would add the Atlantic to every query and be far worse than the status quo, so the move is choreographed as one cutover window, apps and database together, using the same logical replication playbook rehearsed for the 15 to 16 upgrade, which conveniently means we can fold both moves into one maintenance window and one write freeze rather than two; sequencing decided as upgrade first on the new ams machine, so the replication target is already 16 in the target region and the region move and version upgrade collapse into a single cutover. Redis instances are cheap and stateless enough to simply recreate in ams ahead of time, cache warms itself, state instance gets its rate-limit buckets rebuilt from zero which fails safe per the eviction incident design. US users take the mirror-image latency hit, accepted explicitly: they are 30 percent of sessions and the median US user is lighter-usage than the median EU user, and if that changes we revisit with a read replica in iad, noted as the trigger condition rather than built speculatively. Fly-specific homework identified for the execution session: volume snapshots before anything, machine counts and sizes replicated in ams, the deploy pipeline region config, and checking that the scheduled scale commands from the cold-start work carry the region argument correctly. Target date set for next Tuesday 06:00 UTC, rehearsal on scratch copies Friday.

Executed the Fly region move plus Postgres 16 cutover this morning, the combined maintenance window planned last week. Net result: done, 52 seconds of write freeze, one surprise, no rollback. Timeline: 05:40 preflight checks, replication lag zero, ams machines for all three services staged and health-checking against the ams 16 replica in read-only smoke mode; 06:00 freeze, ferrite lanes paused, maintenance mode on Quillbase API and clearharbor; 06:00:41 lag drained, sequence sync applied per the rehearsed script, five text indexes reindexed, amcheck clean; 06:01:12 connection strings flipped via Fly secrets, apps in ams promoted to primary traffic, unfreeze; 06:03 canary save-clip loop green end to end; 06:10 declared stable and the old iad machines demoted to stopped-but-kept status for the one-week rollback window. The surprise: the clearharbor machine in ams came up unable to reach Stripe for its first 40 seconds, TLS handshake timeouts, which turned out to be the lazy-init change from the cold-start work interacting with a cold DNS resolver on the fresh machine, first Stripe call after boot did resolution plus handshake and tripped our aggressive 3-second webhook processing timeout; harmless during the window since webhooks were queued in webhook_events anyway, the consumer retried and succeeded, exactly what that architecture is for, but we lowered the surprise into a fix by adding a non-blocking warmup ping to Stripe at boot. Post-move measurements, six hours in: Frankfurt probe library page p50 610ms down to 240ms, session validation from EU 95ms down to 12ms, ferrite claim round trip 2.1ms down to 0.8ms since the workers sit beside the database again, which incidentally lifted batch claim throughput headroom by a third we do not currently need. Virginia probe shows the expected mirror penalty, library p50 290ms up to 600ms, matching prediction, trigger condition for an iad read replica stands as written. Cost delta is roughly neutral, ams pricing equivalent, old machines stopped not destroyed until next Tuesday costing a few dollars of volume storage as rollback insurance. Loose ends from the window: the Grafana-less alert script had region hardcoded in two probe URLs, fixed; the deploy pipeline still lists iad as fallback region and should list ams, queued; and the scheduled scale commands for clearharbor business hours needed their region argument updated, caught in Friday rehearsal, applied today, verified tonight. The upgrade half deserves its own closing note: Postgres 16 has been serving all traffic since 06:01 with zero plan regressions except one, the tag-suggestions query flipped to a merge join and slowed from 3ms to 19ms, fixed within the hour by an ANALYZE on tags after which the planner behaved; watching for a week per the runbook before dropping the 15 publication machinery.

The cascade. Writing this the same night because the details will blur by morning. At 13:37 UTC Fly performed an unannounced host migration on the machine running our state Redis in ams, about 35 seconds of downtime for that instance, which should have been a non-event and instead became our first genuine all-three-products outage, 41 minutes user-visible, because four systems each behaved reasonably and the composition did not. Chain of events as reconstructed from logs. Link one: state Redis goes away for 35 seconds. Link two: sixty ferrite workers hit connection refused on their rate-limit checks; the reconnect logic does the right thing per the eviction-incident hardening, exponential backoff with jitter, but the rate-limit check itself was written fail-open for the missing-key case, not the connection-error case, and the error path raised, worker.rs treated it as job failure, and 31 in-flight fetch jobs went into retry with their politeness budget unconsumed. Fine so far, genuinely. Link three: Redis comes back 35 seconds later empty, because the state instance persists via AOF and the Fly migration restored from a volume snapshot taken before the appendfsync everysec window flushed, actually worse, investigation showed the machine came back with an empty data dir and AOF rewrite recreated from nothing, still unclear precisely why, open thread number one and an ugly one. Empty means every rate-limit bucket and every dedup key gone, which by the eviction-incident design fails safe individually: limiter fail-open, dedup treats missing as fetch-needed. But composed at fleet scale it means sixty workers simultaneously believe nothing has been fetched recently and no domain is rate limited, and the retry queue from link two plus the normal queue surged through with zero politeness spacing. Link four: our own crawler DDoSed the top newsletter hosting domains for about 90 seconds until buckets repopulated, and two of those domains responded by 429-ing and then tarpitting our IP range, which stretched fetch latencies to 30 seconds and pinned every worker slot on slow sockets. Link five, the one that reached users: with all worker slots pinned, the interactive lane starved despite the reserved-slot design, because reservations govern claim priority, not slot occupancy, once claimed a slow bulk fetch holds its slot for its full duration; interactive jobs queued behind pinned slots, save-a-clip stopped confirming in the UI, and the canary correctly fired at 13:44. Link six: clearharbor felt it too because the webhook consumer shares the worker pool with a small lane, so Stripe event processing lag climbed to 9 minutes, no user damage there but it lit our new billing lag alert and added noise exactly when we needed signal. Recovery: identified tarpitting at 13:55 via the fetch latency histogram bimodality, paused the fetch lane entirely at 13:58, interactive save flow recovered immediately since saves only need enqueue plus parse, index lane drained normally, brought fetch back at 14:10 at a manually configured global concurrency of 4 with a seeded conservative rate limit table, and both tarpitting domains released us within the hour, no lasting reputation damage per subsequent successful crawls. Lessons and decisions, recorded tonight while angry. One: fail-open was the right call per key and the wrong call per fleet, so the limiter gains a global circuit breaker, if more than 20 percent of rate-limit checks fail or miss within a 10-second window, the whole fetch lane drops to a hardcoded crawl floor, one request per domain per 10 seconds, until buckets rebuild; local safety decisions must have a global aggregate guard, that is the sentence to remember from tonight. Two: slot occupancy needs a timeout distinct from job timeout, a per-fetch socket budget of 8 seconds, because 30-second tarpitted sockets holding worker slots is how bulk starves interactive despite every queue-side fairness mechanism we built. Three: the empty-Redis mystery gets a full investigation slot tomorrow, and until then the state instance gets an every-write AOF policy despite the throughput cost, measured tonight at acceptable, 4 percent claim throughput reduction. Four: an unannounced host migration is a thing that happens, so the drill script gains a kill-the-redis-machine scenario, and we will run it quarterly against staging. Five, the meta-lesson that stings: every individual behavior in the chain was something we designed deliberately in a previous postmortem, the failure was emergent from composition, and the only defense against that class is chaos drills of infrastructure failure, not more careful unit-level design. Tomorrow: the empty-volume investigation with Fly support ticket already filed, the circuit breaker implementation in the limiter module, and the socket budget in the fetch client in lib/ingest adjacent code on the ferrite side.

Refactored lib/ingest/parser.ts to stream instead of buffer, closing a memory problem that has been visible on the ferrite fetch workers since the leak investigation put memory graphs in front of us daily. The old path buffered the entire HTTP response into a string, parsed it into a DOM, ran readability extraction over the DOM, then serialized the article; on the p99 pages, think 8mb single-page documentation dumps and image-heavy newsletters, a single worker spiked 120mb, and with eight fetch slots per machine the theoretical worst case exceeded machine memory, which is presumably behind the two unexplained OOM kills in the worker logs last month. New path: the fetch client streams with a hard 4mb body cap enforced at the socket, on the reasoning that no article worth reading exceeds 4mb of HTML and anything bigger is a mis-clipped application page, the cap returns a specific oversized-body error that the UI surfaces as clip failed with reason rather than a silent truncation, decided explicitly because silent partial extraction would be worse than honest failure. Within the cap, parsing now uses the streaming HTML parser with an incremental tree builder that discards script and style subtrees at tokenization time, they never allocate, which alone cuts DOM size by half on the median newsletter, and readability scoring runs on the pruned tree. Peak per-fetch memory on the p99 fixture set dropped from 120mb to 22mb, median from 9mb to 6mb, and the 4mb cap fired on exactly 3 of the 10,000-page replay corpus, all three legitimately garbage clips of app dashboards. One compatibility wrinkle: two extraction heuristics keyed off computed structure that the pruned tree no longer contains, the ad-block heuristic counted script tags per container as a spam signal, ported it to count during tokenization into a side table, and the paywall detector looked for hidden-content styles, ported to a regex pass over style attributes at tokenize time, both verified against the extraction regression corpus, 9,983 of 10,000 byte-identical outputs, 14 diffs improvements from better ad pruning, 3 the garbage clips now correctly failing. Worth recording the process note: the extraction regression corpus, built during the parser rewrite last year, once again converted a scary refactor into a mechanical one, it is the single highest-value test asset we own and the same pattern is still owed to rank.ts scoring. Open threads: the streaming parser handles malformed HTML differently at a low rate, the corpus caught the diffs but real-world drift deserves a week of watching the extraction-failure rate metric; and the 4mb cap constant belongs in config rather than code before someone needs to raise it during an incident at 2am.

Followed the loose thread from the cascade postmortem into lease.rs and found a real bug that the host migration had been quietly exploiting. During the incident review we noticed a handful of leases expiring early in the minutes after the Fly host migration, jobs that were healthy and heartbeating got reclaimed by the reaper and double-executed, harmless for idempotent index jobs but two fetch jobs double-fetched, which we initially wrote off as incident noise. It was not noise. Lease expiry in lease.rs compared last-renewed timestamps captured from the system wall clock against now, and the host migration stepped the machine clock backward by 1.7 seconds on restore; any lease renewed just before the step looked, after the step, as if it had been renewed in the future, and an overflow-guarded subtraction that should have saturated at zero instead wrapped through the guard into a huge apparent age on the next comparison, expiring the lease instantly. The fix has two layers, because clock trouble deserves defense in depth. Layer one: lease age computation now uses monotonic time for the local heartbeat scheduling and treats the database clock as the single authority for expiry decisions, meaning the reaper query computes age as the database now minus the renewal timestamp written by the database itself at renewal time, never a worker-supplied timestamp, so worker clock steps cannot manufacture expiry; this matches the fencing-token decision from the original lease design, the database was already the authority for ownership, it is now also the authority for time. Layer two: renewals that would move a timestamp backward are rejected with a logged warning rather than applied, a tripwire that turns the next clock anomaly into a log line instead of a mystery. Wrote a regression test that simulates the backward step by injecting a shifted clock into the renewal path and asserts the lease survives, plus a property test over random clock jitter sequences asserting the reaper never reclaims a lease within its renewal budget. Deployed with the incident hardening batch. Also cleaned up the double-execution damage surface while present: fetch jobs now carry an idempotency key derived from url hash plus scheduled time bucket, so a double-claimed fetch collapses at the dedup layer even when the politeness state is cold, closing the exact combination the cascade produced. Open thread: the wrapped subtraction deserves a look across the codebase, grepped for the same saturating-subtraction pattern and found one more candidate in the queue depth gauge, benign but fixed for hygiene.

Entitlements caching session in clearharbor, closing the last latency complaint from the cold-start work. Warm-path entitlement checks in src/entitlements.ts were costing a Postgres query per authorized API call, 3 to 5ms each, and Quillbase fans out to three or four entitlement-guarded endpoints per page render, so entitlements were adding 12 to 20ms of pure sequential latency per page and roughly 45 percent of all clearharbor query volume. The design decided and shipped: two-tier look-aside cache, an in-process LRU of 10,000 entries with a 30-second TTL in front of the cache Redis instance with a 5-minute TTL, both keyed by user id plus entitlement version stamp. The version stamp is the interesting part: every entitlement-mutating path, the webhook consumer, the reconciler, the admin override tool, bumps a per-user version integer in the same transaction as the mutation, and the stamp rides in the session token clearharbor already issues, so a stale cache entry is structurally unreachable after a mutation that the user has re-authenticated past, and within a session the worst case staleness is the 30-second process TTL, which product-wise is fine, a user upgrading sees pro features within half a minute and always sees them immediately on the post-checkout redirect because that path bumps the session. We chose this over pub-sub invalidation deliberately: invalidation messages are a second delivery system with its own failure modes, and the cascade incident two weeks ago made us allergic to correctness that depends on a message arriving; TTL plus version stamps fail only toward brief staleness, never toward wrongness that persists. Stampede protection via single-flight per key in process, and the Redis tier populates with a short random TTL jitter so mass expiry cannot synchronize. Measured on staging replay: entitlement check p50 from 3.2ms to 0.04ms process-hit, 0.9ms Redis-hit, hit rates 88 and 9 percent respectively leaving 3 percent to Postgres, and clearharbor total query volume down 41 percent, which also buys headroom on the shared connection pool. One deliberate scope cut recorded: no negative-entitlement caching for missing users, the failure mode of caching an absent user who is mid-signup was not worth the 0.2 percent traffic it addresses. Open thread: the version stamp lives in the session token, so long-lived API tokens for the future public API will need their own stamp transport, noted in the API design doc.

Short maintenance session on the Drizzle tooling. Upgraded drizzle-kit and drizzle-orm to current, mostly painless, one breaking change in how the config file declares the migrations table name which took ten minutes of release-note reading. Used the occasion to squash migration history: we had 61 migration files accumulated since the project started, several of them mutually contradictory relics of the schema refactor era, and a fresh database setup replayed all 61 in sequence taking 40 seconds and occasionally tripping the DROP-check CI guard on its own history. Generated a single consolidated baseline from the current schema state, verified it produces a byte-identical dump against a replay of the old chain on a scratch database, schema diff empty, then archived the old files into migrations/archive rather than deleting them, because the history has archaeological value when tracing when a column changed meaning. New-database setup now runs one file in under 2 seconds. Two rules recorded in the runbook while in the neighborhood: squash only at moments when no migration is mid-rollout anywhere, meaning immediately after a deploy epoch, and the archive directory is append-only. Also fixed the drizzle-kit config to point introspection at the ams database since it still referenced the retired iad hostname, which would have bitten the next person to run a diff. The external-tables drift check sketched during the schema refactor is still not built; bumped it to the top of the maintenance backlog since the schema tooling is now current enough to support it properly.

Incident today, self-contained but worth a full note: Stripe webhook signature verification broke for 40 minutes after this morning's clearharbor dependency deploy, all deliveries 400ing with signature mismatch, caught by the delivery-success-rate alert built after the storm, which is the first time one of our post-incident alerts has caught the exact failure it was designed for, grimly satisfying. Root cause: the deploy included the Node 22 minor bump and a framework patch that together changed how the raw request body reaches the route handler; our verification in src/webhooks.ts signed over a body that had been decoded and re-encoded, a byte-identical operation until a unicode em dash in a customer name field arrived in a normalization form that did not round-trip identically, at which point the computed signature diverged from Stripe's. The failure was therefore intermittent by payload content, which made the first twenty minutes confusing, some events verified fine, and the temptation to blame Stripe was real until we diffed the raw bytes of a failing body against the re-encoded version and found the normalization delta. Fix: capture the true raw bytes before any body parsing middleware touches the stream, verify the signature over those exact bytes, and only then parse; this is what the Stripe docs say to do and what our code appeared to do, the regression being that a framework update quietly moved where parsing happens. To keep it fixed regardless of future framework behavior, added a test that replays three captured real webhook payloads including the em dash one as raw byte fixtures against the live verification path, asserting acceptance, plus a canary in the Stripe CLI fixture suite that fires a test event with deliberately gnarly unicode through staging on every deploy. No data damage: every failed delivery sat in Stripe retry queue and replayed successfully after the fix, webhook_events dedup absorbed the replays exactly as designed, consumer lag peaked at 11 minutes and drained in 4. Decision recorded: raw-body capture now lives in a tiny dedicated middleware registered first, with a comment forbidding anything before it, because the whole class of bug is ordering-dependent middleware and the defense is making the ordering explicit and load-bearing.

Small focused performance session on the remaining N plus one offenders flagged by the dev-mode query counter since the clips listing fix. The folder sidebar was the loudest: it renders the folder tree with per-folder clip counts and unread counts, and the tree component recursively fetched counts per node, 2 queries per folder times typically 15 folders. Collapsed into one grouped query, counts and unread counts computed with a filter clause aggregate grouped by folder id, and the tree assembles from the flat result in memory; 31 queries to 1, sidebar render contribution from 45ms to 6ms on production-sized data. Considered and explicitly rejected a materialized counts column maintained by trigger or by application code: the write amplification on every clip move and read-state flip is real, the invalidation bugs are inevitable, and a 6ms aggregate over an indexed foreign key at our scale does not justify any of it; recorded the rejection with numbers in the code comment so the idea has to beat the measurement next time it gets proposed, because it will get proposed, it always does. Second offender: the tag autocomplete endpoint fetched matching tags then queried usage count per tag for ranking, 1 plus up to 20; folded the count into the main query with a join against the same aggregate pattern. Third: the share-page renderer fetched clip, then author profile, then folder, sequentially, three round trips serialized behind each other adding 5ms of pure latency; combined into one query with two joins, and the share page is public-facing so this one actually moves a user-visible number, TTFB p50 from 90ms to 82ms. Sidebar note for the future: the query counter tripwire that found all three has now paid for itself several times over, and the month-old experiment note wondering whether it would annoy us can be answered, it stays, promoted from experiment to permanent fixture. The only remaining red-flag route in the counter log is search result hydration, which was already on the list from the rank.ts session and remains the last known query storm in the app.

Neighborhood project, nothing to do with work. Got the three-node mesh wifi experiment running across our place, the garage, and the neighbors two doors down who agreed to host a node in exchange for coverage in their garden office. Three refurbished routers flashed with OpenWrt, 802.11s mesh on the 5ghz radios with a dedicated backhaul SSID, client access on 2.4 and the second 5ghz where the hardware allows. The garage node was the problem child: mesh link kept flapping every few minutes, which turned out to be a channel width mismatch, the garage radio negotiated 80mhz while the others sat at 40, and the renegotiation storm looked like interference until iw dev output showed the mismatch plainly. Locked all backhaul radios to 40mhz and the links have been solid for four days. Throughput measured with iperf3: 210mbit between adjacent nodes, 90mbit across the two-hop path to the neighbors, which comfortably beats the powerline adapters it replaces. Set up batman-adv briefly for comparison and went back to plain 802.11s, the added complexity bought nothing measurable at three nodes. Remaining wishlist: a roaming tune since phones cling to the far node when walking between houses, 802.11r is enabled but the transition thresholds need lowering, and a small monitoring page scraping station dump from each node so I can see link quality without sshing into three routers.

Postgres 16 follow-up week concluded, closing the observation window from the combined region move and upgrade. The one open plan regression from cutover day, the tag-suggestions merge join, stayed fixed after the ANALYZE, and a systematic pass over pg_stat_statements comparing the top 30 queries against pre-upgrade captures found two more subtle shifts worth recording. First, the clip listing query picked up an incremental sort node on 16 that is genuinely faster, p95 down 15 percent, free win, no action. Second, the nightly reconciler subscription scan flipped from index scan to bitmap heap scan and doubled to 90 seconds of runtime; it runs at 03:00 and nobody would ever notice, but the cause was interesting enough to chase, the new default for random_page_cost interacts with our volume type such that the planner slightly overestimates random read cost on the ssd-backed Fly volumes, so set random_page_cost from 4.0 to 1.1 cluster-wide, which is the standard ssd setting we should have applied years ago, re-verified the top 30 queries after the change, reconciler back to index scan at 40 seconds, everything else unchanged or marginally improved. Also enabled wal_compression to lz4 while touching config, wal volume down 30 percent, replication bandwidth to the future iad replica cheaper whenever that gets built, no measurable cpu cost at our write rate. Dropped the logical replication artifacts from the retired 15 primary, publication, slot, and the machine itself destroyed after a final volume snapshot archived to the backup bucket, closing the rollback window formally, and the write freeze runbook got its actuals filled in, 52 seconds against the 41 rehearsed, with the delta attributed to the sequence sync running against production sequence counts. Recorded the upgrade retrospective paragraph in the infra doc: logical replication cutover was the right call, rehearsal caught both real traps, sequences and collation, and the single combined window for region plus version was cheaper than two windows, the only cost being a scarier rollback story that we never needed. Next infra item in the queue is the external-tables drift check, which has now survived three sessions of being bumped and is starting to feel like a curse.

Short sharp incident this afternoon, 9 minutes of degraded saves, caught by the canary before either of us noticed manually. The state Redis instance restarted, planned Fly maintenance this time with notice we had ignored in the inbox, and came back with its post-cascade every-write AOF intact, data present, buckets warm, exactly as designed. The degradation came from somewhere stupider: the global circuit breaker added after the cascade watches the rate-limit check failure rate, and the 20-second connection outage tripped it correctly, dropping fetches to the hardcoded crawl floor, but the breaker reset logic required a full 10-minute window of sub-threshold failures before restoring normal throughput, so we crawled at the floor for 10 minutes to recover from a 20-second blip, and interactive saves that needed fresh fetches queued visibly during it. The breaker did its job during the trip and overstayed during the recovery, textbook asymmetric tuning. Fix applied tonight: reset uses a half-open probe pattern instead of a fixed window, after 30 seconds at the floor the breaker admits a small probe cohort of normal-rate fetches, and full restoration follows two consecutive healthy probe cohorts, so recovery from a transient tracks the actual health signal rather than a worst-case timer. Re-ran the kill-the-redis drill against staging with the new reset logic, floor period shrank from 600 seconds to 74 for a simulated 20-second outage while the sustained-outage behavior is unchanged, verified by holding the drill Redis down for five minutes. Also actually subscribed the maintenance notices to the alert channel instead of the inbox where they go to die. Filed the lesson in the cascade postmortem addendum: a circuit breaker has two tunings, trip and reset, and we only designed one of them.

Reworked the ferrite worker execution model in worker.rs, the last big structural item on the performance backlog. The old model spawned a tokio task per claimed job with a global semaphore capping concurrency at 64, which served fine until the workload diversified: fetch jobs are io-bound and cheap to run wide, index jobs are cpu-heavy tokenization and embedding batches that at concurrency 64 thrash the two vcpus, and the post-cascade socket budget work showed how one class of job pinning resources degrades every other class. New model: per-class worker pools with explicit slot counts, fetch pool 48 slots io-weighted, index pool 3 slots matching physical parallelism minus headroom, webhook and misc pool 8, each pool pulling from its lanes through the weighted claim machinery, so the claim-side fairness from the batching work is now matched by execution-side isolation, and a saturated index backfill can no longer add latency to fetches or webhook processing even in principle. Implementation notes: pools are plain structs owning a JoinSet each, the Drop-guard lease heartbeats moved unchanged, and graceful shutdown got properly implemented as part of the rework since the old global semaphore made clean drain awkward, shutdown now closes claim intake, lets in-flight jobs finish against a 25-second deadline chosen to sit inside the Fly 30-second SIGKILL window, and releases surviving leases explicitly so the reaper does not wait out the lease TTL on deploy, which shaves the annoying 60-second post-deploy throughput dip we have had forever and never traced, it was lease-wait on jobs killed mid-flight, diagnosed at last by reading the reaper logs during a staged deploy. Measurements on the staging replay corpus: mixed-workload throughput up 22 percent from reduced cpu thrash on index jobs, index job p95 duration down 40 percent at pool size 3 versus the old free-for-all, fetch throughput unchanged, deploy-time throughput dip gone entirely across three test deploys. One decision debated and settled: pool sizes are static config per machine size rather than runtime-adaptive, same reasoning as the lane weights, adaptive sizing is a control loop we would have to debug during incidents, static sizes are legible, and the config comment carries the sizing arithmetic so resizing a machine comes with instructions. Open threads: the completion-path batching deferred twice is deferred again and honestly may not matter after this rework since completion round trips overlap within pools now, will measure before building it; and the webhook pool sharing a machine with fetch pools means a tarpit-style event could still add scheduling jitter to webhook latency, acceptable now, noted as the trigger for splitting machines if billing latency alerts ever implicate it.

Second round of clearharbor cold-start work, targeting the residual 1.6 to 2.1 seconds left after the first optimization pass. Boot-phase logging, which earned its permanence, showed the remaining time split roughly three ways: 600ms of runtime and machine start we do not control, 500ms of module load even after the barrel-import surgery, and 700ms of first-request warmup, JIT, route compilation, first TLS session to Postgres. Attacked the middle third first: bundled the server with esbuild into a single file per entry point instead of shipping node_modules and letting the runtime resolve 96 modules through the filesystem, and module load dropped to 90ms, the filesystem stat storm was the cost, not parsing; bundle size 3.1mb, source maps shipped alongside for stack traces, and one dynamic-require dependency in the Stripe SDK needed an esbuild plugin shim, documented inline because the error message when it breaks is deeply unhelpful. The last 700ms was harder to move: prewarmed the route table and forced JIT warmth by having the boot sequence issue three synthetic requests against localhost before the health check reports ready, which converts first-user-request warmup into pre-traffic warmup, and the Postgres TLS session moved to boot-concurrent during the synthetic requests. Net cold start now 1.0 to 1.2 seconds measured across ten trials, from the original 6.2 to 8.9 before round one. Decision recorded: this is the stopping point, the remaining second is mostly Fly machine start plus unavoidable runtime boot, and squeezing further means either keeping machines always-on everywhere, already done for business hours, or exotic snapshot-restore tricks that are not worth their operational surface for a sub-second win on overnight logins only. Also recorded the counterintuitive finding for the infra doc: module count mattered enormously and bytes barely mattered, the 3.1mb bundle loads faster than 96 small files totaling 1.9mb ever did.

Cold-start round two on clearharbor, written up after the evening deploy. Starting point was the 1.6 to 2.1 second residual from the first pass, and the boot-phase logs broke it into thirds: machine plus runtime start around 600ms which is Fly's territory, about 500ms of module loading that survived the earlier barrel-import cleanup, and roughly 700ms of first-request costs, route compilation, JIT, initial Postgres TLS handshake. The module-load third fell to an esbuild single-file bundle per entry point, 3.1mb, which took module load from 500ms to 90ms; the surprise there was that filesystem resolution overhead across 96 modules, not parse time or code size, was nearly the whole cost, worth remembering since we have been mentally optimizing bytes when we should count stat calls. One Stripe SDK dynamic require needed a plugin shim to bundle, and the inline comment on the shim exists because the failure mode without it is an inscrutable runtime error. The first-request third was addressed by making boot do the warming: the startup sequence fires three synthetic localhost requests before the health check flips to ready, so route compilation and JIT happen pre-traffic, and the Postgres TLS session establishes concurrently during those synthetic requests rather than on the first real login. Ten-trial measurement after deploy: 1.0 to 1.2 seconds cold start to first real response, versus 6.2 to 8.9 when this effort began two weeks ago. We agreed to stop here and wrote the reasoning down: what remains is dominated by machine start and runtime boot that we do not own, business-hours traffic already sees warm machines from the min-machines schedule, so further work would buy back under a second for overnight logins at the cost of snapshot-restore complexity nobody wants to operate. Logged the general lesson in the infra doc alongside round one: for cold starts, module count beats bundle bytes as the thing to minimize, our 3.1mb single file comfortably outperforms the smaller-but-scattered layout it replaced.

Cleanup session on the Next.js 16 aftermath plus the session-handling edge the migration exposed. The framework's revised middleware execution model changed when our auth guard runs relative to static asset serving, and we noticed clearharbor session validation counts creeping up again after the big prefetch win from the migration; traced it to the middleware matcher, whose pattern was written against the old default exclusions, under 16 the matcher was now catching font files and the manifest, each triggering a pointless session check, roughly 15 percent overhead in validation volume. Rewrote the matcher with an explicit allowlist of guarded path prefixes instead of a denylist of exclusions, app routes, api routes, nothing else, on the general principle that auth guards should name what they protect rather than what they ignore, and the miscounted validations disappeared. While in the session path, fixed a subtle cookie behavior the migration changed: session cookie renewal in src/session.ts wrote the refreshed cookie on every response including cached ones, and under 16's revised caching the renewal header could be captured into a cached response and replayed to the wrong client, not exploitable as session fixation since the cookie is per-user validated against the store, but sloppy and confusing in traces; renewal now happens only on responses explicitly marked dynamic, and an assertion in dev mode throws if a set-cookie header appears on a cacheable response, turning the whole class into a loud failure. Added the middleware matcher to the migration checklist template, since matcher semantics have now shifted in two consecutive major versions and we fell for it once each time, apparently this is a lesson that costs one incident per major to relearn unless written down, so it is written down. Session validation volume is back to the post-migration baseline and the dev assertion has already caught one violation in a draft branch, the new export endpoint, which was setting a cookie on a cacheable response within days of the assertion existing, immediately justifying it.

Queue backlog incident today, the first real stress test of all the ferrite fairness machinery under organic rather than simulated load, mixed grades. At 08:20 UTC the newsletter-import feature shipped last week hit its first viral moment, a productivity forum thread recommended Quillbase for newsletter archives, and 300-odd signups each triggered historical imports averaging 600 issues, flooding the bulk lane with 180,000 fetch jobs in two hours against a normal daily volume of 45,000. The good news first: interactive saves never degraded, reserved slots plus the pool isolation from the worker rework held, canary green throughout, and the politeness limiter with the post-cascade circuit breaker crawled the newsletter hosting domains at sustainable rates without a single 429, so the fleet-level safety lessons from the cascade held up under a completely different trigger. The bad news: bulk backlog drain time, at the politeness-limited crawl rate for the three domains hosting most newsletters, projected at 26 hours, and new importing users watched a progress bar promising their archive sometime tomorrow, four wrote in asking if the import was broken, so the failure here was product experience rather than infrastructure. Mitigations shipped during the day. First, import jobs now fetch newest-first instead of oldest-first, a one-line ORDER BY flip with outsized effect, users see their recent issues, the ones they actually reread, within minutes, and the deep archive fills in behind; embarrassing that it took an incident to think of it. Second, the import progress UI stops pretending to be a linear progress bar and shows newest issues ready, archive filling in, estimated completion, honest framing measured against the same numbers, zero support mail since it deployed midday. Third, per-domain politeness budgets got a temporary manual raise for the two largest newsletter hosts after checking their robots and terms, 4x for 24 hours to drain the burst, with the change logged through the override table the cascade work added rather than config-edited, first real use of that tooling, worked exactly as intended, expires on its own. Backlog fully drained by 22:00, 14 hours actual versus 26 projected thanks to the temporary raise. Decisions recorded for the durable fixes: import volume estimation moves into the signup flow, importing 600 issues should reserve bulk capacity ahead of time so drain projections exist before the jobs enqueue rather than after, sketched as a capacity ledger table consulted at import creation; and the bulk lane needs a per-user fairness dimension on top of per-lane weights, one 5,000-issue import should not sit ahead of fifty 100-issue imports in aggregate wait, the claim query can shard by user hash with round-robin across shards, designed on the whiteboard today, building tomorrow. Meta-note for the incident log: this is the first incident in the ferrite lineage where zero user-facing writes were lost or delayed, every previous queue incident degraded saves, the layered work is visibly compounding.

Quick focused session on session-token verification cost in clearharbor. Profiling after the entitlements caching work showed JWT verification as the new largest line item in the warm path, 1.2ms per verification, dominated by re-fetching and re-parsing the JWKS on a cache that was keyed wrong and missing constantly, effectively re-importing the signing key per request. Fixed the cache key to include the kid header properly, imported keys now cached as parsed key objects rather than raw JWK JSON, and verification dropped to 80 microseconds. Also took the opportunity to precompute the expected issuer and audience strings at boot instead of rebuilding them from config per call, small but free. Verified the disk-cached JWKS staleness metric from the cold-start work still reports correctly with the new key cache layered on top, it does, staleness age currently 3 hours against a 24-hour refresh cycle. Warm-path session validation now totals 0.3ms p50 end to end, down from 4.5ms before this fortnight of caching work began, and clearharbor cpu utilization at peak dropped from 55 to 30 percent, which defers the next machine size bump indefinitely. Noted for the future public API: the parsed-key cache assumes our own single issuer, and third-party token verification if ever added must not share this cache without adding issuer to the key.

Follow-through session on the region move, building the iad read replica whose trigger condition fired sooner than expected: the US probe latency regression noted on cutover day drew three user complaints this week, all from a US-based team account that turns out to be our second-largest customer, which converts the noted trigger condition into an action item with a name attached. Stood up a hot standby in iad via streaming physical replication from the ams primary, wal_compression from the upgrade follow-up paying for itself immediately, replication bandwidth 40 percent lower than the pre-compression estimate.
